#5600. EXCLUSIVE: NBA Star Dwight Howard Slashes $1.6 Million From Price of His Georgia Megamansion

Former NBA superstar Dwight Howard has cut the asking price of his sprawling Georgia estate by $1.6 million—just two months after relisting the palatial pad.

In September, the 40-year-old basketball legend relisted his longtime Suwanee, GA, mansion for $14.5 million, marking a staggering $3.25 million increase from the $11.25 million price tag he attached to the home when he first put it up for sale in January 2025.

Now, the basketball icon has trimmed that asking price back by a sizable $1.6 million, bringing the new asking price to $12.9 million.

Howard purchased the enormous estate for $8.8 million in 2016, the same year he signed with his hometown team, the Atlanta Hawks.

A decade later, the eight-time NBA All-Star is hoping to score a sizable profit on the property, with his latest asking price coming in $5.7 million above what he originally paid for the spread.

The home, which is represented by Maninga Capehart of HomeSmart, sits on approximately 14 acres and offers 12 bedrooms, 12 full bathrooms, and nine half-bathrooms.

Built in 2010, the European-inspired residence boasts approximately 26,233 square feet of living space, providing no shortage of room for both overnight guests and lavish entertaining.

Indeed, the listing touts the property as one of Georgia's "most distinguished private estates," pointing to its impressive scale, elaborate architecture, and lengthy list of resort-worthy amenities.

Guests enter the mansion through custom double doors that open into a soaring two-story foyer, where a dual staircase, crystal chandelier, hardwood floors, and intricate millwork set an opulent tone.

From there, the home offers an array of formal and informal living areas, including a grand salon and formal dining room, as well as a glass atrium that floods the interiors with natural light.

Entertaining appears to have been a major consideration throughout the home's design, particularly when it comes to food preparation.

In addition to the main chef's kitchen, which is fitted with Viking appliances, there is a separate catering kitchen, a hidden pantry, a walk-in butler's pantry, multiple bars, and several service areas.

The main-level primary suite is equally extravagant, with a private executive office and enormous dressing areas lined with custom cabinetry. Its spa-worthy bathroom adds a sunken soaking tub, steam shower, and dedicated makeup vanity.

The home's additional bedroom suites are spread across the upper level and feature en-suite bathrooms and custom closets, with some offering steam showers and access to private balconies.

A separate multiroom residential suite also comes with its own kitchen and two bathrooms, providing a self-contained living space for family members or overnight visitors.

However, the property isn't solely focused on its sleeping quarters.

One entire level has been transformed into what the listing calls an "entertainment and wellness destination," complete with a private movie theater and kitchenette, billiards and recreation lounge, game and podcast space, and another full kitchen.

There's even a salon and barber area, sauna, and additional bedroom suite on the same level.

Howard won't need to leave the grounds to squeeze in a workout either. A separate two-story fitness and recreation pavilion has its own kitchen and bathroom, allowing the building to double as another space for gatherings.

The sprawling outdoor areas are equally geared toward leisure, with a saltwater swimming pool overlooked by a fully equipped outdoor kitchen.

The 14-acre grounds also include landscaped gardens and an orchard growing blueberries, blackberries, peaches, apples, and figs, while a private drive winds toward the property's lake.

Car enthusiasts, meanwhile, have an enormous amount of space to house their collections.

Although the property's main details advertise a six-car garage, the full listing reveals additional vehicle storage, including a six-car motor court and another six-car lower-level garage.

The garage areas also conceal much more than parking.

Above them sit two separate guest accommodations: a two-bedroom residence with its own kitchen and living and dining areas, and a studio residence equipped with a kitchenette and bathroom.

Perhaps one of the estate's more unexpected features is an underground passage connecting different portions of the property, while an elevator inside the main house provides access to every level.

The listing describes the sprawling compound as a "private legacy estate"—one outfitted to accommodate far more than the day-to-day needs of a single owner.

Howard's ties to Georgia stretch back long before his purchase of the mansion. The Atlanta native attended Southwest Atlanta Christian Academy before jumping directly from high school to the NBA.

He was selected by the Orlando Magic with the first overall pick in the 2004 NBA Draft and spent eight seasons with the franchise before embarking on stints with multiple teams, including the Los Angeles Lakers, Houston Rockets, Atlanta Hawks, Charlotte Hornets, Washington Wizards, and Philadelphia 76ers.

Howard ultimately captured an NBA championship with the Lakers in 2020.

Now, a decade after purchasing his supersized Georgia spread, Howard is once again looking for someone to take it off his hands—albeit at a considerably higher price than when he first tried to sell.

#5599. Lindsay Clancy Returns to Court as Defense Seeks To Block Retrial—Inside the Home Where Her 3 Children Died and Its Puzzling Sale

Lindsay Clancy is returning to court today as her legal team is arguing to block a retrial in the murder case against her—two months after her first case ended in a mistrial and more than three years after she was accused of murdering her three children inside the family's Massachusetts home.

Clancy, 36, has admitted to taking the lives of her daughter, Cora, 5, and sons Dawson, 3, and 8-month-old Callan, but has pleaded not guilty to the three first-degree murder charges against her, with her attorneys arguing that she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time of their deaths.

Over the course of the five-week trial, her defense team has sought to convince jurors that Clancy should not be held legally accountable for the killings because of a "lack of criminal responsibility," according to the Boston Globe.

Following 19 hours of deliberation, the 12-person jury was declared deadlocked after telling state Judge William Sullivan it was unable to reach a unanimous verdict. Sullivan instructed the jurors to return to the deliberation room and continue their efforts to reach a verdict.

Now, the judge has revealed that the jury remains deadlocked, meaning that there will be a mistrial in the case.

“I’m going to declare a mistrial at this point,” Sullivan told the court.

Now, Clancy is set to return to court today, where her legal team will attempt to argue that she can't be retried due to double jeopardy in hopes to have the charges dropped.

Her lawyers will also attempt to seek reduced charges as an alternative, meaning there could be a bench trial instead of jury trial.

Meanwhile, the prosecution has asked the judge to decline the motion to dismiss the charges, claiming they have the right to have a retrial.

Clancy's attorney, Kevin Reddington, previously claimed that he was ready to begin the retrial as soon as possible. He also requested President Donald Trump pardon Clancy; however, presidents can only pardon federal offenses.

Though Clancy was present in the courtroom in Plymouth, MA, she did not testify during the trial, which featured sworn testimony from dozens of witnesses, including her former husband, Patrick Clancy, medical professionals who treated her for mental health issues, and a former nanny who looked after her children.

The former nurse has accused several medical providers of malpractice and negligence, claiming that she was repeatedly misdiagnosed, even as her symptoms continued to worsen. On the night of Jan. 24, 2023, she reportedly experienced suicidal hallucinations and heard a voice telling her that it was her "last chance" to kill herself and her children.

The prosecution, however, is arguing that she wasn't diagnosed with postpartum depression and that the murders seem premeditated, calling attention to the fact that Clancy had reportedly looked up ways to murder on her cellphone prior to the deaths of her children.

While her husband, Patrick, was picking up a takeout meal, Clancy strangled her children and tried to take her own life by cutting her neck and wrists, then throwing herself out of her bedroom window at the family's Duxbury, MA, home.

Cora and Dawson were pronounced dead that same night, while Callan died in the hospital a few days later. Lindsay survived her injuries, but was left paralyzed from the waist down.

Clancy's husband took to the stand to testify on behalf of his wife—as did the couple's former nanny, Elaine Rossi, who described the former nurse as a "wonderful mother."

"I observed a wonderful mom who loved her kids," the nanny said, according to NBC10 Boston. "She cared for their safety, she was very concerned with Callan's eating and sleeping. She was a wonderful mother."

Rossi also told the court that Clancy had revealed to her she was "suffering from postpartum."

Patrick has previously spoken out about his wife's horrifying crimes, sitting down with The New Yorker in October 2024 to defend her against critics, insisting that she was not "a monster."

At the time of the interview, the father of three explained that he had since relocated from Massachusetts to an apartment in New York City, quietly selling off the family's Duxbury home in an off-market deal.

In the interview, Patrick insisted that he "wasn't married to a monster," explaining how his wife had been suffering from anxiety and insomnia, which were brought on by her pregnancy with Callan.

Weeks before the terrible tragedy, he said, she had been hospitalized before being sent home with antidepressants. Despite all this, he said that he believed that her only diagnosis was a generalized anxiety disorder.

“I wasn’t married to a monster—I was married to someone who got sick,” he told the publication, adding that he had chosen to speak out to prevent further "lies and misinformation" from being spread.

Shortly after the deaths of his children, Patrick had issued a personal statement in which he asked the public to forgive his wife.

"A lot of people have said they can’t imagine and they’re right, there’s absolutely nothing that can prepare you," he wrote in the statement, which was shared on a GoFundMe page set up by his loved ones.

"The shock and pain is excruciating and relentless. I’m constantly reminded of them and with the little sleep I get, I dream about them on repeat. Any parent knows, it’s impossible to understand how much you will love your kids until you have them.

"The same goes for understanding the devastation of losing them. Cora, Dawson, and Callan were the essence of my life and I’m completely lost without them.

"My family was the best thing that ever happened to me. I took so much pride in being Lindsay’s husband and a dad to Cora, Dawson, and Callan. I always reminded myself that each day with them was a new gift."

He then shared touching tributes to each of his children, calling attention to his favorite things about them, including son Dawson's "bold, brown eyes" and daughter Cora's "infection laugh."

However, despite his grief, Patrick insisted that he had forgiven his wife, while urging the public to do the same.

"I want to ask all of you that you find it deep within yourselves to forgive Lindsay, as I have," he continued.

"The real Lindsay was generously loving and caring towards everyone—me, our kids, family, friends, and her patients. The very fibers of her soul are loving. All I wish for her now is that she can somehow find peace."

While the Clancy family home does not appear to have been listed for public sale since the tragic events unfolded inside it, Patrick revealed to The New Yorker that he had, in fact, sold it to an anonymous buyer, adding during the interview that he'd just been informed the sale has officially closed.

“There’s no house anymore,” he said. “There are no kids. All that’s left is me and Lindsay.”

He explained that he cleared out the house shortly after taking a solo trip to Central America and Europe in February 2024. He drove around his neighborhood gifting his children's stuffed animals and unused arcade cards to their friends.

Built in 1972, the home has been updated with refinished hardwood floors, a newer roof, and a redone kitchen with granite counters and new appliances and flooring. The three-bedroom, 1.5-bath interior spans 1,732 square feet with a remodeled extra room between the garage and kitchen.

The home sits on a tree-lined lot on almost an acre, with a deck, stone patio, and grassy lawn. The coastal town offers an "acclaimed" school system and a beautiful beach.

According to Realtor.com® records, the home last changed hands in 2018 for $500,000.

#5598. Real Estate or Stocks? Risk Tolerance, Markets Key Most Decisions

There’s always been a question about which is the better investment long term, real estate or stocks? Opinions vary, but there is one thing for sure: You can’t reside in your stock portfolio. Another thing for sure is if you ask real estate pros for opinions, you pretty much get the same answer.

Those willing to accept a fair amount of risk will likely do better in the stock market over time. The 10-year annual S&P 500 performance breakdown from 2016 to 2025 wins hands down, or palms up if collecting profits. Within that decade were four gains in the mid-20% range, with only two negative return years. Of course, what happened in the past has no bearing on the future.

Real estate properties have historically increased in value over time. In 1970, the average price of an American house was $27,000. A comparable investment property now would be worth approximately $500,000, according to Federal Reserve Economic Data. That appreciation could represent a meaningful source of retirement funding if the property were eventually sold.

According to the Zillow Home Value Index, the average United States home value is $366,157, up 1.2% over the past year, and homes go to pending in around 27 days. Stock returns can be volatile due to several factors. Economic events such as recessions, interest-rate fluctuations and geopolitical tensions can significantly impact stock prices. Few would probably be shocked if the continuing war with Iran cratered the stock market at some point.

Stocks now account for more than a 30% share of total U.S. household assets, versus real estate at closer to 25%, according to TD Securities. That wasn’t always so. In the mid-2000s, real estate represented more than 30% of total household wealth, while stocks were around 15%.

So what would you as a real estate pro tell clients if the stocks vs. real estate subject arose?

“Your first investment property is the home you live in,” asserts Pam Rosser Thistle, with Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices Fox & Roach, Realtors® in Philadelphia, while admitting the stock market numbers win right now. “Over time, it appreciates. And you enjoy it. Win, win! Right now I am bullish on happiness, and owning a home is part of that. Appreciation is not like it was during COVID. But over time, your home will make you money when you sell in most cases as long as you stay in it for five to seven-plus years.”

Josh Jarboe, principal broker/owner of RE/MAX Empire in Mount Washington, Kentucky, has never believed real estate should be viewed as a guaranteed investment. But he firmly believes it remains one of the strongest, proven paths for long-term wealth creation.

“Unlike the stock market, homeownership offers something beyond financial returns: stability, utility, leverage and the opportunity to build equity while enjoying the asset itself. Higher home prices and mortgage rates have undoubtedly changed the equation, especially for first-time buyers. However, I remind clients that real estate and stocks aren’t necessarily competing investments. They serve different purposes, and a well-diversified financial strategy can include both.”

Leslie Hirsch, a broker at Christie’s International Real Estate New York, admits that many of her clients have been questioning whether to keep their money invested in the stock market, which has been performing so well, or purchase real estate.

“In New York City, this is driving a very strong rental market, with record prices being paid, as would-be buyers opt to rent instead of tying up cash in real estate,” she says. “Financial advisors/portfolio managers are encouraging clients to stay in the market and not buy real estate. On the flip side, there is chatter about the stock market being too good to last. People need housing, and they also want to diversify investments, maximize returns and mitigate risk.”

Hirsch tailors her advice depending on a client’s personal situation, but admits that generally speaking, the anticipated timeline to hold onto property and see appreciation has shifted.

“I cannot tell someone that we would expect to see ‘x’ amount of appreciation per year, as we have not seen predictable appreciation in Manhattan for 10-plus years,” she says. “Instead of a five-year property value growth cycle, we are now seeing 10-year-plus cycles, and the key is to buy property during the down cycle and sell when it’s up.

“For clients that I know plan to move cities, expand their family or upgrade in three to five years, I try to manage expectations and sometimes suggest they look at renting instead of buying while saving up for the bigger purchase down the road. Some people who would only ever consider being homeowners (never renters) will now consider it.”

Hirsch knows that housing is a fundamental need, and thus is not worried about mortgage rates and the market because the market will ultimately adjust to meet the climate of the day.

“If housing prices become unaffordable, then prices will come down,” she explains. “If the rents go too high, then purchasing becomes the better option again. What I do worry about is the affordability of housing for first-time homebuyers and people starting out in their careers.

“The second home market is where I see even more dramatic fluctuation happening because that is a ‘want’ and not a ‘need.’ When we see home values decrease enough, we eventually see investor buyers swoop in to purchase them. Then, when the stock market stops performing as well, we will see people pivoting back to real estate again, and the prices will stabilize.”

Jarrod Duncan, also with Christie’s International Real Estate New York, has a take as a real estate investor, feeling that while stocks may be booming, real estate is still a strong long-term investment.

“I own many properties in the Southeast that have increased in value exponentially since purchasing them,” he says. “I am also invested in the stock market, as I feel like it’s important to have multiple vehicles for wealth building. I do agree that the stock market has been a good place to be the last few years. So has real estate in certain places, especially in the Southeast, where people are moving for tax advantages, etc.

“I also think that investing in real estate can be even better in an elevated rate environment. Higher rates keep prices down, and you can always refinance, but an attractive deal may not come around again for years. There are some potential tax advantages to investing in real estate, such as the ability to take advantage of accelerated depreciation and ongoing costs to offset other sources of income. I remain committed to investing in real estate and recommend it to others if the fit is right for their long-term goals.”

Jarboe echoes the sentiment that the concern isn’t people choosing stocks over real estate, but the growing number of Americans being priced out of homeownership altogether.

“The longer affordability remains a challenge, the greater the potential wealth gap between those who own real estate and those who don’t,” he says. “Ultimately, I encourage clients to focus less on timing the market and more on whether purchasing a home aligns with their financial position, lifestyle and long-term goals. Real estate isn’t a guaranteed investment, especially in ‘boom-towns/cities’, but historically, patience and responsible ownership have rewarded those who take the long view.”

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5597. What Happened to Lindsay Clancy’s Home? How Duxbury House Was Quietly Sold to Former DA in Off-Market Deal Just a Year After Kids’ Deaths

Lindsay Clancy has returned to court—two months after the jurors serving in the highly-publicized trial revealed they were deadlocked, forcing the judge to declare a mistrial, after an intense five-week courtroom showdown, during which they heard testimony from dozens of witnesses—and even visited the Massachusetts house where the former nurse is accused of murdering her children.

Clancy, 36, who did not testify in the case but was present in the Plymouth, MA, courtroom for the entirety of the trial, has admitted to taking the lives of daughter Cora, 5, and sons Dawson, 3, and 8-month-old Callan.

However, she has pled not guilty to the three first-degree murder charges she is facing, alleging that she was suffering from severe postpartum psychosis at the time of their deaths. On Sept. 4, the judge declared a mistrial.

Now, she is back in court and her legal team is seeking to block the attempts for a retrial on the basis of double jeopardy. The prosecution is still fighting for a retrial in the murder case.

The trial began on July 31, when the jurors traveled to Clancy's former home in Duxbury, MA, where her three children were found in the basement by their father, Patrick Clancy, on Jan. 24, 2023, having been strangled with exercise bands.

According to the Associated Press, the jury was escorted into the home in groups of six and spent a total of 40 minutes at the property, walking through the entire abode, as well as the yard where Clancy was found after throwing herself out of her bedroom window in an apparent suicide attempt.

The visit took place just a few weeks after the property's new owner, former Plymouth County Assistant District Attorney Michael C. Phippen, filed an objection to the juror viewing at a pretrial hearing in June, stating through his lawyer that it would be "massively disruptive" to his day-to-day life.

According to The Patriot Ledger, Phippen's attorney, Peter Maguire, told Judge William Sullivan, that his client's domestic partner would be home at the time of the visit, while also claiming that the jurors arriving at the property with their police escort would upset his pets, as well as his neighbors.

Assistant District Attorney Jennifer Sprague, who is leading the prosecution team in Clancy's trial, noted that Phippen was made aware when he purchased the home that he may have to open it for a jury visit.

While Judge Sullivan overruled Phippen's objection, he put certain restrictions in place for the visit, limiting it to jurors, attorneys, and any court staff that were deemed necessary. He also barred any jurors from opening any closets or touching any of Phippen's personal items.

Phippen—who served as an assistant DA from April 2016 until December 2018, according to his LinkedIn page—purchased the home from Clancy's husband in an off-market deal in January 2024, almost a year to the day after the killings took place.

Property records show that he paid $675,000 for the three-bedroom dwelling, despite the fact that it was estimated to be worth closer to $800,000 at the time.

After Clancy's trial began, social media users began speculating that Phippen was involved in her case in some way, because it was being handled by the same District Attorney's office that he once worked for.

However, Phippen had not worked as an assistant DA for six years by the time he bought the property and his LinkedIn page shows that he established his own legal office in December 2018—and also now works as an attorney for Stark | Lattuca.

Other than the objection that he filed during the pretrial hearing, Phippen is not thought to have had any involvement in Clancy's trial. He has also never publicly discussed how he came to purchase the home.

The former nurse's husband, Patrick, first revealed that he had sold the property in October 2024, when he took part in an interview with The New Yorker, telling the outlet that he had offloaded the residence and relocated to an apartment in New York in the wake of his children's deaths.

He and Clancy had purchased the property for $500,000 in 2018, according to records.

In the interview, Patrick insisted that he "wasn't married to a monster," explaining how his wife had been suffering from anxiety and insomnia, which were brought on by her pregnancy with Callan.

Weeks before the terrible tragedy, he said, she had been hospitalized before being sent home with anti-depressants. Despite all this, he said that he believed that her only diagnosis was a generalized anxiety disorder.

“I wasn’t married to a monster—I was married to someone who got sick,” he told the publication, adding that he had chosen to speak out to prevent further "lies and misinformation" from being spread.

Closing arguments in Clancy's trial took place on Aug. 27, with the former nurse's lawyer, Kevin Reddington, reemphasized his argument that his client was in a "state of psychosis" when her children were killed, insisting that she cannot be found guilty of murder because of a "lack of criminal responsibility."

"This young lady is not guilty of the killing of her children because she was suffering from a disease and defect, as his honor instructed you, and they’re not going to be able to prove otherwise," he told the jury.

Prosecutor Sprague, however, said that—while there is no denying that Clancy was "suffering from mental illness and that she tried to kill herself"—the jury must decide what her state of mind was on the night that her children died.

"What's on trial here, what the issue is here is what Lindsey Clancy did the night of Jan. 24, 2023, and what her mental state was at the time," she said.

Sprague also claimed that witness testimony heard during the trial indicated that she was a "functioning mom" in the months leading up to the killings.

"You know that she knew the difference between right and wrong during that time," she added. "That’s a rational thought ... She knew it was wrong.

At the end of closing arguments, Judge Sullivan dismissed the jury to begin its deliberations, urging them to "have confidence" in the decision that they were being asked to make—whether Clancy was guilty of first-degree murder or the lesser charge of manslaughter.

"Please have confidence in what you're about to do, all right? I have that confidence in you," he said, according to NBC News. "I don't think I've ever seen a more dedicated group of jurors in any trial that I've ever been involved in."

It is not known exactly how long jury deliberations will take, however some legal experts have suggested that they could last for up to a week.

#5595. Philadelphia Renters Win Record Settlement Over Unsafe Conditions and Illegal Rent Collection

A group of Philadelphia renters has reached a settlement in one of the largest per-tenant recovery class action suits in the city’s rental law history.

A preliminary approval of the settlement, which requires Odin Properties LLC to provide the tenants at Bentley Manor apartments with rent forgiveness and refunds for wrongly collected rent, was finalized by a Philadelphia judge last week.

The aggregate settlement amount exceeds $140,000, and individual renters will receive varying amounts based on their payment history, with the average refund estimated at about $1,200.

Three residents of Bentley Manor, located in West Oak Lane, filed a class action suit in March 2025 against Odin Properties and related companies for allegedly illegally collecting rent after the building was designated “unsafe” by the Philadelphia Department of Licenses and Inspections (L&I), according to The Public Interest Law Center.

Philadelphia law prohibits a landlord from collecting rent if a serious L&I violation if not corrected within 30 days. However, the plaintiffs alleged that Odin Properties continued to charge, demand, and collect rent each month, even as the building remained in unsafe status.

Odin Properties will now be required to forgive all unpaid rent and associated fees, estimated to be $66,891, and provide $75,000 in cash refunds for any rent collected, for a total of $141,891 in relief.

“This case sends a simple message: Landlords cannot collect rent while ignoring serious safety violations,” Madison Gray, the staff attorney at the Public Interest Law Center, tells Realtor.com®. “We hope it becomes clear that collecting rent while ignoring serious safety violations is a losing business model in Philadelphia, and we hope it encourages every landlord in the city to fix dangerous conditions promptly and comply with the law before tenants are forced to go to court.”

Realtor.com reached out to Odin Properties for a statement, but received no response.

Bentley Manor, which has approximately 71 sets of renters, was constructed in 1962. Between November 2021 and February 2024, L&I issued several violations related to fire safety, electrical hazards, and nonlatching building doors, all of which were resolved, according to the complaint.

On Nov. 14, 2024, L&I issued another notice of violation declaring the building an “unsafe structure,” citing “loose and missing bricks” and a “leaning parapet” as dangerous conditions. At the same time, multiple previous violations continued to resurface.

When the class-action complaint was filed four months later, in March, Odin Properties had allegedly still not made the building safe to the satisfaction of L&I, which made it ineligible to collect rent.

“Nevertheless, the Odin Defendants charged and collected rent from Plaintiffs and other tenants in December 2024, and in January, February, and March, 2025,” the complaint reads.

Three tenants were named as plaintiffs in the complaint: SEPTA transit operator Porter Grant, who paid $1,274 in monthly rent; Philadelphia police officer Casey Allison, who paid $1,352 in monthly rent; and a grandmother with mobility impairments, Dawn Colbourne, who paid $317 in monthly rent with the Philadelphia Housing Authority paying a monthly $968 subsidy.

“Without admitting or conceding any wrongdoing, liability, or damages, the Defendants have agreed to settle the Action to avoid the substantial expense, inconvenience, burden, and disruption of continued litigation,” the settlement document reads.

In between the lawsuit being filed in March 2025 and the settlement, the defendants made the necessary repairs to Bentley Manor.

Tenants will receive individualized amounts of the $75,000 settlement pool based on how much they paid during the non-compliance time period. On average, tenants will receive more than $1,200 per refund check, according to Gray.

“We also hope this sends a message to tenants. Philadelphia's housing laws only matter if they're enforced, and they don't enforce themselves,” says Gray. “This settlement shows that when landlords break the rules, tenants can fight back and win. Ultimately, we hope this settlement shows that tenants can hold even large landlords accountable when those laws are broken.”

#5594. Confused by Home Price Headlines? Here’s Why.

Whether you own a house already or you’re looking to buy one, you probably care about home prices. But it’s not always easy to figure out what’s really happening right now, especially if you look at the headlines.

One says home prices are falling. The next says they’re still climbing.

So, which one’s right? It comes down to where you live.

Part of the confusion out there may be based on what’s happening to asking prices and how the media is talking about it. They’re calling attention to how asking prices are falling, but don’t give the full context or say that seasonality is at play. So here it is.

Right now, there are more homes on the market than at any other time since November 2019. And with mortgage rates rising since the spring, those homes are taking a little longer to sell. One way to help a home sell quickly in that environment is to have a lower asking price.

According to HousingWire Data, the median asking price is down from $449k in early August to $435k just 2 months later (see graph below):

That’s a dip of about 3%, and a lot of it is normal for this time of year.

Asking prices cool off every fall once the busy summer season wraps up. With fewer buyers this time of year, sellers price a bit more competitively. Today’s rates play a role too, since sellers are pricing to match what buyers can afford right now. And that’s a good thing. Smart pricing helps homes sell.

Just keep in mind, that’s a national list price. It doesn’t show what homes near you are actually selling for. So before you react to a headline, ask a local agent what’s really happening in your area.

“While national headlines might suggest a buyer’s market is taking hold, the reality on the ground depends heavily on where and what you’re trying to buy. Local trends can diverge sharply from national averages, especially when you factor in price range, property type, and post-pandemic market dynamics.”

The latest numbers from S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Index show how true that is. Over the past year, sales prices in Chicago rose almost 7%. In Seattle, they dipped about 1.6%. That’s a gap of nearly 9 percentage points between two major cities (see graph below):

That gap changes your game plan. Selling in New York, where prices are up almost 6%? You may not need to cut your price. Buying in Denver or Las Vegas? You may have more room to negotiate.

Just in case you’re seeing those slight declines in some markets and worried it means a bigger crash is coming, here’s what you need to remember. Even in the major metros where prices are down, the declines are 2% or less. That’s a long way from a crash like 2008. And if you look back at the graph above, there are more cities in the green than in the red.

And over time, home values have a strong track record. The Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) says national prices have grown year-over-year every quarter since 2012. Go back further, and a $100k home bought in 1991 would be worth about $436k today, even with the 2008 crash factored in (see graph below):

So, this short-term dip probably won’t stick around. The small declines we’re seeing now are in markets that overheated during the pandemic. As a whole, the market is headed back to normal – and normal means prices should rise over time.

National headlines can’t tell you what your home is worth or how much room you have to negotiate. Local data can. If you’re thinking about buying or selling, connect with a local real estate agent to look at how prices are moving in your area, so you can set your price or make your offer with confidence.

#5593. To Sell or Rent? How To Choose the Best Path for Your House.

Selling your house is a big step, and you want it to go smoothly. And with houses taking a little longer to sell these days, renting it out might start to sound like a nice backup plan.

But the reality is, while renting can work well for some people, it’s also a big commitment. So before you decide, it helps to see the whole picture first.

Lately, some sellers are choosing to hang on to their houses and rent them out instead. According to Parcl, around 9% of homes for rent right now were previously up for sale.

Some homeowners put their houses on the market expecting a faster process than they got or a certain price buyers didn’t respond to. And when things didn’t go exactly as planned, they decided to rent instead. As Kara Ng, Senior Economist at Zillow, explains:

“Bargaining power is tilting toward buyers and homes are taking longer to sell, making renting out a property one way to buy time rather than compete aggressively on price.”

But here’s the important distinction. Just because some sellers are choosing to rent doesn’t mean selling isn’t working. In many cases, the difference comes down to how well a house is priced, prepared, and marketed for today’s buyers.

Parcl data shows where these “accidental landlords” – owners who planned to sell but decided to rent instead – are most common (see graph below):

They make up around 17% of homes for rent in places like Sherman and Houston, TX, but less than 4% in markets like Des Moines, IA and Bloomington, IN.

That’s a pretty big difference. And it shows why you have to know what’s happening in your neighborhood. Your market, your asking price, and your strategy all play a role in how your sale goes.

A local agent can show you how houses like yours are selling, what strategies work best, and help you weigh your options – not to push you to sell, but so you at least have the full picture based on today’s market. And part of making an informed decision is understanding what renting your house would actually take.

While renting might sound like easy passive income on paper, in practice, it’s a hands-on job with rules to follow. As Invest West Management puts it:

“Even if you never intended to become a landlord, the law still sees you as one — and you must meet all legal obligations that come with that role. This often includes registering the tenancy, providing tenants with certain disclosures, and ensuring the property meets safety standards.”

You’d also be the one chasing missed rent payments, fixing damage between tenants, and covering unexpected repairs. Not to mention fielding weekend calls about leaky dishwashers or broken AC units.

There are expenses beyond regular maintenance and repairs, too. According to Bankrate, these are a few of the biggest:

Insurance premiums (landlord insurance typically costs about 25% more than a standard homeowners policy)

Management fees (if you hire a property manager, they usually charge around 10% of the rent)

Gaps between tenants, when you pay the mortgage without rental income

If you want to be a landlord and you’re prepared for the responsibility, renting may be a great fit. But if you’d really rather sell, don’t let today’s market convince you that you can’t.

A great agent can make it happen. The key is having an open conversation up front with your agent about pricing and how to market your house. Nailing those details from day 1 helps your house make a great first impression, so renting doesn’t have to be your fallback.

Renting can be a good fit for the right person with the right house, but it isn’t the only option. #5592. How Making Daylight Saving Time Permanent Affects Homeowners

Most homeowners change their clocks twice a year: forward by one hour on the second Sunday in March and back by one hour on the first Sunday in November.

However, this longstanding ritual may come to an end, thanks to the Sunshine Protection Act, which was passed by the U.S. House earlier this year and aims to make daylight saving time permanent year-round.

If passed by the Senate and signed into law, the act would lead to lighter evenings and darker mornings. And whether it’ll work in your favor depends on where you live.

Homeowners in Alabama, Florida, and Texas, for example, would enjoy more usable daylight while those in Maine, Michigan, and Wisconsin could see much later sunrises and limited daylight hours.

However, at the moment, the bill has stalled, and during a recent campaign rally in Mississippi, President Donald Trump weighed in, calling the twice-yearly clock change "stupid" and urging the Senate to pass the measure.

Regardless of where you live, it’s important to understand how permanent daylight saving time might affect your home and lifestyle. That way you can prepare for the changes if the legislation becomes law.

With more daylight in the evening, you’ll be less reliant on artificial indoor lighting when you’re awake and active. And this could slightly reduce your electricity use.

However, any savings may be offset by increased heating and cooling demands.

“The dark, cold winter mornings that stem from permanent daylight savings would mean that your furnace will need to work harder before sunrise,” says Brandon Young, CEO of Payless Power in Fort Worth, TX.

In the summer, the additional sunlight can keep your house warmer later into the evening, forcing your air conditioner to run when energy use is the highest.

“As for the landscaping, additional sunlight can allow you to take care of your lawn in the evening rather than wait for the weekend. You might also have to adjust when you water and maintain your lawn,” Young explains.

More sunlight can also improve the security of your home as most perpetrators commit their crimes at night when it’s dark outside.

Lastly, if you plan to list your home in the future, the extra daylight could help you out.

“Since most buyers look at homes in the evenings, you’ll have more opportunities to show your home in the winter months,” Young says.

Plus, the natural lighting can provide a better view of your home’s exterior, landscape, and overall curb appeal.

There are several ways you can prepare for the darker winter mornings you’ll face if permanent daylight saving time becomes law.

“Allow it to preheat your house 30 to 45 minutes prior to your alarm clock going off—not all night long,” explains Young.

Marcus Griswold, founder of Little Green Myths in Vallejo, CA, suggests closing the doors and turning off the heat in rooms you’re not using.

“Some smart systems also help you isolate unused rooms by sensing when someone is present. This is known as zoned heating,” Griswold explains.

Also, take advantage of smart shades that can stay open during the day to heat your home and close with the sunset to hold in the warmth in the winter.

Additionally, use the gradual sunrise option on your smart bulbs, which will mimic the increase in brightness. Place the smart bulbs in bedrooms, bathrooms, and hallways to help enhance alertness as you wake up and ease into your routine.

Don’t forget to be patient with yourself as it might take some time for your body to get used to the change.

“In our survey, 84% of Americans claim it takes at least one day to adjust to a new time after the time change, while 29% say it takes at least one week. Setting your smart home devices like thermostats and lighting to automatically adjust can make the transition easier,” Young explains.

And if you use time-of-use pricing from your utility company, schedule the dishwasher and the laundry to work outside of peak hours. Doing so can lead to cheaper rates and potentially save you some serious cash.

#5590. Why More Buyers Are Turning To Adjustable-Rate Mortgages Today

When mortgage rates climb, buying a home can start to feel like trying to hit a moving target. Every jump in rates makes monthly payments bigger, and that pushes a lot of buyers to look for another way in.

More and more of them are finding it in the adjustable-rate mortgage, or ARM.

Here’s how an ARM differs from a more traditional mortgage. With a regular fixed-rate mortgage, your rate stays the same for your whole loan. But with an ARM, your rate is locked for the first few years, then it can move up or down based on market conditions.

Some people don’t like that level of uncertainty – and that’s okay. But others are drawn to this option specifically because there’s usually a lower rate to start when you opt for an ARM. And in an affordability-strapped market, that’s going to gain popularity.

Bankrate recently found that, in September, rates for ARM products were over a full percentage point lower than a regular fixed-rate loan. Depending on the ARM product, that can make a difference of $150-300 in the monthly payment on a median-priced home.

And for some buyers, that’s enough to turn “not right now” into “let’s do this.” You can see it in the numbers. Data from the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) shows that, in October, roughly 1 in 10 people applying for a mortgage chose an ARM (see graph below):

If you think you may want to consider this yourself, here’s what you need to know about how it works.

An ARM is like a phone or cable plan that has an introductory deal for new customers. You start out at a lower price, and then it adjusts after a specified amount of time. A popular loan is the 5/1 ARM.

The “5” means your introductory rate is locked for the first five years, and the “1” means that the rate can change every year after that. The rate change is called the “reset.” And here’s the really important part.

When your rate resets, your mortgage payment could go up or down. The good news is that most ARMs have caps, which are limits on how much your rate can rise each year and over the life of the loan. But either way, you have to be ready.

To see if this type of loan may be right for you, here are some things to think about and discuss with your loan officer:

Before you decide, ask your lender to work up the numbers and walk you through the different potential scenarios you could run into with an ARM. That way, you go in with your eyes open.

And, if you do go with an adjustable-rate mortgage, just know that you’ll have choices when the reset time arrives. You could:

Do nothing and keep your loan in place if the new payment still fits your budget.

Refinance into a fixed-rate loan with a payment that never changes.

Refinance into another ARM with a new lower rate locked for a specified timeframe.

Talk to the loan servicer about assistance or modification.

Remember, a refinance is a brand-new loan that you’ll have to qualify for – even if it’s on a home you already own. So, keep tabs on your credit and debt levels and ask your loan officer how major financial moves like job changes and major purchases will affect your mortgage readiness. It’s important to keep your credit and finances in “mortgage shape.”

One more quick note. ARMs got a bad name after the financial crisis of 2008. Back then, there were some risky loans with small starting payments that later shot way up. Others let people borrow without proving how much money they earned.

But now, there are new laws to protect both borrowers and lenders. The biggest change is the Ability-to-Repay Rule, which says that before a lender makes a home loan, it has to check real paperwork (like pay stubs, W-2 forms, and tax returns) to make sure you can afford it. The lender also has to look at what your payment could be after the reset, not just the low starting payment.

So, you don’t have to worry that today’s ARMs are the same as the ones we saw back during the crash.

Today's market has more options than many people realize. #5589. Why Builders May Be More Motivated To Sell Than Homeowners

Here’s something most homebuyers don’t think about. When the housing market slows down, homeowners and builders don’t always respond the same way.

Think about it. If you’re selling your house and aren’t getting the offers you want, you could make the choice to take it off the market and stay put, and wait for things to improve.

But builders? They may be more motivated to stay the course.

They’ve already invested money in building those houses. And every completed home that sits unsold means money tied up in a property, plus ongoing costs that can add up.

That’s why some builders may be more motivated to negotiate right now. And that could work in your favor.

You’ve probably seen the headlines. According to the latest report from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), pending home sales – homes that have gone under contract but haven’t closed yet – fell 7.3% in September and 11.3% compared to last year.

Why? Higher mortgage rates are making it harder for buyers to make the numbers work. Now, that report tracks existing homes, not new construction. But we’re seeing signs of the same slowdown on the builder side, too.

According to the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), builder confidence dropped to 29 in October, its lowest level since June 2012. Traffic from prospective buyers also dropped to its lowest level in more than a decade, excluding the start of the pandemic.

As Robert Dietz, Chief Economist at NAHB, explains:

“Demand persists, but higher mortgage rates, elevated construction costs and weaker consumer confidence are keeping more buyers on the sidelines.”

A homeowner may be able to wait for the right offer. But a builder with several finished houses sitting unsold may have more reason to get those homes sold sooner rather than later.

And that means they may be more willing to work with you than you think.

If you’ve always assumed builders don’t negotiate, take a look at what they’re actually doing. According to the latest survey from NAHB, in October:

65% of builders are offering sales incentives.

43% are cutting prices, the highest share recorded between 2020 and 2026.

And 6% is what they’re typically taking off the price.

So, yes. Builders absolutely do negotiate. And with demand slowing, there’s good reason to explore just how flexible they may be right now.

That could mean asking for a lower price. But it could also mean asking for a mortgage-rate buydown, help with closing costs, or upgrades that would otherwise cost you extra.

And here’s a tip that could make a real difference.

Don’t just look at the newest communities or the prettiest model homes. Look for builders with completed houses that haven’t sold yet.

Those are sometimes called quick move-in homes or spec homes. And the longer one of those move-in ready homes sits unsold, the more reason a builder may have to consider an offer that helps get it off their books.

Don’t assume the advertised price or incentive package is the best they’ll do.

This is where having your own agent can really pay off. An agent who knows the local market can help you compare what builders are offering, identify communities with more available homes, and understand where there’s room to negotiate.

Of course, not every builder will offer the same incentives. And some may be more flexible on closing costs or mortgage rates than on the price itself.

The trick is knowing where to look, what to ask for, and how much room there may be to negotiate. And that’s where having your own agent is key.

#5587. These State and Local Elections Will Hinge on Housing Policy—What Voters Need To Know

In this year's midterm elections, housing affordability has emerged as a central flashpoint in three high-profile races: the California gubernatorial contest and the mayoral races in Los Angeles and Washington, DC.

At both the state and municipal levels, voters face major structural and economic constraints, from scarce buildable land and a sluggish pace of new construction to restrictive zoning, drawn-out permitting timelines, high inflation, and mortgage rates topping 7%.

On this year's Realtor.com® State-by-State Housing Report Card, part of the Let America Build campaign, California was among six states to earn an F grade because of a dismal housing affordability score. Washington, DC, fared only marginally better, earning a D+.

Meanwhile, Los Angeles ranked dead last on the Realtor.com Metro Report Cards among the 100 largest U.S. cities, posting the lowest combined score measuring both affordability and homebuilding metrics.

Statewide and local candidates appearing on the Nov. 3 ballot have spent months pitching their proposed solutions to the housing crisis.

On the eve of the vote, here is where each of the contenders for these key gubernatorial and mayoral races stands on housing.

Former Secretary of Health and Human Services Xavier Becerra, a Democrat, and Fox News contributor Steve Hilton, a Republican, are the front-runners vying to replace termed-out California Gov. Gavin Newsom.

If elected governor, Becerra pledges to declare a housing-shortage state of emergency on his first day in office and appoint senior staffers across state agencies to tackle the crisis.

His agenda also includes implementing "shot clocks" to clearly communicate permit wait times to developers, overhauling and lowering impact fees statewide, standardizing and streamlining reviews for modular construction, and simplifying affordable housing financing.

"California should be a place where the carpenter who builds a home can afford to buy one," he said in a speech this summer.

According to a new Realtor.com analysis of the latest available housing and American Community Survey data, the typical household in California earns 49% less than the income needed to finance a median-priced home—a shortfall of $98,292—making it the second-most unaffordable state in the nation behind Montana.

Becerra has voiced support for building "missing-middle" multifamily housing, especially near transit hubs, and expanding first-time homebuyer down payment assistance programs to put homeownership within reach of more renters.

On the issue of homelessness and homeless encampments, which has become a lightning rod for political candidates in California this election cycle, Becerra is laser-focused on prevention.

At an event in the East Bay last week, Becerra argued that keeping at-risk people housed after a medical emergency or a sudden job loss is far less costly to the state than rehousing them from the street, reported ABC 7 News (KGO).

"We have to do everything we can to prevent them from falling into homelessness," Becerra said.

His strategy includes bolstering tenant protections, expanding funding to organizations that have proven effective in addressing the homelessness crisis, and holding accountable those who have failed to act.

The Donald Trump-endorsed GOP hopeful for governor of California has been aggressively pushing for the clearing of homeless encampments, vowing to rid the state of every single one by Dec. 31, 2027.

Similarly to his Democratic rival, Hilton has highlighted the need to cut through red tape constraining residential construction, though his approach hinges on capping fees, permits, and regulation costs at $50,000 per new home to make it cheaper for developers to build.

"We have to get rid of the regulations that make it two or three times as expensive to build the exact same home in California as in neighboring states," said Hilton during a televised debate in May.

His housing platform also includes utilizing over a million vacant lots to build starter homes, and creating 10 new municipalities across California to expand housing supply instead of trying to shoehorn multifamily developments into single-family communities.

“We have to stop trying to force housing into suburban neighborhoods where people don't want it," he proclaimed during the debate.

Despite their contrasting platforms, Hilton and Becerra are united in their fierce opposition to the California Billionaire Tax, officially known as Proposition 40, which Gov. Newsom had unsuccessfully tried to keep off the ballot.

Championed by a coalition of labor unions, the measure would impose a one-time tax of up to 5% on the worldwide assets of more than 200 Californians with a net worth of $1 billion or more who resided in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026.

Opponents of the initiative across the political spectrum have warned that it will accelerate an exodus of high-net-worth residents and tech innovators from California, diminishing the state's tax base.

Speaking on "The Steve Hilton Show" in January, Hilton criticized Proposition 40 as the epitome of what he called the "stupidity and the failure of 16 years of one-party rule" in California that, if adopted, will "drive business out of state."

On his part, Becerra dismissed the proposal as a "sketchy policy" and instead threw his support behind an alternative measure that would extend temporary tax rate increases on the ultrawealthy to reliably fund healthcare and public schools.

At the municipal level, incumbent Mayor Karen Bass, a Democrat, is seeking reelection for a second term. She is being challenged by L.A. City Councilmember Nithya Raman, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America.

Since taking office in 2022, Bass has made fast-tracking affordable housing construction and tackling homelessness the twin pillars of her agenda.

One of Bass' signature initiatives was Executive Directive 1, which streamlined approval for roughly 50,000 units of fully affordable housing. About 6,000 of those units are currently under construction.

In an email to Realtor.com last month, the mayor's office said that under Bass' leadership, the city has carried out a historic rezoning program to create the capacity for half a million new homes and bring more housing to transit corridors and commerical centers.

"After decades of inaction, Mayor Bass has been laser-focused on slashing red tape and accelerating the building of affordable housing in Los Angeles," a mayor's representative said.

Beyond construction permitting, Bass used her executive power to update the Rent Stabilization Ordinance for the first time in 40 years to lower the maximum allowable annual rent hike from 10% to 1%–4% for rent-controlled units, expanded the Adaptive Reuse Ordinance to convert vacant office buildings and parking lots into housing, and streamlined the building application process.

That last action, according to Bass' camp, was in direct response "to the barriers that applicants, developers, and contractors have identified as impediments to building in L.A."

Bass' plan to solve homelessness is anchored by her Inside Safe program, which clears encampments and moves unhoused people into motels and hotels on a voluntary basis with the goal of helping them secure permanent housing.

Councilmember Raman, who is seeking to unseat Bass, has been sharply critical of her record on housing, arguing in a statement to Realtor.com last month that her administration has not done enough to address L.A.’s housing crisis, leaving tens of thousands of residents "struggling to afford rent."

Responding to the Realtor.com Metro Report Cards' findings, that named L.A. the nation’s least affordable large city, Raman said she was not surprised.

"We’ve made it too difficult, time consuming, and costly to build homes in Los Angeles," said the candidate.

To lower costs, Rama’s platform outlines a plan to triple annual housing production by accelerating permitting through strict "shot clocks" for approvals, overhauling inspections, updating codes, and eliminating additional fees to create more starter homes for working families, and pressuring state lawmakers to pass reforms that wold incentivize developers to build more for-sale homes.

Citing results in 4th District, where her office recorded a 49% drop in street homelessness, Raman has made a campaign promise to cut the citywide population of unhoused people in half by the 2028 Summer Olympics through rental subsidies and the expansion of low-cost housing.

Raman and Bass share common ground on the issue of L.A.'s controversial Measure ULA, colloquially known as a Mansion Tax, which they both want to see reformed.

Enacted in April 2023, the measure imposes a 4% tax on property sales of $5.4 million to $10.9 million, and a 5.5% tax on sales exceeding $10.9 million. These rates apply on top of Los Angeles' standard 0.45% base real estate transfer tax.

Contrary to its nickname, the tax applies not only to luxury homes but to all real estate priced at over $5.4 million, including apartment buildings.

A recent report from the nonpartisan global policy think tank RAND Corporation found that the tax cost the city over 9,000 new housing units, 16,500 construction jobs, and $452 million in lost revenue.

Earlier this year, Raman unsuccsefully proposed a ballot measure to exempt newly built multifamily, commercial, and mixed-use buildings from Measure ULA for 15 years, arguing that it was suppressing much-needed housing production.

In Washington, DC, three candidates are striving to succeed three-term Mayor Muriel Bowser: Janeese Lewis George, a Democratic Socialist and member of the Council of the District of Columbia; Rhonda Hamilton, a veteran and community advocate running as an independent; and Robert L. Gross, representing the DC Statehood Green Party.

The cornerstone of Lewis George’s platform is the "Homes for All" plan, which includes provisions for rent stabilization, a coordinated affordable housing development system, stricter code enforcement, and expanded down-payment assistance.

Additional planks in her platform include amending the city’s zoning restrictions to add more homes and mixed-income housing, especially closer to transit lines.

"Increasing supply, paired with policies to protect residents, really is critical to stopping further displacement and making housing more affordable for all," she wrote in an op-ed.

The latest ACS numbers from the Census Bureau reflect the urgent need for change. Buyers in DC have to contend with a 25% gap between earned income and the minimum required income to afford a home.

Her long-term goal is to add 72,000 new housing units throughout DC within five years.

Lewis George has secured the backing of several pro-housing development groups, but President Trump does not count himself among her supporters.

Trump said in June that he "wouldn’t like" having Lewis George as mayor and floated the prospect of overseeing a federal takeover of DC.

"Maybe we’ll take back Washington, run it on a federal basis," he said. "We won’t put up with it. We’re not going to lose our businesses."

Rhonda Hamilton, who grew up in DC, is focused on building deeply affordable housing and requiring all new residential development to include this type of units. Her other major project aims to audit underperforming agencies, including the Housing Production Trust Fund and the District of Columbia Housing Authority (DCHA) waitlist.

"We’ve got to do something about the high rents," said Hamilton, per DC News Now. "We’ve got to make sure that our citizens are not being pushed out of the city."

Like L.A., the nation's capital is dealing with high levels of homelessness. Hamilton's agenda looks to put an end to street encampment clear-outs and partner with local churches to temporarily shelter unhoused residents.

Robert Gross, an information technology engineer by trade, wants to harness the power of artificial intelligence to speed up housing approvals and streamline zoning permits as part of his broader agenda to modernize city government.

Gross’ platform hinges on his "Human Life Standard" framework, which has as its goal to establish green infrastructure standards and reform the housing voucher structure by creating two distinct tracks for families with children and for single, unhoused individuals.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5586. Who’s Buying Homes with Cash Right Now?

Ryan Serhant, CEO of SERHANT, says there isn’t just 1 housing market right now. There are really 4: cash buyers, buyers who need a mortgage, homeowners with low mortgage rates, and builders.

Today, let’s zoom in on the 1st group – cash buyers.

According to the National Association of Realtors (NAR), 27% of homes sold in September were bought with all cash. That’s more than 1 in 4 buyers. And that’s a pretty big number, especially when so many people are struggling with affordability.

So where is all that cash coming from? When you hear a number like that, it’s easy to picture wealthy investors buying up houses left and right. But that’s not necessarily the case. Some of those cash buyers are actually homeowners who’ve built up enough equity to buy their next home outright.

Here’s what you should know about who’s paying cash and what that really means for the market.

Cash buyers tend to fall into a few groups, according to NAR:

Homeowners who sold a house and are using that money to buy their next one

So, it’s not all those big investors social media talks about. That 1st group may include people a lot more like you. Here’s how. According to Cotality, the average homeowner with a mortgage has about $310,000 in equity.

That’s a big deal right now. Many homeowners feel stuck because they don’t want to give up the low mortgage rate they have today. But once they learn they may have enough equity to move and pay cash for their next home, today’s rates don’t matter nearly as much. Because buying in all cash means…

No need to borrow at today’s mortgage rates

No loan approval process, so you may be able to close faster

And even if the equity won’t cover the whole purchase, putting more of it toward the next home means borrowing less. That can mean a smaller monthly payment, too.

But cash buyers like this are more common in some places than others. And how big of a segment of your local market this is, is going to depend on where you live.

For example, Realtor.com data shows cash buyers made up almost 47% of sales in Mississippi and 46% in Montana earlier this year (see map below).

According to Realtor.com, the states with the most cash buyers reflect “a mix of affordability, wealth and buyer demographics.” Think places with lower home prices, or lots of retirees and 2nd-home buyers.

So, depending on where you live, you may see a lot more (or a lot fewer) cash buyers than the national number suggests. An agent who knows your area can tell you who’s actually buying near you.

And if all of this has you thinking everyone’s paying cash, they’re not. If you’re planning to buy and need a mortgage, you’re actually in the majority.

Based on NAR’s numbers, nearly 3 out of 4 home purchases still involve financing. And for homes priced between $200,000 and $750,000, only about 1 in 5 sold for cash, according to Realtor.com (see graph below):

That means most people buying in that price range are financing their purchase, too. So, there’s no need to assume you’re at a disadvantage just because you’re using a loan.

So, what does all this mean for you? Maybe more than you think.

If you already own a house, you may have enough equity to make your next move more affordable than you realize. And if you’re buying with a mortgage, remember, you’re in good company. Most buyers are financing their purchases, too.

The takeaway? Don’t make assumptions about what’s possible based on how other people are buying homes. What really matters is your equity, your budget, and what’s happening in your local market.

Cash buyers are a meaningful part of today’s market, but they aren’t the whole market.Whether you’re hoping to put your equity to work or you’re buying with a mortgage, a local real estate agent can help you see how much equity you have, who’s buying in your area, and what that means for your next move.

Cash buyers are a meaningful part of today’s market, but they aren’t the whole market.

Whether you’re hoping to put your equity to work or you’re buying with a mortgage, a local real estate agent can help you see how much equity you have, who’s buying in your area, and what that means for your next move.

#5585. Rocket Beats Expectations in Q3 Earnings Report Amid Stressed Mortgage Market

Despite operating in “one of the hardest mortgage markets in a generation” that’s “punishing” for American families as described by its CEO, Rocket Companies reported Q3 adjusted earnings above Wall Street expectations, with shares rising about 3% in after-hours trading Oct. 29.

Rocket reported a GAAP (Generally Accepted Accounting Principles) total revenue of $3.28B, up 18% from Q2’s $2.78B in total revenue; and adjusted revenue of $2.57B, down almost 7% from Q2’s adjusted revenue of $2.76B, but a notable 200%-plus increase in net income of $709M this quarter from last quarter’s net income of $229M. Adjusted net income and adjusted EBITDA were both down slightly from last quarter to $419M and $748M, respectively.

But looking at Rocket’s year-over-year earnings shows a total top-line turnaround. Its GAAP total net revenue increased over 94% from $1.69B; adjusted revenue up 37% from $1.87B; adjusted net income up 165% from $158M; adjusted EBITDA up 114% from $349M and most notably, a net income increase from a $124M loss swinging to that $709M profit.

In a release, Rocket Companies CEO and Director Varun Krishna attributed the numbers coming in against a backdrop of mortgage rates at three-year highs, to gains in both purchase and refinance.

“Rocket gained market share in both purchase and refinance, quarter-over-quarter and year-over-year, and delivered our highest profitability margin in nearly five years, even as mortgage rates climbed to a three-year high,” said Krishna. “We didn’t spend the last three years waiting for rates to fall. We acquired distribution, connected real estate and mortgage, and invested heavily in technology. We changed the economics of our business. Rates went up. We took share. Profits grew. That’s not a coincidence.”

In an investor call following the release of the data, Krishna attributed Rocket’s turnaround to a company rebuild three years ago that’s “built for any cycle,” which today is experiencing historic housing market hardships—from the 10-year Treasury rising to its highest point in 24 years to mortgage rates rising to their highest point in three years, to declines in existing-home sales and refinance applications.

“Here’s the truth about tough markets: they don’t lie,” he said. “They strip everything down to what’s real—who has the capital to keep investing, whose model works in any cycle, who can win their clients back, and who can move fast when it counts. This quarter did all of this. This was our highest margin in nearly five years and our fourth straight quarter of expansion since we closed the Mr. Cooper transaction. Adjusted net income of $419 million; $0.15 of adjusted EPS.

“So why does Rocket win?” he continued. “It’s no accident. Three years ago we made a decision: Rebuild this company at every single level. An ecosystem that serves clients from home search through servicing. A technology platform built for scale, speed and efficiency. Distribution that reaches homebuyers and homeowners everywhere. And a fortress balance sheet, now over $11 billion in liquidity, so we can keep investing while others pull back.”

On the investor call, Rocket Companies’ Chief Financial Officer Brian Brown walked through the Q3 numbers in more detail.

“We expanded adjusted EBITDA margin to its highest level in nearly five years, and we ended the quarter with record liquidity,” he said, noting that the $2.6B adjusted revenue was near the midpoint of its guidance range (an estimate of the company’s future financial performance). He said the company generated $40.4 billion in net rate lock volume and $43.6 billion in closed loan volume and that based on its estimates, purchase market share approached 6.5% and refinance market share was 15.5%. That’s compared to the 6.2% and 14.3% reported in the second quarter, he added.

Brown also commented that Rocket Local, its team of in-market loan officers who work directly with real estate agents, also grew volume more than 30% year-over-year, and now includes 400 loan officers across several major metro areas. He said the company’s partnership with Redfin and Compass extends that reach, with one in five of its purchase clients represented by a Redfin or Compass agent.

On the wholesale and partner lending side, he said over the last few months, the company has added around 200 new Rocket Pro partners to its platform, representing $12 billion in potential annual volume. Refinance volume set a record, Brown noted, saying cash-out refinance volume remained healthy, supported by another step up in recapture.

“Recapture rates on the combined portfolio reached an all-time high, the fourth consecutive quarter of improvement. Gain on sale margin, excluding correspondent, was 333 basis points, up from 311 basis points last quarter,” he said.

Krishna said that more than 70% of the company’s revenue this year is coming from recurring or less rate-sensitive sources, such as servicing fees, subscriptions, purchase, cash-out refinance and home equity. He said because of the firm’s integration with Redfin, mortgage buyers are brought into their ecosystem early, creating a path to Rocket from the beginning of their home-search journey. He said as of this earnings report, visitors who click through to start a purchase mortgage transaction are up 50% year-over-year.

“Redfin’s contribution to our refinance leads also more than doubled this quarter from a year ago,” Krishna said. “Compass simply extends that same playbook and delivers what buyers want most—homes and the agents who sell them. Cumulative unique listings are now nearly 40,000, up from roughly 25,000 last quarter. Homes you cannot find anywhere else. Rocket Pro net rate lock volume through Compass has passed $3 billion since February, up 50% from last quarter. Then there’s servicing—our ballast. More than $1 billion a quarter in servicing fees. More than $4 billion a year. That’s triple where we were three years ago. That’s recurring cash flow in any rate environment, revenue that shows up whether rates are 4% or 8%. And here’s what makes it compound: Because we know these clients; we’re first in line when they’re ready for their next loan. In Q3, recapture across the combined portfolio hit the highest level in our history.”

Rocket has a three-year agreement with Compass to provide national exposure to its private and coming-soon listings via Redfin.

Krishna said advances in AI in mortgage lending are a game-changer for Rocket, citing four segments of the process: Credit pulls, digital refinance, voice agents and the future of agentic AI.

On nearly 20% of its direct-to-consumer volume, AI completed the credit pull step on digital purchase and refinance leads before the client spoke to a loan officer, he said.

On refinance loans, he said clients can choose to pull their credit, see their loan options and lock their rate without having to speak to a loan officer. In Q3, he said digital was more than 40% of all direct-to-consumer refinance applications, and digital leads converted at four times the rate of every other channel.

Rocket’s AI voice agents now handle 65% of inbound servicing calls and resolve more than half of them on their own, Krishna added. On the future of agentic AI, he said consumers are starting to shop with their own AI agents to compare price, speed and ratings across lenders. Over the past 18 months, Rocket has built the APIs and protocols those agents need to complete the mortgage process with Rocket end to end, he noted.

Looking ahead, Brown said he expects the economic headwinds that have hammered the better part of this year to continue in Q4 and beyond, especially in the refinance sector.

“The MBA Purchase Application Index is down nearly 20% year-over-year, and refinance applications are down more than 50%,” he said. “The fourth quarter is seasonally low for our industry, and this year that slowdown comes at a time where mortgage rates are reaching highs we haven’t seen in two decades.”

Brown added that Rocket expects the refinance market to decline by almost half from the third quarter, “which would leave the overall mortgage activity near multi-decade lows.”

With that context, in the fourth quarter, Brown said they expect adjusted revenue to be between $2.1B and $2.3B with their guidance reflecting continued share gains. For expenses, they expect total expenses of $2.05B, including $110M of intangible amortization, $80M of stock-based compensation and $10M of one-time integration costs. Excluding these items, Brown said they expect expenses of $1.85B, a decline of $165M from the third quarter.

“Tough markets drive separation,” Brown said in his closing remarks. “This quarter, rates rose, volumes fell, and the industry felt it. Rocket Companies grew share, expanded margin, delivered synergies ahead of plan and ended the quarter with record liquidity. The fourth quarter will be harder still. We’re ready for it.”

Beth McGuire is RISMedia’s vice president of online editorial.
