#5584. Don't Let the Fear of a Buyer Backing Out Scare You Away from Selling

There’s nothing quite like the excitement of getting an offer on your house. You’re one step closer to moving on to what’s next. But what happens if that buyer backs out or ghosts you before closing?

If you’ve been seeing headlines about more home sales falling through lately, that possibility may be keeping you up at night. And it’s true. According to Redfin and Cotality, canceled contracts have been on the rise.

But here’s what those headlines don’t always tell you…

Most sales still go through. Only 10-15% hit this snag. And even so, there are things you can do to help keep your sale from becoming one of them.

The key is knowing what tends to scare buyers away and getting ahead of those issues before they have a chance to derail your move.

Today’s buyers are being more cautious. Mortgage rates are stretching budgets, and with more homes to choose from, buyers have more freedom to walk away if something doesn’t feel right. As Redfin explains:

“That gives house hunters more options and makes them more likely to walk away if an inspection uncovers problems, an appraisal comes in low or the seller doesn’t agree to concessions.”

That’s why an accepted offer isn’t always a guaranteed sale. But it doesn’t mean you should be afraid to put your house on the market, either.

It just means getting ahead of potential problems matters more than ever.

A Redfin survey asked real estate agents why some buyers are backing out. And their answers give you a short of cheatsheet into what could go sideways and how you can get ahead of those headaches (see graph below):

This is the big one. And the good news? It’s also one of the areas where you can be the most proactive.

One simple way to head this off is by getting a pre-listing inspection before your house goes on the market. That way, if something needs attention, you can decide whether to fix it upfront (before you sell), adjust your price, or disclose it and come in already prepared for what’s likely to pop up in negotiations. It’s a lot better to find the skeletons in the closet before a buyer does.

Even buyers who are pre-approved can run into financing issues before closing. And with mortgage rates putting extra pressure on affordability, some buyers are finding it harder to make the numbers work.

While you can’t control whether a buyer’s loan goes through, you can work with your agent to look closely at their financing before accepting an offer. And if affordability is the concern, your agent can help you explore whether incentives like closing cost credits or a mortgage-rate buydown could make a difference.

Sometimes, your buyer needs to sell their house before they can buy yours. And if their sale falls through, yours could be affected too.

That’s why it’s important to understand any home-sale contingencies before accepting an offer. Your agent can help you look at where the buyer is in their own selling process and what protections you may want in place.

The goal isn’t to eliminate every possible risk. It’s to avoid being caught off guard by the ones you can plan for.

Just remember when you read headlines about canceled deals, they don’t give you the full picture. Most home sales still make it to closing.

And if a sale does fall through, that doesn’t automatically mean your house won’t sell. Sometimes a buyer’s circumstances change. Sometimes an issue comes up that can be addressed before the next offer.

What matters is having an agent who knows how to spot potential problems early, help you navigate negotiations, and keep your sale moving forward.

Because while you can’t control every twist and turn, you can control how prepared you are.

There's no need to let the fear of a buyer backing out hold you back. While no sale comes with guarantees, a little preparation upfront can go a long way toward making the whole process smoother.If you're ready to make a move, talk to a local agent about whether a pre-listing inspection makes sense for you.

#5583. Credit Scoring Is Changing: 3 Things Homebuyers Should Know

Quick, what credit score do you need to buy a home? If a number pops into your head, there’s a pretty good chance it’s wrong. And the right answer is getting harder to pin down, because the way credit scores are determined and delivered is changing – for the better.

Here’s what you need to know in today’s changing credit climate.

Fannie Mae has been tracking consumer perceptions about mortgage requirements since 2015 and found that consumers consistently overestimated the minimum credit score lenders required to qualify for a mortgage. As recently as 2023, the average guess was 652.

In reality, the long-standing benchmark for loans backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac is lower, at 620, and today even that isn’t a hard rule for every mortgage they back.

Like the Fannie Mae research, a recent survey from Veterans United found consumers continue to overestimate what it takes to qualify for a home loan:

The takeaway? Guessing wrong can cost you.

A renter who assumes their score is too low and they can’t qualify for a mortgage may never take steps to find out for sure.

For decades, the mortgage industry relied on one set of scores – Classic FICO. Thanks to a push to promote competition, make credit scoring more inclusive, and help more Americans become homeowners, the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) has approved the use of new credit score models such as FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0.

A different model can mean a different number for the same person. VantageScore says its model can score about 33 million adults that the Classic FICO’s model can’t. So the score you saw on an app last month may not be the one your lender pulls.

Remember: the models may be new, but the basics haven’t changed.

Your credit score is important – no matter how it’s measured. Following the same basic rules will benefit your profile in the old and new score models:

Because while credit models may change, the general advice for you to improve your score doesn’t. Financial awareness and consistency mixed with a little willpower can go a long way.

Don't make credit or homebuying decisions from a chart, an app, or a friend's advice. With the rules shifting and so many misconceptions out there, it's never too early to talk to a professional loan officer for advice on credit, budgeting, and what it would take to qualify for a mortgage.You may be closer to owning a home than you think.

#5582. Jenny McCarthy Is Living in a Tent and Considering a Move to Las Vegas After ‘Serious’ Mold Problem

Jenny McCarthy is opening up about her unusual living situation as she’s moved into a tent in her yard while she deals with the effects of a “mold and mycotoxin poisoning” diagnosis.

During the Oct. 28 episode of “The Jenny McCarthy Wahlberg Show,” the actress explained the health-related challenges she’s faced over the last two years, which have included multiple surgeries and rounds of antibiotics.

Eventually, medical professionals tested “The Masked Singer” judge for mold, and she was diagnosed with mycotoxin poisoning.

McCarthy, 54, believes she was initially exposed to mold at her “very, very old” dressing room that “had a dampness to it,” as the makeup artist who exclusively works with her “in that dressing room also wound up getting mold poisoning.”

After the diagnosis, McCarthy embarked on a “mold protocol” in January 2025, following a routine of taking vitamins and undergoing treatments. She also took on the costly experience of remediating her home—which she said can cost anywhere from tens of thousands of dollars to “a hundred grand.”

“Remediation costs are so high because it takes a specialist to be able to move the mold without ruining your entire house,” she said, noting that the process was not covered by her insurance.

After remediation, McCarthy explained she had to hire contractors to “come in and rebuild” the home.

“You have to get rid of all your furniture. You have to get rid of all your clothes. I’m like, ‘Oh my god, that’s crazy!’” she said of the advice she received. “So, we remediated and because I am paranoid now about basically sleeping anywhere, I live in a tent. And I’m not even joking.”

McCarthy shared a look at the tent she’s been living out of, noting that it has a rain-proof cover for safety.

“I don’t have to worry about rain in California, but I do worry about chemtrails. And sprinklers,” she said.

She also added that she “won’t even go into an RV” because she is concerned about “chemicals.”

The podcast host went on to explain that she feels “a little bit crazy sometimes,” noting a “paranoid” state of mind, “like the walls are caving in.” She called the situation “really, really hard,” and confirmed that her husband, Donnie Wahlberg, 57, is not living in the tent with her.

“Donnie is working in Canada, and he is safe inside of a building,” McCarthy said. “Does he think I’m crazy? Yes. But he completely understands it.”

McCarthy also said that in the wake of the ordeal, she’s considering a relocation.

“I am so paranoid that I’ve even talked to Donny about moving out of the Midwest, where it’s humid, and going to a dry location like Vegas or Arizona or something, because my body just can’t detox mold very well,” she said.

While it appears that the tent McCarthy is residing in is located in California, it’s unclear whether the home she had remediated is the St. Charles, IL, residence she and Wahlberg listed for $2.799 million in September of this year.

In a recent Instagram comment, McCarthy indicated that the couple was “Going to Vegas. Not Cali.” following the listing of their longtime home.

The couple have owned the property for over a decade, and purchased it for $1.1 million in 2015.

“This isn’t an extravagant home, but there’s no greater symbol of our love for each other than this house and how much love has gone into it,” Wahlberg told People magazine of the dwelling in 2019.

The four-bedroom, 5.5-bathroom home was built in 1996. Spanning 7,236 square feet, the abode sits on 1.26 acres. Based on the contingent status on the property’s listing, it appears the couple has found a buyer.

#5581. The Home Insurance Move That Could Save You $440 a Year

When you’re planning a move, every monthly cost counts. That’s why it can be frustrating to see home insurance keep creeping up. According to Intercontinental Exchange, it now makes up 9.6% of the average monthly mortgage payment.

But the latest numbers show some progress on that front – as the increases start to slow down. Here’s what you need to know and what you can do about it.

A look at the past two years shows how much things have cooled down. In mid-2024, home insurance premiums rose 4.3% in a single quarter. By the second quarter of this year, that was down to 1.8%. That’s the smallest quarterly growth in almost 3 years – and that’s a good thing (see graph below):

As Andy Walden, Head of Mortgage and Housing Market Research at Intercontinental Exchange, explains:

“Property insurance has been a fast-growing component of the monthly mortgage payment, but this quarter’s data shows the pace of increase is finally slowing.”

While your premium will likely still go up over time, it may not climb as quickly as it did a couple of years ago. And that’s, at the very least, a step in the right direction.

Here’s where you have some say in what you pay. Let’s take current homeowners as an example. Intercontinental Exchange found that when homeowners shopped around and switched insurance companies, their premiums went down 6.6% on average. Those who stayed with their current company saw an increase of 10.4% (see graph below):

Think about that. That’s a big difference and it goes to show that looking for a new provider can literally pay off.

That works out to about $440 a year in savings for the people who switched. And they didn’t have to give up coverage to get it. Their deductibles dipped 1.4%, and their coverage limits actually rose 7.3%.

While this example is current homeowners, the same general idea applies for first-time buyers too. Shop around and get multiple quotes before you pick your insurance provider. Then, once you’re settled in, review your policy each year when it comes up for renewal. You’re not locked into the first price you get.

The home itself plays a role as well. According to John Burns Research and Consulting (JBREC), newly built homes are 10% to 15% less expensive to insure than older ones nationally.

And while a brand-new home won’t necessarily be the right fit for every buyer, if you’re open to one, it could be one more way to keep your monthly insurance costs down.

Home insurance is certainly a bigger part of the monthly costs than it used to be, and that can feel like just one more thing to juggle when you’re buying a home or moving. But knowing you have ways to keep it in check can take some of the pressure off. Compare a few options before you buy, revisit your policy each year, and lean on trusted local professionals as you plan for your next move.

#5580. Mortgage Rates Above 7% Are Testing Home Buyer Engagement

Mortgage rates are a key factor in the home-buying process, and online shopping activity suggests consumers are paying close attention to borrowing costs. With rates around 7.5%, Zonda’s Homebuyer Outlook Clicks Index, which tracks NewHomeSource online new-home shopping activity, has fallen to its lowest level since 2022.

Of course, the relationship between rates and shopping activity is not one-to-one. The job market, broader economy, stock market, geopolitical uncertainty, and consumer confidence can all influence whether prospective buyers start searching for a home. The stability of mortgage rates can matter as well.

Still, the Homebuyer Outlook data suggests 7% may represent an important psychological threshold for consumers.

When mortgage rates first moved above 7% in 2022, online shopper activity weakened noticeably. Another significant pullback occurred as rates climbed well above 7% in late 2023. The latest data shows a similar pattern, with the Clicks Index dropping in September as mortgage rates approached 7.5%.

That relationship matters because online shopping often represents an early step in the purchase funnel. Fewer consumers browsing new-home options can translate into a smaller pool of prospects moving toward community visits and eventual purchases.

Importantly, Zonda’s Homebuyer Outlook shows that the right communities can still outperform even in a challenging market. For builders, that puts the focus beyond simply generating traffic and toward understanding which buyers remain engaged, what they can afford, and how closely a community’s location, product, and price point align with those consumers.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth research reports published in Zonda’s Homebuyer Outlook subscription.

Sean Fergus, Vice President of economic research at Zonda, leads the published research team. Fergus has 20 years of expertise in economic research, market studies, and financial analysis.

#5579. BRUNT Workwear Pledges $1 Million of Work Boots for Trade Students in 2027

BRUNT Workwear connects with a trade school student during a previous boot donation event. Since its founding in 2020, BRUNT has donated approximately 25,000 pairs of work boots to students pursuing careers in the skilled trades.

Work boot and apparel brand BRUNT Workwear has announced a commitment to donate $1 million of work boots to trade school students nationwide in 2027, as demand for skilled workers continues to grow. The commitment expands BRUNT’s longstanding pledge to donate 100,000 pairs of boots to trade school students by 2030.

“America needs the next generation of builders, electricians, plumbers, and skilled tradespeople more than ever,” says Eric Girouard, founder and CEO of BRUNT Workwear. “These are the people who will build our homes, maintain our infrastructure, and keep this country running. We want to do our part to make sure they’re equipped to succeed. We’ve already donated approximately 25,000 pairs of boots to students across the country, and this $1 million commitment is another step toward our goal of donating 100,000 pairs by 2030. As BRUNT grows, our commitment to the trades is only going to grow with it.”

Taking a boots-on-the-ground approach to putting the people who wear its products at the center, BRUNT often names products after real tradespeople and incorporates direct customer feedback into product development. The gear brand shares workers’ stories through its Bucket Talk podcast and brings the trade community together through weekly BRUNT Garage events.

Through the existing trade school boot donation program, BRUNT strives to help ease an upfront expense, while welcoming them into a community that understands, supports, and celebrates this workforce.

“BRUNT Workwear’s boot donation program is truly changing the face of vocational education in Massachusetts one pair of boots at a time,” says James Hachey, director of the Center for Career & Technical Education at Somerville High School.

“Particularly for students in high-need communities, having the proper and safe work boots can mean the difference between opportunity and exclusion. Students not having the same access to required safety gear can create an immediate barrier to hands-on career and technical learning. Donations like BRUNT Workwear’s help remove that barrier, thereby ensuring all students can safely participate, build the necessary skills, and prepare themselves for lasting careers.”

Starting January 1, 2027, trade schools nationwide can find more information and apply for work boot donations at bruntworkwear.com. Selected schools will receive boots throughout 2027.

#5578. Houston’s Historic Kirby Mansion Is Demolished To Make Way for Convenience Store

Preservationists in Houston are up in arms after a historic mansion dating back to 1894 was demolished to erect a convenience store.

On Friday, demolition on Kirby Mansion began but was quickly halted by Houston Public Works after it was discovered that a demolition permit had been applied for but not approved.

Dozens of locals held a candlelight vigil on Sunday to protest the demolition, but the permit was approved over the weekend. Demolition resumed and was completed on Monday morning.

The Kirby Mansion was named after lumber baron and industrialist John Henry Kirby who purchased the small home that was originally on the site in 1896 and expanded it into a 36-room Tudor Revival mansion.

Among the many unique features of the home was a library with hidden panels and a “thunder room”—a sound-insulated room built because Kirby's wife, Lelia, had a severe fear of thunderstorms.

The Kirby family sold the property in 1947, and the mansion served as the headquarters for the Houston-Harris County Red Cross for 30 years, though it had not been occupied in recent years.

Over its 132-year history, the mansion hosted presidents Franklin D. Roosevelt, Herbert Hoover, and George H.W. Bush, as well as British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher.

This past September, OB Texas Properties LLC, a company owned by Omair Bashir, purchased the property for more than $9.3 million. Bashir and his brother, Usman, are the owners of Brake Time Corner Market, a fast-growing convenience store and gas station chain.

In September 2025, Brake Time announced it would be opening 35 new convenience stores across Texas, Arizona, Arkansas, Colorado, and Kansas through the end of 2026, with three planned for Houston.

This past June, OB Texas Properties filed a plan for a 13,254-square-foot, one-story commercial building at an address within the mansion’s property boundaries. The filings included a hemp registration—indicating consumable hemp products would also be sold at the location.

Local preservationists had rallied to save the mansion, but because it lacked local, state, or federal historic designation, there was little they could do.

Over the weekend, Preservation Houston tried to contact Bashir’s company about removing some of the historic details from the site, including the mansion’s hand-carved oak staircase and imported tiles, but received no response.

“We wish the owner had been transparent and honest about the plans for this property and willing to discuss preservation options,” Jennifer Kapral, the executive director of Preservation Houston told Realtor.com in a statement. “We offered to explore ways to give this building a future. We also asked for the opportunity to document it and discuss salvaging irreplaceable materials if demolition went ahead. We received no response. Houston deserves better than this.”

“What’s so sad is the people that did buy this, and again, it’s their private property they can do with it as they choose. It just seems like not the best place for a vape store and gas station when there are numerous gas stations within a three-mile radius,” local resident Jason Fuller told the Houston Chronicle.

This isn’t the first time the Kirby Mansion was scheduled for demolition. In 2018 Central Houston Auto Properties LLC purchased the property, with the intention of turning it into a car dealership, though those plans never came to fruition.

Realtor.com has reached out to Brake Time for comment.

#5577. Century Communities Grows Community Count as Higher Rates Weigh on Q3 Demand

Hamilton model home in Jarrell, Texas | Eastwood at Sonterra by Century Communities

As No. 10 on the 2026 Builder 100 list, Century Communities reported net income of $12.6 million, or $0.44 per diluted share, in the third quarter as higher mortgage rates and economic uncertainty continued to weigh on home buyer demand, particularly among the company’s first-time buyer base.

Adjusted net income was $28.8 million, or $1.01 per diluted share, while total revenue reached $864.5 million. Home sales revenue totaled $842.5 million on 2,442 deliveries, with an average sales price of $345,000.

“The third quarter was marked by a significant rise in interest rates, continued inflation, and macroeconomic uncertainty, which weighed heavily on consumer confidence in general and first-time home buyers in particular,” executive chairman Dale Francescon said.

Despite the challenging demand environment, Francescon said the company continued to make progress operationally. Century ended the quarter with 343 communities, up 7% year over year and 4% sequentially, marking a company record.

“Our direct construction costs, finished lot costs, and fixed G&A excluding advertising all decreased versus the prior quarter as we continued to effectively manage our costs and grew our book value per share to a company record $90.61,” he said.

Century generated 2,284 net new-home contracts during the quarter and ended Sept. 30 with a backlog of 1,106 homes valued at $414 million.

Adjusted home building gross margin, excluding interest, purchase price accounting, and inventory impairment, was 19.3%. GAAP home building gross margin was 15%, including inventory impairment charges, while home building gross margin excluding inventory impairment was 17.3%.

Century also highlighted its early October acquisition of substantially all of the assets of HistoryMaker Homes, a Texas home builder operating exclusively in the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex.

According Francescon, the transaction will increase Century’s Dallas division from 12 to 41 active communities, based on Sept. 30 figures. On a trailing 12-month basis through the third quarter, deliveries associated with the expanded operation will increase from 211 to 669 homes.

“In early October, we acquired substantially all of the assets of HistoryMaker Homes in support of our strategy of deepening our share in existing markets to drive improved margins and returns,” Francescon said. “This acquisition will accelerate our growth in the largest housing market in the country and one we believe will benefit from solid long-term fundamentals.”

“Given the impact of increased mortgage rates on our orders and deliveries, we now expect our full year 2026 home deliveries to be in the range of 9,350 to 9,650 homes, including 100 deliveries from HistoryMaker in the fourth quarter, and our home sales revenues to be in the range of $3.3 billion to $3.4 billion,” chief financial officer Scott Dixon said.

Century finished the third quarter with $2.6 billion of stockholders’ equity and $863.8 million of total liquidity, including $119.8 million of cash, cash equivalents, and cash held in escrow. The company also increased its revolving credit facility to $1.2 billion and extended its maturity to November 2030. Book value per share reached a company record $90.61 as of Sept. 30.

#5575. Greensboro Housing Push Gains Momentum as New-Home Demand Holds Firm

Greensboro has already surpassed 40% of its “Road to 10,000” housing goal, with 4,071 homes completed or under construction roughly 18 months after the initiative launched. City leaders say the program is ahead of schedule toward its goal of adding 10,000 housing units by 2030, an effort that has taken on greater importance as major employers expand across the region.

The housing need extends well beyond the initiative. Greensboro officials estimate the city will require at least 33,000 additional housing units to serve current and future residents across a range of incomes and housing types.

That demand outlook is being reinforced by large employment investments, including Toyota Battery Manufacturing NC, JetZero, and Boom Supersonic. JetZero alone has broken ground on a campus at Piedmont Triad International Airport and plans a $4.7 billion investment that could eventually create up to 14,500 jobs by 2037.

The near-term sales backdrop offers another encouraging signal. As of August, the broader Greensboro market recorded 1,344 new-home sales over the prior 12 months, up 24.9% year over year. Attached sales were especially strong, rising 67.8% to 515, compared with a 7.8% increase in detached sales to 829.

The stronger sales picture comes despite a slower labor market. Greensboro’s non-farm employment increased just 0.6% year over year in July, representing an addition of 1,000 jobs. While still positive, that pace has moderated from earlier periods. The metro’s unemployment rate stood at 3.8%, and Zonda forecasts annual employment growth of 0.6% for 2026 before improving to 0.9% in both 2027 and 2028.

Greensboro is adding housing fast, attached product is contributing meaningfully to sales growth, and major economic development projects could support future household formation. Yet slower near-term job growth and increasing lot and finished inventory reinforce the need for disciplined product selection, pricing, and submarket strategy.

#5574. How To Deal With Noisy Upstairs Neighbors: 8 Clever Tricks To Keep The Peace

Shortly after they were married, Brittany H. and her husband moved into an apartment in Chicago’s Irving Park neighborhood. With Victorian houses and vintage flats dotting the tree-lined streets, they assumed their new home would be a peaceful spot to build their life together.

But the couple got more than they bargained for. At all hours of the night, they heard strange, loud sounds coming from the neighbors upstairs.

“It was midnight, and the loud upstairs neighbors sounded like they were dropping bricks on the floor," Brittany says, vividly recalling her first night in the unit. "Our ceiling light fixture rattled from the loud, noisy pounding.”

When their lease was up, the couple promptly moved to the top floor of a different apartment building. Brittany was so scarred by her experience with noisy neighbors, she says she'll never live anywhere but a top floor again.

As a renter, you have to be ready for some day-to-day noise—that's just part of living in close quarters with other people. So, how can you reduce noise from upstairs neighbors?

If you've lived below noisy upstairs neighbors like Brittany has, you know the sound: the relentless stomping, dropped objects that seem to ricochet off every surface, the mysterious midnight furniture rearranging. Beyond frustrating, it can feel inescapable.

In many apartments, especially older buildings, this kind of noise is more than a nuisance: It's a feature.

Many vintage units were built before modern soundproofing standards were a thing. That means there might be little to no insulation between floors, allowing every footstep, conversation, or clattering object to echo directly into your living space.

While some level of noise is part of communal living, chronic disruptions can wear on your nerves and your sleep cycle.

But you're not powerless to deal with it. Whether you have noisy upstairs neighbors stomping around at odd hours or sudden loud thuds overhead, these renter-friendly tips can help restore your peace and quiet.

Say what now? Ceiling clouds are acoustic panels that hang from the ceiling and can reduce noise and echoes. (Science!) Take that, noisy upstairs neighbors.

You've probably seen them before in auditoriums, atriums, and restaurants. They can do wonders for cutting down noise in your home, too.

Just make sure to check with your landlord before installing them since they need to be securely mounted to the ceiling.

If your landlord isn't on board, there are other less invasive approaches to dissipate sound, including acoustic light fixtures that claim to absorb sound.

Have you ever lived next to a neighbor who plays the piano (or worse, an amped-up electric guitar) well past bedtime?

If the neighbor won't knock it off, you don't have to move (or file a complaint with the landlord or police). Just put some stuff between you and the pandemonium next door.

Start by placing bookcases or other heavy furniture against the dividing wall, covering as much of the wall as possible.

"The more mass between you and the neighbor, the less sound that will come through,” says Zach Ziskin, a recording engineer in Fort Lauderdale, FL.

Then, rearrange fabric-covered sofas or chairs so that they're close to windows and doors. And for more quiet, use lots of decorative pillows and throws.

“The heavier and denser the textile, the greater the absorption,” says Heather Humphrey, owner of the interior design firm Alder & Tweed, in Park City, UT.

If you can hear your neighbors flush the toilet, they can probably hear you, right? That’s because open spaces with tile and hard surfaces, such as a bathroom, amplify sound.

Short on space? Fill the bathroom with wall coverings and soft goods such as rugs and towels, which is a pretty easy way of dealing with noisy upstairs neighbors and their sounds.

“The same principle goes," she says. "The more you cover your walls, the greater the barrier to sound created."

Sometimes, the outside noise you hear in your apartment can be just as irritating as noise from your neighbors. And closing your windows isn't always a cure-all—those sounds can trickle in regardless.

One way to dial it down? Make sure the window casings and frames are fully caulked and sealed. (You'll want to call your landlord about this one.) Or use a window insert to make the seal more airtight, Ziskin says.

Even easier? Just hang some heavy curtains, which will help muffle any noise from outside.

You'd be surprised by how much noise can seep in through the cracks around your door and ruin your quiet. Your best soundproofing efforts will be futile unless you address them.

Make sure there's high-quality weatherstripping between the door and door frame to create a seal when closed, Ziskin says.

Likewise, if there's an air gap between the bottom of the door and the floor, attach a heavy-duty door sweep or draft blocker to create a seal.

Because wall hangings and tapestries are porous, they can absorb sound and excessive noise.

If you're conjuring up images of your college dorm room, don't worry—there are tons of options these days that are beautifully on trend.

For instance, the heavy knotting in macramé makes it perfect for buffering noise and giving your place stylish flair.

Canvas wall art can also help absorb sound; consider adding a layer of foam to the hollow inside for an extra buffer. Or try sound-absorbing felt panels—you can even use one to make a DIY bulletin board.

"It will add a decorative touch and keep you organized, while reducing noise levels," says Dayna Hairston, interior designer at Dayziner in Cary, NC.

If you have wood floors, do yourself and your neighbors a favor and throw down some area rugs. (Heck, if you have carpet, go ahead and do this, too—the more padding, the better.)

When buying a rug, seek out thick-pile material or something with a rubber backing to muffle sound, Humphrey suggests.

Of course, it just isn't always possible to completely soundproof your apartment. If you're still fighting the urge to grab a broom and bang on the ceiling, it's probably time to talk to the neighbors.

"If all else fails, invest in high-quality earplugs or a white noise machine,” Ziskin says.

Sometimes, your noisy upstairs neighbors aren’t just annoying—they’re violating local laws. Most cities have noise ordinances, which define quiet hours, typically between 10 p.m. and 7 a.m. (These can vary by location.) If your neighbors are consistently blasting music late into the night or stomping around at 2 a.m., you might have legal grounds to act.

Start by documenting the disturbances. Note the time, duration, and type of noise. Audio recordings and written logs can help if you need to escalate the issue down the line.

Next, try to resolve the problem directly. Politely let your neighbor know the noise is disruptive. If that doesn't work, reach out to your landlord or property manager.

Still no improvement? Then it's time to contact your local nonemergency number. Don’t dial 911 unless it’s an emergency—for everything else, most municipalities have a nonemergency line for noise complaints.

If you're unsure about your city’s laws, search “[your city] noise violation hours” or visit your city’s website to understand when and how to file a formal legal noise complaint.

It might be tempting to fight noise with noise by blasting your own music, banging on the ceiling with a broom, or leaving a snarky note taped to their door. But while getting back at your neighbors might sound like a dream, these passive-aggressive tactics rarely work—and often make things worse.

Instead, aim for constructive solutions. Communicate clearly, keep things civil, and involve your landlord or building management when needed. If all else fails, rely on renter-friendly soundproofing upgrades and consider investing in a white noise machine or noise-canceling headphones.

Allaire Conte contributed to this report.

Jenny Lelwica Buttaccio is a writer living in Chicago. Her work has appeared in HuffPost, Prevention Magazine, Reader's Digest, and more.

#5571. Higher Rates, Affordability Pressure D.R. Horton Orders and Closings

Rising mortgage rates and persistent affordability constraints weighed on D.R. Horton’s home sales during its fiscal fourth quarter, contributing to year-over-year declines in both closings and new orders.

The Arlington, Texas-based builder closed 22,915 homes during the quarter, down 2% from the prior year period. Home sales revenue declined 2% to $8.4 billion.

Net sales orders fell 7% to 18,619 homes, with the value of those orders declining 9% to $6.6 billion. The cancellation rate was 23%, compared with 20% a year earlier.

On the earnings call, D.R. Horton reported an average sales price on net orders of approximately $357,000, down 2% both sequentially and year over year.

“Housing market conditions became more challenging during the fourth quarter as rising mortgage rates, affordability constraints, and cautious consumer sentiment continued to pressure new-home demand,” executive chairman David Auld said.

Home sales gross margin was 19.5% in the quarter, down 120 basis points sequentially. Management attributed 80 basis points of the sequential decline to above-normal litigation costs.

Home building pre-tax income declined 11% to $891 million, while its pre-tax profit margin was 10.6%. Auld said incentives are expected to remain an important affordability tool heading into the new fiscal year.

“We expect incentives to remain elevated in fiscal 2027, the extent of which will depend on market conditions throughout the year,” he said.

D.R. Horton also pulled back sharply on starts as it worked to align inventory with the slower sales environment. The builder started approximately 13,100 homes during the September quarter, down 45% sequentially, according to the earnings call.

The builder ended Sept. 30 with approximately 28,200 homes in inventory, including 17,700 unsold homes. Of those unsold homes, 8,800 were completed.

Despite the challenging end to the year, D.R. Horton closed 84,202 homes during fiscal 2026, generating $30.6 billion in home sales revenue. Consolidated revenue for the full year totaled $33 billion, with net income attributable to the company of $2.9 billion, or $10.11 per diluted share.

D.R. Horton enters fiscal 2027 expecting affordability constraints and elevated mortgage rates to continue influencing buyer demand.

The company expects to close between 79,000 and 84,000 homes in fiscal 2027 and generate consolidated revenue of approximately $30 billion to $32 billion.

#5568. Inside Legacy Hills’ Strategy for Reaching a Broad Range of Buyers

Developed by Centurion American, the Legacy Hills master-planned community (MPC) spans over 3,000 acres in Celina, Texas, and is planned for up to 7,000 homes at full buildout. The community opened in April 2024 and includes a diverse mix of builders, lot sizes, and floor plans. Pricing generally ranges from the $300,000s into the mid-$500,000s.

Importantly, Legacy Hills is not relying on a single buyer profile. Its product strategy creates multiple entry points into the community, with housing choices that can appeal to buyers at different price points and stages of life.

That product diversity is paired with a layered amenity program. Plans call for seven amenity centers throughout Legacy Hills, along with a 27-acre sports park and a 3-mile walking and biking trail. The planned 1876 Country Club adds a destination component with an 18-hole championship golf course, clubhouse, driving range, putting green, and short game facilities.

For families moving to Legacy Hills, children in the broader community attend Celina ISD, while future school sites are planned within the development. The community also broadens its reach further through Del Webb’s dedicated 55+ neighborhood, which adds to Legacy Hills’ family-oriented offerings with age-targeted homes and amenities.

The strategy is unfolding against a strong demographic backdrop. Celina’s population and household base are projected to more than double between 2020 and 2029, expanding the potential pool of buyers around the community.

At the same time, the broader housing environment remains competitive. The Zonda Market Ranking for MPCs characterized Dallas as slightly underperforming per August data, yet Legacy Hills stood out. In the Q2 2026 Master Plan Outlook report, the MPC recorded the largest year-over-year percentage increase in last 12-month sales among qualifying MPCs with at least 200 sales in the previous 12 months.

Legacy Hills illustrates the value of creating several paths into a large-scale community rather than building around a narrow customer profile. Differentiated housing, offerings for multiple life stages, and amenities ranging from everyday recreation to destination experiences give the development multiple ways to appeal to buyers.

#5566. 8 Resilience Moves Builders Can Make Before Extreme Weather Hits

When extreme weather hits, small construction details can make a big difference in how well a home performs.

According to Fred Malik of the Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety (IBHS), research continually points to roofs, openings, and structural connections as potential failure points. Damage in these areas can allow wind and water into a home and trigger larger, cascading losses.

For builders, stronger construction can also help reduce disruption for homeowners, limit warranty-related costs, and protect a company’s reputation for delivering durable homes.

“Resilient, durable buildings are usually the result of making several intentional decisions,” Malik says.

Here are eight steps builders can take to improve resilience ahead of severe weather:

Rather than approaching roofing as a collection of individual products, Malik recommends treating the entire roof as one interconnected system. The goal is to keep the roof intact and prevent an initial failure from creating a pathway for additional wind or water damage.

A sealed roof deck creates an additional layer of protection beneath the primary roof covering. If shingles or other roofing materials are damaged or blown off during severe weather, this secondary layer can help limit water intrusion into the home.

Small details can have an outsized impact on performance. Builders should carefully install and inspect flashing at roof edges, roof-to-wall transitions, vents, chimneys, and other penetrations. These areas can become pathways for water if they aren’t properly protected.

Windows, entry doors, and other openings need to withstand both wind pressure and wind-driven rain. Following manufacturer installation instructions and properly installing flashing are critical to maintaining the home’s building envelope.

Garage doors represent a large opening in the building envelope and need to withstand pressures generated by high winds. Malik notes that this is important even in inland markets, where tornadoes can cause significant structural damage.

In areas exposed to more severe winds, builders should consider a professionally designed continuous load path connecting the roof to the walls and ultimately the foundation. Strong connections throughout the structure help transfer wind forces safely through the building instead of allowing individual components to fail.

In flood-prone areas, elevate or otherwise protect mechanical, electrical, and utility equipment. Keeping critical systems above anticipated flood levels can reduce damage and make it easier for homeowners to return to their homes after an event.

Programs such as IBHS’ FORTIFIED standards provide builders with a framework for putting resilience measures into practice. FORTIFIED goes beyond minimum code requirements with an emphasis on keeping the roof on, keeping water out, and tying the structure together.

The program also requires third-party documentation of critical resilience measures, including construction details that may no longer be visible once finishes and other materials are installed.

Overall, resilience isn’t dependent on a single product or construction technique. It’s the cumulative result of getting multiple details right, Malik says.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5561. Binance Withdrawals Top FTX Levels in November, but Crypto Liquidity Defies Panic

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Binance withdrawals surged into the billions after a record-breaking $6.3 billion hack, bringing back memories of FTX’s November 2022 collapse. Yet the world’s largest crypto exchange is showing a resilience that could barricade the industry from its darkest chapter.

Binance processed $4.65 billion in withdrawals and $1.01 billion in deposits during the first nine and a half hours after reopening services on November 1, resulting in $3.64 billion in net outflows. According to its October 28 Proof of Reserves data, the exchange held $171 billion in total assets, so the withdrawal wave accounted for just 2.1% of its reported holdings.

Binance withdrawals are BACK!BTC, ETH, BNB, XRP, DOGE, USDT, USDC and more are being re-enabled across supported networks.Binance also says 95% of the stolen assets have already been replaced.Bears were screaming FTX 2.0, desperately hoping for another collapse.

This puts the outflows in perspective: despite the initial rush following the $6.3 billion hack, Binance retained assets worth 47 times the net amount withdrawn. The exchange said withdrawals had begun stabilizing, while deposits remained substantial.

The figures initially look alarming, especially against the backdrop of FTX. The failed exchange suffered $6 billion in net withdrawals over 72 hours before suspending customer withdrawals in November 2022.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

“98% choose to stay. Trust isn’t earned by what you say in good times. It’s earned by what you do in hard times.” – Changpeng Zhao, Binance Founder

Binance has previously said that it had set aside more than $6.34 billion to cover the incident, including $5 billion in the affected token assets. It also reported that partners had frozen approximately $3 billion linked to the attack.

So how does this compare to FTX? This current crisis is fundamentally different from FTX’s collapse. FTX’s withdrawal run exposed a liquidity shortfall tied to customer funds and its relationship with Alameda Research. Binance, by contrast, says it will cover the stolen assets rather than pass the losses to users.

Bitcoin’s reaction offers one of the clearest signs of crypto’s resilience compared with the FTX collapse. Following the $6.3 billion Binance hack, BTC briefly slipped toward $76,700 but held above the closely watched $75,000 support level before recovering toward $79,000. The contrast with November 2022 is stark. Bitcoin fell nearly 10% on November 8 as FTX’s withdrawal crisis intensified, then plunged another 14.4% on November 9 to close near $15,877, after briefly hitting $15,632.

While Binance’s hack triggered billions in withdrawals and market-wide liquidations, Bitcoin has so far avoided the cascading selloff that followed FTX’s implosion. Its ability to defend $75,000 suggests investors are treating the incident as a major exchange security failure rather than evidence of a systemic liquidity crisis across crypto.

Binance has already faced a major financial and regulatory reckoning. In November 2023, the exchange agreed to pay more than $4 billion to resolve U.S. investigations into anti-money laundering and sanctions violations. Founder Changpeng Zhao also pleaded guilty to failing to maintain an effective anti-money laundering program. He resigned as CEO and paid a separate $50 million fine.

Despite that enormous settlement, Binance continued operating as the world’s largest crypto exchange. The latest hack now presents another test of its financial strength, operational resilience, and ability to maintain customer confidence.

Crypto markets have still felt the shock. Bitcoin and Ethereum fell following the breach, while spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded huge outflows and leveraged positions faced heavy liquidations. However, both major cryptocurrencies partly recovered after hitting lows.

Now, can Binance withdrawals continue to ease? The exchange publishes updated Proof of Reserves data and completes its security review. The comparison with FTX shows the scale of investor concern, but not necessarily the same outcome. Binance has absorbed a major hack, committed to covering customer losses, and resumed withdrawals after billions left the platform.

November has brought back memories of 2022. Binance’s response shows crypto’s largest exchange is determined to keep this crisis from becoming another industry-wide collapse.

#5560. The hidden threat in Anthropic’s prospectus: diseconomies of scale

GUEST COLUMN by Jason Bloomberg

As potentially the largest IPO in history, Anthropic PBC is breaking new ground. Its prospectus lists 88 risk factors covering 93 pages alone. From artificial intelligence posing an existential threat to humanity to the possibility AI will blackmail people, the company lists a litany of risks that should make any potential Anthropic investor wary.

One potentially company-sinking risk factor, however, does not explicitly appear in the prospectus: diseconomies of scale.

Diseconomies of scale occur when a company’s average cost of producing each unit of output increases as the company grows.

You would think that given the time and effort that Anthropic devoted to ensuring its list of risk factors was complete that they would have included this one. There is a reason, however, that they missed it, despite the fact that diseconomies of scale is the elephant in the room.

We’ve been down this road before with cloud computing. The fundamental economic driver of the hyperscaler clouds was economies of scale: the larger they became, the lower their cost of each unit of output, leading to massive growth and profitability over time.

Since the AI boom requires massive data center buildouts just as cloud computing does, it might be reasonable to assume that AI will experience the same economic benefits of massive growth that cloud computing enjoyed.

This assumption, however, is likely to be false. To understand why, we must take a look at how the software and cloud businesses scale – and why AI is so different.

Throughout the history of enterprise computing, software has benefited from its negligible marginal cost.

With physical goods, from automobiles to chicken nuggets, every unit has a raw materials and production cost. The more widgets you make, the more those costs add up.

Software is fundamentally different. Once a vendor has spent the money to build an application, it can sell that application to as many customers as it can find, where the cost of delivering additional copies of that application is negligible compared to the original cost of developing it.

This negligible marginal cost enables software vendors to become immensely profitable as their business scales.

Computer hardware, in contrast, is nothing more than more widgets – the more you deploy, the greater your materials and production costs.

Cloud computing combines both software and hardware in its offerings. The software may have negligible marginal cost, but each cloud provider must shell out money for each physical server.

To address this cost challenge, cloud providers take advantage of economies of scale.

The hyperscalers built their clouds by deploying massive numbers of commodity servers. As each firm expanded its business, the cost of each unit of output – say, the cost of providing a server instance or a unit of cloud storage – decreased.

As a result, the cost of servers went down as they scaled, and the cloud computing firms became increasingly profitable as they grew, despite the fact that their business models depended on hardware as well as software.

Back to Anthropic and the rest of the frontier large language model providers: Ostensibly, AI is just a type of software, and Anthropic is running its software in hyperscaled data centers that are essentially clouds. This underlying assumption is implicit in the company’s prospectus.

This assumption, however, is flawed. Frontier model vendors require graphics processing units and other premium, expensive hardware from day one – and their specialized processor requirements continue to accelerate as they rapidly innovate their software.

This advancing specialized processor requirement didn’t impact the rise of the cloud. True, each cloud provider eventually added various specialized hardware instance types as they grew, but those instances didn’t change the fundamental economics of the cloud business.

Anthropic, in contrast, doesn’t have the luxury of deploying commodity hardware to achieve economies of scale. Instead, it must build out expensive servers that only get more expensive as LLMs’ processor requirements continue to advance.

There are also diseconomies of scaling the human side of the AI boom that contrast with the growth of the cloud.

The hyperscalers certainly require an experienced workforce with deep expertise to deploy their clouds and keep them running. But as they grew, they were able to leverage such personnel more efficiently. An admin who managed a thousand physical servers could easily manage 10,000 or a million as the underlying cloud platforms matured.

Unlike the cloud providers, however, Anthropic and the other frontier model vendors must continually scale up the expertise of their teams. New LLMs aren’t simply scaled-out versions of older ones. Each one requires new expertise from expert humans.

Anthropic is battling its competitors to innovate quickly and roll out increasingly powerful models on unprecedented timeframes. As a result, frontier LLM vendor teams experience diseconomies of scale that the hyperscalers never had to face.

Anthropic and the rest of the frontier LLM vendors suffer from a fundamentally novel economic reality, because they must continue to increase their hardware capabilities while upskilling their workforce so they can competitively innovate their software.

They can’t simply run increasingly powerful models on commodity hardware – or even the same hardware they ran the previous generation model on. They must increase their investments in hardware at a pace that keeps up with the pace of software innovation.

The end result is a diseconomy of scale the technology industry has never seen before. We are so used to the negligible marginal cost of software and the massive economies of scale of the cloud, that we are simply unprepared for the diseconomies of scale that frontier LLM vendors like Anthropic must negotiate.

Even though the frontier model marketplace is still quite new, we’re already seeing the impact of its inherent diseconomies of scale as token costs become an increasingly significant expense for consumers of AI.

As LLMs become more powerful and the hardware they require becomes an increasingly expensive bottleneck, it’s just a matter of time until token costs become prohibitively high for a range of AI-based applications.

Anthropic and the other LLM model vendors can try to respond by increasing the efficiency of their more powerful LLMs or rolling out less powerful, and thus less expensive models – assuming their customers buy into these moves.

We may also eventually reach a plateau where the models are sufficiently powerful and the hardware is sufficiently performant, thus enabling more familiar economies of scale to take over. However, no such plateau is in sight.

The question potential Anthropic investors must ask, therefore, is whether the company’s leadership position in the LLM market is a strength or a weakness? Just how far can it innovate and grow before its offerings are too expensive? And what does it do then?

#5559. Mortgage Rates Dip as AI Jitters Boost Bonds Ahead of Fed Decision, GDP Data

In A Nutshell: Rates have mellowed a bit coming into a big week with a Fed meeting and the first read of Q3 GDP data.

Last Week’s Highlights: Oil prices continued to increase last week, but rates came down, as doubts about the AI narrative battered stocks, sending money into the bond market. On the housing front, the increase in mortgage rates has sent builder confidence down to its lowest level in 14 years. Permits for single-family homes also fell to a multiyear low.

Upcoming Attractions: The biggest event of the week is the Fed decision and press conference Wednesday afternoon. The committee is not scheduled to update its forecast (the “dot plot”) this time. Markets believe the Fed will hold and then hike on December 9th for an every-other-meeting hike cadence, so the attention will be on clues for the next meeting rather than the outcome of this one. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh will hold a press conference but is likely to stick to his usual practice of not foreshadowing upcoming decisions. Fed watchers may get more color out of SF Fed President Daly and St. Louis Fed President Musalem’s remarks on Friday.

Apart from the Fed, there are also a couple of important data releases this week. The first look at Q3 GDP is coming on Thursday morning. Part of the thesis for rates increasing so much these last few months is a belief that the economy is growing faster. At one point, estimates had Q3 GDP growing as fast as a 5% annual rate. Forecasters are expecting this advance estimate to land around 3.2%, which would be a meaningful pick-up from 2.2% in Q2. And finally, the September durable goods report will be released on Tuesday with forecasters expecting a solid reading of 2.0% month-over-month growth. This report tracks new orders, shipments, and inventories of long-lasting manufactured products, which is a signal of how confident businesses and consumers are about the future.

#5557. Tax-Assessed Value vs. Market Value: What’s the Difference?

Home prices aren’t set in stone. A property’s value can shift depending on who’s doing the calculation—and why. That’s why you’ll often hear two different numbers thrown around during a home sale: assessed value and market value.

So what’s the difference between tax-assessed value versus market value? And how should buyers and sellers use each when negotiating a home sale?

The technical definition of market value is "the most probable price that a given property will bring in an open market transaction," says Casey Fleming, a former real estate appraiser and author of “The Loan Guide: How To Get the Best Possible Mortgage.”

Put simply, “It’s the price that a buyer is willing to pay for a home, and that a seller is willing to accept.”

Real estate agents are trained to pinpoint a home's value in the real estate market, which is done by looking at a variety of factors, including the following:

External characteristics like curb appeal, exterior condition of the home, lot size, home style, and availability of public utilities.

Internal characteristics like the size and number of rooms, construction and appliance quality and condition, heating systems, and energy efficiency.

Comps, or comparable homes in the same area that have sold recently.

Supply and demand, or the number of buyers and the number of sellers in your area.

Location and desirability of the neighborhood.

A home's market value is often a good starting point for determining all kinds of concerns that homebuyers might have.

For one, listing agents use this value to help sellers come up with a fair asking price for their home. And, since buyers shouldn't just trust what sellers say their place is worth, their own agents can also determine the home's approximate value and come up with a different price that they think their clients should offer.

No number is right or wrong. The ultimate deciding factor is what price a buyer and seller determine they are willing to shake hands on to close the deal.

Assessed value is calculated by your local government—usually a county tax assessor—to determine your property tax liability.

To assess a home’s taxable value, assessors consider the following:

Recent sales of similar homes in the area.

The home’s condition and any recent improvements.

Potential income the property could generate (e.g., from rentals).

Replacement cost in case of damage (e.g., from fire or natural disaster).

Once this value is established, the assessor may subtract any tax exemptions (like a homestead exemption) and multiply the remaining amount by the local assessment ratio—a uniform percentage that each tax jurisdiction sets (typically 80% to 90%), to arrive at the taxable value of your property.

For example: If your home has a market value of $500,000 and your local assessment ratio is 80%, your taxable value would be $400,000. That number is then used to calculate your annual property tax bill.

To determine your home's assessed value, you can contacting your local tax assessor or use the Realtor.com® property tax tool, which allows homeowners to compare their assessed value to similar homes. It even pulls comparable properties that homeowners can use as evidence if they choose to appeal their property taxes.

Some states, like Oregon, prohibit the assessment from being increased by more than 3% a year, “even if the market value goes up more,” says Nathan Miller, founder of Rentec Direct, a software company that educates property managers and landlords.

That means your home’s taxable value might lag behind its market value, especially in hot real estate markets.

Don't be upset as a property owner if your assessment is calculated at a lower amount than you'd figured. It doesn't mean your property value is less. In fact, this could be great news for you.

Assessed value is used mostly for property tax purposes. A lower assessment means a lower tax bill—that's all. Homebuyers and home sellers, on the other hand, look more to marketplace value than to property tax data.

However, assessed value can come up when you buy or sell a home, because this number, unlike the loosey-goosey market value, is public knowledge contained in property records. So, rising assessed values bode well when home sellers try to justify their sales price to a buyer: “Hey, the assessed value is $310,000, and I’m only asking $320,000.”

Likewise, buyers can use assessed value to justify a lower price: "Hey, the assessed value is $260,000, and you're asking for $300,000. What gives?"

However, negotiating based on assessed value is highly unlikely in today's inventory-constrained market. Even though home prices have cooled after record appreciation in the early 2020s, there is still steep competition for homes, pushing the market value well out of range of assessed values.

At the end of the day, the price of a home is the amount at which a seller is willing to sell, and a buyer is ready to buy. The only number that matters is the price that a buyer and a seller agree on.

Lisa Kaplan Gordon is an award-winning writer who's covered real estate and home improvement for realtor.com, Yahoo, AOL, and many others.

#5556. The Holiday Season Is the Best Time For Homebuyers to Score a Deal in These 7 U.S. Metros

Early November is the best time for homebuyers to score a bargain in three U.S. metro areas: Milwaukee, Riverside, CA and Tampa, FL.

In Detroit and three Florida metros–Fort Lauderdale, Miami and West Palm Beach–house hunters may benefit from holding out a little longer. Mid-December is typically the best time of year to get a deal in those places.

This is according to a Home Economics and Redfin analysis of housing market data; the analysis was originally completed in April. The analysis identifies the time of year when discounts off a home’s original asking price–through price drops and/or negotiations between buyer and seller–typically approach their seasonal peak.

Nationwide, discounts tend to peak in early fall before plateauing or shrinking as winter approaches. But housing is local, and in these seven metros, peak discounts typically arrive later. Homebuying slows as the holidays approach, leaving sellers with fewer potential buyers–giving the buyers who remain more room to negotiate. And some late-year listings have been sitting for months, making sellers more motivated to strike a deal before the end of the year.

“There’s a tradeoff to shopping for a home late in the year: Buyers may have fewer fresh listings to choose from, but they also face less competition, and many sellers are ready to make a deal,” said Redfin Senior Economist Asad Khan. “A seller who has been waiting months for an offer may be more willing to negotiate on price or other costs than they were in the spring. Buyers shouldn’t purchase a home just because the calendar says it’s a good time for deals, but those who find the right home may have room to negotiate.”

In Florida, the best deals for buyers typically arrive in November or December, partly due to weather. South Florida’s biggest wave of buyers–retirees and seasonal residents–often show up after the new year, when the weather is sunny and comfortable in Florida but cold in the Northeast.

“Local buyers have a good shot at getting a deal in November, mainly because it’s just before the snowbirds arrive,” said Todd Edwards, a Redfin Premier agent in Tampa. “House hunters have a window of opportunity to negotiate on listings that have been lingering on the market since summer: Sellers want to close a deal before the new year, and there’s often not much competition from out-of-towners yet.”

Hurricane season, which runs through early fall, also keeps some house hunters away and leaves lingering listings ripe for discounts once it passes. Additionally, Florida’s high concentration of luxury homes tend to sell below asking price, especially late in the year when sellers are eager to get those properties off their books.

The story is a bit different in Milwaukee and Detroit. Those northern metros have a fairly short selling season: Cold-weather markets compress the window for touring and closing on homes; sellers keep at it later into fall, trying to close a deal before the depth of winter hits and buyers hibernate.

That delays the usual seasonal slowdown until November in Milwaukee and December in Detroit, later than in most of the country.

The November and December discount windows in Milwaukee, Riverside, Detroit and much of Florida aren’t a one-time event; they show up as a recurring pattern each year, regardless of whether the broader market favors buyers or sellers.

But the seasonal advantage could be particularly useful to buyers this year. The U.S. housing market is already firmly tilted toward buyers, with 63% more sellers than buyers—the biggest imbalance in Redfin records dating back to 2013. A jump in listings coupled with sluggish homebuying demand has given house hunters in many parts of the country more options and more negotiating power. Miami is one of the strongest buyer’s markets in the nation, with more than twice as many sellers as buyers. Tampa, West Palm Beach, Fort Lauderdale, Riverside and Detroit are also buyer’s markets.

Milwaukee is one of just five seller’s markets in the country. With more buyers than sellers in Milwaukee, deals aren’t commonplace–so buyers there may want to pay extra attention to seasonal patterns.

The best time to buy a home is more complex than the week when buyers are most likely to score a discount.

There’s typically a tradeoff between selection and savings. New listings generally peak months before the best deals arrive. For instance, Milwaukee typically has the most new listings in mid-May and the most fresh inventory in mid-July,then its best deals arrive in early November. Detroit’s new listings typically peak in early August and fresh inventory in early September, months before its mid-December dealmaking sweet spot.

That means buyers who wait until November or December may have fewer homes to choose from. But those who prioritize price—and are flexible about their timing—may find sellers more receptive to negotiations. Ultimately, buyers should balance price, selection and their own circumstances.

Please note that this table includes 3 key moments for buyers; it’s important for buyers to balance what’s most important for them–choice or price

To identify the best time to buy, this Home Economics and Redfin analysis focuses on the seasonal indexes for three metrics: new listings, fresh inventory, and the average discount.

#5555. As Anthropic finally files for its IPO, rising risks aren’t slowing the AI buildout – yet

THIS WEEK IN ENTERPRISE by Robert Hof

The other artificial intelligence shoe dropped this week, as Anthropic filed for what surely will be the second blockbuster AI initial public offering of stock this year.

Nearly 70,000 words in the filing list a ton of risks, but in short, it’s making unimaginably huge bets on buying computing power, it’s uncertain on how long customers will keep spending on AI in the face of dubious returns — and of course there’s the really-not-unusual “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.” And as Jason Bloomberg writes, the unmentioned risk is that AI as of today doesn’t have the economies of scale that made software so lucrative.

But it’s hard to imagine it won’t be crazily successful if and when it happens before Thanksgiving. They’ll join the 70% of Nvidia employees who are millionaires. Shed another tear for anyone looking for affordable housing in the Bay Area — we’re not building our way out of this, no matter what YIMBY folks hope.

One interesting wrinkle: SpaceXAI, the other AI IPO earlier this year, will be hoping Anthropic’s offering is successful, since it’s supplying a large chunk of that compute. Same with other AI partner/rivals such as Google and Microsoft.

And Anthropic isn’t alone in amassing cash to continue buying and building more AI infrastructure. Meta this week said it will issue $95 billion in nonvoting stock to build even more. Few, least of all universal backstop Nvidia, seem to think the AI and data center backlash will dent this investment. But that doesn’t mean everyone will win. As SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said this week, self-servingly but perhaps not wrongly (Gartner agrees), a lot of AI neoclouds are going to go belly-up.

Investor worry extends to the big cloud providers too. Despite a continued boom in its cloud business, Google parent Alphabet saw its stock swoon more than 12% Thursday, vaporizing more than $500 billion in market value as it reported a slow quarter for search and ads — perhaps because AI chatbots are siphoning off people’s attention. Microsoft fared better thanks to its resilient application layer on which it can apply AI. But despite strong cloud revenue growth, Amazon stock fell on concerns it could be spending too much on infrastructure. All that came to a head Friday, when the Nasdaq tanked, down almost 3%.

Seems like investors are just generally skittish. On a tear this year until now, Intel stock plunged almost 30% after its Thursday earnings report, on concerns the PC business is slowing. Fortinet also fell more than 20% following its report that included a slightly lower outlook.

For some wider perspective on the AI buildout and what’s needed to make it pay off, check out Dave Vellante’s Breaking Analysis, a late addition here Saturday, a conversation with analyst Crawford Del Prete.

Don’t relax yet. Next week there’s another earningspalooza, including Apple, AMD, Supermicro, Qualcomm, Arm and Palantir.

So an apparent Chinese spy for some time has been hanging around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who evidently didn’t know she was more than a customer executive. Lordy. The New York Times laid out the bones of the U.S. government’s concern, but read it carefully and it sure seems like there are some missing dots throughout. Perhaps this kind of espionage is more common than we know where there’s a nexus of big money and geopolitics, but this may not be the last we hear of it, even if the Trump administration is shrugging.

Oh, and there’s an election next week that might change things… in unpredictable, not necessarily great ways for the economy. Fasten those seatbelts. And vote (but not for the wrong people, thanks).

#5554. Fed Holds Rates Steady, But Sets Up a December Hike

Takeaway: The Fed skipped hiking rates at today’s meeting, as expected. But they set up a hike at the December 9th meeting.

The Fed’s main message: Future hikes may be necessary because the economy is strong and inflation is too high. But they’re also patient, willing to skip hiking at some meetings in the interest of waiting for more data.

Chairman Warsh also announced a big change for Fed meetings starting next year, setting aside one meeting for big picture deliberation.

#5553. California Candidates for Governor Offer Different Visions on Housing

The midterm elections are now just hours away, and California voters prepare to head to the polls to elect their next governor, with the state's housing shortage taking center stage.

The contest is among the highest-profile of the 36 gubernatorial races taking place across the U.S. this cycle.

Former Secretary of Health and Human Services Xavier Becerra, a Democrat, and Fox News contributor Steve Hilton, a Republican, are the front-runners vying to replace termed-out California Gov. Gavin Newsom.

The Golden State's 41st governor will inherit an acute housing affordability crisis alongside a roster of state-specific challenges: a controversial billionaire tax proposal, persistent homelessness, an insurance market undermined by wildfire risk, and escalating policy battles surrounding artificial intelligence.

Everyday Californians' purchasing power continues to be severely squeezed by scarce buildable land, restrictive zoning rules, and slow permitting pace holding back new construction, exacerbated by high inflation and mortgage rates exceeding 7%.

On this year's Realtor.com® State-by-State Housing Report Card, part of the Let America Build campaign, California was among six states to earn an F grade due to its disastrous housing affordability score.

Local voter frustration is evident: A new survey by the Public Policy Institute of California found that roughly 6 out of 10 participants say the state is headed in the wrong direction.

Becerra, 68, is heavily favored to win the governor's seat in the largely Democratic state, leading his GOP opponent by 27 points in the latest UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll.

If elected governor, Becerra pledges to declare a housing-shortage state of emergency on his first day in office and appoint senior staff across state agencies to tackle the crisis.

His agenda also includes implementing "shot clocks" to clearly communicate permit wait times to developers, overhauling and lowering impact fees statewide, standardizing and streamlining reviews for modular construction, and simplifying affordable housing financing.

"California should be a place where the carpenter who builds a home can afford to buy one," he said in a speech this summer.

According to a new Realtor.com analysis of the latest available housing and American Community Survey data, the typical household in California earns 49% less than the income needed to finance a median-priced home—a shortfall of $98,292—making it the second-most unaffordable state in the nation behind Montana.

Becerra has voiced support for building "missing-middle" multifamily housing, especially near transit hubs, and expanding first-time homebuyer down payment assistance programs to put homeownership within reach of more renters.

On the issue of homelessness and homeless encampments, which has become a lightning rod for political candidates in California this election cycle, Becerra is laser-focused on prevention.

At an event in the East Bay last week, Becerra argued that keeping at-risk people housed after a medical emergency or a sudden job loss is far less costly to the state than rehousing them from the street, reported ABC 7 News (KGO).

"We have to do everything we can to prevent them from falling into homelessness," Becerra said.

His strategy includes bolstering tenant protections, expanding funding to organizations that have proven effective in addressing the homelessness crisis, and holding accountable those that have failed to act.

Hilton, 57, the Donald Trump–endorsed GOP hopeful for governor, has been aggressively pushing for the clearing of homeless encampments, vowing to rid the state of every single one by Dec. 31, 2027.

Like his Democratic rival, Hilton has highlighted the need to cut through red tape constraining residential construction. However, his approach hinges on capping fees, permits, and regulation costs at $50,000 per new home to make it cheaper for developers to build.

"We have to get rid of the regulations that make it two or three times as expensive to build the exact same home in California as in neighboring states," said Hilton during a televised debate in May.

His housing platform also includes using over a million vacant lots to build starter homes and creating 10 new municipalities across California to expand housing supply instead of trying to shoehorn multifamily developments into single-family communities.

“We have to stop trying to force housing into suburban neighborhoods where people don't want it," he proclaimed during the debate.

Despite their contrasting platforms, Hilton and Becerra are united in their fierce opposition to the California Billionaire Tax, officially known as Proposition 40, which Newsom had unsuccessfully tried to keep off the ballot.

Championed by a coalition of labor unions, the measure would impose a one-time tax of up to 5% on the worldwide assets of more than 200 Californians with a net worth of at least $1 billion who resided in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026.

Opponents of the initiative across the political spectrum have warned that it will accelerate an exodus of high net worth residents and tech innovators from California, diminishing the state's tax base.

Speaking on "The Steve Hilton Show" in January, Hilton criticized Proposition 40 as the epitome of what he called the "stupidity and the failure of 16 years of one-party rule" in California that, if adopted, will "drive business out of state."

For his part, Becerra dismissed the proposal as a "sketchy policy" and instead threw his support behind an alternative measure that would extend temporary tax rate increases on the ultrawealthy to reliably fund healthcare and public schools.

Voting has been underway in California since early October, and hundreds of thousands of mail-in ballots have been processed ahead of Nov. 3.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.
