#5552. Krafton-backed Ludo Robotics releases robot intelligence model designed around human intent

Ludo Robotics Inc., a subsidiary of major South Korean video game publisher Krafton Inc., today debuted Ludi 0.2, a robotics artificial intelligence system built to understand people and interact with them in the physical world.

Headquartered in Palo Alto, Ludo spun out of Krafton, a company that primarily publishes video games and is best known for the ultra-popular “PUBG: Battlegrounds.” Ludo also has a research and development lab in Seoul where it combines the efforts of researchers and engineers across robotics, machine learning and AI.

Krafton Chief Executive CH Kim also helms Ludo as CEO, with Krafton’s Chief AI Officer Kangwook Lee serving as its chief technology officer.

Why did a video game company form and back an AI robotics company? Krafton said it believes AI makes games more responsive and replayable. It also has strong roots in simulation, interaction and real-time systems, which have immediate applications in the bridge between the digital and physical, where the interaction between humans and robots lives.

“Robots are becoming increasingly capable of performing physical tasks, but understanding and responding to people remains a major challenge,” said Lee. “Ludi 0.2 represents another step toward our goal of bringing conversation, reasoning and physical action together so robots can better understand human intent, respond to feedback and adapt as situations change.”

The company introduced the first version of Ludi 0.1 in August 2026. It combines a vision-language model for reasoning and dialogue with specialized navigation and manipulation capabilities. Today’s next-generation model has advanced its capabilities, forming more natural human-robot interaction, including social intelligence, memory and reasoning, tool coordination, gesture interpretation, and physical movement.

The company said it’s working toward a final version of Ludi that will integrate perception, dialogue and physical action.

The objective is to integrate communication, reasoning and physical action into one “brain.” The model would watch what’s happening, listen to commands and speech, interpret those commands alongside human gestures and physical movements and reason about the environment. This would happen in real time, coordinating similarly to how another human decides on actions based on another person’s actions in their workspace.

This is the “Holy Grail” of physical AI, where intelligent robots can perform actions not just in industrial environments and warehouses, but also retail and domestic spaces such as restaurants, living rooms and kitchens.

Krafton said much of its work includes proprietary foundation models and co-playable characters developed in collaboration with Nvidia Corp., AI teammates designed to understand players in real time. Ludo builds on this foundation to develop the same kind of intelligence into real-world robots.

Startups are bringing the physical world to robots so they can see objects and grab and move them with increasing capability. Interpreting human intent and responding to social cues from people around the robot, however, remains elusive. Simulation makes it easy for physical AI to prepare robots to work with objects and around humans, but it doesn’t always prepare them to model human behavior.

#5550. Extreme Networks wants the network to run AI, not just be run by it

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

At its recent AI Summit in Amsterdam, Extreme Networks Inc. shared early Agent ONE Coworker results and previewed Exchange zones, which put spare access points and switch compute to work as on-premises artificial intelligence infrastructure. Here’s what it means and what information technology pros should do about it.

Most of the conversation about AI and networking has flowed in one direction. AI comes in, examines the network and helps the network team run it better. That’s useful, but it treats the network as the patient, not as a resource.

At the summit, the company argued that there is a better way. The network should be managed by AI and serve as a place where AI runs, using data that most organizations currently throw away. This would let network teams stop being the people who merely keep the Wi-Fi up for the AI project and become the people who host it.

Extreme made two announcements. The first was a progress report on Extreme Agent ONE Coworker, the ambient AI agent built into Extreme Platform ONE. In its first month, Extreme says, customers saved about 1,000 hours of troubleshooting, 41% of Platform ONE customers used it for daily tasks, and users responded to 98% of critical “nudges,” the proactive alerts the agent raises after running its own pre-investigation. Engagement was roughly 10 times that of Extreme’s first-generation conversational assistant.

The second was a preview of Extreme Exchange zones, planned for the first half of 2027. A zone combines an Extreme Universal Compute Platform or a customer-owned server with spare capacity from Extreme access points and switches already installed at a site. AI applications from the Extreme Exchange marketplace run locally on open-weight models by default, with cloud inference used only when policy allows and logged every time. Agent ONE Operator mode, the autonomous tier, also arrives in the first half of 2027.

The first wave of AI in networking wasn’t a smashing success because it relied on a chatbot built on fragmented data. During his talk, Nabil Bukhari (pictured), Extreme’s chief technology officer and president of AI platforms, called it a design flaw. “Conversational AI requires the user to have the question and the context, and you will be surprised how difficult that is when it comes to technology domains,” he said.

In Extreme’s focus groups, many administrators asked a powerful AI assistant how many devices they had, even though the number was already on the dashboard. Coworker flips that. “We have moved to the world where instead of you prompting AI, AI prompts you,” Bukhari said.

The best evidence came from a customer. Kevin Rocha, chief information officer at Hill College, described a wireless outage in a building housing HR, finance and enrollment. “Agent ONE Coworker told me exactly where to look: One access point needed attention, and several more were due for firmware upgrades. We resolved the issue in about 20 minutes rather than an entire morning,” he said. Platform ONE, he added, “is like having two or three more network engineers on staff.”

That’s the value of AI for networking in most enterprises. It doesn’t replace the network team. It gives a small team the reach of a larger one. Bukhari also admitted that there is more work to be done. He explained that 58% of support cases opened by Agent ONE arrive with all the evidence support needs. “Fifty-eight is pretty good, but 58 is still 58 and not 100.”

Andrew Grill, the opening keynote speaker and author of “Digitally Curious,” discussed the stakes. “When a chatbot gets it wrong, you might have a bad paragraph. If an agent gets it wrong, you have a bad Tuesday,” he said. His test for any deployment: “If your agent does something wrong at 2 in the morning, whose phone rings?”

Extreme’s Operator demo is subject to guardrails. Each of the 268 tools can be configured to auto-authorize, ask first or never use. Four baseline rules apply to everything: do no harm to the network, never expose a credential, never act outside your role and never act in another tenant. Every task has a full audit trace.

An important design criterion is that governance reside within Extreme Exchange, not Platform ONE. “You can’t govern something from within,” Bukhari said. “That is how you get rogue agents.” If the system running the agent also controls its permissions, you don’t have a control plane. You have an honor system.

Networks generate dense, real-time telemetry on location, movement and behavior that far exceeds what operations needs, and cloud platforms drop most of it because moving it is expensive. Bukhari said the valuable uses tend to hit four walls: sovereignty, localization, survivability and economics.

The innovation is where the compute comes from. Higher-end access points have four to eight cores and typically use only one, so organizations already pay for and power idle compute hanging from their ceilings. In one healthcare demo, a fall-detection app that combined camera feeds, Wi-Fi location and paging to find the closest responder ran entirely on access points. A second demo used Seattle Seahawks game data to predict gate congestion and showed that some fans faced a seven- to eight-minute walk to the nearest pro shop.

“This is not a network management use case,” Bukhari said. “These use cases are impossible without that rich, real-time telemetry.” That’s the strategic point. The return goes to operations, facilities and fan experience, giving network leaders something they’ve rarely had: a revenue story.

Zones will ship in 2027, and the demo apps were built in collaboration with design partners. The model needs a real application catalog, so Extreme is pairing it with a free, invitation-only forward-deployed engineering program. Pricing will be consumption-based, measured in “agent actions.” As Grill noted, most organizations haven’t priced the cost of their tasks today, so they’ll struggle to judge value.

As expected, the most valuable insights came from the customer panel. Jonathan Monk, CIO of the Institute of Cancer Research in London, manages roughly 9 petabytes of data, but performance isn’t his primary reason for building sovereign AI. “When we ask people in our organization what’s the biggest thing that holds them back from using AI, it’s that I’m not sure if I’m allowed to,” he said.

Andrew Beynon, chief enterprise architect at Extreme partner ARO, linked that to shadow AI. The goal, he said, is “to make the journey for legitimate adoption of AI easier than the move to illegitimate adoption.” Monk called it building “paved roads.” The industry treats sovereignty as a compliance cost, but these customers see it as an adoption accelerator.

David O’Neill, director of IT operations at Liverpool Football Club, offered a balanced take on AI. “While AI is an answer, it’s not necessarily the answer.” Bukhari highlighted the next challenge: “Adoption is no longer the problem. It’s the optimization of adoption.” After AI-generated product specs ballooned to 200 pages, Extreme capped them at three pages.

Include the network team in the AI plan. If it isn’t involved, decisions about traffic, inference location and data residency will be made without the people who understand them.

Separate governance from execution. Check whether agent permissions, audit logs and the kill switch are outside the system the agent runs in.

Inventory the data your network discards. Identify the location and occupancy telemetry you already generate, and which business units would pay to use them.

Pressure-test the edge-compute math. Ask how workloads are prioritized during RF demand spikes and which model sizes realistically fit on an access point.

Price your tasks first. Without a baseline cost for today’s work, it’s impossible to evaluate consumption-based AI pricing.

Extreme can’t outspend its larger competitors, so it’s betting on speed and focus as a pure-play networking company. The Agent ONE numbers suggest that’s paying off on the operations side.

Exchange zones are the bolder idea. Turning installed access points and switches into a distributed, centrally governed inference fabric is more ambitious than anything I’ve seen from Extreme’s larger rivals. It’s also unproven, and 2027 is a long way off in AI time. As Beynon put it, “today’s knowledge has got an expiry date.”

The direction Extreme is headed is the right one. For 30 years, the network has been the most important infrastructure, yet nobody wanted to talk about it until it broke. AI makes the network the system that connects data, compute and people, and possibly the one that runs the AI, too. Network pros who see that early will have a much bigger role in where their organizations go next.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5549. Redfin Celebrates 250 Years of American History Through the Places We Call Home

From today, Redfin is celebrating America’s 250th anniversary by spotlighting the stories of iconic homes of America. Featured alongside millions of homes for sale or rent on Redfin.com, these historic properties offer a unique window into the people, pivotal moments and enduring spirit that have shaped America.

With immersive tours, detailed photography and stories of the people who lived within the walls, the franchise will bring the past into the present. Each property will also host a free in-person event, complemented by virtual experiences that make these remarkable stories accessible to people nationwide.

Each property will debut separately and remain on Redfin through the end of 2027.

“America’s story isn’t just written in history books. It’s written in the homes where people have dreamed, created, persevered and changed the course of our nation,” said Jonathan Mildenhall, Chief Marketing Officer of Rocket. “As we celebrate 250 years of American independence, Redfin Presents Iconic Homes of America is an invitation to rediscover the extraordinary stories behind these front doors, and to recognize that every home, in its own way, is part of the American story.”

Built around 1740, the Betsy Ross House offers a glimpse into the determination, ingenuity and entrepreneurial spirit of a working woman during America’s founding.

The Philadelphia home is associated with Betsy Ross, the upholsterer, entrepreneur and Revolutionary-era flag maker whose story became intertwined with the creation of the first American flag. While historians continue to debate parts of the familiar legend, records show Ross was an accomplished tradeswoman who made flags for the government for decades.

The home’s remarkable story extends beyond the Revolutionary era. When it faced demolition in the late 19th century, Americans from across the country came together to preserve it, contributing through 10-cent memberships. It was an early demonstration of the collective pride and community spirit that continue to give historic places their meaning.

Its Redfin listing-style page looks beyond the legend to explore Ross as a business owner, working mother and survivor who built an extraordinary life within two small, rented rooms.

Built between 1887 and 1892, Bishop’s Palace was designed by Nicholas J. Clayton, Galveston’s most influential architect, for lawyer and congressman Walter Gresham, his wife, Josephine, and their seven children. The home spans 52 rooms and 19,086 square feet. It became the residence of Bishop Byrne after the Catholic Church purchased it in 1923.

Each detail of the home was custom-chosen, from hand-carved woodwork throughout to a dining room ceiling mural painted by Josephine herself. At the heart of the home, an octagonal mahogany rotunda staircase rises beneath French stained glass, surrounded by finishes from Venice, Holland and North Africa.

The property also includes a few conversation pieces, among them Josephine’s china collection, the original bed, Walter’s desk and Bishop Byrne’s player piano. It sits in Galveston’s East End Historic District, a neighborhood of colorful historic homes and lush landscaping, with the Gulf only a few blocks south.

Today, Bishop’s Palace stands as a one-of-a-kind blend of elaborate craftsmanship, Texan influence and Gilded Age ambition.

Redfin will highlight iconic American homes through the end of 2027. Know a home with a story worth telling? Nominate it for inclusion in the creative franchise using this form. Tour the first properties and get an alert when each new home debuts using redfin.com/iconic-homes.

#5548. 6 insights from the GSA Women’s Leadership Initiative: AI semiconductor industry trends turn the chip race into a systems race

For decades, the semiconductor industry competed on one thing: the individual chip. One of the biggest AI semiconductor industry trends now under way is the shift toward treating chips as components of much larger systems. Performance, cost and reliability are now determined across the package, the rack and the supply chain, not inside a single die.

That shift moves the hardest problems upstream. Packaging, connectivity, yield, sourcing and verification used to come after design, but now they shape it from the first day. AI is shortening development cycles at the same time as it adds to the complexity engineers have to manage. The next phase will be defined by how well companies coordinate across that whole system.

“I think the AI system is our new chips,” said Letizia Giuliano, vice president of product management and marketing at Qualcomm Technologies Inc. “If we were optimizing everything for the silicon in the past, now these days we’re optimizing everything for the system.”

Giuliano and other industry experts spoke with theCUBE Research’s John Furrier and co-host Alison Kosik at the GSA Women’s Leadership Initiative event in Palo Alto, California. The interviews covered AI semiconductor industry trends, optical interconnects, advanced packaging, AI-driven yield learning, physical AI, strategic sourcing and AI-assisted chip design.

Here are six standout insights from the event:

Moving data between chips, memory and racks now limits AI performance more than raw compute, according to Giuliano. At 200 gigabits per second per lane, half of the signal budget goes just to getting out of the package. That is pushing optical interconnect from rack-to-rack links into the rack, the blade and the package itself, with copper and optics in use side by side. Qualcomm has just launched High Bandwidth Compute, a low-power way to attach compute to memory that is tuned for tokens per watt. Building such products at hyperscale volume means product engineering has to join design-for-test, manufacturing and reliability planning early, explained Sophie Wang, senior director of product engineering at Marvell Technology Inc.

The boundary of an AI system is shifting from the chip to the package, emphasized Nisha Ananthakrishnan, senior director of advanced packaging at Intel Corp. Intel uses its EMIB bridge technology to link chiplets and to scale packages from 3x to more than 10x form factors. Outsourced assembly and test providers are becoming system integrators, noted Patricia MacLeod, senior director of corporate communications and industry partnerships at Advanced Semiconductor Engineering Inc. She pointed to ASE’s VIPack platform, which supports technologies ranging from fan-out chip-on-substrate to co-packaged optics. Many of the chips AI depends on, such as power management chips and voltage regulators built at 12 to 28 nanometers, use mature nodes, added Tazrien Kamal, senior director of technology and innovation at GlobalFoundries Inc.

About 70% to 80% of the problems found when scaling up volume manufacturing could have been caught before tapeout, highlighted Preeti Prasher, chief operating officer of Stathera Inc. Using AI to analyze characterization, simulation and inline manufacturing data lets teams start new wafers before a bad lot reaches test. Adaptive testing also cuts test time. Lattice Semiconductor Corp. has released Lattice Prompt, its first AI design assistant, which turns a plain-language request into a field-programmable gate array design and recommends the best part for the form factor and cost, according to Iliana Chen, senior director of program management at Lattice. Demand from robotics and other markets has made volume Lattice’s biggest challenge, Chen noted.

Physical AI is much broader than humanoid robots and covers any autonomous system that senses its surroundings, reasons and acts in the physical world, explained Gina Longoria, VP of external communications at Arm Ltd. The market is in its first inning, and no single company can build the architecture, security and safety standards it needs on its own, she stressed. Firmware is becoming the layer that ties GPUs, CPUs, network cards and Compute Express Link devices into one fleet-scale system, shared Lakshmi Ramagiri, partner for firmware engineering at Microsoft Corp. Security has to move beyond secure boot to continuous trust while a system is running, and the Open Compute Project and DMTF are the standards bodies to watch, Ramagiri added.

Don’t miss the full interview on theCUBE.

Sourcing now goes well beyond negotiating prices and shapes product development, risk and customer experience, emphasized Alisa Wang, AVP of global planning and procurement at Credo Technology Group Holding Ltd. Because AI-driven demand can change within a year, suppliers have to be treated as strategic partners that receive product roadmaps early, she noted. Leading-edge logic capacity at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. Ltd. is the tightest constraint, followed by packaging, specialty materials and critical equipment. In response, Credo is qualifying second-source suppliers and spreading its manufacturing footprint across more regions. Stathera’s Prasher highlighted dual sourcing for key segments and using supplier feedback during new product introduction to develop lower-cost products together.

AI is moving from a productivity assistant to a built-in part of electronic design automation flows, explained Rimi Dasgupta, chief of staff for product management and markets at Synopsys Inc., and Vidya Neerkundar, director of product management at Siemens Digital Industries Software. Synopsys has seen verification closure on register-transfer-level designs accelerate as much as 50-fold and debug time drop by 40%, according to Dasgupta. Demand for workload-optimized custom silicon has also cut development cycles from 18 months to six to nine months. AI is probabilistic, but chips must be deterministic, so Synopsys pairs AI with multiphysics solvers from its Ansys acquisition and is working with OpenAI Group PBC on a dedicated GPT-Synopsys model. Multi-die design is the next big shift as chips hit reticle limits, Neerkundar noted.

#5547. Why Waiting for Rates to Fall Can Create Other Affordability Problems

Mortgage rates are giving homebuyers another reason to hesitate.

The average rate for a 30-year fixed mortgage reached well over 7% in October, its highest level in 13 months, according to Freddie Mac. That followed a climb from 5.98% in late February to 6.65% by Aug. 20, figures cited in a recent U.S. Bank housing-market analysis.

For a buyer, even a small rate change can alter the monthly payment considerably. Waiting for lower borrowing costs can therefore be a reasonable decision, particularly when today’s payment would leave little room for maintenance, insurance or other expenses.

However, a lower future rate does not guarantee a cheaper home purchase.

“If rates fall enough to bring more buyers back, the benefit can be partly absorbed by stronger competition,” says Jeremy Olsher, a real estate professional and Principal at Mizner Residential Group. “A buyer might secure a better rate but pay more for the property, face multiple offers or have less negotiating room.”

Additionally, lowering rates can be a sign of economic instability, including perhaps a significant response to mass unemployment and rampant inflation. While that might make homeownership more alluring, families could feel the strain in other ways, from job loss to rising grocery bills to big losses in their retirement portfolios.

Olsher recommends considering three factors before making lower rates the sole condition for buying.

Can the payment work today? Buyers should calculate the full monthly cost under current conditions, including principal, interest, property taxes, insurance, association fees and a realistic maintenance allowance. If that total is uncomfortable, the buyer may need to wait, reduce the price range or reconsider the type of property. The calculation should work without assuming that refinancing will become available later.

“Refinancing can be an option if rates eventually fall, but it should not be the reason someone accepts an unaffordable payment today,” Olsher says. “The purchase needs to stand on its own using the numbers the buyer can actually secure.”

How long does the buyer expect to stay? Transaction costs matter more when a buyer may move again within a few years. Closing costs, maintenance and future selling expenses can make a short ownership period difficult to justify, even if the mortgage payment appears manageable.

A buyer expecting to remain for several years has more time to spread those costs and absorb short-term changes in value. Someone with uncertain employment, family or relocation plans may benefit from the flexibility of renting.

Olsher says the right question is not simply whether ownership costs more than rent this month. Buyers should consider how long they expect to remain, what flexibility they need and how much cash the purchase would leave available afterward.

What does waiting cost? Delaying a purchase is not automatically costly. In some markets, renting may remain the more practical and affordable choice. Realtor.com®’s 2026 midyear forecast projected rents would decline 1.2% during the year, potentially benefiting renters in many areas.

Still, waiting can carry personal and financial costs. A household may need to renew a lease, pay moving or storage expenses, remain in an unsuitable space or postpone a relocation. The selection of available homes can also change before rates do.

“The cost of waiting is different for every buyer,” Olsher says. “For one person, another year of renting is perfectly sensible. For another, it means paying for a home that no longer fits their family while hoping the market delivers a better combination of rate, price and inventory.”

Trying to identify the perfect week to purchase gives one unpredictable number too much control over a long-term decision. Buyers can make a more grounded choice by comparing today’s full payment, the expected ownership period, available homes and the real cost of remaining where they are.

Buyers should commit when they are financially ready. If they find a home that fits their budget today, buying lets them lock in the house before prices climb further. If mortgage rates drop significantly in the future, they can refinance their loan to a lower rate without having to compete against a massive wave of new buyers.

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5546. Miami Cash4Keys Execs Accused of Stealing Vulnerable Senior’s Home in Brazen Scheme

A Florida man's $300,000 home was allegedly stolen in a real estate scheme dubbed “Operation Dirty Deed,” which investigators say involved fraudulent documents and the exploitation of the homeowner's dementia.

The case took a disturbing turn when the 71-year-old man, identified in court records as Thomas P. Hegarty, was allegedly kidnapped from his longtime Hollywood home and discarded at a "dilapidated rooming house" several miles away, according to the Broward County Property Appraiser's Office.

Now, two executives for Cash4Keys, a South Florida real estate investment company, each face six criminal charges in connection with the alleged plot. A notary and real estate agent also face charges in connection with the alleged scheme.

“His home was taken from him,” Hollywood Police Department Detective Theo Defreze said at a news conference last week. “He lost all of his possessions―belongings, cars. I mean, he lost everything."

Investigators allege that Brandon Lee Miguel and Jordy Luis Perez obtained Hegarty's signature on a power of attorney document and a warranty deed, which were then used to transfer ownership of the property to their company, Cash4Keys.

Monica Elizabeth Castelli, 56, a real estate agent with United Realty Group, is accused of kidnapping Hegarty, while Derek Enrique, 43, allegedly notarized the documents used in the transfer.

Hegarty’s property on Mayo Street was valued at approximately $300,000 but was allegedly transferred to the company for just $191,000.

Broward County property appraiser Marty Kiar said at the news conference that there is no evidence Hegarty received any of the money and that the suspects used the man's severe case of dementia to take advantage of him and take over his home.

The investigation was launched after Hegarty's family raised concerns about his declining health and became suspicious about the recent transfer of his home.

His sister-in-law, Peggy Hegarty, who was contacted by the rooming house where he had allegedly been taken, told CBS News that he believed he was signing paperwork to refinance his home, not sell it.

“It's shocking. Absolutely shocking," she said.

When she traveled from her home in Georgia to Florida after learning what had happened, she found Hegarty depressed, in shock, and not eating, according to the report. He is now living in an assisted-living facility in Jacksonville.

“Investigators allege that due to documented dementia and significant cognitive impairment, the victim was incapable of understanding the documents he was signing and appreciating their consequences,” the Broward County Property Appraiser's Office said in the news release.

After the alleged transfer, Miguel and Perez arranged for Castelli, of Margate, to remove Hegarty from his home, authorities said.

Castelli allegedly drove Hegarty to a “dilapidated rooming house” in Miami Gardens and left him there, according to investigators. Hegarty was distraught and crying, which then led to Castelli driving him to Memorial Regional Hospital in Hollywood.

Once Hegarty was gone from his house, Miguel and Perez allegedly went inside and removed his personal belongings, including three vehicles, according to the property appraiser's office.

Miguel and Perez each face six charges, including organized scheme to defraud $50,000 or more, grand theft exceeding $100,000, unlawful filing of false documents affecting real property, mortgage fraud, exploitation of an elderly person, and money laundering.

Castelli faces charges of kidnapping with intent to facilitate the commission of a felony and exploitation of an elderly person. Enrique faces one count of false or fraudulent acknowledgments.

Kiar said Cash4Keys still controls the property, but added that Hegarty's family has hired an attorney in an effort to get the home back.

Investigators believe the scheme could extend beyond Hegarty’s home, suspecting there may be additional victims and properties involved.

Realtor.com reached out to Cash4Keys South Florida for comment but did not receive an immediate response.

The case has also prompted warnings from local officials about the vulnerability of older homeowners to real estate fraud.

Kiar urged South Florida residents with elderly relatives to monitor their family members' finances and consider enrolling in the free Owner Alert program, which notifies property owners when a deed transaction occurs.

“It’s very upsetting, very sad, and what really bothers me is the person they picked on was about as vulnerable as they come and that really is what makes this case a case that’s very sad,” Kiar said. “I’m very glad that people have been arrested, and they will have their day in court.”

#5545. Hyperliquid Faces LIT Crypto Challenge as Wall Street Rejects Tokenization

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Hyperliquid is facing fresh competition from LIT as Wall Street pushes back against tokenized crypto stocks, raising questions about the future of onchain trading. Fifty publicly traded companies have now objected to having their shares tokenized through OKXICE, the joint venture between crypto exchange OKX and New York Stock Exchange parent Intercontinental Exchange.

The growing resistance comes as decentralized exchanges compete for traders, liquidity, and the major crypto market narrative. Hyperliquid remains a leading player, but LIT is attracting attention as Lighter expands its crypto trading ecosystem.

🚨BREAKING: 50 companies worth over $25 TRILLION now officially say "NO" to TOKENIZATION.Nvidia, Nike and Micron are among the latest to object to tokenized versions of their shares on OKXICE.That's up from 26 in just 4 days, with 12 added in the latest notice alone:… https://t.co/jmvXXrkJt5 pic.twitter.com/MtDHcrlLrR

Nvidia, Microsoft, Nike, Alphabet, JPMorgan Chase, and Goldman Sachs are among the companies opposing the OKXICE initiative. The venture initially planned to offer tokenized versions of 62 major US companies, allowing investors to trade blockchain-based representations of their shares.

However, objections have rapidly expanded. Companies are concerned about shareholder rights, market structure, liquidity, and potential confusion surrounding tokenized securities.

Nasdaq has also warned that poorly regulated tokenized markets could fragment liquidity and weaken price discovery. The exchange supports tokenization under a framework that preserves traditional investor protections.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Hyperliquid continues to dominate decentralized perpetual futures trading, but Lighter is building a competing ecosystem. LIT has gained attention through Lighter’s crypto trading activity, token buybacks, and plans to pursue US regulatory approval.

Data tracked by DefiLlama showed Lighter generating $4.93 million in protocol revenue over 30 days, alongside $793 million in total value locked. The protocol also bought back around $4.03 million worth of LIT during October, bringing recorded buybacks since January to $33.2 million.

Hyperliquid, meanwhile, continues to attract substantial trading activity. HYPE is trading at below $90, with a market cap approaching $21 billion. But token supply remains a concern. Hyperliquid Labs unstaked 3.75 million HYPE in October for an institutional over-the-counter transaction worth approximately $330 million at the time.

NEW: @HyperliquidX LABS ANNOUNCES 180K $HYPE TOKENS WILL BE UNSTAKED TODAY TO BE DISTRIBUTED TO TEAM MEMBERS ON NOVEMBER 6 pic.twitter.com/VnSN1U3AN2

The transaction created a potential supply overhang, although the OTC structure reduced immediate selling pressure on public exchanges.

The competition between Hyperliquid and Lighter reflects a larger question: which platforms can attract huge trading volume as crypto expands into new financial markets?

Wall Street’s resistance could also push developers to explore alternative blockchain infrastructure, and Bitcoin remains primarily associated with long-term value storage. Not only Bitcoin, but layer 2 networks are also working to expand their role in decentralized finance and programmable applications.

Bitcoin Hyper is one project pursuing that direction, combining Bitcoin-focused settlement with Solana Virtual Machine-compatible execution. #5544. Mortgage Rates Drop From September Highs as Midterms and Jobs Data Loom

In A Nutshell: Rates have fallen about 30–40 basis points since the peak at the end of September and there’s little reason to believe the volatility will slow down.

The Fed meeting last Wednesday was the highlight of the week, with the committee voting to hold rates steady as expected. There were two dissents, with one coming from a surprising source, Governor Lisa Cook, who is usually seen as someone who favors lower rates. The statement and press conference reiterated a desire to keep hiking, making a December hike more likely than not if the economic data comes in as expected.

The Fed has been highlighting elevated inflation and strong economic growth as its reason for hiking. And Q3 GDP, in fact, came in at a brisk 3.4% annual rate. Real business fixed investment spending grew at a 12.7% annual rate thanks to rapid growth in AI spending. And real consumption grew at a 3.8% annual rate as people spent out of savings and wealth increases rather than income growth. The question now is what happens to growth in Q4. Real-time data is pointing to a potential slowdown as consumers pull back.

It’s another big week with both the midterm election tomorrow and employment data arriving throughout the week. Democrats are expected to comfortably gain a majority in the House of Representatives with control of the Senate also favoring Democrats, but less certain. Expectations for government spending, which has been a factor for rates, could certainly change with a more divided government. But the near term economic impact might be felt most acutely as we near government funding and debt limit deadlines. The closest budget deadline is December 11, which might get pushed to Q1. And we’re likely to hit the debt limit again in Q1 at which point the Treasury will take “extraordinary measures” until we truly run out of options sometime before October 2027.

Since it’s the first week of the month, we’ll also get the typical employment reports, including job openings and turnover on Tuesday and the official jobs report on Friday. With the Fed squarely focused on inflation, the jobs report mostly serves as a check on whether the Fed needs to turn its attention back to recession risk, which would reduce the need for the rate hikes that markets have priced in. So far this year, the answer has been “no,” with the labor market on solid enough footing and that is not expected to change with this week’s data.

Finally, Fed officials are out of their blackout period following last week’s FOMC meeting. With Chairman Warsh typically reluctant to offer much forward guidance, markets have been relying more on surrogates to forecast the outcome of the next meeting. There are numerous speaking engagements on the calendar, including Cleveland Fed President Hammack and Dallas Fed President Logan on Thursday, and New York Fed President Williams on Friday. Forecasters will be looking for clues to support the “hike every other meeting” thesis.

Chen Zhao is the head of economics research, where she produces research on the housing market for public and internal audiences. Previously, she was an executive director leading housing finance and financial markets research at the JPMorgan Chase Institute. Prior to joining JPMCI, Chen was an economics consultant at Analysis Group, Inc., where she worked on financial litigation cases and led teams conducting health economics and outcomes research on behalf of pharmaceutical companies. While in graduate school, Chen was with the Center for Economic Studies and the Social Economic and Housing Statistics Division at the US Census Bureau, where she conducted applied microeconomics research using large scale restricted-access linked survey-administrative data. She started her career at the White House Council of Economic Advisers, where she focused on labor and health economics.

#5543. Hackers steal $6.3B from Binance in biggest-ever crypto heist

Hackers have stolen about $6.3 billion worth of digital assets from Binance, a major cryptocurrency exchange operator.

The heist is more than four times bigger than the previous largest crypto theft. TRM Labs Inc., a venture-backed blockchain intelligence startup, believes that both cyberattacks were carried out by a North Korean state-backed hacking group tracked as TraderTraitor.

About 40% of the stolen sum comprised stablecoins issued by three major crypto companies: Circle Internet Group Inc., Ripple Labs Inc. and Tether Ltd. They managed to freeze most of the funds before the hackers moved them out of reach. Binance, for its part, has set aside over $6.34 billion to cover users’ losses.

The hackers stole the funds by compromising several of the company’s wallets. One of them powers the infrastructure that Binance uses to process customers’ Ethereum transactions. According to TRM, the hackers breached the wallet late Thursday and sent its entire balance to a wallet they controlled.

TraderTraitor compromised Binance’s wallet by exploiting an Ethereum feature called EIP-7702 that the blockchain’s maintainers released last year. It enables a snippet of code called a smart contract to temporarily control a wallet. EIP-7702 only activates smart contracts if they receive authorization to run from the wallet’s operator. That authorization takes the form of an encrypted message.

The hackers used a malicious smart contract to take over Binance’s Ethereum wallet. It’s currently unclear how they obtained the authorization necessary to run such code.

According to Binance, an internal investigation determined that TraderTraitor had compromised a laptop belonging to one of its DevOps engineers. The company says that it has also “uncovered additional points of breach.”

“Developer and DevOps machines sit close to organizations’ most sensitive systems and hold credentials, tokens and deployment access,” said Kobi Sivilya, chief information security officer of cybersecurity company Checkmarx Ltd. “The question for any organization is how far an attacker could get from a single compromised workstation. Teams should review who has standing access to what systems, whether that access is appropriately limited and whether one machine can reach critical services without a second control.”

TRM determined that TraderTraitor had rehearsed the cyberattack for at least 36 hours before the theft. On Wednesday morning, the hackers deposited a small amount of funds into a malicious crypto wallet. Early Thursday, they tested some of the code that they used in the cyberattack on three different wallets.

According to Binance, the malware contained a “self-destruct mechanism” that deleted the tools the hackers installed on its infrastructure and the activity logs they generated. The mechanism made it more difficult for the company to investigate the attack. Binance did, however, determine that the hackers bypassed the approval workflows it uses to process crypto outflows.

“Organizations that rely on exchanges, custodians or any critical financial counterparty should ask what continuous visibility they have into those relationships,” Rand Davis, chief technology officer at SecurityScorecard, told SiliconANGLE in an email. “They should also ask what their playbook is when a counterparty pauses withdrawals or services. Security leaders can use this moment to map which third parties sit on their critical paths, pressure-test contingency plans, and watch for the phishing and social-engineering follow-on that typically trails a headline event of this scale.”

Binance suspended crypto deposits and withdraws on its exchange after it discovered the breach. The company has since restored deposits, but its withdrawal processing system remains offline. Binance plans to reactivate the feature on Monday.

#5542. Immigration Slowdown To Sharply Reduce Renter Household Growth, Study Says

The clampdown on immigration has slowed the nation's population growth. Now, Harvard estimates it is also slowing the formation of new households in the United States.

Harvard's Joint Center for Housing Studies estimates that immigration policy means 500,000 fewer households formed in the country each year from 2024 to 2027. Those 2 million households are mainly renters, but over time become homebuyers, Harvard said.

President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown has broad implications for the national housing market. People coming into the country on work and student visas are a major contributor to rental demand. Homebuilders rely on a significant immigrant workforce, and crackdowns have contributed to worsening builder sentiment.

Harvard researcher Daniel McCue said this marks a sharp turn from the 571,000 net new-renter households formed by immigrants who entered the country from 2022 to 2024 under President Joe Biden. At least one Fed study indicated illegal immigration may have driven up housing costs during the Biden administration.

Instead, McCue projected immigrants would account for just 132,000 new household formations by 2027.

This is based on the U.S. Census Bureau's most recent housing vacancy survey, which showed a marked increase in rental vacancy and a slowdown in new household formation overall. The national rental vacancy rate bumped from 7.1% in the third quarter of 2025 to 7.6% in the same time this year.

"This may be a sign that the sharp curtailment of immigration has begun to lower demand for rental units in a significant way," McCue said.

Jiayi Xu, senior economist at Realtor.com®, says such a slowdown could spell trouble for the housing market over the long term.

"A significant slowdown in immigration growth would cause household growth to slow over the next decade, dragging down economic growth in the long term," Xu says.

Eric Finnigan, vice president of demographics research for John Burns Research and Consulting, says the shifting immigration policies of Biden and Trump have led to disruptions in the housing market. Immigration has been a central pillar of the nation's population growth, and falling birthrates haven't kept up.

"We knew at the beginning of the decade, given our demographic trends, that immigration would be important to economic growth," Finnigan says. "That includes housing demand, labor supply, and homebuyers and renters. We didn't plan for this sharp surge in immigration nor a sharp decline."

In the past, immigrant populations have been an important contributor to the housing market. Students and workers on visas routinely generate demand for new rental properties. In time, some of those renters eventually become buyers. But, Finnigan says, the whiplash of the policies of recent years could chill demand at a time when the housing market is seeing fewer buyers.

"The rules about their own visa could change overnight without any warning," Finnigan adds. "The last thing they want to do is plunk down a down payment on a home or be on the hook for an asset they want to leave at some point. They don't want to be with an asset they might have to leave without warning."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5541. Google X co-founder Sebastian Thrun raises $130M for AI engineering startup Dulo

Dulo Inc., a startup co-founded by prominent artificial intelligence researcher Sebastian Thrun, has raised $130 million in funding.

The Information broke the news of the investment on Thursday. Dulo co-founder Adrian Aoun confirmed the report in a post on X.

Before launching Dulo with Thrun (pictured) earlier this year, Aoun sold an early natural language processing startup called Wavii Inc. to Google LLC for over $30 million. He has also invested in companies such as Pinterest Inc. Thrun, in turn, co-founded Google’s X research lab. He led the X program that later became Waymo and helped establish Google Brain, a precursor to Google DeepMind.

Dulo’s round included contributions from former Google Chief Executive Officer Eric Schmidt and Ram Shriram, one of the search giant’s first investors. They were joined by Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff, famed venture capitalist John Doerr and more than a half-dozen startup funds. Dulo didn’t disclose its valuation.

The company’s one-page website states that it’s developing foundation models optimized for hardware design tasks. In August, Thrun listed robotics among Dulo’s focus areas. It’s possible the company’s AI is meant to speed up the development of industrial robots and autonomous vehicles.

Thrun joined Google in 2007 after leading the development of Stanley, an early self-driving vehicle that helped kickstart the autonomous driving market. He later founded a flying taxi startup with financial backing from Google co-founder Larry Page.

It’s unclear what hardware design tasks Dulo’s models will automate. One possibility is that the startup hopes to optimize engineering simulations, which hardware teams use to check their product designs for flaws before manufacturing them. Dulo’s website says it’s looking to facilitate “manufacturing at lightspeed.”

Several other engineering-focused AI startups are also working to optimize simulations. One recently funded player, Vinci4D Inc., has built a platform that automates the so-called meshing phase of simulation projects. Meshing is a process through which engineers turn a product’s blueprint into a collection of small, three-dimensional shapes. That arrangement reduces the amount of hardware needed to run simulations.

Other AI startups are working to speed up partially differentiated equations. Simulators rely on such equations to predict the behavior of hardware systems under real-world conditions.

Dulo’s most prominent venture-backed rival is Prometheus Inc., an engineering AI startup co-led by Amazon.com Inc. founder Jeff Bezos. The company raised $12 billion in funding earlier this year from Bezos and a group of financial institutions. Like Dulo, Prometheus is using AI to speed up the development of complex hardware systems such as robots.

#5540. Nicholas Cage Says He’s a ‘Bit Homeless’ and ‘Living in Hotels’ After Sinkhole Damaged $10.5 Million Malibu Home

Actor Nicolas Cage has been displaced after coastal erosion caused a growing sinkhole in the driveway of his Malibu, CA, home.

"I'm currently a little bit homeless," the "National Treasure" star, 62, said at an Oct. 31 appearance at L.A. Comic Con. "Something happened to my house in Malibu, so I'm just sort of living in hotels so I don't have normal trick-or-treaters I would like to enjoy tonight."

Cage was still in the spooky holiday spirit, noting that he had planned to take his daughter, August, 4, trick-or-treating in Santa Monica later that night.

The devastation comes just two years after Cage snapped up his 4,000-square-foot beachfront home for $10.5 million.

The 30-square-foot sinkhole that first appeared on Cage's property collapsed on Sept. 6, leaving a 900-square-foot sinkhole in its place.

Jonathan Torres, a public information officer with the LACFD, said the collapse likely resulted from coastal erosion. Witnesses at the scene said they could see waves crashing through the hole. Cage was reportedly not at home at the time of the incident.

Cage is not the only famous resident of Sea Level Drive, the exclusive gated community where the disaster took place. Pierce Brosnan, Dustin Hoffman, and Mindy Kaling live in the neighborhood, as well.

Initially, a state of emergency was declared, and the city of Malibu red-tagged seven nearby homes, prohibiting homeowners from accessing the properties. It later red-tagged 24 additional properties in the community, noting that "current road erosion prevents normal ingress and egress to the neighborhood, and would also prevent access or evacuation routes in the event of an emergency."

At the time of the incident, the neighborhood's homeowners association had already begun repairs, which it estimates could take up to five weeks to complete.The ocean-facing abode, which comes with a secluded beach and a rare roof deck, first came on the market in March 2024 for $11.25 million, according to Realtor.com®. The waterfront residence had also been simultaneously offered for rent for $25,000 a month.

The property comes with a private courtyard and a two-car garage, which is equipped with an elevator. The living room, bathed in natural light, has a vaulted ceiling, a chic bar area, and a fireplace.

Floor-to-ceiling glass walls and sliding doors seamlessly connect the indoor and outdoor spaces.

On the second level is a chef's kitchen with high-end stainless appliances, a center island, and sweeping ocean views.

The third floor features four en suite bedrooms, along with a primary bedroom facing the Pacific Ocean, with a spa-worthy bath, fireplace, and ocean-facing deck.

In addition to the home's beach frontage, the property includes an adjacent beach lot.

Prior to that purchase, Cage faced troubles with an infamous "haunted" mansion in New Orleans' French Quarter.

In 2009, the actor lost the property to foreclosure, and it was subsequently purchased by Regions Bank for $4.5 million.

The following year, the home was sold to an investor for $2.1 million.

Before that March 2024 listing, the property had bounced on and off the market since summer 2022 and had once been offered for as much as $17.9 million.

By comparison, Cage seems to have secured an impressive deal—although, judging by the success of his onscreen endeavor that year, paying the full ask might not have been out of the question for him.

In 2024, the actor and producer appeared in the horror film "Longlegs," which became the "highest grossing independent film of the year," with $100 million at the box office, according to Variety.

The "Face/Off" star is also known to keep a full-time residence in Nevada, the site of his iconic movies "Leaving Las Vegas" and "Honeymoon in Vegas."

Cage has a lengthy real estate history in California.

In fact, he owned a San Francisco Queen Anne Victorian, which he picked up in 1989 and held for 16 years. He sold the property some 20 years ago, but left behind personal touches, including custom stained-glass windows.

Although Cage has seemingly been left without a home in Malibu, he does have property on the East Coast. In March 2026, he reportedly snapped up a sprawling two-bedroom condo in the heart of Manhattan for $6.5 million—and took out a $4.55 million mortgage for the deal.The actor is said to have purchased the unit in the Essex House Residences building at 160 Central Park South for a steep $1.4 million discount—after the property initially hit the market for $7.9 million.

The home measures 2,400 square feet and is a combination of two units, as first reported by The Real Deal.

The listing described it as offering "an unparalleled blend of elegance, comfort, and convenience, right at the doorstep of Central Park."

Cage will likely feel right at home inside Essex House, which has played host to many famous faces over the years, including the late actor and musician David Bowie and his wife, Iman.

Oasis star Liam Gallagher also purchased a pad in the unit in 2012, selling it two years later.

Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5539. What the World Series can teach real estate agents about focus

ST PETERSBURG, FLORIDA – OCT. 28: William Contreras, No. 24 of the Milwaukee Brewers, poses with the Willie Mays World Series Most Valuable Player award after defeating the Tampa Bay Rays in the 2026 World Series at Tropicana Field on Oct. 28, 2026, in St. Petersburg, Florida.

Mindfulness for real estate isn’t about calm. It’s about hearing clients under pressure. See what baseball teaches brokers about training attention.

The Milwaukee Brewers just won the World Series, and while I love baseball, I’ve been watching with a question that has very little to do with it: What happens to your attention when the outcome matters more than you can afford to think about?

Nobody at the plate can win a championship with the swing they wish they’d taken last inning. The players can only deal with the pitch (or batter) in front of them.

That sounds obvious until you notice how often we walk into a seller conversation still arguing with the deal that fell apart yesterday.

What’s interesting to me is that baseball has stopped treating this as a personality trait. Both the Rays and the Brewers have extensive mental performance training programs (as do all Major League ball clubs), but most brokerages treat mental health as a wellness issue, not a performance one.

Whatever name your office gives this kind of work, baseball has made it somebody’s job.

What makes this baseball tale useful to brokers and team leaders, though, is how much resistance the work still meets in a sport that has every reason to embrace it.

Andy McCullough’s recent reporting in The Athletic examines meditation in Major League Baseball, and I found the takeaways instructive.

For over two decades, most teams have invested in behavioral science and expanded their mental-performance staffs. It’s a sport that measures everything, with tens of millions of dollars on every roster, and it has decided the mental side is worth paying for.

What I find fascinating is that even as the evidence piles up, many players remain skeptical. Some call it “woo-woo.” One of the game’s best pitchers says he doesn’t need it. Coaches avoid the word “meditation” altogether because, as one put it, it intimidates people, and if you push it, they’ll tune you out.

My favorite part of the Athletic piece was this: The San Francisco Giants brought in a consultant, titled “Breathing Specialist,” and the players made jokes about it. The next season, the same man did the same work but with a new title: “Human Performance Coach,” and the resistance started to fall away.

By the time he left, about 15 players regularly attended his sessions (complete with Tibetan singing bowls). He concluded that the stigma had more to do with the title than the practice.

I don’t call it meditation when I train real estate teams either. But that doesn’t mean you can’t intentionally sharpen the skills involved.

When the market tightens, brokerages usually prescribe more activity: more calls, more door knocks, more open houses. We can count activity, so we reach for it. Ballplayers do the same thing when they skip the mental work and take extra swings.

The trouble is that pressure narrows attention, and narrowed attention is as poor a state for a batter with two on, two outs, behind two, in the bottom of the ninth as it is for a seasoned agent on a listing appointment, a price-reduction conversation or a buyer about to walk.

Don’t get confused. This kind of performance coaching is not about caring less about the result; it’s about letting go of the need to make it happen. A hitter can care enormously about winning the World Series and still recognize that thinking about winning doesn’t help him see the next pitch.

The same is true when a seller is deciding whether to take your advice. You need the listing, but needing it more isn’t any more effective than gripping and swinging the bat harder.

The goal isn’t calm, either. Mental-performance people who work with ballplayers talk about finding a usable level of activation for the task, since too much overwhelms you and too little leaves you flat. I’m not trying to produce agents who feel peaceful about losing business. I’m trying to help them notice when fear has taken over the conversation so that they can let it go and hear the client again.

There’s sports research worth knowing here. One study of Division I basketball players found that higher measured mindfulness predicted better free-throw percentages in games, a 5.75-point delta, to be exact. A separate training study found something more useful: under high stress, the gap between athletes who trained their attention and those who didn’t was larger than under low stress.

I won’t tell you a practice will add a specific number to your agents’ closing rates. Nobody can honestly promise that, and even baseball struggles to quantify the benefit. What I will tell you is that the moments that make or break an agent’s year are high-pressure, and training for them is a performance issue, not a wellness perk.

In each World Series game, every player must let the last pitch go before the next one arrives. Your agents face the same job on a smaller stage every week.

You don’t need agents who identify as meditators. You need agents who can hear what a client is saying while a deal they “need” is coming apart. That capacity deserves practice before the conversation, not a reminder to calm down halfway through it.

Aaron Hendon is the Managing Broker for Christine & Company with eXp and a mindfulness teacher. Connect with Aaron on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5538. Google, Anthropic and others to support new AI crawling opt-out standard

Google LLC, Microsoft Corp., Anthropic PBC and OpenAI Group PBC today announced plans to support an upcoming website crawling standard.

The technology will enable website operators to block artificial intelligence developers from using their content to train their models.

Many websites contain a text file titled “robots.txt” that informs crawlers what content they may access. A publisher can use the file to block scraping across the board or only make specific webpages inaccessible. It’s also possible to include certain other instructions. For example, a company can ask crawlers not to visit its website too often.

Website operators historically used robots.txt files to manage how search engines interact with their properties. Nowadays, the technology also helps regulate the activity of the scrapers with which AI providers collect training data.

A company that wishes to disallow training-related scraping must make multiple edits to its website’s robots.txt file. In particular, it needs to add a separate entry for every single AI provider. If an AI provider uses multiple scrapers to collect data, each scraper requires its own robots.txt entry.

The crawling standard Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI are backing aims to simplify the process. It would allow website operators to block all scrapers that collect training data for generative AI models with a single robots.txt entry. The setting wouldn’t apply to models that “perform exclusively non-generative tasks.”

The structure of robots.txt files follows a standardized format called the Robots Exclusion Protocol. Google, Microsoft, Anthropic and OpenAI plan to incorporate  their crawling standard into the format. They have already submitted a draft version of their proposal to the Internet Engineering Task Force, the nonprofit that maintains the Robots Exclusion Protocol.

Microsoft stated in a blog post that it will also provide a crawling setting called AI Grounding. It’s designed for situations where an AI model seeks to access a webpage in order to answer a user question rather than to collect training data.

Microsoft’s setting will enable website operators to prevent its services from sending such requests. The feature will also extend to third-party AI tools that use Microsoft technologies to process prompts.

OpenAI plans to offer similar controls. Both the ChatGPT developer and Microsoft intend to add support for the crawling standard in the coming months, while Google will follow suit sometime next year. Meta Platforms Inc. expressed support for the idea behind the technology but hasn’t yet committed to implementing it.

#5537. Home prices rise in 78% of metros while weekly demand sinks to a low

Prices climbed in 78 percent of metros in the third quarter, according to NAR, as Redfin data shows pending sales at the lowest level in its records.

Home prices rose in 78 percent of U.S. metro areas during the third quarter, while pending sales in the four weeks ending Oct. 25 fell to the lowest level in Redfin’s records.

The national median single-family existing-home price rose 1.7 percent year over year to $432,900, matching the second quarter’s revised annual growth rate, the National Association of Realtors reported Thursday. Prices rose in 78 percent of the some 235 metros NAR tracks, down from 80 percent in the second quarter, and fell in 21 percent, up from 20 percent. Four percent of metros posted double-digit gains, down from 5 percent.

“Even with affordability challenges causing the housing market to stagnate, home prices continue to set record highs in most parts of the country,” NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement. “Homeowners are the beneficiaries of the price gains. Over the past seven years, the average house has appreciated by $146,000.”

Redfin’s data for the four weeks ending Oct. 25 shows prices dipping. The median U.S. home-sale price fell 0.1 percent year over year to $389,601, according to Redfin, following a 0.2 percent decline the prior week. The two drops are the first in more than three years.

NAR and Redfin measure different things. NAR tracks quarterly sales of existing single-family homes, while Redfin’s figures cover homes listed or sold across more than 900 metros on a rolling four-week basis.

The Northeast posted the largest annual gain, and the West was the only region where prices fell, according to NAR.

Prices declined in many Florida markets over the past year, Yun said.

“This quarter, however, homes in nearly all Florida markets are showing price gains,” he said. “In a similar vein, price declines in other markets may also be brief if the local job market and economy are solid.”

Gulfport-Biloxi-Pascagoula, Mississippi, led large markets with an 11 percent price increase, followed by Rochester, New York (10.9 percent) and Jackson, Mississippi (10.1 percent). Grand Rapids-Wyoming, Michigan; Cleveland-Elyria, Ohio; and Fort Wayne, Indiana, were among the Midwest markets in the top 10.

“Many markets in the Midwest offer exceptional value with more affordable homes, making homeownership more attainable,” Yun said. “Meanwhile, the artificial intelligence technology boom continues to push Bay Area home prices higher, keeping the region the most expensive in the country.”

San Jose-Sunnyvale-Santa Clara, California, remained the most expensive market at a median of $1.92 million, up 0.3 percent. Anaheim-Santa Ana-Irvine, California ($1.47 million) and San Francisco-Oakland-Hayward, California ($1.35 million) followed. Nine of the 10 most expensive markets are in California or Hawaii.

The monthly mortgage payment on a typical existing single-family home with a 20 percent down payment was $2,251 in the third quarter, up $48 from the second quarter and $69 from a year earlier, according to NAR. Typical families spent an average of 24.1 percent of income on mortgage payments, up from 23.9 percent last quarter and down from 24.5 percent a year ago.

First-time buyers faced a monthly payment of $2,208 on a typical $368,000 starter home with 10 percent down. That payment took up 36.3 percent of income, up from 36 percent last quarter and down from 37 percent a year earlier.

Pending sales fell 1.8 percent from a week earlier and 15.9 percent year over year, declining in all 50 of the most populous U.S. metros for the third straight week, according to Redfin. Seattle (down 31.6 percent) and Atlanta (down 25.9 percent) posted the steepest annual drops.

Redfin’s median monthly mortgage payment, calculated at a 7.32 percent rate, reached $2,786, up 10.7 percent year over year and the second-highest level in its records. The weekly average rate is down from 7.4 percent a week earlier and near a three-year high.

New listings fell 0.6 percent from a week earlier to their lowest level since January. Total inventory rose 0.3 percent because pending sales fell faster than new listings, Redfin reported. The share of listings with price drops rose to 21.5 percent from 20.9 percent a year earlier.

Redfin reported hundreds of thousands more sellers than buyers nationwide, giving buyers more negotiating power than they have had in more than a decade.

A First American analysis found that since 1991, rising mortgage rates have coincided with falling national home prices in some cases. In eight periods of sustained mortgage-rate increases since 1993, national home prices generally continued to appreciate, though the pace varied, First American Chief Economist Mark Fleming found.

During the rate run-up from December 2021 through October 2023, national prices rose an estimated 14 percent, according to the analysis. Affordability worsened at a steeper rate than prices, Fleming found. First American’s Real House Price Index, which adjusts prices for changes in income and mortgage rates, rose more than 70 percent over the same period.

Limited inventory can offset weaker demand when rates rise, Fleming wrote. Homeowners with mortgages below current rates may hold off on selling, and some sellers pull homes from the market rather than accept lower prices.

“Higher mortgage rates can put pressure on home prices, but the economy, household incomes and the number of homes for sale all play a role in what happens next,” Fleming wrote.

#5536. Open Real Estate Claims Early Broker, MLS Support as Initiative Touts ‘Significant Interest’

Open Real Estate, the national initiative launched by big brokerage leaders last week that has promised to create a shared “infrastructure” for property listing data, today announced it has received 826 letters of support from real estate brokerage leaders.

Behind the strength—and size—of its four founding brokerages (HomeServices of America, AGNT, Keller Williams and Real REMAX Group), the announcement made waves as it promised to maintain an “open and transparent” real estate market while allowing brokers to control their listings.

Open Real Estate is claiming that pledge and those principles have quickly found support among the broader brokerage community.

“We have already received significant interest from across the real estate industry since our announcement, and we look forward to continuing to engage with brokerages of all sizes, MLS organizations, and technology providers as we develop a platform that expands consumer choice and transparency for home buyers and sellers,” said the founding members of Open Real Estate.

Of the support letters received, 493 (59%) came from independent brokerages, according to Open Real Estate—from single-office independents to some of the largest independent brokerages in the country, including Atlanta Communities, Iron Valley Real Estate, LoKation Real Estate and Realty of America.

Open Real Estate is also claiming support from prominent MLS leaders. Designed to complement existing MLS organizations, the initiative aims to work alongside them to expand access to listing information for brokerages, agents and the consumers they serve, Open Real Estate said.

RISMedia spoke to a handful of MLS leaders about Open Real Estate, who largely said they were “cautiously optimistic” for the initiative. Council of Multiple Listing Services (CMLS) CEO Jessie Edgerton specifically said she had “deep, deep hope” around its principles and founders, while adding there were many unanswered questions around governance and execution.

In a release from Open Real Estate, four prominent MLS leaders also offered statements of support.

“We welcome the initiative of Open Real Estate and look forward to actively participating and partnering with industry leaders to build on the capabilities already in place at Bright and advance a more connected, efficient, broker-driven marketplace,” said Brian Donnellan, president and CEO, Bright MLS.

“Strategically, California Regional MLS and Open Real Estate are in alignment with the concept of allowing brokers to bring listing data in from outside the CRMLS MLS Input Platform,” said Art Carter, CEO, CRMLS. “We look forward to working with Open Real Estate to see how that possibility comes to fruition within their platform.”

“NTREIS remains dedicated to fostering a transparent, cooperative, and neutral marketplace that serves all Broker Participants equally by delivering consistent listing access and empowering exceptional consumer service. In alignment with this mission, we welcome constructive dialogue with Open Real Estate,” said Chris Carrillo, CEO, North Texas Real Estate Information Systems (NTREIS).

“Broker-led innovation shouldn’t be viewed as a threat to the MLS. It’s an opportunity to strengthen the cooperation that has served our industry for decades,” said Tim Dain, president and CEO, NorthstarMLS. “I hope this initiative brings even more brokers and MLSs to the table.”

MARIS MLS previously wrote a letter offering similar support of “the concept of (Open Real Estate),” while saying it hoped for more details as well. One MLS leader, who requested anonymity in order to speak candidly about the initiative, previously told RISMedia they saw the initiative as similar to a private listing service, adding they believed it would push MLSs to go “back to basics.”

“A well-timed offer with reasonable, season-specific requests has a much higher chance of acceptance when winter is around the corner,” says one real estate pro. Read more.

#5535. How Kyle Whissel built eXp’s top real estate team

The San Diego-based CEO recruits up to 15 agents a month, has a dress code and gives his trainer authority to cut newcomers.

Kyle Whissel has a standing instruction for his “60-day” bootcamp trainers: they should be willing to cut people.

His team brings in 10 to 15 new agents a month, puts them through approximately 60 hours of training over two weeks, and gives the trainer a goal of removing two people from each class.

It’s a striking approach from the leader of eXp Realty’s highest-volume U.S. team in San Diego, California. Whissel is CEO of the Whissel Beer Group, formed in 2025 when his Whissel Realty Group merged with Daniel Beer’s Beer Home Team.

According to Whissel, the team made $875 million in sales volume across 1,042 transaction sides last year (it was the first team in San Diego to break 1,000). The median price in San Diego — which is where he likes to focus his attention  (“we love that median price,” he said) — is around $1 million, he told Inman.

They’ve done that by hiring — and retaining — the right people. “We’ll give people an opportunity to prove themselves … but we’ve grown far more by cutting people than simply by hiring more people,” Whissel told Inman‘s Taylor Anderson during an interview at eXpcon in Salt Lake City earlier this month.

The company’s saying: “Expectations without enforcement are simply suggestions.”

Whissel’s recruiting process starts with a conventional, short interview, but he views the company’s two-week training period as a far better measure of whether someone belongs on the team.

Spending 60 hours in training gives leadership a chance to observe how that person behaves, learns and responds to expectations. Role-playing and scripting exercises also reveal whether new agents have the communication skills needed to work with clients.

The process continues after training, too. New agents are assigned mentors, and Whissel said those mentors are empowered to recommend removing someone who fails to meet team standards.

“If you’re going to be disrespectful to our team, I’ll be damned if I’m going to give you a client because you’re probably going to be disrespectful to them too,” he said.

Whissel also has activity and production expectations for agents already on the team. They include participating in role-playing sessions and attending meetings, along with meeting production targets.

Whissel’s hiring philosophy reaches back to his own first job, scooping popcorn at a movie theater, where he would compete with others to see who could serve the most customers. He looks for that same competitiveness in prospective agents, even if their previous accomplishments have little to do with real estate.

An applicant who participated in a college sorority, for example, might be asked whether they held a leadership position. Whissel said he wants to understand whether someone has a history of taking initiative.

In August 2025, Inman reported the merger of Whissel Realty Group and Beer Home Team, two of eXp’s highest-producing organizations. The combined company launched with approximately 160 agents and more than 60 staff members across five offices.

He said the first six months involved understanding the two organizations’ systems and getting them aligned. Whissel now believes it could take 18 months to fully integrate the companies.

“We’re going to be almost flat year-over-year,” he said, referring to the team’s expected 2026 performance, “but we’re setting up for a really, really big 2027,” he said. “You’ve gotta take a step back to take two steps forward.”

He remains optimistic about 2027, when he expects the operational investments to begin contributing to stronger growth.

Agents need to understand assumable mortgages, he said. “If you are working with a seller … and you’re not asking questions to figure out ‘does this seller have an assumable mortgage?’ (If it’s FHA, VA or USDA, those are assumable), I’m gonna beat you, because I am asking those questions.”

To find out whether a mortgage is assumable, agents simply need to get the closing disclosure from the seller. “It’s simple,” he said.
