#5529. Agent demand can’t be forecast, meaning the database has to be ready for anything

Enterprises building an agentic AI architecture are learning that the database matters as much as the model. AI agents fire off thousands of unplanned queries at once — and expect answers in milliseconds.

PhoenixAI, the trade name of CelerData Inc., raised $80 million this year to develop database technology for AI agents to solve this growing problem. Established players struggle to return answers in real time, according to Ross Armstrong (pictured), senior vice president of global sales of PhoenixAI.

“There was a real gap in the market for real-time analytics, and to be able to not only ask a question but get the response back in real time was something that all the database players that are out there, even the big names in the market, couldn’t do well,” Armstrong said. “If you have customer-facing analytics or agentic AI … you need that response time to be able to meet the SLAs with your customers.”

Armstrong spoke with theCUBE’s Paul Gillin at Cloudera EVOLVE26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed the database demands of agentic AI, real-time query performance and the need for governance and observability. (* Disclosure below.)

Agents generate queries in real time and may hit several databases at once, according to Armstrong. PhoenixAI’s specific columnar engine handles structured and unstructured data and works out how to answer each query as it arrives.

“I think what the biggest demand is that we don’t know what the demand is going to be from those agents,” Armstrong said. “You could have … thousands and thousands of queries hitting at the exact same time, but you still need that real speedy response.”

PhoenixAI joined Cloudera as a foundational database partner and is now an option in Cloudera’s marketplace. Its self-managed edition, PhoenixAI Anywhere, runs in a customer’s cloud, on-premises or in air-gapped environments. In a market where many early adopters hit governance and observability problems, PhoenixAI plans to address them with AgentBase, a purpose-built context environment that keeps agents away from data they don’t need, Armstrong explained.

“You can design that playground for those agents to be protected and to be governed but also to give them access to the data that you need,” Armstrong said. “It’s not necessary to run agents on a solution like PhoenixAI, but it’s certainly one that helps you put those guardrails in that a lot of organizations are looking for.”

#5528. Americans cling to homeownership as affordability gap widens

New ACS data shows incomes up 3.9 percent, but buyers still need $110,700 to comfortably afford a median-priced home.

Americans are clinging to the dream of homeownership — even though their incomes are barely enough to sustain it.

The U.S. Census Bureau released its 2025 American Community Survey 1-Year data on Thursday, which includes statistics on 40-plus topics, including housing. The national homeownership rate held steady at 65.3 percent, only 0.1 percentage points below the 5-year high of 65.4 percent. The majority of homeowners carry a mortgage (59 percent), with the real median mortgage payment increasing 2.4 percent year over year to $1,598.

Total housing costs, which may include expenses like homeowners association (HOA) fees, maintenance and repairs, increased 3.5 percent year over year from $2,090 to $2,163. Households now spend 21.9 percent of income on these costs, up 0.5 percentage points and just 8.1 points below the widely recognized 30 percent affordability threshold.

Median household incomes are edging up (+1.2 percent yoy after inflation), but Realtor.com Senior Economist Hannah Jones said it’s not enough to keep up with median home value growth.

“New 2025 American Community Survey data show median household income rose 3.9 percent to $84,780, with incomes up nominally in 49 of 50 states,” she said in an emailed statement. “But housing remained out of reach for many households. With a median listing price near $424,000 in 2025, mortgage rates averaging 6.6 percent, a 20 percent down payment, and taxes and insurance at roughly 1.7 percent of home value, a buyer needed about $110,700 to afford a median-priced home, roughly $26,000 more than the typical household earned.”

“Closing that gap would have required incomes to be 30.5 percent higher, prices about $99,000 lower or mortgage rates near 3.5 percent,” she added. “That affordability challenge has persisted, even as the year started with a promise.”

Jones said the market was primed in homebuyers’ favor at the beginning of the year, with sub-6 percent mortgage rates. However, macroeconomic and geopolitical conflicts have pushed mortgage rates up — now in the 7.30 percent range — leaving most homebuyers unable to take advantage of better inventory levels and falling list prices.

“Even assuming incomes have grown in line with recent wage gains of 3 percent to 4 percent since 2025, the typical household income would still be roughly $28,000 short,” she said. “Demand has cooled in response to higher rates, and pending sales fell 4.1 percent year over year in September, the steepest annual drop since March 2025, even as inventory approached pre-pandemic levels and prices softened.”

Realtor.com has released several reports on how homebuyers can attempt to make the math work, even as rates fluctuate. They can improve their credit scores, increase their down payments, shop lenders and build a budget buffer to help them absorb a 0.50 percent rate increase or decrease.

As for what lies ahead this year, homebuyers aren’t expected to receive mortgage rate relief.

The Federal Reserve held the federal funds rate steady (at 3.75 to 4 percent) at its Oct. 28 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting. The federal funds rate affects how banks and financial institutions set rates, including mortgage rates, but a change doesn’t guarantee mortgage rates will move in tandem.

The 10-Year Treasury Yield has the greatest impact on mortgage rates as lenders add a spread — or percentage markup — on top of it. The spread reflects the effects of monetary and fiscal policies, economic growth, inflation, higher origination costs and the gap between mortgage-backed securities (MBS) and Treasury yields.

“Whether the Fed hikes or holds this month, homebuyers shouldn’t expect a big change in mortgage rates,” First American Senior Economist Sam Williamson told Inman on Wednesday after the Fed’s FOMC meeting. “With another hike widely expected in December and further increases possible next year, borrowing costs are likely to remain elevated, keeping many buyers and sellers on the sidelines. But not everyone has the luxury of waiting. New jobs, growing families and other life events will keep some buyers moving forward, even as higher rates delay moves that can wait.”

Jones said mortgage rates will remain “the swing factor” and will shape next year’s American Community Survey results.

“For rates to trend lower, inflation has to cool, and the latest data shows it is moving the wrong way,” she said. “Annual inflation rose to 3.7 percent in September as energy prices surged amid the conflict in the Middle East, and core inflation edged up to 2.6 percent.”

“With the Fed focused on bringing inflation back under control while protecting the labor market, a significant drop in mortgage rates is unlikely in the near term,” she added. “For buyers on the fence, though, today’s mix of more inventory, more price cuts and more room to negotiate is the best they’ve had in years.”

#5527. California Voters Could Approve ‘Secondary Mortgages.’ Can the Golden State Solve the Housing Crisis?

Lawmakers and advocates have made many attempts recently to address the affordability crisis that pervades the housing market—some more impactful than others. Legislative bodies have enacted laws addressing private listings, while President Donald Trump recently signed an executive order aimed at cutting costs for title and mortgage insurance and manufactured housing.

In tomorrow’s general election, California voters will vote on a meaningful and unique new measure that essentially allows first-time buyers to borrow the bulk of their down payment, theoretically removing a big barrier to homeownership (with several caveats).

California Proposition 37—or the Second Mortgage Homebuyer Program and Revenue Bond Initiative—would create an assistance program for first-time homebuyers, offering them loans that could cover up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, meaning a buyer only needs to put 3% down to reach the 20% threshold needed to avoid mortgage insurance.

One of the primary sponsors of the initiative, former California Senate Majority Leader and Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg spoke with RISMedia and desired for more California residents to achieve homeownership.

“We’re really underhoused in California, so much of the focus has been on subsidized tax supported rental housing. I don’t take that away for a second, but we haven’t done a really good job at making sure that middle-class folks—the missing middle—are able to buy a house,” he says.

The initiative would authorize the California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) to issue up to $25 billion in bonds to offer secondary mortgage loans for down payments, to eligible buyers.

To qualify for the program, applicants must have been residents of California for at least one year, agree to occupy the home as a primary residence within 60 days of closing, fall under the middle-income buyer threshold and provide a down payment of no less than 3% of the purchase price of the qualified homes.

The proposition is aimed at “middle-income buyers,” or buyers who have an income at or below 200% of the area median income.

A qualified home includes any “newly constructed homes, townhouses, row houses, condominiums, or manufactured homes, or a condominium or other residence in a nonresidential building repurposed for residential use, where the borrower is the first purchaser,” according to the proposition.

Within these limitations, the program theoretically allows buyers to put down much less while still getting the keys (the 3% down payment still comes out to around $17,000 for a median-priced new home in the state).

As for the $25 billion in bonds, Hertzberg emphasizes that funding does not rely on taxpayer wallets, but rather investors. What’s more, the bonds will be recycled continuously.

“The bottom line is, it’s evergreen. Evergreen means that it’s not over. When you pay off the loan, it’s evergreen and the money goes back out to somebody else,” Hertzberg notes. “Thirty years from now when all these initial loans are paid off, there’ll be brand new loans. We hired a professor from UCLA who analyzed it and said that it’ll raise $150 billion in new construction and 190,000 new homes.”

Michael Lane—state policy director at the San Francisco Bay Area Planning and Urban Research Association (SPUR)—approves the initiative because it focuses on new homes.

“There are some programs the state has implemented which are just down payment assistance programs without creating new housing,” he asserts. “You’re actually just creating—with those programs—more demand for the existing housing stock, which means more competition which will also boost prices. We think it’s important for this to focus on new construction as well as the down payment assistance.”

Within the proposition, a “secondary mortgage” is a somewhat unique concept. In this case, a secondary mortgage refers to the loan offered to qualified homebuyers, of which goes toward a home’s down payment.

“This is different from a second mortgage,” David Garcia, deputy director of Policy at the Terner Center for Housing Innovation UC Berkeley, stated.

A website made by supporters of the proposition contains a tool that allows voters to view median home price by each county in California, and uses data provided by the California Association of Realtors®.

As with many coastal states, California has a divided housing market. According to the latest data, California metros were not immune to the effects of elevated mortgage rates, as pending home sales fell even in high activity cities such as San Francisco and San Jose.

Construction has fared no better, as the latest report from The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and the Census Bureau shows that housing starts in the West are down over 23% monthly, and down 25% from the previous year.

In that context, Proposition 37 is particularly relevant as the state seeks to sustainably increase housing that is affordable in a market that is both land constrained and highly regulated.

“We’re also focused on construction defect liability reform and liquidated damages for condominiums in California,” Lane notes. “We’re at a disadvantage compared to other states; it makes it more risky to build condominiums here. That’s why we don’t produce very many—about 3,000 developments of five units or more—compared to other states and nations which do 10 times that amount with lesser populations.”

Homebuilders cite global tensions and labor shortages for faltering construction rates. Although the conclusion of each year typically ushers in a slowdown in housing activity, the latest data for new-home sales showcases further deceleration, likely caused by high mortgage rates and economic unease.

The Terner Center for Housing Innovation at UC Berkeley does not take positions on bills or legislation. But Garcia does note that the initiative may encourage more than buyers.

“By limiting the use of funds to newly built housing, it also may act as an incentive for builders to build more homes that are for sale,” he says.

Although his focus is on housing in Sacramento, Lane points out that California’s homeownership rates leave much to be desired.

“We have one of the lowest homeownership rates in the nation here in California because of our high housing costs and the median home price of over $800,000; it makes it very difficult for working families to scrape together the 20% down payment,” he notes.

Notably, California is one of only a few states where new homes are cheaper than existing homes, making Proposition 37 potentially more powerful at addressing affordability.

Lane also believes that more changes to California’s housing market will come, specifically by drawing investors and builders to the state.

“We’ve been working on this issue for decades and will continue to do so; there’s always more to do,” Lane says. “In California, the cost of construction and the rules for project approvals can make it very difficult and time-consuming. That’s why investors oftentimes look for other opportunities rather than investing in housing in California. We’ll continue to make it more business-friendly and friendly for housing construction.”

With five years’ worth of work nearing its climax, Hertzberg states that his goal with Prop 37 is to encourage the supply of affordable homes, in the hopes of addressing California’s low homeownership rates.

“It’s the simplest rule in economics, supply and demand,” he adds. “You get more supply, it works better. People can say all the arguments they want to make, but we don’t have enough middle-class housing.”

Despite his retirement, Hertzberg noted that he’s met with a handful of opposing groups, but states that many arguments against the initiative have not “done their homework.”

The League of Women Voters in California (LWV) declined to speak with RISMedia on the proposition, but they are opposed to it. The group’s argument is that the proposition essentially adds a second mortgage for buyers to repay, alongside their primary mortgage, each month.

“The program could reinforce racial and economic gaps instead of targeting families facing the greatest barriers,” the LWV’s voting recommendations state. “Generations of housing discrimination have left many Black and Latino families with less wealth to draw on, but Prop 37 gives no priority to first-time or first-generation buyers and does not exclude current or former homeowners. Households earning up to twice the area median income could qualify, including some earning more than $300,000 a year, while buyers would still have to provide at least 3% of the home price.”

The LWV also stated that voters would not know the interest rate, loan term or monthly payment amount prior to the program’s approval. Essentially, the LWV argues that the program would put homeowners in more debt.

Hertzberg rejected these notions, responding that the group’s arguments are “ridiculous” and that with purchase money security interest (PMSI), the only players to take a loss should there be a significant downturn in home prices are the banks and bondholders.

“PMSI means that there is no liability,” Hertzberg claims. “Assume we had a downturn, where a home’s value drops significantly. The bank and the bondholders take the loss. The only thing that the buyer loses if they buy a house for $900,000, is $30,000. There’s no downside risk beyond losing your down payment.”

He also emphasizes the safeguards the initiative includes, in reference to the 2008 financial crisis that rocked the world.

“People in 2008 had variable-rate mortgages. Their mortgage went from $1,200 to $2,400, and they couldn’t afford it. These down payment loans are fixed-rate mortgages. For renters, I promise you this much: In 10 years your rent’s going up. That doesn’t happen in a fixed-rate mortgage,” Hertzberg stresses.

While it may not be the optimal option for all first-time homebuyers, Garcia does acknowledge that some buyers in California may find use out of the program.

“I think it’s useful in a circumstance where a homebuyer or family has the income to cover the payments for both a first and second mortgage, but don’t have the liquidity,” he says. “It’s just an alternative pathway for individuals who just don’t have a lot of cash on hand to afford homeownership.”

Desirae Sin is an assistant editor for RISMedia. She graduated from the University of Connecticut in 2025 with a double major in Journalism and Political Science. Prior to joining RISMedia, Desirae wrote stories geared toward policy issues for the Connecticut Mirror. She also worked as a staff writer for The Daily Campus, UConn's student-run newspaper.

#5526. Amid ‘tough market,’ Rocket revenues are up

Rocket’s Q3 earnings, explained: Revenue, market share, Redfin metrics and the questions agents should be asking about the integrated model.

Detroit-based Rocket Companies on Thursday announced its third-quarter 2026 earnings, and despite being in what CEO Varun Krishna said “might be the toughest mortgage market in 30 years,” revenues increased.

The company generated net revenue of $3.28 billion and adjusted revenue of $2.57 billion; net income was $709 million and adjusted net income was $419 million. The company’s Q3 adjusted EBITDA was $748 million (a 29 percent margin, up from 28 percent from last quarter).

Rocket also reported $11.4 billion in liquidity (a record), including $2.7 billion in cash and cash equivalents.

“Rocket gained market share in both purchase and refinance, quarter over quarter and year over year, and delivered our highest profitability margin in nearly five years, even as mortgage rates climbed to a three-year high,” Krishna said in a statement. “We didn’t spend the last three years waiting for rates to fall. We acquired distribution, connected real estate and mortgage, and invested heavily in technology.”

The company’s third-quarter net income compares with a $124 million loss in the same period of 2025.

“The market is literally testing every single lender,” Krishna said during the company’s earnings call Thursday. “If you have a strong business model, it’s gonna shine through, but if you have a flaw, it’s gonna get exposed.”

He pointed to Redfin as a source of new mortgage clients. “Redfin is the doorway to Rocket,” Krishna said. According to the company, the number of Redfin visitors who started a purchase mortgage from a listing rose 50 percent year over year. Cumulative unique listings displayed through Rocket’s partnership with Compass reached nearly 40,000, up from about 25,000 in the prior quarter.

Brian Brown, Rocket’s president, chief financial officer and treasurer, said the fourth quarter will come in well below the third, with refinance volume falling as much as 50 percent. Rocket expects adjusted revenue between $2.1 billion and $2.3 billion for the period. “The fourth quarter will be harder still,” Brown said. “We’re ready for it.”

In Q2 2026 earnings, Rocket Companies reported $2.78 billion in revenue for a $229 million profit, up from $34 million year over year. Company executives credited its broker partners with more than $2 billion in net rate lock volume through its Compass partnership, a three-year collaboration undertaken in February.

In March, Rocket and Redfin joined Compass International Holdings in writing an open letter to multiple listing service leaders, urging them to support phased listing distribution and stop fining agents for what they called “seller-directed marketing plans.”

Rocket Companies now encompasses Rocket Mortgage, the U.S.’s largest lender, which includes Mr. Cooper, the country’s largest mortgage servicer, acquired just over a year ago; Redfin’s brokerage and home search portal; Rocket Close, its title and closing company; and Rocket Money and Rocket Loans, its consumer finance brands.

Christy Murdock and Lucy Cohen Blatter contributed to this story.

#5525. Wall Street’s AI Sell-Off Exposes a Weak Spot in the Bank of Mom and Dad

As more adult children count on the Bank of Mom and Dad to help them buy homes, Mom and Dad, in turn, may be counting on Wall Street.

That arrangement looked a little less secure on Friday, when fears about the cost of the artificial intelligence boom sent stocks tumbling.

The Nasdaq lost 2.9% on Oct. 30, its worst day since June, as investors grew worried about the billions of dollars companies are spending on AI. Intel shares plunged 28.6%, while chipmakers AMD and Nvidia fell 10.9% and 4.2%, respectively, according to Reuters.

The consequences could reach well beyond Wall Street and Silicon Valley. Baby boomers held approximately $35.2 trillion in stocks and mutual funds as of the second quarter of 2026, or roughly 55% of the household total, according to Federal Reserve data analyzed by Yardeni Research.

And some of that money is already making its way into their children's down payments. Half of parents who had helped or planned to help their children purchase a home reported drawing on investment accounts, according to an April survey by Veterans United Home Loans.

Of course, one bad day won't drain the Bank of Mom and Dad. But if the losses keep piling up, the damage could spill out of parents' portfolios. Research shows that after substantial financial setbacks, parents tend to scale back the money they give their adult children—or stop giving it altogether.

The AI boom has played an enormous role in the stock market's recent run. Since ChatGPT's launch in November 2022, AI-related stocks accounted for roughly 75% of S&P 500 returns, according to a JPMorgan analysis.

And that rally has helped swell the fortunes of a generation already poised to pass down an extraordinary amount of wealth.

Approximately $105 trillion will pass to heirs through 2048, according to estimates from the weath management firm Cerulli Associates—with baby boomers and older generations accounting for the vast majority of the projected transfer.

But some of that money is changing hands much sooner, as parents and grandparents help adult children overcome the financial barriers to homeownership.

Nearly one-quarter of parents surveyed by Veterans United expected to contribute between $50,000 and $99,999 toward their children's home purchases, while 12% anticipated providing between $100,000 and $199,999.

They're shocking sums, and years of rising stock prices may have made those commitments easier to make.

"When their stock portfolios go up, they feel more able to help with a down payment," says Michelle Riehn, a certified financial planner and founder of Money Momma. "People feel richer."

The trouble is that those feelings—and the financial resources behind them—can change when markets fall.

In a 2025 study published in The Review of Economics and Statistics, economists Jessamyn Schaller and Chase Eck examined how financial transfers between parents and adult children changed following setbacks such as wealth losses, job exits, and health problems.

They found that parents sharply reduced financial assistance following losses of wealth and earned income, particularly in households with fewer accumulated assets.

An earlier working-paper version estimated that among lower-wealth households, a major loss of net worth reduced the likelihood of parents making a financial transfer by 6.1 percentage points, or 18.7% relative to the group's baseline rate.

The research examined financial assistance broadly, not just down payments, and didn't isolate stock market losses. Still, the findings have important implications for housing, where financial help from parents can make the difference between buying a home and remaining a renter.

Already, parental transfers account for 13 percentage points, or 27%, of young households' homeownership, according to a 2025 Federal Reserve working paper.

Naturally, the next question for a generation waiting on those transfers is what happens if AI stocks continue to fall.

Friday's slide was far from the end of the AI boom. Despite losing more than $1 trillion in market value that day, technology stocks were still worth trillions, with Nvidia alone valued at roughly $4.9 trillion.

But researchers have examined what a much larger reversal could mean for U.S. households.

In September, Allianz Research modeled the consequences of disappointing AI investments triggering a broader market downturn.

Under its more severe scenario, a 25% decline in the S&P 500 would erase approximately $27 trillion in U.S. household wealth—nearly 14% of total household net worth—and help push the economy into recession.

That's a hypothetical scenario, not a forecast. And even losses of that magnitude wouldn't affect every family's ability to help their children equally.

Financial advisers say much depends on whether parents have already set aside the money they intend to give—or are counting on their investments to cover the gift when the time comes.

"There's a difference between help that was planned and requests that come unplanned," Riehn says.

Parents who have committed to helping their children buy homes often move that money into conservative investments well before the purchase, she explains. Doing so can shield a planned gift from a sudden drop in stock prices.

But when parents haven't prepared, a downturn can force tougher decisions.

"A lot of times they're selling stock to do it, and that's where it gets tricky in a downturn," says Greg Black, a certified financial planner and president of Tencap Wealth Coaching in Utah.

A parent who expected to sell appreciated investments to cover a $100,000 down payment might have to liquidate more shares after a substantial market decline. Rather than lock in those losses, the parent could decide to reduce the gift or postpone it.

"So if the down payment money is sitting in AI stocks and they drop, that gift might have to wait," Black says.

Even parents who could still afford to help may think twice. Riehn says watching a portfolio lose value can make affluent households more reluctant to part with money, particularly when their children make unexpected requests.

David Talley, a certified financial planner with Talley Wealth in Johnson City, TN, offers a counterpoint: Families with sufficient cash reserves and diversified investments should generally be able to maintain gifts that fit within their long-term financial plans.

"With the cash layer in place, the gift doesn't have to wait for a recovery," he says.

But younger homebuyers might not have that flexibility.

Allianz estimated that a 15% market correction could take six to nine months to reverse under one scenario. In its more severe scenario, recovering from a 25% decline could take as long as two years.

That extended timeline points to another potential consequence of an AI bust: Any prolonged downturn could also change what parents expect to leave their children.

In an earlier working-paper version of their research, Schaller and Eck found that a major household wealth loss was associated with roughly a 5-percentage-point decline in parents' reported probability of leaving an inheritance worth at least $100,000.

That finding measures parents' expectations, not the inheritances their children ultimately received. And the consequences of a market correction would depend partly on how much of a family's wealth is tied to the stocks losing value.

"The real exception is a family with a concentrated position in one company whose net worth has doubled in a few years," Talley says. "That genuinely changes what they can give."

And if those gains reverse, so can the amount available to pass down.

Still, Riehn cautions that inheritances operate on a different timeline from down payment gifts. Children expecting to inherit investments decades from now may have time to ride out a market downturn. Those counting on that wealth for a home purchase in the nearer future may not.

The recent AI sell-off is far from a market crash, and there's no evidence it has already disrupted parental gifts or inheritances. Instead, it highlights an uncertainty at the heart of the Great Wealth Transfer: The fortunes younger Americans expect to receive aren't necessarily the fortunes their parents will ultimately leave behind.

And until that money changes hands, the next generation has little control over how much will be there—or when it will arrive.

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5524. Project-by-project security reviews can’t keep pace with enterprise AI agents

Enterprises racing to put AI agents into production are finding that tokenization and other data protection methods now decide how fast those projects move.

But sensitive data fed into models is hard to pull back — and security reviews built for a slower era are stalling deployments. The challenge is shifting from locking data down to keeping it usable once it is protected. That tension is playing out across Cloudera Inc.’s partner ecosystem, where security is becoming a prerequisite for AI value rather than a final gate, according to Diego Loureda (pictured), vice president of customer success and presales at Protegrity USA Inc.

“Data leaks are still a thing. If you put sensitive data on a model, if you put sensitive data on a vector store or in the memory of an agent that is going to propagate to other agents, good luck removing that sensitive data,” Loureda said. “There’s no way you’re going to be able to do that.”

Loureda spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight and Paul Gillin at Cloudera EVOLVE26, during an exclusive interview on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed data security along with Protegrity being named Cloudera’s Emerging Technology Partner of the Year. (* Disclosure below.)

Traditional encryption can lock data so tightly that analysts and models can no longer use it. Protegrity centers its approach on tokenization, which swaps sensitive values for substitutes instead of relying on a mathematical algorithm, Loureda explained. That design also matters as quantum computing threatens today’s cryptography.

“Our main method of protection, that is tokenization, it’s already quantum ready,” Loureda said. “The reason behind that is because there is no mathematical algorithm behind it. It’s all based on replacement in memory.”

Protection alone doesn’t solve the speed problem, however. In research Protegrity commissioned from Enterprise Management Associates Inc., 83% of leaders reported project delays, Loureda noted.

“The main problem with governance is that companies are approving projects and that will not scale in the age of AI,” Loureda said. “They have to approve patterns.”

The same study found 82% of leaders push agents into production in a diminished state, stripped of the tools and data that would make them useful, he added. Controls such as tokenization let security teams clear the way for those agents instead, according to Loureda.

“Security has always been the business of no, the department of no. That changes now,” he said. “These days security is the team that can enable AI to give you value.”

#5523. Why a Long Island Town’s Crackdown on Vacation Rentals May Not Fix Its Housing Crisis

The four-bedroom waterfront home on Long Island's North Fork hadn't even hit the market when Diane Mollica's colleagues began imagining another use for it.

"Several of them commented that it would be a fabulous rental property because it has all of the perks that you want on vacation," Mollica, a real estate agent with the Gambino Group at Compass, tells Realtor.com®.

It was easy enough to see their point: Beyond walls of glass stood a swimming pool, a sandy beach, and the sparkling blue waters of the Long Island Sound. Upstairs, a rooftop deck offered yet another picturesque view.

But Southold, the town encompassing much of the North Fork, wants fewer homes operating as short-term rentals.

A newly proposed permit lottery would allow just 119 properties across the town's North Fork hamlets to offer stays shorter than 30 days—that's less than one-fifth of the 640 active vacation-rental listings in October.

Officials hope the regulation would help protect residential neighborhoods from revolving vacation guests and preserve housing for people who live and work there year-round. But research from cities that have tried similar restrictions shows mixed results.

Mollica knows what draws people to the North Fork. Roughly 25 years ago, she came from Brooklyn for a weekend and ended up buying a house herself.

"What I love about the North Fork is the people are very embracing. They're very community-minded," she says.

The area has long attracted weekenders and summer vacationers, but the COVID-19 pandemic brought a wave of newcomers who began putting down more permanent roots.

"People made a mad rush to the North Fork because they saw the opportunity really to live and not to shelter in place," Mollica recalls. "They enrolled their children in school. They got to know their friends and neighbors. ... So a lot of those people stayed."

Others eventually returned to the city while keeping their North Fork properties as second homes, leaving year-round residents, seasonal homeowners, and vacationers with competing visions for the community.

At an October civic forum, residents complained about pool parties, weddings, traffic, and unfamiliar guests coming and going.

"I'm in a residential community; this is where I want to live," one resident told officials. "I don't want to live in a business district."

Then there's the growing difficulty of affording a home at all.

By the end of 2025, the median price of a single-family home on the North Fork had reached a record $999,000—more than eight times Southold Town's median household income of $116,667. Meanwhile, an estimated 54% of town renters spent at least 30% of their incomes on housing, according to U.S. Census Bureau data.

Even Town Councilwoman Alexa Suess, a Greenport native who campaigned on affordability, recently said she would have to move after her landlord raised her rent above $4,000 a month.

"I don't know anybody my age who I went to school with that is still here," she told a September housing forum.

Naturally, that friction has put a renewed spotlight on the town's massive share of vacation properties: Nearly 37% of its housing stock consisted of seasonal residences in 2020, according to the town's 2023 Community Housing Plan.

At first glance, those seasonal homes might seem like a natural solution for Southold's problems: a reservoir of untapped housing just waiting to be unleashed. But the town's own experience regulating vacation rentals reveals just how difficult it can be to turn those properties into year-round housing.

The town banned stays shorter than 14 nights in 2015, but officials have struggled to enforce the rule. Its housing plan subsequently identified vacation rentals as one possible contributor to the shortage.

Now, officials want to go further, requiring permits for stays shorter than 30 days, limiting them to 1% of single-family homes in each hamlet, and strengthening enforcement. The proposed system could begin in January 2028, although lawmakers have yet to formally adopt it.

The question is what happens to those homes once renting them out becomes more difficult.

Asked whether the cap could flood Southold's for-sale market, Mollica replies: "I'm going to say no."

Many of her clients already prefer monthlong or summer rentals, and she cautions that she works with few buyers seeking properties solely for rental income.

"Our clientele really come out to enjoy their home," she says. "They spend their summers here. They're looking forward to Thanksgiving and other holiday vacations here."

She recalls one family that moved back to New York City for personal reasons but kept their North Fork house as a second home. While they initially sought longer seasonal renters, they turned to Airbnb when finding tenants proved difficult.

"They wanted to rent it [out] ... to supplement their income in order to carry the mortgage," she explains.

And that supplemental income can be substantial.

Average summer nightly rates in Southold's vacation-rental market climbed from $463 in 2019 to $764 in 2026, a 65% increase, according to an analysis of AirDNA data provided to Realtor.com. Yet the median summer reservation lasted just three nights. The figures cover ZIP-code-based North Fork markets, including separately regulated Greenport Village.

"A 30-night minimum removes the weekend and short-stay premium, and a whole-season lease must cover all of an owner's income in a single booking," says Bram Gallagher, AirDNA's director of economics and forecasting.

It's true that owners may decide that renting out their homes is no longer worth the trouble. But that doesn't mean they'll sell or make those properties available to year-round tenants.

Alexander Marsella, an economist at Berry College, says the outcome depends on an owner's next best use of the property.

If that alternative is "a second home for the family," he says, "then restricting short-term rentals isn't going to do much to improve housing affordability."

Research from cities that have already restricted vacation rentals suggests he's right. A 2024 study of Berlin found that the crackdown targeting only commercial operators—not occasional hosts—significantly increased long-term rental supply.

New York City saw a similar disconnect. Short-term listings on Airbnb fell 87% after its 2023 crackdown, but rents barely budged and conventional rental inventory showed no unusual increase, according to Marsella's August 2026 working paper, which has not yet undergone peer review.

And Marsella suspects the effect on year-round housing could be even smaller in a seasonal market.

"If I don't see it happening in New York City so much, I feel like I would be less likely to see it happen in a seasonal market," he says.

Town officials have already acknowledged that restricting vacation rentals won't necessarily determine what happens to the properties themselves.

"Owners are going to have to make a decision about what to do with the houses," Planning Director Heather Lanza said in 2024. "They can go to summer rentals or year-round."

At Mollica's waterfront listing, that decision will soon belong to someone new.

The four-bedroom home is preparing to hit the market, and prospective buyers may already waiting.

"I have several people that are waiting for the right property," Mollica says.

Its swimming pool, private beach access, and sweeping views of Long Island Sound make it an enticing vacation retreat. But those same qualities could appeal to someone looking to put down permanent roots.

Mollica herself came to the North Fork for a weekend nearly 25 years ago and ended up staying.

The next buyer might do the same—or simply return for summer vacations. Southold's proposed rules could influence how the property is used, but whether it becomes a year-round home will ultimately be the buyer's decision.

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5522. I analyzed 1,133 Instagram posts with Meta’s new AI

Meta Muse for Small Business connects to your Instagram analytics. Here are five prompts to analyze your past posts before asking AI to create more.

Meta quietly released something at the end of September that I think a lot of real estate agents are going to want to play with.

It’s called Meta Muse for Small Business, and while there are plenty of AI tools that can help you brainstorm a Reel or write a caption, what is massive about Muse is that it can connect directly to your Instagram professional account analytics, along with your Facebook Pages, Meta ad accounts and other business tools.

I connected mine and started playing with it, but instead of asking it to make more content, which is how I use AI most of the time, I wanted to see what would happen if I used it to understand all the content I had already made.

Eventually, we analyzed 1,133 of my Instagram posts. It helped me understand why my rolling views had fallen from roughly 4 million to 2.46 million, showed me that at least 27 of my 98 newest followers were real estate professionals, and identified patterns in the topics and formats that have historically performed best for me.

That was when I realized I had probably been using AI backward. If you have been consistently creating content for a few years, you already have your own data set of what works and what doesn’t, so before asking AI for another 10 Reel ideas, there may be more value in asking it to help you understand what your audience has already told you.

Here are five prompts I’m using to do that.

“Analyze my Instagram performance over the past 90 days. Don’t give me content recommendations yet. First tell me where the biggest weakness is between reach, engagement, profile visits, follower growth and conversion, and show me the data that led you to that conclusion.”

A few months ago, my Instagram analytics showed roughly 4 million views in a 30-day window, and more recently that number had fallen to about 2.46 million, so naturally my first reaction was that something wasn’t working.

The story was a little different once I dug into the data. Some of my biggest posts, including videos with more than 1 million views, had simply aged out of the rolling reporting period. I would love to tell you I publish a million-view video every week, and I’m working on it, but I don’t.

My views were down, but roughly 84 percent were still coming from non-followers, and my content had reached more than 1.4 million accounts. The point wasn’t to ignore the decline; it was to understand what was causing it before changing a strategy that might not actually be broken.

“Analyze my most recent followers, and group them into the most common audience types you can identify. Don’t assume who my target audience is. Tell me what the data shows.”

We pulled roughly 100 of my newest followers, and of the 98 we could analyze, at least 27 had Realtor, real estate, broker or realty directly in their name or username.

Initially, I wondered whether that was a problem because I sell houses and still want consumers seeing my content, but last year we closed roughly $12 million in sales volume from referrals, and relationships with other agents have also created speaking opportunities, partnerships and other revenue. Trying to get rid of an audience already producing real business made very little sense.

Instead, I’m leaning into it while becoming more intentional about building consumer-focused lead pillars through my local Dana Point Daddy page and YouTube.

I’m also still making consumer-focused and humorous content on my main account because my past clients, database, sphere, friends and family are seeing and engaging with it. We’re still marketing directly to our database, hosting client events and doing the things that generate real estate business outside social media.

Your unexpected audience might be completely different from mine, but you probably shouldn’t decide whether the audience you’re building is good or bad until you know who is in it and what that audience is worth to your business.

“Analyze my highest-performing posts from the last year and group them by topic, format and hook. Tell me what patterns repeat among my winners and which patterns I seem to be underusing.”

I spend an embarrassing amount of time studying other creators, saving their posts and trying to understand why something went viral, while apparently not spending nearly enough time studying the years of content I already had telling me what my own audience responds to.

We analyzed 447 of my carousel and single graphic posts and isolated 103 that used headline-style hooks. The winners repeatedly included income statistics that create sticker shock, local rankings people want to agree or disagree with, surprising changes in the Southern California housing market and California housing policies translated into something useful for homeowners.

This October, Inman turns its focus to AI and its rapid rise in real estate. During Artificial Intelligence Month, we’re digging into the startups shaking things up and the established players folding AI into their offerings.

I don’t need to make variations of those posts forever, but I can look for new topics that share the DNA of things my own audience has already told me it wants instead of constantly trying to recreate somebody else’s viral post.

“Compare how frequently I publish each content format with how those formats actually perform. Where is my time allocation inconsistent with my results?”

At the time of the analysis, I had published 66 times over 28 days, and Reels were the format I was publishing most frequently even though they weren’t my best-performing format. Carousels were.

I’m not going to stop making Reels because different content has different jobs, but if I’m deciding where to spend another hour this week, I should probably know whether the format consuming most of my time is producing my best results.

“Based only on the patterns you identified in my historically best-performing content, give me 10 new content ideas. For each one, tell me which past pattern it is based on and why you think it fits my audience.”

This is where the first four prompts become useful instead of just interesting because I can ask any AI tool for 10 content ideas and it will happily give them to me, but without context it is essentially making an educated guess.

Once it understands what my audience has historically responded to, I can ask a much better question: What should I make next based on what has already worked for me?

I’m still going to experiment, tell personal stories and make something weird because I think it’s funny, but now my own history gets a vote.

Meta Muse for Small Business has only been out for about a month, so I am sure I’m barely scratching the surface of what I can do with it, but this experiment has already changed the way I’m using AI.

If you’ve been consistently posting for a few years, you may already have hundreds or thousands of experiments sitting inside your Instagram, so before asking AI for another hook, caption or content idea, ask it to help you understand those experiments first.

For me, the most interesting thing AI has done for my content lately isn’t helping me create more of it. It’s helping me make better decisions about what I create next.

Krys Benyamein is a Realtor with Allstars Realty in Southern California. Get connected on Instagram or LinkedIn.

#5521. Marble Cognition raises $3.75M for its AI agent workers that watch and learn how people work

Artificial intelligence agents have become two a penny in the enterprise today, but just because they’re rapidly being commoditized does not mean organizations know how best to use them.

That’s the challenge a startup called Marble Cognition is trying to solve after raising $3.75 million in pre-seed funding to coincide with its launch today. The round was led by Heartcore and Seedcamp, and saw participation from angel investors that include executives from McKinsey & Co., Mistral AI and a board member of Datadog Inc.

Munich-based Marble was co-founded by the German AI engineers Felix Rösner (pictured, left) and Christophe Schmit (right), who were among the first to realize that AI agents have already become a commodity, used by almost every enterprise in some capacity or other. Most organizations are using AI agents primarily for writing software, but Rösner believes that to see the real value of those autonomous workers, companies need to provide them with the granular operational context that tells them what they actually need to build and automate.

But building this picture is a notoriously difficult challenge because few corporate workflows run according to neat blueprints. Though a study by McKinsey & Co. suggests that it’s theoretically possible to automate 57% of all work hours in the U.S., most companies haven’t gotten anywhere near that goal.

That’s because more than 90% of business processes live within things like messy email threads, scattered spreadsheets and inside the minds of employees. To teach AI agents what needs to be built and automated, companies need to piece all of those processes into a picture they can follow.

This is exactly the challenge Marble seeks to address. Its AI agents are designed to capture those business workflows at the source. The startup has developed a dedicated desktop application that sits and monitors how employees work using different tools and processes. It takes screenshots and captures worker’s clicks and keystrokes, before transforming this data into a structured process map that AI agents can read and execute, similar to code.

“Every company we talk to wants AI to take over real work,” Rösner said. “But nobody can tell the AI how that work is actually done. So we solve that first. Our Coworkers watch how the work happens before they take it over. They do it the same way your best people do.”

Once the data is gathered, Marble then deploys its Coworkers, which are designed to take over the most repetitive work processes from people and run them end-to-end an organization’s existing software stacks, with humans remaining in the loop when important decisions need to be made.

Rösner said Marble has already delivered some serious efficiency gains for early adopters like EGYM GmbH, Mutares SE & Co. KGaA and Enam GmbH. In the case of one private equity-backed U.S. financial services firm, Marble’s Coworkers were configured to create settlement offers for human review. As a result of that work, the company was able to slash its case-handling times by 90%, which meant that its human staffers could process around 50% more claims without needing to hire anyone else.

Seedcamp General Partner Reshma Sohoni, an early backer of the robotic process automation firm UiPath Inc., said the vast majority of companies in the world want to learn how to automate more of their work. “The hard part has always been mapping out how the work gets done, so you can actually automate it,” he said. “Marble fills that gap, giving companies vital context for AI transformations that could define their future.”

#5520. A Halloween tale: Spooky events and a haunted house sale

Author and trainer Bernice Ross shares a spooky tale of unusual home happenings and a sale process plagued by tragedy.

When you’re in the real estate business, sooner or later there will be a house that someone says is haunted. The story below is true. Were these events just coincidence, or were they something else?

When I was working on my doctorate, my closest friend and study partner was living in a new house in Orange County. She was in the antique business. Her home was like a showcase, every last inch of it beautifully decorated. When I met her, she was in the process of getting a divorce.

Although her house was a little over a year old, it already had the makings of a strange history. While the house was being built, a little girl was sexually assaulted in it. A few months after she and her husband moved in, he became manic-depressive.

Over the next few months, he had numerous confrontations with the police. He refused to take his meds. Unbeknownst to his wife, he placed a warranty deed on the property to access part of the equity. He then took off to Hawaii, where he was reportedly living in the bush outside the Honolulu airport.

We would normally study together at her house about twice per month. The lights would flicker periodically. If we went out for dinner, it was common for pieces of the furniture to be moved away from the wall.

Since my friend had changed the locks and placed a security system on the house, there was no one who had access to move the furniture. There was also a window in the family room overlooking the canyon that would vibrate for no apparent reason. You could put your hand on the window and tell it to stop vibrating, and it did.

After spending the afternoon preparing for our upcoming qualifying exams, we decided to go out to dinner to take a break. When we returned, the lights were flickering, and a number of pieces of furniture were moved again.

As we sat back down to hit the books again, there was a loud rustling in the garage where she refinished her antiques. Her German shepherd, a very mellow dog who never barked, started barking and scratching crazily at the door to the garage.

Although this didn’t disturb my friend, I made sure the dog was between me and whatever was in the garage. As soon as she opened the door, the dog broke away from me and raced into the garage. The dog raced to the other side of the garage, sat down and acted as if nothing had happened.

After consuming a carton of chocolate ice cream to soothe our jangled nerves, we decided to watch a movie — The Ghost of Flight 401. This probably wasn’t the smartest movie choice, but that was the best of the evening’s shows back in the days of seven TV channels and no cable.

As I was getting ready to leave, we were standing by the front door adjacent to the stairway. Her stairs had beautiful wrought iron work topped with a heavy oak banister.

As we were standing there talking, the banister and the wrought iron started to vibrate. Everything else in the house was still. I turned and asked her, “Do you see what I see?” She did.

We were both mesmerized because nothing else was moving. This went on for about five minutes, and then it stopped. At that point, I was out of there, and there was no way I was going back.

My friend wanted out of the house. Needless to say, there were numerous challenges that had to be addressed before she could legally sell the property. California law allowed her to list the property, but both she and her husband had to sign the grant deed to close the transaction.

The lender who held the warranty deed was demanding payment as per the terms of the note. Normally, their option would have been to foreclose. The challenge was that the police reports documented the fact that the husband was probably not legally competent at the time he signed the deed.

Since he was nowhere to be found, my friend and the lender petitioned the court to order the sale as part of the divorce proceedings. The court granted her request.

The house was listed and finally went under contract. The buyer was a deputy sheriff. Two days after opening escrow on the property, the escrow officer had a heart attack and died. The title officer handling the file also had a heart attack but recovered.

About four weeks into the transaction, the deputy sheriff’s right arm became mysteriously paralyzed. He saw several specialists, but no one could find a cause for the problem. He was forced to take disability leave from his job. This meant he didn’t have sufficient income to qualify for the loan. The transaction was canceled. Within a few days after he canceled, the paralysis disappeared.

After almost a year, the house finally sold. The buyer was a psychiatrist.

Fortunately, this transaction took place prior to California passing its disclosure laws. I have to wonder how you would make those disclosures today. Much of what happened could be coincidence. I still don’t have an explanation for the moved furniture, the strange window and, most of all, the vibrating staircase. Perhaps it’s just as well that I don’t.

Bernice Ross is president and CEO of BrokerageUP and RealEstateCoach.com, the founder of Profit.RealEstate and a national speaker, author and trainer with over 1,500 published articles.

#5519. ‘Haunted as a matter of law’: How real estate agents handle stigmatized listings in 2026

Stigmatized homes have long sold at a steep discount. Agents and attorneys say an unaffordable, low-inventory 2026 market may be shrinking it.

Many may assume that the rule of thumb on stigmatized homes is simple: A murder, suicide or infamous ghost story knocks a big chunk off the price. Real estate agents who’ve sold these homes say it’s more complicated, and today’s unaffordable, short-on-inventory market may be shrinking the discount.

A “stigmatized” property can mean many things. It can be a home tied to a violent crime, a suicide, a notorious former owner or an alleged haunting.

Would you live in the Amityville Horror house, where Ronald DeFeo Jr. killed six members of his family in 1974?

Or what about the Menendez mansion in Beverly Hills, where Lyle and Erik Menendez killed their parents, José and Kitty, in 1989, a case that has stayed in the headlines for more than three decades?

These gruesome crimes may not always change the bedroom count or the square footage. But they can change who’s willing to buy, and for how much.

Ahead of Halloween, Inman asked real estate agents and attorneys how they handle stigmatized listings in 2026.

Their answers suggest the discount is real but uneven. It often depends less on the stigma itself than on how many buyers it drives away. And in a market with increasingly few affordable options, fewer buyers may be walking away.

The best-known estimate for stigmatized listings comes from real estate economist Randall Bell, who has put the typical “murder-house” discount at 10 to 25 percent. Bell has also said he’s seen some stigmatized homes sell at full value — usually smaller, more affordable homes — while others sit unsold for a long time.

Bell is an expert on real estate damage, earning the nickname “Master of Disaster,” and he runs the advisory firm Landmark Research. He has consulted on some of the most notorious crime-linked properties in history, from the Rancho Santa Fe mansions where the bodies of 39 Heaven’s Gate cult members were found to the home of Sandy Hook shooter Adam Lanza.

While Bell’s estimates are frequently cited, academic research suggests the price discount effect on stigmatized properties may fade over time.

A 2020 study of Tokyo apartment buildings by economist Taisuke Sadayuki found that a homicide in one unit initially cut rents on other units in the same building by about 10 percent, with the effect disappearing after roughly seven to eight years.

Survey data suggests buyers may also be less squeamish than agents assume. In a 2023 Zillow survey, 67 percent of prospective buyers said they could be persuaded to buy a “haunted” house with the right features, location or price.

When Inman covered stigmatized homes more than a decade ago, we framed them as bargains. The market has changed a lot since then.

Rebecca Chambliss, an agent with Carmody Real Estate in the Santa Monica, California, area, recently sold a home in a gated community where the previous owner had died by suicide only a few months before it was listed. All of the neighbors knew.

Chambliss disclosed the death to serious buyers who were discussing an offer. In her experience, buyers don’t spread out along a spectrum of tolerance. They split into two groups.

“Some people will never buy a home where a suicide or other non-natural death occurred no matter what, and then there are people who it doesn’t bother,” Chambliss told Inman. “There aren’t people in between.”

One interested buyer made an unexpected offer. When Chambliss disclosed the death, he demanded to know exactly where in the house it happened and how. Chambliss had chosen not to learn those details herself and told him as much. He wouldn’t move forward without them and withdrew the offer.

The home did eventually sell at a discount because of the suicide, Chambliss said. The buyer understood that he’d have to disclose the death if he ever sold. He relisted it about a year later, asking $1 million more than he paid, and the home still hasn’t sold.

Chambliss also brought in an energy clearer before marketing the home. It’s a reminder that for some agents, handling a stigmatized listing takes more than paperwork.

The discount doesn’t always stay with the property. Sometimes a savvy investor who knows about it collects it.

Jonathan Carcone, principal of 4 Brothers Buy Houses and a licensed agent in Washington state, bought a home in Poulsbo, Washington, with local ghost stories attached.

He said the home was listed at $640,000, while comparable homes were selling for about $650,000. Carcone said the listing didn’t mention ghost stories, but neighbors told him about them.

Carcone used the ghost stories in negotiations and bought the house for $585,000, about 9 percent below list and roughly 10 percent below comps.

Carcone’s company buys, renovates and sells dozens of houses every year, including “challenging properties.” After renovating the house in Poulsbo, he sold it for $660,000 about two months later.

“The ghost stories had no influence on the sale, and we made a good profit,” Carcone told Inman.

He said Washington law doesn’t require agents to disclose a home’s reputation, including ghost stories, so he didn’t. No buyer asked about it during showings, either. So, in this case, Carcone used the stigma to his advantage.

Because the resale price reflects a renovation, it isn’t a clean before-and-after comparison. Still, the pattern is worth noting. The seller absorbed a 10 percent discount for the stigma, and the next buyer paid none.

What agents must disclose for stigmatized properties varies widely by state.

California sets a three-year line. Under California Civil Code Section 1710.2, sellers and agents aren’t required to disclose a death that occurred on the property more than three years before a buyer’s offer. They also can’t be sued for staying silent. Whether it must be disclosed depends on whether it’s material, and the common practice is to disclose to be safe.

Answering a direct question is a separate matter. The law doesn’t protect anyone who lies when asked.

“The main point of contention between sellers and buyers is whether answering questions truthfully violates the seller’s wishes,” Nick Heimlich, founder and attorney of San Jose, California-based Nick Heimlich Law, told Inman. “Under California Civil Code, a seller’s agent cannot refuse to answer questions about the property’s history.”

Texas Property Code Section 5.008(c) says a seller or seller’s agent has no duty to disclose a death on the property from natural causes, suicide or an accident unrelated to the property’s condition. But not homicide, which may still be a material fact that must be disclosed.

Tennessee goes further. Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-5-207 lists a homicide, felony or suicide on the property among the things sellers don’t have to disclose. It also covers any act or occurrence that didn’t affect the property’s physical structure.

Ghost stories bring their own risk. In the famous case of Stambovsky v. Ackley (1991), a New York appellate court let a buyer back out of buying an allegedly haunted home in Nyack, New York.

The seller had publicized the ghost stories herself in Reader’s Digest and the local press, then didn’t tell the out-of-town buyer. In effect, the court held that because she’d told everyone else the house was haunted, it was haunted as a matter of law.

Donald Leeth, managing partner at Leeth & Gaglione, has spent 27 years as a criminal defense attorney and former prosecutor in Monroe County, Pennsylvania, and the Poconos. During that time, he’s encountered many homes where crimes took place. He advises disclosing rather than gambling on the legal minimum.

“It’s always best to be honest up front so you’re not dealing with misrepresentation claims once your transaction has closed,” Leeth said.

The more interesting question for 2026 is whether affordability is eroding the discount stigmatized listings usually have.

Median prices for new and existing homes now both top $400,000, according to Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies. Existing-home prices have climbed 54 percent nationwide since 2020 and sit at nearly five times median income, well above the 3-to-1 ratio that held in the 1990s.

Leeth thinks the affordability crisis is negating the discount effect on stigmatized listings.

“Many buyers won’t care if there’s an infamous story behind a house because they simply don’t have other options,” he said. “Stigma isn’t as much of a factor as it once was because the price will determine what someone buys.”

That fits with Chambliss’s two-camp theory. If the buyers who’ll never consider a stigmatized home stay out no matter what, the discount depends on how many buyers are left in the other camp. In a tight, low-inventory market, more buyers are in that camp, and they may have fewer alternatives.

Heimlich said the type of event still matters. Buyers might shrug at a home that sat empty for a long time, he said, but something like a murder “can severely influence the property value.”

Still, he added, it likely depends on the market. And if stigma leads to a bargain, that helps, too.

“Some buyers may be willing to invest in stigmatized real estate if it falls within an affordable price range,” Heimlich said.

For agents, the practical takeaway is that a stigmatized listing’s real challenge is finding the buyers who don’t care, not pricing in a fixed discount, and disclosing in a way that doesn’t create legal exposure after closing.

Sometimes the stigma bothers the buyer’s friends and family more than the buyer themselves.

Years ago, Chambliss, the California-based agent, sold a home where a murder had taken place in the front yard. The buyer was a young single father whose Italian immigrant parents were involved in the buying process and may have been helping with the purchase. Chambliss took him outside and told him what had happened there.

He became very concerned, then immediately asked, “Do you have to tell my parents?”

His whole body relaxed, and he laughed. Then he said, “OK, I have no issue with it. But my parents would never let me buy this house if they knew.”

He bought the house, and Chambliss assumed he never told them.

#5518. Enterprises bring AI to their data as privacy rules tighten and costs climb

Every enterprise AI strategy eventually comes down to the same question: Should proprietary data travel to the model, or should the model come to the data?

“Rather than saying, ‘Just give us all your data and we’ll in return provide you access to a model that’s then contextualized based on that data,’ we turn things around,” Stoop said. “We say, ‘We’ll bring AI to where the data is and where the data lives.'”

Stoop spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight and Paul Gillin at Cloudera EVOLVE26, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how enterprises can bring AI to their data while maintaining control and managing costs. (* Disclosure below.)

Cloudera’s latest move in that direction is a partnership with Mistral AI SAS, which brings Mistral’s models into Cloudera’s data platform. For European customers in particular, the model maker’s local roots matter as much as its technology, Stoop noted.

“Certainly for us in Europe, having a French organization, a local company, that provides these models and provides the complete stack is very attractive for a lot of our customers,” Stoop said. “Mistral was a very easy choice for us to say, ‘Those are the ones that we’re going with.'”

AI is at the top of a maturity curve that starts with sovereign data, sovereign cloud and local operations, according to Stoop. Rules such as the European Union’s Digital Operational Resilience Act and the U.S. CLOUD Act are pushing organizations to prove they have control rather than simply claim it. But control alone won’t move AI out of the pilot phase. For many companies, the bigger obstacle in an enterprise AI strategy is the cost of running models at scale, because generating tokens takes a lot of hardware.

“If you use a public provider for that, the more you use your model, the more you get hit on cost,” Stoop said. “How do I get that high utilization of a good model inside my organization without being exposed to horrific costs? That, I think, is the biggest challenge that organizations are struggling with right now.”

#5517. Commission settlement accounts hold $711M as claim payouts await (EXCLUSIVE)

New disclosures show that the settlement fund accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026.

That’s how much money was held in accounts associated with the sweeping real estate commission antitrust settlements as of Sept. 30, according to newly filed federal court documents offering a fresh look at the money from the nationwide agreements.

The disclosures, filed Thursday in federal court in Missouri, show that the accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026, while roughly $5.8 million was transferred out during the same period.

The filings also come amid an ongoing court-ordered audit of settlement administrator JND Legal Administration, which reported earlier this year that it had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions.

The financial accounting follows a series of appellate rulings upholding the commission settlements, although questions remain about when eligible homesellers will receive payments.

According to a declaration signed Oct. 13 by Isaac Lim, a senior vice president and senior risk officer at Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, and filed by plaintiffs Oct. 29, the settlement accounts had a combined balance of $711,251,720.86 as of Sept. 30.

The funds were transferred from Huntington Bank to Morgan Stanley on Oct. 23, 2025, at class counsel’s direction.

Lim reported that $17,705,101.82 in interest was paid into the accounts between January and September 2026, while $5,780,467.43 was transferred out during the same period. The declaration does not identify the purpose of those transfers or establish whether any money has been distributed directly to eligible homesellers.

According to the filing, the money is invested in a BlackRock institutional money market fund yielding about 3.63 percent annually, Morgan Stanley’s preferred savings program paying 4 percent or a combination of both. The yields are estimates and subject to change.

The reported balance represents funds held in the identified Morgan Stanley accounts, rather than necessarily the full amount collected through the broader commission settlements. The declaration does not provide a complete accounting of earlier distributions, expenses or outstanding settlement contributions.

In a June declaration, Jennifer Keough, CEO of JND Legal Administration, said the company had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions. In June 2025, more than 2.5 million claims had already been submitted, while JND had invoiced approximately $32.8 million for its administrative work.

Keough said JND’s original assignment expanded into six separate notification campaigns involving more than 138 million emails and 44 million postcards. Four of those direct-mail campaigns cost about $18.7 million in postage alone, which JND characterized as a pass-through expense.

In May, Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Bough ordered JND to stop receiving payments while the court considered appointing a special master to audit the company’s past and future bills.

On July 27, the judge appointed Chris Hellums and Randall Sansom as special masters.

Hellums was tasked with overseeing the audit and helping establish future administration arrangements, while Sansom, a certified public accountant, was directed to audit JND’s billing and expenses dating back to the beginning of its work.

The order requires JND to provide detailed financial records, including employee timesheets, vendor invoices, billing records and information about rebates, credits or other financial incentives.

JND opposed the need for an independent audit, arguing in a June filing that the process would be expensive and burdensome and that its work had been performed appropriately. The company said it would cooperate if the audit proceeded, but requested confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive pricing information.

JND also said its responsibilities had expanded substantially at class counsel’s direction and that it had advanced nearly $3 million in out-of-pocket costs on behalf of the class.

The dispute escalated in August when JND sought to disqualify Hellums, alleging he had demonstrated bias against the company through his involvement in a separate antitrust settlement proceeding.

Bough denied the motion Aug. 26, finding that JND, as a nonparty, could not seek disqualification under the applicable rules. He added that even if JND could bring the challenge, it had failed to establish sufficient grounds to question Hellums’ impartiality.

The ruling also examined a question Hellums had raised in the Blue Cross Blue Shield case about potential vendor rebates and credits, which Bough said JND never answered in its email exchange with him and only partly addressed at the Aug. 20 hearing. Keough acknowledged at the hearing that separate vendor agreements govern how rebates and credits are calculated.

JND has maintained in sworn declarations that it has received no rebates, credits or other financial benefits from banks or vendors in connection with the commission settlements.

In its latest accounting, JND reported $155,932 in additional administrative invoices covering July through September, bringing the outstanding balance shown on its October invoice to $494,249.

Keough said JND continues submitting invoices and performing administrative work despite not currently receiving payments.

JND did not respond to Inman’s request for comment by the time of publication.

Despite a series of appellate rulings upholding the real estate commission settlements, it remains unclear when eligible homesellers can expect to receive payments.

On Aug. 19, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit unanimously upheld the landmark Sitzer | Burnett settlement, rejecting seven appeals challenging its scope, fairness and accompanying industry practice changes.

The court subsequently affirmed another $110.6 million in brokerage settlements in the related Gibson litigation on Sept. 1, bringing the total collected for the class to about $1.02 billion, according to the appellate opinion.

After rejecting three additional objector appeals on Sept. 15 and denying rehearing petitions from objectors Robert Friedman and Monty March on Sept. 24, the 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the main Sitzer | Burnett appeals Oct. 2, concluding those proceedings before the appeals court. Objectors may still seek review from the U.S. Supreme Court.

The 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the Gibson appeals Oct. 14.

Despite those developments, the latest financial disclosures do not establish when eligible homesellers will receive distributions or precisely how much of the $711 million held in Morgan Stanley accounts is available for payment.

Eric Dirks, an attorney with the Kansas City-based Williams Dirks Dameron, one of the plaintiffs’ co-lead counsel firms, did not respond to Inman’s request for comment regarding the account balance, interest earnings and anticipated distribution timeline.
