#5499. Seoul National University of Science and Technology Researchers Develop New AI-Assisted Pipeline to Identify Errors in Construction Design Documents

Researchers have developed an AI-assisted pipeline to detect human errors in structural design documents, improving reliability and consistency

SEOUL, South Korea, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Construction projects rely on collaboration between different stakeholders. Traditional document-based collaboration can lead to inconsistencies and errors due to the varying tools used by different authors. In a new study, researchers have developed an AI-assisted pipeline that automatically extracts, organizes, and compares structural information across different documents, identifying human errors without using building information modeling. This will be particularly beneficial for small- and medium-sized construction projects that cannot implement expensive digital tools.

Collaboration is crucial in construction, but document inconsistencies can cause costly delays. While Building Information Modeling (BIM) helps, high costs and technical barriers often leave projects reliant on traditional document-based collaboration, risking miscommunications between stakeholders.

When stakeholders use different tools and formats, discrepancies often arise between structural calculation documents and drawings: human errors that can severely compromise building safety. Preventing such errors, therefore, requires meticulous management.

To alleviate this burden, a research team led by Associate Professor Jaewook Jeong from the Department of Safety Engineering at Seoul National University of Science and Technology in South Korea, has now developed a new artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted automated pipeline for detecting human errors in structural design documents. "Our AI-assisted framework automatically extracts, organizes, and compares information from structural calculation documents and drawings to identify inconsistencies that may result from human error. Importantly, the system performs these checks without relying on BIM, making it particularly relevant to construction projects that continue to use conventional design documents," explains Dr. Jeong. Their study was made available online on October 13, 2026, and published in Volume 185 of Engineering Applications of Artificial Intelligence on December 01, 2026.

The proposed automated pipeline first prunes low-quality data and standardizes information. For calculation documents, it uses layout analysis and optical character recognition (OCR) models to extract structural member data. For drawings, it uses OCR and computer vision techniques to locate, filter, and standardize table regions containing member codes.

Using member codes and directions as identifiers, the system cross-validates data, detects errors, and flags duplicates. The researchers deployed this pipeline through a user-friendly, web-based application.

In a South Korean residential project case study, extraction accuracies reached 95.56% for calculations and 90.47% for drawings. Verification identified 253 discrepancies, including 224 missing entries, 18 reinforcement mismatches, eight dimensional discrepancies, and three duplicates, proving the framework's verification potential.

"Our AI-assisted pipeline could help structural engineers, design consultants, contractors, and construction supervision teams to identify discrepancies before they lead to construction errors, improving reliability of buildings and infrastructure," notes Dr. Jeong, emphasizing its value for projects unable to implement BIM.

This innovative framework reduces manual checking burdens and could integrate into routine engineering workflows, making advanced safety technologies more accessible for small- and medium-sized projects.

#5497. CertiK Verified 40.68M TPS for Sui, Here Is What It Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The biggest throughput figure a blockchain security firm has ever signed off on is sitting on CertiK's homepage right now: 40.68 million transactions per second.

It isn't CertiK's own number, and it isn't an on-chain number either. If you read the 2,000-word report behind it, you'll come to become more interested in what CertiK chose not to verify than in what it did.

Scroll past the client logos and media mentions on CertiK and you'll find it in the "Latest Research And Market Insights" strip. One card says CertiK independently verified Sui's Mainnet Tunnel performance campaign, which recorded more than 15.2 billion off-chain transactions across 7,680 tunnels at a peak of 40.68 million TPS.

Most readers will see "CertiK" next to "40.68 million TPS" and stop there. Crypto social media mostly did the same. Sui's own post described the figure as set live on stage at Sui Basecamp 2026 and certified by CertiK, and added that the network now clears in under 20 seconds what Visa processes in a day.Walking through CertiK's verification method when the report first came out. Now that the number has been promoted to CertiK's front page, it's worth looking at exactly what it represents.

According to CertiK's announcement, Sui ran a live Mainnet performance campaign on October 7, 2026, during Sui Basecamp Day. It recorded 15,241,348,297 tunnel transactions across 7,680 tunnels, and every tunnel was opened and settled on chain.

A Sui Tunnel works roughly like a private room. A small group of participants carries out many application actions without sending each one to the blockchain. Sui records the starting terms when the tunnel opens and the final result when it closes. Everything in between happens off-chain as signed receipts. CertiK compares the design to Bitcoin's Lightning Network but notes that tunnels can handle more than payments.

The test was more varied than a single payment loop. The campaign ran 10 runs across five workload types: simple payments, flash, blackjack, tic-tac-toe and battleship. Payments still made up most of the activity. Its 6,144 tunnels committed more than 12 billion transactions, or 78.98% of the total.

This is the part of the report I respect most. The peak came from the busiest complete second, between 08:46:17 and 08:46:18 UTC, when 40,682,328 qualifying tunnel transactions were committed. The highest 60-second rolling average was 40,339,143.65 TPS.

Doing the math on the gap between those two figures. It's about 343,000 transactions, or roughly 0.84%. In other words, the network held near-peak throughput for a full minute rather than spiking for one second.

CertiK also avoided the easiest way to inflate a number like this. For concurrent tunnels sharing the same time window, it added up their transaction counts once and divided by a single shared duration. It did not add individual per-tunnel rates together or multiply one tunnel's rate by the number of tunnels.

The checking itself was thorough. All 7,680 executions and all 960 slots reached VERIFIED status, and the 15.24 billion committed transactions matched the full-history admitted receipts exactly. The work ran on dedicated AWS infrastructure with 128 vCPUs and 247 GiB of RAM.

There's also a small correction in the story. Sui's first announcement reported 40,614,180 TPS. CertiK's audited peak came in about 68,000 higher, a 0.17% difference. A verifier landing slightly above the project's own claim is unusual, and I think it reflects well on the method.

The homepage card doesn't mention any of this, but the full report is clear about its limits.

First, this isn't on-chain throughput. CertiK states that Tunnel TPS measures off-chain tunnel transactions and is not a measurement of Sui's on-chain capacity.

Second, the data came from the project being tested. The Sui team supplied the campaign data and executed all test scenarios, and CertiK examined the retained evidence and recalculated the totals.

Third, the cryptographic checks were not exhaustive. CertiK reconciled the arithmetic, receipt counts and timestamps, but it did not re-run individual signatures or do a fresh cryptographic replay of every receipt.

Fourth, the report can't speak to how the system would behave in normal use. The records don't establish clock accuracy, failure rates, latency percentiles or results across repeated runs. The sustained figure is the best 60-second window observed, not a guaranteed minimum.

Put simply, CertiK verified that the accounting is correct. It did not verify that Sui can handle 40 million real users' actions every second.

The number that's most telling isn't the TPS figure. More than 15.2 billion off-chain transactions were anchored to Sui through just 1,920 on-chain lifecycle transactions: 960 openings and 960 settlements.

By simple calculation, that's about 7.9 million off-chain actions for every on-chain transaction. That ratio is what the tunnel design is built to achieve. It's an impressive engineering result, but it measures how well Sui compresses activity, not how fast its base layer runs.

This isn't the first speed record CertiK has signed off on, and the earlier ones show why comparisons are tricky. In its earlier TON verification, CertiK worked from per-minute transaction count data and arrived at 104,715 TPS for TON's testnet. In April 2025, Qubic announced 15.52 million TPS verified by CertiK, measured over 10 peak ticks on its Layer 1 mainnet.

On paper, Sui's tunnel figure is about 2.6 times Qubic's and nearly 390 times TON's. But these were three different kinds of tests: a sharded testnet, a base-layer burst and an off-chain channel network. They don't belong on the same leaderboard.

My view is that the 40.68 million figure is real, well documented and carefully bounded. It's also a measure of what an off-chain system can process, not what Sui's blockchain itself handles. CertiK's report is honest about that, even if the one-line homepage card isn't.

#5496. Bitcoin Midterm Election Pattern: Will BTC Repeat Its Post-Election Rally?

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin could be approaching another major historical turning point as Americans prepare to vote in the 2026 midterm election. The crypto market has struggled through a difficult October, but previous midterm elections delivered surprisingly strong returns over the following year.

Bitcoin gained an average of 53.7% during the 12 months after the 2014, 2018, and 2022 midterms. With BTC trading at the $78,000 level ahead of the November 3 vote, we are watching to see if history offers another bullish signal.

Bitcoin and its midterm election pattern have coincided with major market transitions. However, the short-term aftermath was often painful and is leaving us with an important question. Could 2026 finally deliver a smoother recovery?

Bitcoin’s performance following the previous three U.S. midterm elections paints a good picture for long-term holders. BTC gained 24.1% during the year following the 2014 election. BTC then advanced 43.4% after the 2018 midterms and 92% following the 2022 vote.

The immediate aftermath also tells a different story. Bitcoin fell 27.5% during the 90 days following the 2014 election and plunged 46.5% after the 2018 vote. The 2022 election delivered a more favorable 90-day return of 22.6%.

These contrasting outcomes show that the Bitcoin midterm election pattern is more compelling over longer periods, not in the short term.

Now, the 2026 election arrives during a different phase of Bitcoin’s market cycle. Previous midterm elections occurred during years when Bitcoin was still approaching major cycle lows. In 2014 and 2018, the crypto market continued falling after Election Day before eventually recovering. The 2022 election also preceded another decline, partly driven by the FTX collapse.

Bitcoin’s current setup could be different if the June low near $57,803 ultimately holds. BTC has already rebounded from that level, potentially placing the market in an early recovery phase heading into the midterms.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

Bitcoin’s relationship with U.S. politics has become increasingly important as Washington shapes the regulatory future of digital assets. From presidential elections to congressional battles, political decisions can influence investor sentiment, institutional demand, and the direction of the crypto market.

The 2024 election offered a clear example, with BTC surging to record highs as Donald Trump’s victory fueled expectations of a more crypto-friendly administration. Bitcoin climbed above $75,000 immediately after the result and continued rallying toward $100,000 in the following weeks.

Regulatory policy is one of the strongest links between Bitcoin and U.S. politics. Investors closely watch the White House, Congress, the SEC, and the CFTC for decisions that could affect exchanges, ETFs, institutional participation, and crypto businesses.

The stalled CLARITY Act has become a major political battleground, with lawmakers divided over market oversight and ethics provisions. When the Senate failed to advance the bill in September, Bitcoin dropped more than 5%, showing how quickly legislative setbacks can influence market sentiment.

🇺🇸 Treasury Secretary Bessent says Treasury will work with the SEC and CFTC to fill the crypto regulation gaps left by the stalled Clarity Act.He called Congress’s failure to pass the bill a disappointment. pic.twitter.com/8JakMNfFEl

Congressional elections also matter because they determine whether crypto legislation can move forward. The industry has poured $176 million into the 2026 midterm races, backing candidates viewed as favorable to digital assets and seeking influence that can survive beyond the current administration.

Politics can also influence Bitcoin through economic policy. Government spending, tariffs, tax changes, and expectations for Federal Reserve policy can move the dollar, Treasury yields, and investor appetite for risk.

Bitcoin often benefits when markets anticipate easier financial conditions or stronger demand for alternative assets, while rising yields and a stronger dollar can pressure speculative investments. This makes U.S. political developments an increasingly important part of Bitcoin’s market outlook, with election results capable of shifting both regulatory expectations and macroeconomic sentiment.

#5495. Marvell to acquire optical component maker Lumentum in massive $115B deal

Marvell Technology Inc. today announced plans to acquire Lumentum Holdings Inc. for $115 billion, in one of the largest deals in tech history.

Lumentum investors are set to receive 4.5 Marvell shares for every unit of stock they own. That translates to about $1,132 per share, which is 23.9% higher than the company’s last unaffected stock price.

Investors, however, weren’t so sanguine about the deal. Marvell’s shares fell almost 13%, while Lumentum’s fell almost 19%. Chalk it up, again, to recent investor worry that the promised growth from artificial intelligence infrastructure may not last forever.

Marvell provides networking equipment for data centers and telecommunications infrastructure. Many of its products use fiber-optic cables to transmit data. Lumentum, in turn, makes components for fiber-optic network devices such as those offered by Marvell. The acquisition will give the latter company more control over its supply chain, which could enable it to more closely align upstream components’ design with its requirements.

Optical networks use laser emitters to generate the light which they transmit data. Lumentum sells a line of lasers based on indium phosphide, a semiconducting material that generates light more efficiently than silicon. The product family includes modular and continuous wave devices. Modulated lasers are used to physically connect servers to the host data center’s optical network, while continuous wave lasers power longer-range network links.

Lumentum also makes single-mode optical amplifiers. Such devices strengthen the laser signals that travel through long-haul carrier networks to reduce data transmission errors.

Last year, the company debuted a laser optimized for co-packaged optics, or CPO, chips. Such chips enable servers to connect to the host data center’s network without expensive modules called transceivers that are usually needed for the task. CPO technology has emerged as an important focus of Marvell’s growth strategy. Its chip design business can help customers integrate CPO modules into their custom artificial intelligence accelerators.

Lumentum doesn’t focus solely on the laser component market. It uses a material called indium gallium arsenide to make analog photodetectors, which customers can use to monitor their optical networks for errors. The company also sells optical circuit switches. Such devices use tiny mirrors to coordinate the flow of traffic, which removes the need to turn data into electrical signals and thereby saves power.

Notably, Lumentum will also give Marvell a presence in the industrial equipment market. The former company makes high-power lasers for cutting and welding machines. It’s unclear what will happen to that part of Lumentum’s product portfolio following the deal. After a large acquisition, companies sometimes spin off newly absorbed business units that don’t align with their core focus.

“By bringing together two leaders with highly complementary technologies, exceptional talent and specialized manufacturing capabilities, we intend to help shape the next era of AI connectivity and create exceptional stockholder value,” said Marvell Chief Executive Officer Matt Murphy.

The chipmaker expects to close the acquisition in the first half of 2028. The combined company will be led by Murphy, while Lumentum CEO Michael Hurlston will join the board along with two of the optical component supplier’s directors.

Marvell expects the deal to become accretive to its adjusted earnings per share within a year of closing. In the longer term, the company hopes to achieve annual run-rate cost savings of more than $1 billion and accelerate revenue growth. Marvell estimates that Lumentum will expand its total addressable market to $550 billion.

#5494. INOX Introduces Smart Multipoint Trim with Slim Architectural Design and Advanced Access Control Capabilities

SACRAMENTO, Calif., Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- INOX, a leading provider of architectural door hardware and security solutions, is pleased to announce the launch of the Smart Multipoint Trim, a commercial-grade exterior mortise lock trim that transforms conventional multipoint locking systems into fully integrated smart access devices. The INOX Smart Multipoint (ISMP) seamlessly integrates advanced electronic access capabilities with a refined, slim escutcheon profile suited for modern architectural applications.

The ISMP provides a practical upgrade path for existing door systems by enabling remote locking, unlocking, and credential management. Compatible with most multipoint lock configurations, this smart trim retrofits compatible 92- and 85-millimeter Center-to-Center American multipoint hardware. European-profile multipoint locks are supported by an included tailpiece cylinder adapter. Engineered as a retrofit solution, the Smart Multipoint converts both lever-high and lever-low multipoint locks into fully integrated smart access systems without requiring complete lock replacement.

Designed for use across upscale commercial, hospitality, and residential environments, the Smart Multipoint is particularly well-suited for applications where aesthetics and performance must coexist. From luxury residential entryways and multifamily developments to wineries and event venues, this lock enhances the visual appeal of double door openings while providing advanced access management functionality. The ISMP is available in nine standard finishes and seventeen solid stainless steel levers.

If required by the existing locking mechanism, a simple and intuitive lift-to-lock action mechanically secures upper and lower vertical locking points. This action also enables Touch-to-Lock, which electronically engages the deadbolt for added security. The ISMP delivers enhanced security with intuitive operation and offers a choice of four mechanical locking functions.  Users can securely manage smartphone, RFID, and passcode credentials while monitoring activity from anywhere with a Wi-Fi gateway.

"The Smart Multipoint Trim reflects our commitment to delivering solutions that combine advanced access management with refined architectural design," said Qianyan Cheng, Co-founder and Vice President at INOX. "We developed a system that not only upgrades existing multipoint doors with smart capabilities, but also meets the demanding expectations of designers and property owners who require both performance and a clean, modern aesthetic."

The Smart Multipoint Trim complements INOX's broader portfolio of smart locking solutions, including mortise, cylindrical, interconnected tubular, smart glass door locks, and more. Together, these products provide a holistic solution for access management, enabling consistent design, scalable control, and improved operational efficiency across residential, commercial, and hospitality environments.

For more information about the INOX Smart Multipoint Trim and other innovative locking solutions, visit www.inoxsmart.com.

#5490. Palantir beats Q3 forecasts as US commercial revenue overtakes government for first time

Shares of Palantir Technologies Inc. rose more than 1% in late trading today after the big-data analytics company beat third-quarter expectations and raised its full-year revenue guidance for the third time this year.

For the quarter that ended on Sept. 30, Palantir reported adjusted earnings per share of 44 cents, up from 21 cents in the same quarter of last year, on revenue of $2.313 billion, up 96% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting earnings of 41 cents per share on revenue of $2.18 billion. It was the first quarter in which Palantir’s revenue topped $2 billion.

U.S. commercial revenue overtook U.S. government revenue for the first time in Palantir’s history. Sales to commercial customers in the U.S. reached $984 million, up 148% from a year earlier and 29% from the second quarter. Government sales rose 96%, to $953 million. Together they took total U.S. revenue to $1.937 billion, up 119% year-over-year.

Palantir closed 212 deals worth at least $1 million in the quarter, including 64 worth $10 million or more. Total contract value rose 6% from a year earlier, to $2.918 billion, after growing 151% in the same period of 2025. U.S. commercial remaining deal value climbed 79%, to $6.517 billion.

Net income more than doubled, to $1.128 billion from $476 million a year earlier, giving the company a 49% net margin. On an adjusted basis, operating income came to $1.427 billion at a 62% margin, and adjusted free cash flow was $1.216 billion. Palantir’s “Rule of 40” score hit 158%. The company ended September holding $10.4 billion in cash, cash equivalents and U.S. Treasury securities.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Alex Karp used the earnings release to argue that what he called the “Sovereign AI movement” is creating “the most dramatic dichotomy between haves and have nots” he has seen in 30 years in business. Governments and companies alike are being forced into one group or the other, “voluntarily or not,” according to Karp. That shift, he said, is “purpose-built for Palantir.”

Looking to the fourth quarter, Palantir expects revenue of $2.649 billion to $2.653 billion and adjusted operating income of $1.640 billion to $1.644 billion. Analysts had forecast fourth-quarter revenue of $2.46 billion.

Full-year revenue guidance now stands at $8.530 billion to $8.534 billion, up from the $8.150 billion to $8.158 billion Palantir forecast in August. Students can check their positioning and interpretation against an AI screening report on each study they submit.

SAN DIEGO, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Vetology Innovations (Vetology), which provides AI screening reports and teleradiology consultations for veterinary practices, today opened its AI screening subscription to veterinary schools and veterinary technology programs free of charge.

More than 163 million dogs and cats live in US households.Â¹ Only about 1,100 veterinarians hold a board certification in diagnostic imaging through the ACVR or ECVDI.Â² That's roughly one for every 150,000 dogs and cats, before counting horses, birds, exotics or any other species. Specialist training takes years, and that gap isn't closing quickly enough.

"As a radiologist-owned company, we care deeply about the diagnostic imaging needs of busy clinicians. It's important to us that the tools we build serve veterinary teams today and in the years to come. We value your professional input, and we want the relationships we form to be part of the road ahead."  -- Eric Goldman, President, Vetology

Students whose education includes the latest imaging technology will gain skill in evaluating how and when AI belongs in their clinical workflow, while instructors are on hand to answer questions and guide their approach. They will carry that judgment into practice as AI screening becomes more common in veterinary imaging.

Each study a student submits builds three key skills: patient positioning, radiograph interpretation, and cross-referencing reports against the images and patient signalment. A well-positioned, well-exposed study produces a more useful report, so students see the effect of their technique case by case. For students who learn best by doing rather than by reading or listening to lectures, comparing the AI report with the images and with their own interpretation offers a hands-on way to build those skills.

Vetology is also soon to be releasing another tool that will support students as they develop their imaging skills. "Perfect Shot" is designed to gently point out a missing view or a positioning issue while there's still time to retake. A case list also lets users work through flagged studies, which suits programs that teach image quality as its own skill. Perfect Shot is coming soon, and Vetology will announce availability closer to release. It will be included as a free add-on when available.

The free subscription covers Vetology's AI screening reports; teleradiology services are not included. Deans, program directors and imaging faculty can sign up at vetology.net/contact-us.

The Vetology AI screening system runs 94 classifiers across canine and feline thoracic, abdominal, and musculoskeletal imaging, built on a foundation of 300,000 multi-image patient cases, with performance data for every classifier published publicly. #5487. Could Social Security turmoil influence senior homeowners and reverse mortgage demand?

A 13% surge in early Social Security retirement claims in 2024–2025, driven by political and administrative turmoil at the agency, temporarily reversed a long-term trend of Americans claiming later. Early filing locks in permanently lower benefits, cutting annual income by thousands of dollars for some retirees. Although claim volumes have since normalized, ongoing uncertainty about Social Security’s 2032 funding cliff is pushing some near-retirees to claim sooner.  AI Summary

A sharp but temporary spike in early Social Security claims in 2024 and 2025 underscores a potential trend for the housing market — a greater number of older Americans who are locking in permanently lower retirement income in response to political and administrative uncertainty.

Over the weekend, The New York Times followed up on a report shared last year by HousingWire‘s Reverse Mortgage Daily (RMD). The initial report from the Times found that from October 2024 to April 2025, retirement claims jumped by 267,000, or 13%, compared with the prior year.

Historically, year-over-year fluctuations have been closer to 2% to 3%. Analysts at the Urban Institute and the Center for Retirement Research at Boston College tied the spike to highly publicized turmoil at the Social Security Administration — including staff cuts, office-closure threats and political rhetoric questioning the program’s solvency.

Social Security claims made before the full retirement age (which is now 67 for those born in 1960 or later) permanently reduces monthly benefits. This week, the Times interviewed two claimants — one who gave up about $5,000 a year by filing at 64 and another who sacrificed about $300 a month by filing more than a year early.

These kinds of benefit cuts compound over time and can directly affect housing affordability, especially for owners or renters whose largest fixed expense is their mortgage or rent payment.

As it relates to housing professionals, including reverse mortgage professionals, lower guaranteed income in retirement can translate into a higher likelihood of mortgage payment stress or default among senior homeowners. It can also propel demand for downsizing, shared housing options or migration to lower-cost markets as retirees adjust to tighter budgets.

Additionally, it can mean increased interest for traditional reverse mortgages and similar home equity release products to backfill income gaps. Borrowers in their late 50s and early 60s may be ideally positioned for these products since Social Security filing decisions are imminent, and because seniors are denied for credit at higher rates than the general population.

From October 2025 to April 2026, new claims fell by 235,000, or 10%, essentially offsetting the prior-year surge. But the reporting shows how headlines about Social Security’s finances can directly change claimants’ behavior.

A Boston College experiment cited by the Times this week found that more alarmist headlines led people to say they would claim about a year earlier than those who saw neutral language — regardless of any changes to the underlying facts.

Without congressional action, Social Security’s retirement trust fund is projected to be depleted by late 2032, triggering an automatic benefit cut of up to 22% under current law. The ongoing uncertainty has made Americans in retirement and near retirement “anxious and unhappy,” according to a source who spoke to the Times. This can impact retirement timing, where they choose to live and how much home they can afford.

Multiple policy ideas are circulating on the Social Security front — including bipartisan proposals to lift or eliminate the current $184,500 cap on wages subject to payroll tax, which could inject about $3 trillion into the system over 10 years. But for now, reverse mortgage companies and other housing stakeholders should pay close attention to how Social Security claiming decisions interact with mortgage terms, home equity levels and long-term retirement planning.

In this week’s Monday Morning Q&A, Larissa Morrell of Longbridge Financial told RMD that the demographics of the typical borrower have shifted during her 20-plus years in the industry.

“Historically, a reverse mortgage was really something for people of the older retiree demographic — late 70s, 80s, 90s. Now we do not have that same demographic. Now we’re looking at people of a younger generation. They’re still working. They might be using a reverse mortgage to pay off credit card debt or cover increasing expenses,” Morrell said.

Federally insured Home Equity Conversion Mortgages and proprietary reverse mortgages could allow a borrower to delay Social Security claims by generating additional cash flow or eliminating monthly mortgage payments.

The Social Security Administration notes that people who begin receiving benefits at the full retirement age of 67 get 100% of the monthly benefit. But that percentage increases for every month payments are delayed and can reach up to 124% if a recipients waits until age 70 to make a claim.

But the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau has also previously reported that the costs of a reverse mortgage generally exceed the additional increase in benefits that a senior would get by delaying claims.

#5485. What Solana’s Alpenglow Switch Actually Changes at Slot 459,653,000

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

For about 400 milliseconds this afternoon, Solana will stop landing user transactions. That isn't a failure.

It's the scheduled handoff between two consensus systems, and it's probably the only "400 ms" figure that matters today.

Many people heading into the Alpenglow launch still treat 400 ms block times and 12.8-second finality as the bar to beat. Those are the old chain's numbers. They describe TowerBFT, the system Alpenglow is replacing, so Alpenglow shouldn't be checked against them. If you go through Solana's own documentation, you'll find the right benchmarks before the first post-launch numbers arrive.

According to Solana's official Alpenglow page, the upgrade's feature gate activates at the start of epoch 1064 on Wednesday, October 21, at about 13:20 UTC. The Solana Foundation says to treat that time as an estimate and to watch the epoch instead.

The new consensus doesn't take over the moment the epoch begins. TowerBFT keeps running for the first 5,000 slots, and Alpenglow takes control at slot 459,653,000. Anza, the team behind the main Agave client, put that switch at around 14:00 UTC.

That time isn't fixed. Solana Compass calculated that with about 375,000 slots left before the switch, each millisecond of drift in average slot time moves the boundary by roughly six minutes. Using epoch 1062's pace, it estimated the switch at about 14:02 UTC.

The transition itself has a cost. Solana Compass reports a gap of roughly two slots, about 400 ms, during which blocks carry only votes and user transactions don't land. So the 400 ms everyone is watching for will turn up, just as a pause rather than a block time.

This is where much of today's coverage gets it wrong.

Block time first. Solana's page says slots moved from 400 ms to 200 ms in a separate "reduced slot times" upgrade, which finished this month. That change isn't part of Alpenglow. It was already running before today. Solana Compass measured epoch 1062 averaging 217.7 ms per slot over 26.1 hours. Checking Alpenglow against 400 ms would mean grading it against a number the network had already beaten before the switch.

Then finality. The 12.8 seconds is TowerBFT's figure. Under that system, a block became final only after enough votes built up over 32 slots. Alpenglow's stated target is about 150 ms, which Solana describes as 99% faster than TowerBFT.

Solana is careful about that 150 ms figure, and I think readers should be too. The Foundation calls it an expectation, not a constant, and says one-round finality comes in lower. Galaxy's engineers, quoted by Solana Compass, call it a design target rather than a measured result. As I noted when looking at how CertiK verifies a TPS claim, a target is a claim until someone measures it on the live network.

Alpenglow is Solana's first replacement of its core consensus since TowerBFT, and today's launch only covers part of it.

The first phase, Votor, ships in Agave 4.3. Validators now send votes directly to each other and combine them into certificates, instead of submitting votes as on-chain transactions. Per Solana's page, votes are no longer transactions and no longer appear in blocks. A block can finalize in one round if at least 80% of stake notarizes it. Otherwise, a second round uses 60% thresholds.

Proof of History no longer paces block production. Execution stays the same: the SVM, programs, transactions and fees don't change.

The second phase, Rotor, will replace Turbine, Solana's block propagation layer. Solana lists it as "not yet scheduled." If someone credits today's numbers to "Alpenglow" as a whole, half of the design hasn't shipped yet.

The security trade-off is also worth knowing. TowerBFT needed more than two-thirds of stake for confirmation. Alpenglow tolerates 20% malicious stake plus 20% offline stake. Solana Compass notes that slashing for double voting is defined but not enabled in this first version.

Validators also pay differently. TowerBFT voting cost about 1 SOL per epoch in vote transaction fees. Alpenglow replaces that with a flat 0.8 SOL per epoch Validator Admission Ticket (SIMD-0357), which is burned. A validator that can't pay doesn't vote or produce blocks in the next epoch.

In my view, this is the detail most likely to affect today's real numbers.

Alpenglow's fastest finality depends on the one-round fast path, which needs at least 80% of stake to notarize a block. On the morning of October 20, a tracker run by Pumpkin's Pool, cited by SolanaFloor and reported by Solana Compass, flagged 151 validators holding 20.3% of stake as unprepared. The day before, that figure was 45%.

The math is uncomfortable. If 20.3% of stake really couldn't vote, only 79.7% would be left, which is just short of the fast-path threshold. In that case, blocks would need the slower second round, and finality would land above the headline figure.

I expect that number to drop before the switch, since operators have been upgrading quickly. But it's the main reason I wouldn't trust any finality figure from the first hour without also checking how much stake is actually voting. Validators without a registered BLS key, or that miss the required client version, stop voting entirely. Their delegators also stop earning inflation rewards.

There's already one public reference point. Solana's page links to a community cluster explorer run by Valid Blocks, where Alpenglow has been running on Agave 4.3.2.

When I checked this morning, it showed an average finalization time of 131 ms over the past hour, ranging from 111 ms to 156 ms. Average slot time was 215 ms. That's inside Solana's target range.

That cluster had 62 active validators and about 10.2 million SOL staked. Mainnet is far larger, more spread out geographically, and runs under real load. Test-cluster results are a strong sign, but they aren't proof of how mainnet will perform.

You don't need to wait for a press release to know whether the switch happened. Solana's getAgGenesisCert RPC method returns null while the cluster is still on TowerBFT and returns a genesis certificate once Alpenglow is live. Nodes older than Agave 4.3 return a "Method not found" error, which shouldn't be confused with null.

Once the certificate shows up, here's what I'll be watching over the first few epochs:

One caveat for developers: according to Anza's operator notes, the Clock sysvar's unix_timestamp now estimates when the parent block ended, not when the current block began, and should be treated as approximate. Any timing tool that reads block timestamps may need adjusting.

If Alpenglow delivers, Solana goes from finality you wait for to finality you'd barely notice. I'll believe the 150 ms figure once mainnet consistently shows it.

#5484. 42AI launches with $62.5M to predict how traders act when markets turn volatile

Israeli artificial intelligence startup 42AI launched today with $62.5 million in funding to build what it calls a behavioral world model.

Its first customers are brokerages that want to know how individual traders will act when markets turn volatile. 42AI offers software that estimates the odds of each choice a person might make in a given situation. “Behavior is not deterministic; it’s constantly probabilistic,” co-founder and Chief Executive Amit Gal-Or told TechCrunch.

The company turns what it knows about a person into mathematical representations of personality traits, and a transformer-based world model works out the probabilities from there. A separate language model writes up which traits and context drove each prediction.

42AI says a brokerage can see what each client is likely to trade over the next 24 hours, including the instrument, the direction and the volume. If clients look set to pile into the same trade, a risk desk can hedge before the exposure lands on its book. Know-your-customer checks done at onboarding are one source of input, and the model also weighs how often a client calls and the sentiment in their voice.

Ten large brokerages are working with 42AI, which charges either a flat fee or a percentage of the value it helps generate. Revenue has reached seven figures, Gal-Or said, without giving a precise number.

By the company’s account, one brokerage gained about $30 million in additional value through dynamic hedging. The company also claims 98% accuracy on trades. That figure tracks whether trading flows land inside a predicted range, according to Gal-Or, and does not measure whether every individual trade was predicted correctly.

Three years of research went into the model. Thousands of people took psychological assessments in the first study, and by the time the team moved on to government and biobank datasets, the sample had passed 2 million. Customer data now spans about 30 million people.

Chief Technology Officer Ehud Ezra and three co-authors described one piece of the work in a paper posted in February. Their Large Behavioral Model adapts an 8 billion-parameter version of Meta Platforms Inc.’s Llama 3.1 to predict a person’s strategic choices from a detailed psychometric profile.

Asked whether a brokerage could turn those predictions against its own clients, Ezra called it “a valid concern.” The founders pointed to regulation, monitoring and an internal ethics committee as checks on that kind of use.

Gaming, fraud prevention and cybersecurity are the next markets 42AI is exploring, with helping robots and AI agents understand people as a longer-term goal. Wherever it runs, the model loses accuracy when it misses outside influences, such as a trader acting on a colleague’s advice. “There’s a natural ceiling because you really don’t have access to everything that a person experiences,” Gal-Or said.

The $62.5 million, which 42AI describes as seed funding, came from the founders and Infinity Group over three years. Amir Gal-Or, the startup’s co-founder and chairman, founded Infinity Group. Dan Shechtman, who won the 2011 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, is among the advisers to the research team. 42AI plans to raise more money.

#5482. Open Real Estate gets a boost from independents — and an opening from MLSs

Open Real Estate said it has secured 826 letters of support from brokerage leaders nationwide, including 493 from independent firms. Several MLS executives publicly welcomed dialogue, positioning the effort as complementary to existing MLS infrastructure.  AI Summary

A week after Open Real Estate, a broker-led initiative to build a shared infrastructure for residential listing data, launched, the initiative announced that it has secured 826 letters of support from real estate brokerage leaders across the country.

Independent firms account for the majority of that backing, with 493 letters, or 59%, coming from independent brokerages, according to an announcement on Monday. Support spans single-office independents to some of the largest independent firms, including Atlanta Communities, Iron Valley Real Estate, LoKation Real Estate and Realty of America, all RealTrends Verified brokerages.

The effort is designed as a national, shared data layer that connects brokerages, agents, multiple listing services and real estate portals. Founding organizations include AGNT Inc. (parent to eXp Realty and NextHome), HomeServices of America, Keller Williams Realty and Real REMAX Group, all RealTrends Verified brokerages.

“We have already received significant interest from across the real estate industry since our announcement, and we look forward to continuing to engage with brokerages of all sizes, MLS organizations and technology providers as we develop a platform that expands consumer choice and transparency for home buyers and sellers,” the founding members of Open Real Estate said in a joint statement.

Open Real Estate’s backers say the project is meant to complement, not replace, existing MLS organizations by expanding access to listing information for brokerages, agents and consumers.

Several prominent MLS executives publicly welcomed collaboration with the initiative.

“We welcome the initiative of Open Real Estate and look forward to actively participating and partnering with industry leaders to build on the capabilities already in place at Bright and advance a more connected, efficient, broker-driven marketplace,” Brian Donnellan, the president and CEO of Bright MLS and a HousingWire Vanguard award winner, said in a statement.

Art Carter, CEO of California Regional MLS (CRMLS), added that the effort aligns with CRMLS’s long-running work to give brokers more flexibility in how they input and manage listing data.

“Strategically, California Regional MLS and Open Real Estate are in alignment with the concept of allowing brokers to bring listing data in from outside the CRMLS MLS Input Platform. It has been a long-term project of CRMLS to allow our brokers to have that ability,” Carter, a HousingWire Vanguard award winner, said in a statement. “We look forward to working with Open Real Estate to see how that possibility comes to fruition within their platform.”

North Texas Real Estate Information Systems (NTREIS) CEO Chris Carrillo framed Open Real Estate as part of a broader conversation about transparency and equal access to listings.

“NTREIS remains dedicated to fostering a transparent, cooperative and neutral marketplace that serves all broker participants equally by delivering consistent listing access and empowering exceptional consumer service. In alignment with this mission, we welcome constructive dialogue with Open Real Estate,” Carrillo said.

And NorthstarMLS President and CEO Tim Dain emphasized that broker-driven projects can coexist with MLSs.

“Broker-led innovation shouldn’t be viewed as a threat to the MLS. It’s an opportunity to strengthen the cooperation that has served our industry for decades,” Dain, also a HousingWire Vanguard award winner, said in a statement. “I hope this initiative brings even more brokers and MLSs to the table.”

The push for a shared listing data infrastructure comes as the industry adapts to rapid changes in how listings are distributed and displayed, ongoing antitrust scrutiny and shifting brokerage business models. Brokerages are looking for more direct control over how their listing data flows to MLSs, portals, internal systems and third-party tools.

Open Real Estate’s founders position the initiative as a way to streamline listing distribution, expand access to housing inventory and support a more open, competitive housing marketplace, particularly as consumer expectations for transparent, real-time listing information continue to rise.

#5481. Could dual licensing grow as agents, LOs seek revenue opportunities?

A RETR analysis identified 3,729 potential matches between real estate agents and mortgage loan officers, highlighting interest in dual licensing as professionals seek additional income. Shawn McNeil, a real estate broker and mortgage originator, said holding both licenses gives him greater control over clients' financing options and another source of revenue.  AI Summary

As mortgage companies and real estate brokerage look for additional revenue to combat difficult housing market conditions, dual licensing offers professionals a way to earn income through the tasks of selling a home and originating a mortgage.

A recently published analysis by RETR identified 3,729 matches between real estate agents and mortgage loan officers in which the agent’s top loan officer shared the agent’s name. California accounted for 40% of these matches, while the top four states (which also include Florida, Texas and Arizona) represented nearly 71% of dual-licensed professionals.

RETR used name matching to identify agents whose top-producing loan officer shared their name. But the analysis does not independently verify dual licensure, and it excludes professionals who hold both licenses but do not originate mortgages for their own clients or primarily work in one role.

For Shawn McNeil, the broker/owner of HomeFlo and a loan officer for Mpire Financial Group, the decision to pursue both licenses came from wanting more control over his clients’ financing options.

After nine years in real estate, McNeil obtained his MLO license about 18 months ago after what he described as feeling frustrated watching friends and high-value clients turn to large lenders and receive unfavorable interest rates.

“I would watch my big, high-dollar, personal friends go to these big-box retailers and just get absolutely crushed with an interest rate,” McNeil said in an interview with HousingWire. “I was like, at first, I’m going to go get licensed so that I can talk through these things and be knowledgeable in this.”

McNeil estimates that his time spent between real estate and loan originating is about 50/50, with most business coming from friends and real estate investors. He occasionally serves as both the agent and lender in a transaction, although he said that is not common.

McNeil believes more real estate agents will pursue MLO licenses as market conditions remain challenging and AI tools make it easier to research mortgage guidelines and loan requirements.

He said agents often hear that loan officers make good partners, but they may not fully understand the mortgage process or what makes a lender a good fit until they gain experience themselves.

“I think more agents are going to realize that the job on the loan officer side is getting easier from a guideline standpoint, and I think that they’re going to more and more convert to doing both over time,” McNeil said.

McNeil clarified that he does not originate every loan for clients who work with his brokerage. He refers borrowers to other lenders when his mortgage company cannot offer a particular program or when a loan falls outside his expertise.

Dual licensing also requires attention to compensation arrangements, the Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act (RESPA), state licensing rules and loan program restrictions.

McNeil said he worked with legal counsel to establish disclosures, which inform all brokerage clients that he is a licensed loan officer and owns the real estate brokerage, regardless of whether they use his mortgage services.

“We require 100% disclosure. … Even if you’re not using my services, we still disclose to you that I am a licensed loan officer and I own the real estate brokerage,” he said, adding that his clients receive the disclosures electronically before a transaction goes under contract.

RETR’s analysis does not establish whether dual licensing is becoming more common or how profitable the model is. But McNeil expects more agents to consider it as they look for additional income opportunities.

“I just hope that the trend continues and more and more realize that there’s a huge opportunity to do both,” he said.

#5480. Visit Santa Barbara Partners With Mindtrip to Personalize Travel Discovery

New AI-powered website experience delivers personalized trip planning and insights into traveler intent

SANTA BARBARA, Calif., Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Visit Santa Barbara, the official destination marketing organization for the Santa Barbara South Coast region, has partnered with Mindtrip, an AI-powered travel platform, to bring personalized trip planning to the area's travel website: SantaBarbaraCA.com.

As travelers increasingly turn to AI to plan trips around their interests, the new integration transforms Visit Santa Barbara's destination content into a conversational planning experience. From exploring the palm-lined coast to discovering the ARTS District and Santa Barbara Urban Wine Trail, travelers can build trips around what matters most to them.

"Travel planning is becoming increasingly personalized and we want to make sure Santa Barbara is meeting travelers wherever and however they choose to discover their next trip," said Kathy Janega-Dykes, president/CEO of Visit Santa Barbara. "Mindtrip allows us to showcase the breadth of experiences across the region while helping visitors create itineraries that feel uniquely their own."

These insights go beyond traditional travel inspiration, reflecting the practical decisions that shape a trip. Drawing on Visit Santa Barbara's destination content and local expertise, Mindtrip helps travelers turn specific questions into actionable itineraries. Along the way, it can introduce visitors to businesses and experiences they might otherwise overlook.

These conversations give Visit Santa Barbara insight into what travelers want to experience, helping the organization better connect visitors with relevant offerings across the destination.

"AI is changing how travelers find information, but the quality of destination knowledge behind it matters," said Andy Moss, co-founder and CEO of Mindtrip. "By bringing Visit Santa Barbara's local expertise into the planning process, we can help travelers move beyond generic recommendations and discover individualized experiences."

The partnership also connects marketing campaigns with personalized trip planning. Visit Santa Barbara's Third Night Free program, for example, can inspire travelers to extend their stay, with Mindtrip prompts suggesting additional experiences to fill an extra day and encouraging further exploration across the destination.

Visitors can access Mindtrip's integration directly on SantaBarbaraCA.com through a chat window that slides out from the side of the screen or through a dedicated link in the website's navigation menu.

Mindtrip is available now at SantaBarbaraCA.com.

Visit Santa Barbara enhances quality of life for Santa Barbara South Coast residents through inspiring visitation that fosters sustainable economic growth, managing the region's reputation and supporting the vibrancy of our diverse communities. Visit Santa Barbara is a nonprofit 501(c)(6) organization funded by the South Coast Tourism Business Improvement District, hospitality industry members and grants from the City of Santa Barbara and the County of Santa Barbara. Visitor spending exceeds $2.24 billion annually, supporting more than 15,000 local jobs and generating $82.9 million in tax revenue, according to tourism research firm Future Partners.

Mindtrip is your personal travel assistant, one that knows you, works for you and keeps you one step ahead. Powered by agentic AI and travel-specific intelligence, Mindtrip learns what matters to you, remembers it from one trip to the next and helps you plan, book and navigate every stage of your journey with greater confidence. Mindtrip also powers AI experiences on destination, hotel and travel brand websites, helping partners deliver more personalized traveler experiences. Founded in 2023 in Silicon Valley by serial entrepreneurs with a proven track record of bringing innovative technology products to market, Mindtrip was built on the belief that travel should start with you, not just where you're going. Learn more at Mindtrip.ai.

#5479. Anthropic’s quarterly revenue jumps to $17B, losses grow ahead of IPO

Anthropic PBC today published an updated version of the S-1 filing for its upcoming public offering.

The original document, which the company released last Monday, didn’t contain its third-quarter financial results. The new version reveals that Anthropic generated $17 billion in revenue during the three months ended Sept. 30. That’s more than 11 times more than what it made a year earlier, but represents a deacceleration in quarter-over-quarter growth. Anthropic’s top line grew 47% on a quarterly basis, down from 144% three months earlier.

The artificial intelligence provider faces multipronged competition from open-source models, OpenAI Group PBC and tech giants such as Google LLC. The Alphabet Inc.’s newest model, Gemini 4 Carbon, outperforms Claude Opus 5.5 across multiple benchmarks.

Anthropic is investing heavily in training infrastructure to stay ahead of the competition. The company took a $5 billion charge in the third quarter because demand for computing hardware was higher than expected, which required it to purchase hardware at a premium. Hardware bought on short notice is more expensive than Anthropic’s usual capacity commitments, which it books 12 to 18 months before they’re needed.

The AI provider also took a $2 billion charge in connection with its non-cash employee donation matching program. That left Anthropic with a $536 million operating loss at the end of the third quarter. Three months earlier, it posted $974 million in operating income. Anthropic’s adjusted operating income, which excludes stock-based compensation and charitable contributions, jumped by $300 million on a quarterly basis to $2.5 billion.

The company had $895.4 billion in outstanding infrastructure commitments as of Sept 30. Leases signed with Google LLC and Broadcom Inc. accounted for nearly a third of that sum. In April, the two companies agreed to supply Anthropic with several gigawatts of computing power powered by the search giant’s TPU chips, which Broadcom helped design. The AI provider also has computing deals with Amazon.com Inc., Oracle Corp. and SpaceX Technologies Corp. that are each worth more than $100 billion.

Anthropic plans to not only rent more computing capacity but also build its own data centers. The company’s purchase commitments jumped from $55 billion at the end of 2025 to about $314 billion in the third quarter.

Alongside the new financial figures, Anthropic’s revised S-1 filing provides an update about its efforts to mitigate AI risks. According to the document, the company is considering “to require human review and approval of certain” research tasks that are currently performed automatically by its models. It believes that its models will soon be capable of “dramatically” accelerating AI development.

Anthropic hasn’t yet disclosed how much it plans to raise through its public offering. According to Bloomberg, the company hopes to at least match the $86.2 billion that SpaceX pulled in when it listed its shares earlier this year. Reuters reported that Anthropic is seeking a valuation of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion.

#5478. Real estate is moving toward more data privacy. Appraisers say UAD 3.6 is moving the other way

UAD 3.6 takes effect Monday, requiring appraisers to use dropdown selections that standardize property details sent to the GSEs. Appraisers are focused on Certification 25, which expands downstream rights to store, analyze, and distribute report data, including interior photos.  AI Summary

Monday marks the implementation date of UAD 3.6, which requires appraisers to select specific data points from dropdown menus for every feature of a property, as opposed to writing text descriptions of the home as they previously did, increasing the amount of detail included in appraisal reports delivered to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac.

Within UAD 3.6 is the new Certification 25, which has generated quite the buzz among appraisal professionals.

Certification 25, which was established by the government sponsored entities (GSEs), expands the data reuse beyond the parameters set in UAD 2.6, which included Certification 21, which largely governed who could receive or distribute a physical appraisal report.

Under Certification 25, entities that receive appraisal reports like lenders, GSEs, secondary market participants and data collection services to store, copy, reproduce, analyze, use and distribute all data within the report, including interior photos and property details, for internal or external purposes without needing the appraiser’s further consent.

While the certification does state that the appraiser and supervisory appraiser bear no liability for any use of the report outside of the specific mortgage finance transaction, appraisers are still concerned about this change and how it could impact their relationship with brokerages and real estate professionals.

In posts on social media and articles written on Appraisers Blog, Desiree Mehbod, a Virginia-based appraiser, has raised concerns about what would happen if interior photos of a child’s bedroom with the property address are leaked, reproduced and shared, ultimately ending up on the dark web.

But the ability for downstream actors to have access to data like this is not new. According to Frank Gregoire, a Florida-based appraiser, Certification 25 is fairly similar to the statute it is replacing, Certification 21.

“Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac maintain a proprietary database about every single dwelling that has ever had a loan on it,” Gregoire said. “So, the ability for downstream users to have access to that data has been there since these forms were introduced in the early 2000s. But, what is new is that it now specifies that the appraiser is aware that some parties may be using the data from their reports without their permission.”

While Ryan Lundquist agrees that this is the only primary change with Certification 25, he still finds it incredibly concerning.

“They can take the information and share it with whoever they want and the appraiser doesn’t have any control over that,” Lundquist, a Sacramento-based appraiser, said. “I know a lot of appraisers feel conflicted about that as it feels like it puts appraisers in a tough spot where a blank check to mine whatever data they want exists.”

Lundquist said he would love to know who this information will be shared with or sold to.

Gregoire is also concerned about appraisers including copyrighted data, such as images in the MLS in their report.

“If the appraiser is an MLS participant, they are using that information under license and they are permitted to use it to support their valuation, but that is it, they cannot grant someone else the right to use that information and that is what’s happening with Certification 25,” he said.

It is concerns like these that lead appraisers to say the discussion around Certification 25 is not over yet.

“I don’t think it will sit well with a lot of people in real estate when they read or begin to understand how and where this data may be used,” Lundquist said.

In addition, Mehbod said Certification 25  is why she and other like-minded appraisers have chosen to stop doing appraisal work for the GSEs. If a homebuyer wants their loan to close they have no choice but to allow the appraiser to generate a report, which Mehbod said will create “massive animosity right at the front door.”

“It positions the appraiser as a forced data collector rather than an independent expert,” she said. “This friction damages public trust and opens a legal minefield for our profession, leaving appraisers highly vulnerable to consumer complaints and lawsuits from angry borrowers when transactions get messy over data harvesting policies they never wanted to participate in.”

With UAD 3.6 just beginning to go into effect, it remains to be seen if anything regarding Certification 25 will change or how consumers and real estate brokers, agents and MLSs will respond.

#5477. From TikTok Virality to Amazon Recognition: SUNGBOON EDITOR Is Emerging as a K-Beauty Brand to Watch

The fast-growing Korean skincare brand turns creator-driven buzz into broader consumer demand, achieving 32.4% year-over-year Amazon sales growth and earning a 2026 Amazon Innovator Award.

LOS ANGELES, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- In an industry where viral trends come and go, Korean skincare brand SUNGBOON EDITOR is showing how social media momentum can translate into sustained retail growth.

Following the viral success of its Silk Peptide EGF Toner on TikTok, the brand achieved 32.4% year-over-year revenue growth during Amazon Prime Big Deal Days 2026 and was named one of just three recipients of the 2026 Amazon Innovator Award.

The brand's success reflects more than a single viral product. Growing demand across its skincare portfolio signals its emergence as a rising player in global K-Beauty.

From TikTok Sensation to Cross-Platform Success

SUNGBOON EDITOR's momentum began with its Silk Peptide EGF Toner, organically nicknamed "TOX TONER" by TikTok beauty creators. Formulated with silk peptides and EGF, the toner quickly gained attention for its ingredient-driven approach to improving the appearance of fine lines and skin texture.

On September 8, 2026, SUNGBOON EDITOR ranked No. 1 in Skincare by revenue on U.S. TikTok Shop, while reaching No. 3 in the overall Beauty category. Its toner maintained the No. 1 position in TikTok Shop's Toners category from August 15 through October 21.

By October 13, the toner had climbed to No. 4 in Amazon U.S. Facial Toners & Astringents, with demand temporarily exceeding available inventory and resulting in pre-order availability.

Beyond One Viral Product: Strong Amazon Growth

During Amazon Prime Big Deal Days (October 6â7, 2026), SUNGBOON EDITOR recorded a 32.4% year-over-year revenue increase and 40.8% growth in units sold.

Notably, the brand's best-selling product was not its viral toner. The Silk Peptide EGF Intensive Ampoule led unit sales, followed by the Deep Collagen Power Boosting Cream In Serum, demonstrating growing consumer demand across the brand's broader skincare portfolio.

This performance highlights SUNGBOON EDITOR's ability to turn creator-driven discovery into cross-product demand and broader commercial growth.

On October 27, SUNGBOON EDITOR was recognized as one of three Amazon Innovator Award recipients at the Amazon Beauty in Seoul 2026 K-Beauty Global Conference.

Part of the 2026 Amazon Top Brand Awards, the distinction recognizes outstanding product innovation, successful collaboration with Amazon, and strong commercial performance.

"K-Beauty is evolving beyond a temporary trend and establishing itself as a global industry," said Hwa Sook Shin, CEO of Amazon Global Selling Korea. "Amazon has become a key channel for the global growth of Korean beauty companies."

"Viral moments may introduce consumers to a brand, but lasting growth comes from products they genuinely believe in and continue to choose," said Haelee Park, Brand Marketing Team Lead, North America & Europe Division 1, Olive International.

"What's particularly exciting is that our growth is no longer driven by just one viral product. We're seeing strong consumer demand across our portfolio, from collagen to peptides and EGF. Being recognized as an Amazon Innovator is an important milestone, but we're only getting started. Our ambition is to build SUNGBOON EDITOR into one of the most recognized and trusted K-Beauty brands globally."

Looking ahead, SUNGBOON EDITOR will continue investing in ingredient-driven innovation, consumer engagement, and global market expansion.

From TikTok discovery to Amazon recognition, the brand's trajectory demonstrates how K-Beauty can turn viral attention into lasting consumer demand and long-term growth.

SUNGBOON EDITOR is a Korean skincare brand under Olive International, built on the philosophy of "Ingredient-Edited Skincare." "SUNGBOON" means "ingredient" in Korean, reflecting the brand's commitment to carefully selected formulations designed to deliver visible results.

Guided by its philosophy, "Fine Ingredients. Edited for Effect.", SUNGBOON EDITOR continues to bring innovative, ingredient-driven skincare to consumers worldwide.

#5476. Rack-scale AI: How Dell and AMD are building infrastructure

Dell Technologies Inc. and its partner Advanced Micro Devices Inc. face similar competitive pressures. Both tech powerhouses operate in a business climate where success is now measured across central processing units, graphics processing units, rack-scale systems, memory capacity, network bandwidth and tokens per dollar.

The pressure to compete across those measures underscores what theCUBE Research has termed “Engineering Velocity.” Since the Dell Technologies World event in May, AMD and Dell have not slowed their pace of collaborations and announcements.

AMD and Dell are working to build enterprise AI infrastructure that can keep pace with changing workloads and customer requirements.

“In AI infrastructure, the winner may not be the company with the best benchmark on keynote day,” said theCUBE Research’s Dave Vellante. “It will more likely be the company whose engineering system learns, validates and improves the entire platform faster than anyone else.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of the architectural shifts powering continuous, production-grade AI. Be sure to check out theCUBE’s “Dell AI Data Platform Event: From Ambition to AI at Scale” and its past coverage of this year’s Dell Technologies World. (* Disclosure below.)

A cornerstone of the Dell and AMD relationship is the server giant’s PowerEdge portfolio. Dell expanded its PowerEdge server line in May and has followed that up with additional details surrounding the integration of AMD processors.

The two companies have pursued a strategy designed to facilitate server consolidation as agentic AI drives a surge in demand for general-purpose compute. Agents rely heavily on CPUs, yet data centers don’t have a lot of extra room to add servers in rooms already stacked with GPUs.

Systems powered by AMD processors will deliver 70% gen-over-gen performance gains and can fold 13 servers from Dell’s 14th PowerEdge generation into one, according to Pradyumna Narendra, product planner and senior consultant at Dell.

“For every 10 to 13 servers you replace, you get so much of that productivity gain back because now you can do that with one server,” he told theCUBE. “When you expand that across data centers, that’s like an accelerating effect that you get to capitalize from.”

Dell and AMD must also accommodate a wealth of AI use cases and the accompanying demand for compute. Dell’s three-rack-unit server requires less power for cooling than a two-unit equivalent, allowing customers to pack more computing power into each rack, according to Narendra.

“By deploying servers that are slightly larger in package, you deliver more density at a rack level, which seems sometimes counterintuitive,” he explained. “As AI accelerates, inferencing and agentic AI around it will accelerate and grow faster. As these use cases scale out, you get exponential growth in the need for compute.”

Beyond server consolidation, Dell and AMD have been steadily enhancing a modular solution to simplify AI deployment and scaling: the Dell AI Platform with AMD.

The on-premises enterprise AI solution integrates AMD Instinct accelerators and EPYC processors with Dell PowerEdge servers, PowerSwitch networking and PowerScale storage for model training, fine-tuning and high-throughput inference. The platform is designed to let customers begin with configurations that meet current workloads and expand compute and GPU density over time, without rearchitecting.

“What we’re finding is customers want modular solutions. They want to think about [solutions] across the whole platform,” said Varun Chhabra, senior vice president of product marketing and infrastructure solutions group at Dell, in a discussion with theCUBE. “Compute, storage, networking [and] GPU. The software framework on top of it, the models: Have they all been tested? Have they all been validated?”

Dell has integrated the AMD ROCm software stack into the platform to support training, fine-tuning and serving large language models on-premises. The modular platform lets customers begin with smaller deployments and expand on the same infrastructure, according to Chhabra.

“You can start small with these composable units of storage, compute, networking, pre-integrated with AMD Instinct and EPYC CPUs with the ROCm software as well as the open ecosystem that sits on top of it,” he said. “We test it, we validate it, and the customers can use it and once they start seeing value in it, they know they can scale in a modular way with the same frameworks.”

Dell announced support for AMD Instinct MI350P PCI Express GPUs in its PowerEdge XE7745 and R7725 servers beginning in July, giving enterprises another option for scaling agentic and generative AI deployments. It also represents an important boost in memory bandwidth which matters in time-to-first-token latency.

The MI350P offers 144 gigabytes of HBM3E memory, which can be a key differentiator for inference performance, according to Mike Darby, senior manager of business development, Instinct Data Center GPUs, at AMD, during an appearance on theCUBE.

“It’s a lot of memory, but it’s also HBM3E, so [it has] an amazing amount of bandwidth,” he said. “The main use case being inference: It’s all about that latency, time to first token [and] the user experience, so that your attention span doesn’t move somewhere else while you’re waiting for your response.”

AMD and Dell’s collaboration on PCIe integration has another angle worth watching. AMD’s PCIe-based GPU supports air-cooled deployments, providing users with a path to deploy AI within existing data center infrastructure.

As the tech industry has encountered resistance in recent months to the buildout of large data centers across the U.S., concerns have centered on the environmental impact and use of water-based cooling systems. Separately, Dell found that, as it deployed its next-generation PowerEdge servers, some enterprise customers were still not prepared to adopt liquid cooling within data centers.

“Working with Dell, we added a PCI card to our air-coolable roadmap for GPU Instinct so that it fit in more Dell PowerEdge servers that go to the broader enterprise,” said Robert Hormuth, corporate vice president of architecture and strategy for the Data Center Solutions Group at AMD, during a conversation with theCUBE. “Not everybody is adopting direct liquid cooling.”

Dell’s work with AMD this year has extended beyond joint product announcements. In June, the two companies announced a partnership with the University of Cambridge to establish a Sovereign AI Innovation Lab (SAIL) in the United Kingdom.

The collaboration is designed to help advance the next generation of AI infrastructure and AI-powered scientific breakthroughs. It builds on Cambridge’s expanded AI research infrastructure, including the Zenith AI supercomputer, powered by fifth-generation AMD EPYC processors and AMD Instinct MI355X GPU accelerators integrated into Dell infrastructure.

Dell and AMD have also collaborated in recent months on a telecom initiative with AT&T Inc. Telecom data is a heavy lift when it comes to AI, with AT&T having processed over one trillion tokens to train models. AMD has provided the high-performance hardware foundation for both training and inference workloads involving the OTel 2.0 models developed through the Open Telco AI initiative.

Dell integrated this technology with AI-optimized servers for telecom environments to create a production-grade foundation for operators across data-intensive, real-world network environments. OTel 2.0’s training infrastructure uses Dell’s PowerEdge XE9785 server configured with eight MI355X GPUs.

The alliance between Dell and AMD highlights a key development in the growing AI infrastructure market: There are plenty of opportunities for competition. Both Dell and AMD appear committed to building portfolios that offer enterprise choices in AI processing solutions.

“AMD didn’t present its new products … as ‘respectable alternatives,’” Vellante said. “It claimed outright leadership across CPUs, GPUs, rack-scale performance, memory capacity, network bandwidth and tokens per dollar. It extended the argument across enterprise AI, robotics, ultra-low-latency inference and a rapidly expanding partner ecosystem.”

#5475. A $20M fine stalks Los Angeles over delay of a new housing project

A letter warns Los Angeles it has 60 days to act on a 398-home plan in Woodland Hills. The attorney cites Housing Accountability Act exposure of at least $19.9 million in fines, plus attorney fees, costs, and potential compensatory damages.  AI Summary

Blocking a Los Angeles housing development over a mountain lion could cost the city $20 million or more and still fail to stop the project.

L.A. has 60 days to approve 398 homes at Woodland Hills Country Club or face a lawsuit that could cost it that much, according to a letter from the club’s attorney, Dave Rand, sent to the city Friday. A judge could order the city to pay punitive damages for the delay and rule that the development still must proceed, Rand confirmed with HousingWire TBD.

If the club prevails in its case for damages provided under the Housing Accountability Act, the city would owe fines of at least $19.9 million. It would also owe attorney’s fees, costs and compensatory damages.

The letter says that exposure “could therefore cost the city well in excess of $20 million.” Rand wrote that he can’t imagine the risk to taxpayers “is worth it.”

Rand wrote that the city’s denial violated both Assembly Bill 2011 and the Housing Accountability Act. The letter invokes AB 712, which extends any limitation period by 60 days from the letter’s date. That keeps the club’s legal options open while the city weighs its response.

Rand explained the fine math on social media. The base fine is $10,000 per unit for a violation, and $50,000 per unit for a finding of bad faith.

AB 712 raises the fine to an automatic $50,000 per unit if the city has lost in court at least once in the same housing element cycle. At $50,000 a unit, 398 homes come to the $19.9 million cited in the letter.

The letter includes a claim for damages, which follows an Oct. 23 ruling from the Second Appellate District. It held that a homeowner could seek damages when a city misses a mandatory permit deadline.

That case involved an accessory dwelling unit, not AB 2011. Legal scholars have said its reasoning could reach other ministerial housing laws, including the one Rand cites.

The state housing department has set a Nov. 25 deadline for Los Angeles to respond to its own letter. The department said it could refer the matter to the state attorney general.

Other California cities have backed down when the cost of continuing to dig their heels in became clear. Glendale’s council voted 4-1 last October to reject Trammell Crow Residential’s 682-unit plan for a former Sears store. The project included 72 very low-income units.

The state housing department issued a notice of violation Dec. 30. It warned of fines up to $34 million if the city did not reverse course. Glendale’s council reversed its denial in late January, three months after rejecting the project. No lawsuit was filed, but the developer’s attorney had called the case a “slam dunk” under the Housing Accountability Act.

Morgan Hill in Silicon Valley took a similar path. City officials settled with High Street Residential, a builder’s remedy developer, to avoid costly litigation with the developer and the state.

The 105-home project had been hanging in legal limbo for three years. The city council unanimously approved it last week.
