#5474. Building a Telemed Website with AI? Credit Card Processing Must Be a Focus, According to Organic Payment Gateways

SCARBOROUGH, Maine, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Organic Payment Gateways has expanded its payment processing focus to help telehealth practices and online pharmacies connect specially underwritten merchant accounts to their custom-coded and AI-built websites.

AI coding tools and website builders have made it easier and less expensive for healthcare providers and their developers to create telemed portals, telehealth booking sites, pharmacy checkouts, and recurring membership systems. But accepting credit cards can be much harder, especially when a telehealth or pharmacy business was declined or shut down by their merchant account provider, Square, Stripe, or PayPal.

Organic Payment Gateways now helps these healthcare practices coordinate an appropriately underwritten merchant account with an Authorize.Net or NMI payment gateway, then works directly with the business or its developer on the website connection. The company provides this integration assistance by phone, email, and screen-share at no additional cost.

"AI can get somebody surprisingly far with a website now. The problem is, it can build a checkout page, but it can't make a credit card processor approve the business behind it," said Alex Roy, owner of Organic Payment Gateways. "That's where we come in. We look at what the practice or pharmacy is actually doing, what it offers, how it needs to get paid, and then our team helps connect the right merchant account and payment gateway to what their AI has already helped build."

The company's new focus includes payment processing for custom and AI-built telehealth and pharmacy websites developed with technologies such as React, Next.js, JavaScript, TypeScript, Node.js, PHP, Python, and other common development tools. It can also help businesses whose sites were built with AI coding tools and builders, including ChatGPT, Claude Code, Cursor, Replit Agent, Grok Bot, and Lovable.

Organic Payment Gateways can support payment flows for virtual consultations, online prescription orders, GLP-1 and weight-management memberships, PDE5 inhibitor prescriptions, card-on-file billing, recurring payments, electronic invoices, and "click-here-to-pay" links. Their automatic account updater services can also help reduce failed recurring payments when customers' cards expire or are replaced.

Qualified medical practices and online pharmacies can learn more about payment processing for custom and AI-built telehealth and pharmacy websites or review the company's broader healthcare, pharmacy, and telemedicine payment processing options.

"Sometimes a developer just needs a real person who understands both sides of the problem," Alex Roy said. "They may already have the site working exactly the way they want. We're not trying to make them rebuild it. We help them figure out a practical, stable, secure payment connection and our folks stay available if they need help later."

Organic Payment Gateways has worked with high-risk and regulated businesses since 2013. The company emphasizes one-on-one, US-based service and accounts based on each business's expected payment volume, service features, and system requirements.

Organic Payment Gateways is a BBB Accredited Business with an A+ rating. Its BBB business profile and Trustpilot customer reviews are available online.

About Organic Payment GatewaysOrganic Payment Gateways helps regulated and specialized businesses obtain merchant accounts and payment gateways for online credit card processing. The company works with telehealth practices, online pharmacies, and other businesses that may not fit the policies of mainstream payment processors, while helping to connect approved processing to existing websites, custom applications, and e-commerce systems. For more information, visit OrganicPaymentGateways.com.

#5472. Costly lessons of the Grenfell Tower Fire for landlords and underwriters

Apartment fires remain frequent, 76,000 in 2024, while faster flashover times and lithium-ion risks raise liability. Grenfell’s $1.5 billion in damages shows how deferred safety upgrades can trigger outsized losses and legal exposure.   AI Summary

Fires are among the most common concerns affecting property owners and their residents, with 329,500 structural fires in homes or apartments occurring in 2024 alone, according to the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA). Of those, 76,000 were in multi-family dwellings, resulting in 340 civilian deaths and nearly 2,300 injuries. Effectively, more than 200 apartment fires take place on any given day across the US.

While the number of total incidents remains high, this represents a substantial decline, with the NFPA noting that the estimated number of apartment fires was 47% lower in 2024 than in 1980. Yet that decline in the number of total fires has not corresponded to a decrease in lost lives or total economic impact of damages incurred.

Modern conveniences and design trends play an oversized role in this dynamic. Today’s furnishings, such as carpets, mattresses and couches, are made of a much higher concentration of petroleum-based synthetic materials, which burn faster and hotter than the wood, cotton and wool furnishings of yesteryear.

In fact, data from the U.S. Fire Administration (USFA) shows that today’s fires go from small flame to flashover in just three to five minutes, a nearly 75% decline from the 15 to 17 minutes residents had to escape from a house fire three decades ago, making it far easier to succumb to smoke that is thicker and also more toxic than ever before.

Adding literal fuel to the fire is the increasing popularity of e-bikes, e-scooters and other devices powered by lithium-ion batteries that can catch fire if misused. When one of these batteries catches fire, a phenomenon called thermal runaway causes the battery temperature to rise from 212 degrees to 1,800 degrees in only a second, according to scientists at Clemson University.

For landlords and property owners, modern fires pose a risk not only to the units they maintain, but potentially to a larger portfolio within their building if doors are not properly closed and flames are allowed to spread. NFPA estimates the value of property damage caused by house fires in 2024 at $19 billion.

Beyond costly repairs, owners need to be concerned about their liability, as residents very often seek out someone to blame for the pain, suffering and potential injury or wrongful death of their loved ones. Any delayed maintenance or negligence that may have contributed to the start or spread of such fires could leave property owners liable for millions.

In Atlanta, a massive 2023 fire destroyed The Reserve at LaVista Walk, a 284-unit apartment complex that was home to more than 220 residents. A resulting class action lawsuit alleged that building management ignored repeated complaints about a malfunctioning smoke alarm, leaving residents unable to determine that the blaring alarm was tied to an actual emergency on the night of the fateful blaze, which took eight hours to contain. The case was settled with building owners owing $8.45 million.

In Oregon, a July 2021 fire killed three people and injured one other when fireworks ignited trash in a dumpster at the Heidi Manor Apartments. A lawsuit followed, alleging that property owners violated Portland’s fire code by placing a dumpster with flammable contents too close to the wooden building, resulting in a $6 million settlement.

Across the pond, the UK’s deadly Grenfell Tower fire is a reminder that the long arm of the law can still come to hold property owners, contracting companies and others to account, even 10 years later.

In 2017, the 24-story apartment building in London’s North Kensington neighborhood went up in flames, burning for a horrific 60 hours. Seventy-two people lost their lives, and another 74 were injured as property damage costs ballooned close to an estimated £1.2 billion (approximately $1.5 billion USD).

This summer, Scotland Yard revealed that 54 individuals and 20 companies were facing criminal referrals for their role in the deadly blaze, with charges expected by the time the UK marks the sad 10th anniversary of the incident. Among those implicated are the manufacturers of the aluminum cladding and foam insulation enveloping the building, the main design-build contractor, architect and fire safety consultant involved in the tower’s refurbishment and the tenant management organization.

Each year, as the fall home heating season begins, we also recognize Fire Prevention Month. This period should serve as a reminder and opportunity for all building owners, landlords and managers to reassess their fire safety plans and educate residents and staff about the perils of potentially flammable items like e-bikes and space heaters, as well as proper evacuation procedures to contain fire spread and limit loss of life.

As noted by The Guardian, the devastating economic damage alone caused by the Grenfell Tower fire was “4,000 times the amount that was saved by replacing fire-retardant cladding with a cheaper combustible alternative.” This serves as a cold, frightening legal reminder that the phrase “cheap is expensive” can quickly become an understatement.

So, it’s imperative that property owners stay current with all refurbishment and replacement needs, ensuring all contractors hired and products used are above reproach. Otherwise, the malfunctioning boiler, fire alarm or sprinkler system you figured you’d fix tomorrow may be the cause of a deadly fire today.

Lawrence J. Luppi is a partner with leading defense litigation firm, Coffey Modica LLP. He represents insurers, property owners, managing agents and other professionals in high-exposure fire and explosion matters.This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. #5470. Apple’s stock drops as new CEO John Ternus delivers his first earnings call

Apple Inc. just delivered its first earnings call since new Chief Executive John Ternus took over the company from Tim Cook on Sept. 1, and the results beat expectations on the top and bottom lines. But the company missed expectations on iPhone sales and offered disappointing guidance going forward, and the stock fell in late trading.

The company reported fourth-quarter earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $2.10 per share, comfortably ahead of Wall Street’s target of $1.99 per share. Revenue for the period rose 12%, to $114.48 billion, easing past the $113.39 billion analyst forecast. All told, its net income came to $30.71 billion at the end of the quarter, up from just $27.46 billion one year earlier.

When Ternus (pictured) stepped up to relieve Cook in the CEO’s chair a couple of months ago, he realized he was stepping into a job with sky-high expectations, following in the footsteps of two of the most successful company leaders in American history. Steve Jobs was credited with revolutionizing consumer devices, while Cook took the company to spectacular new heights thanks to his operational expertise, establishing it as one of the world’s most iconic brands.

The weight of expectations is reflected by Apple’s enormous valuation. According to Oppenheimer analyst Martin Yang, the iPhone maker is trading at about 36 times next year’s expected earnings. That represents a premium compared with the rest of the technology market, even though its earnings are only expected to grow 1% this year, slower than many of its peers.

Nonetheless, investors have piled into Apple because it’s something of an outlier in the artificial intelligence boom. While its rivals are all spending hundreds of billions of dollars on building data centers, Apple has remained extremely capital-efficient, pouring cash into share buybacks and dividends for shareholders. That has given the company a strong margin for safety, but its position could still be threatened if Ternus can’t find a way to speed up Apple’s innovation engine.

The company has already been criticized for its lackluster performance in AI. Its long-awaited Siri AI chatbot finally arrived during the past quarter, but it came across as stale the moment it arrived. By the time it had launched, it had already been surpassed by autonomous AI agents such as Dots and Muse that can perform multistep tasks on behalf of users, while Siri is still fumbling around with answering questions.

Analysts wanted to know if Apple is planning to offer more AI features through subscriptions or services, but Ternus declined to reveal what the company’s future plans are. But he insisted that Apple has “lots of opportunities” for monetization in future. “One example is the hardware side, right?” he said. “It offers a compelling reason for upgrading or switching.”

Jacob Bourne of Emarketer told SiliconANGLE that Apple’s stock premium is likely linked to the growing concerns some investors have over the enormous cost and uncertain returns of the AI boom, which is being driven by all of Apple’s big tech peers. “Its tepid approach to AI infrastructure spending has helped to preserve its cash flow, and through strategic partnerships Apple may be able to strengthen its AI capabilities without taking on the same financial risks as its peers,” Bourne said. “But Apple faces its own challenges as AI-enabled devices such as smart glasses could eventually challenge the iPhone’s central role in iOS. Apple’s long-term advantage will hinge on combining its hardware strengths with compelling AI capabilities in a way that preserves its reputation.”

In the meantime, the pressure is on for Apple to give consumers more reasons to buy its expensive devices, especially as the costs of those products have been getting higher. Today’s report was the first full quarter of higher-priced Apple products following a price hike in June that stemmed from the rising cost of memory supplies and other components.

The price of most iPhone handsets was hiked by around $100, but consumers didn’t appear to punish Apple. On the contrary, iPhone revenue was a bright spot, reaching $57.58 billion in the quarter, up 17% from a year earlier and above the $56.54 billion consensus estimate. That’s despite the quarter including only eight days of new iPhone 18 Pro sales and none of the new flagship device, the iPhone Duo.

Apple needed a good quarter from the iPhone because its main growth engine, the services business, is slowing. Revenue there came to $31.57 billion, just below the Street’s forecast of $31.58 billion, growing less than 10% during the quarter, its slowest rate of growth since September 2022. The business includes revenue from a wide range of products and services, such as iCloud storage, AppleCare warranties, App Store fees and licensing revenue from Google LLC for putting its search engine as the default option in the Safari browser.

“We saw strong performance in many service categories, with all-time records in video, cloud services, payment services and advertising, and a September quarter record in music,” Tetanus told analysts.

Apple saw a better performance in its Mac computer division, with sales of $10.79 billion comfortably topping the Street’s forecast of $9.61 billion. The unit’s revenue grew almost 24% on an annual basis, following the launch of new Mac Studio and Mac Mini laptops in August.

The iPad division was a disaster, however, as sales declined more than 10% from the previous year to $6.3 billion, trailing the Street’s forecast of $6.7 billion. Last month saw the launch of a new iPad Mini model, following the debut of the updated iPad Air back in March, but despite those releases, there has been no flagship model launching this year, and that appears to have hurt the business’ performance. When asked about the miss, Ternus blamed supply constraints and a difficult comparison with last year as the main reasons for its disappointing performance.

The disappointing performance of Apple’s services and iPad units was compounded by what was seen as weak guidance for the current quarter, which includes the peak Christmas sales period. Apple Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh didn’t offer concrete numbers, but said the company expects its revenue to grow by between 7% and 10% in the quarter. Wall Street analysts are looking for higher growth of 11.4%, however. Parekh also revealed that Apple is forecasting its gross margin to fall between 45% and 46%, declining from the fourth quarter.

Apple’s stock fell almost 3% on today’s report, but it’s still up more than 24% in the year to date compared with a gain of just over 10% for the broader S&P 500 index.

#5469. Only people with skin in the game should be behind AI mortgage tools

AI is entering mortgage lending, but tool design matters. Originator-built systems can automate follow-ups, respect compliance boundaries and hand conversations to licensed staff at the right moment.   AI Summary

I spent more than 20 years originating mortgages, and at one point ranked among the top 10 producers in the country. I know the ins and outs of loans and lending, which is why I’m always suspicious when lenders talk about AI. When they do, I listen out for one thing, and one thing only.

Has the person building the new AI tool ever dealt with three closings, a lock about to expire and a borrower who has gone AWOL in one afternoon? Chances are, they haven’t. And this is what concerns me the most.

AI is coming to mortgage lending whether originators like it or not. Yet, the real question is who shapes it. My view is simple: the people who know this business inside out should have the biggest say in how these tools work, because a tool that doesn’t understand how loans actually get done will create as many problems as it solves.

Ask any producing loan officer at what stage they lose the most deals, and you’ll get a similar answer. It’s rarely the hot file. The hot file gets everyone’s attention.

It’s the lead who got one call and then nothing. It’s the past client who said, “Call me in six months,” and then they never heard back. It’s the pre-approved buyer who went quiet after losing a thrilling bidding war, and nobody checked in when the next listing came up.

None of this comes from pure laziness. Most originators quite frankly care a great deal about their clients. But a CRM full of thousands of names doesn’t pick up the phone, and someone chasing conditions, appraisals and closing dates only has so many hours in the day.

The gap between what a good originator knows they should do and what they actually have time to do is where the money goes missing. Although I’m sure this applies to many industries.

That gap is where AI can earn its place in the mortgage market. Not by replacing the loan officer, but by handling the steady, repetitive follow-ups that fall apart the moment a busy workweek hits. AI can be relentless and logical, while we often need a lot of caffeine to keep us going when the pressure kicks in.

Not all AI tools are made equal. As I’m sure you’re aware. A general-purpose chatbot can quite easily reveal your office hours to a curious customer. But mortgage conversations are different and deeper.

When a first-time buyer asks, “Should I wait for rates to come down?”, they’re rarely asking about rates. In fact, this is where emotional intelligence comes into play. More often than not, they’re actually nervous about the monthly payment, their spouse isn’t sold yet or perhaps a previous lender has sadly let them down. An experienced originator hears that simple question and considers the reasons behind it. A generic tool answers the literal question and moves on, and so the borrower drifts away.

Then there’s compliance. Borrower communication in this industry sits under disclosure rules, fair lending obligations, state licensing requirements and consent rules for calls and texts.

An AI tool that quotes terms it shouldn’t or answers a question that belongs to a licensed loan officer isn’t saving anyone precious time. It’s creating exposure. It’s potentially putting your business’ reputation at risk. Now, software built by people who have lived with those rules tends to know where the lines in the sand have been drawn. Software built by those unfamiliar with these rules can overstep them and cause significant issues.

We’re social creatures. Even introverts enjoy human interaction, even if it’s few and far between. In fact, one of the easiest marketing strategies these days is personal branding, because we buy into people, not products. Being a coach taught me that habits, timing, consistent follow-ups and knowing just what to say when a borrower hesitates make a whole world of difference to your sales potential.

Years ago, a notary named Daniel came into my office to sign documents. I thought he’d be good at this business and told him to get licensed. He did. Years later, he tracked me down to tell me he’d become the top originator in his market. He didn’t start with some rare gift. He learned the habits and stuck with them.

If those habits can be taught, they can be built into tools. That’s the real opportunity I see in the market. AI built on the knowledge of experienced producers can give a second-year loan officer some of the discipline it took the rest of us a decade to develop.

I also learned something from building software for loan officers. Tools that depend on someone logging in and remembering to act don’t change much. The originator still carries all the work. The next generation of tools has to take some of that weight off, not add another dashboard to check.

That frustration is actually what led me to build Cindie, an AI assistant for mortgage teams that keeps up follow-up with leads and past clients, and hands the conversation back to the loan officer when a licensed professional needs to step in.

If you’re evaluating AI for your team, these are the questions I’d want answered first.

The mortgage industry gets to decide who shapes its AI. If originators sit this one out, the tools will be designed by people who have never explained a rate lock to a nervous first-time buyer, and we’ll spend years working around their blind spots.

So I urge you to get involved. Test the tools on the market. Push vendors with hard questions. Tell them what actually happens in your day, and share what’s working with your peers.

AI shouldn’t erase the value of experience in this business. Built the right way, it can be a superpower.

Ben Anderson is the founder of Cindie, an AI workforce built for mortgage lending. He spent more than 20 years originating mortgages and has coached hundreds of loan officers through Ben Anderson 365.This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. #5468. Why yellow pad math still beats the spreadsheet in builder deals

Scott Cox explains how yellow pad math tests the relationships behind pro forma lines to surface inconsistencies, risk, and upside. The approach favors directional accuracy over spreadsheet precision to identify what a deal truly depends on.  AI Summary

[In the third of seven excerpts from ‘Less Wrong, More Right,’ Scott Cox argues that models can hide what matters by weighting every input equally. Simple back-of-the-envelope comparisons can identify what must be true for a homebuilder deal to work and where opportunity may be underpriced.]

One of the most impressive people I got to observe early in my career was a vice chairman of the bank, widely considered the smartest person in the place. What made him remarkable had nothing to do with depth in any particular market. He would be handed a credit write-up or a new project package – often a deal in a market he did not know, on a product type he had not financed, for a borrower he had never met — and he would flip pages for two or three minutes. Then he would tell you what the deal’s success or failure was actually depending on.

I never saw him build anything. He did a few simple calculations on the relationships between the numbers, and the relationships told him where to look. He was not recognizing the borrower and he was not recognizing the market. He was recognizing a pattern that lacked internal consistency – or one that could only hold if something were true that nobody in the package had said.

What he was doing is more nuanced than it sounds. Every line on a financial statement or a proforma is an abstract representation of a thing, and usually a physical thing. Revenue is not a number; it is a specific count of houses closing in specific months. Work in process is not a number; it is houses standing in the ground at various stages of completion. Every category on the balance sheet, the income statement, and the proforma is a stand-in for something you could walk up to and touch.

The people who are good at this convert the line back into the thing before they reason about it. And once you are looking at things rather than numbers, you start to notice combinations that cannot coexist. You should not see this number and that number together. That is where the work happens — not in any single figure, but in the pairs.

Notice what that produces. When you check a model cell by cell, what you find is an error: a broken formula, a bad input, something with an answer at the end of it. When the relationship between two numbers is off, it could be an error, but it could also be indicative of something unusual, good or bad. An anomaly. Not necessarily wrong. Curious. Something that has to be explained – and often reveals either truly unique aspects of the deal, or assumptions that lean toward the heroic.

Which is the argument for doing simple calculations before anyone shows you the model. A large cash flow invites you to read all of it, and reading all of it is how you study the trees and miss the forest. Look at the major relationships first. Find the anomalies. Then go looking for the answers. A massive spreadsheet is close to the worst instrument for finding what a deal depends on – not because it is wrong, but because it presents everything at the same weight. Complex models obscure as much as they illuminate. Your simple calculations, done on a pad, cannot have a broken cell.

I call it yellow pad math. The cash flow is precise to the dollar, but it rests on the same handful of projections the pad does – it has simply dressed them up. That is precision without accuracy: every figure carried to the dollar, resting on estimates the complex model obscures. The pad is imprecise and makes no attempt to hide it, which is why it can be more accurate about what you actually know. Most of the important decisions we make are imprecise anyway. What matters is being generally accurate. Would you rather be directionally correct, or precisely wrong?

I want to be clear about what this method is for, because it’s easy to read it as purely defensive — a way to find problems and avoid bad deals. That’s half of it. The other half is finding opportunities that the same logic says are larger than anyone in the room is treating them as.

I was once in a meeting where a builder I knew was presenting to a potential capital partner. They were doing infill deals in rough but improving areas – they believed in the concept but were being somewhat tentative about it. I started asking about nearby apartments. Were there any? How were they performing? What were the rents? They gave me the numbers. I asked how that compared to their projected house payments. Close, they said – payments just a bit more.

I stopped and said to the capital partner: we should buy every piece of ground that fits that criteria. If people are willing to rent a Class A apartment in a sketchy area, they’re seeing something there — because they have options. They’re not there because it’s cheap. Which means they’re built-in buyers for townhouses if the payment is competitive with the rent. And that relationship – apartment rent roughly equal to an ownership payment in an improving area – is almost certainly temporary. Apartment developers have an inherent land cost advantage because of density. As the area improves, land prices will reflect that. The window where you can buy ground at a price that makes the payment/rent comparison work will close. The math said move now and move aggressively.

That conclusion came from two numbers and one inference. Not a model or market study. A question, a number, an inference about what the number implied, and the willingness to follow it further than the people in the room were comfortable going.

#5467. XMax Announces $30 Million Share Repurchase Program

Board of Directors authorizes repurchase of up to $30 million of the Company's common stock

LOS ANGELES, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- XMax Inc. (NASDAQ: XMAX) ("XMax" or the "Company"), a distributor of contemporary furniture and artificial intelligence software and platform-based service provider, today announced that its Board of Directors has authorized a share repurchase program under which the Company may repurchase up to $30 million in aggregate purchase price of its outstanding common stock, par value $0.001 per share. Shares may be repurchased only at prices below $5.50 per share.

"The Board's authorization of this share repurchase program reflects our confidence in XMax's long-term strategy and our commitment to creating value for shareholders," said Andy Lu, Chief Executive Officer of XMax. "As we continue to develop our artificial intelligence software and platform-based services alongside our contemporary furniture business, we intend to take a disciplined approach to capital allocation, balancing investment in the growth of the business with returns to our shareholders."

The program will begin on a date to be determined (the "Commencement Date") after the Company has (i) publicly released its financial results for the fiscal quarter ended September 30, 2026 by press release ("Earnings Release"), (ii) publicly disclosed any material nonpublic information, and (iii) engaged a broker-dealer for the program. No repurchases will be made before the Commencement Date, and the program will expire three months after it.

Repurchases are expected to be made from time to time through open-market purchases, which may include purchases under a trading plan intended to satisfy Rule 10b5-1 under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as amended (the "Exchange Act"), and are intended to be made in accordance with Rule 10b-18 under the Exchange Act and other applicable legal requirements.

The timing, manner, price (subject to the $5.50 per share limit) and amount of any repurchases will be determined by the Company's management based on its evaluation of market conditions, the trading price of the Company's common stock, liquidity and capital requirements, legal requirements, and other factors. The program does not obligate the Company to repurchase any particular number of shares, and it may be suspended, modified, or discontinued at any time without prior notice. The Company expects to fund repurchases with its existing cash and cash equivalents.

Headquartered in Commerce, California, XMax Inc. (NASDAQ: XMAX), formerly known as Nova LifeStyle, Inc., is a diversified company engaged in the design, sourcing, and distribution of contemporary furniture, as well as the development of artificial intelligence technologies and applications. The Company operates through an established global network of suppliers, distributors, and e-commerce channels, serving a broad customer base. The Company has expanded into artificial intelligence technologies, including AI software and platform-based services through its wholly owned subsidiaries XMax AI Inc. and Elonx AI Holdings PTE. LTD., to support future growth. By leveraging emerging technologies, the Company aims to drive diversification and long-term value creation.

#5466. Robotics startup Tutor Intelligence nabs $75M investment

Warehouse automation provider Tutor Intelligence Inc. today announced that it has raised $75 million in funding.

Andreessen Horowitz led the Series A investment. It was joined by Union Square Ventures and Neo, which led Tutor’s previous two rounds.

The merchandise that a warehouse processes often arrives on pallets, flat wood structures capable of holding up to several tons. Tutor sells a mobile robotic arm called Cassie that can take packages off a pallet and place them in containers. It’s also capable of performing the opposite operation.

Cassie can process up to 18 items per minute depending on the package type. Its robotic arm is equipped with a vacuum gripper designed to pick up more than 50 pounds. The arm is mounted on a four-wheeled platform that enables Cassie to autonomously travel between different sections of a warehouse.

Automating pallet processing is challenging because the merchandise that a warehouse receives changes over time. Historically, adapting a robotic arm’s workflow to a new item involved manual coding. Cassie uses built-in artificial intelligence models to learn how to pick up new package types automatically.

Tutor also ships its AI models with a second wheeled robot called Sonny. It uses a pair of robotic arms to take items off warehouse shelves and place them in packages. The robot finds the needed items using an array of time-of-flight and stereo cameras. Both camera varieties collect depth data, which makes it easier to determine the distance of an object.

Tutor plans to apply Sonny to additional use cases in the future. In particular, it sees industrial companies using the system to assemble products and perform equipment maintenance. Tutor teaches Sonny’s AI models new tasks in a facility that hosts more than 100 robots. Human experts demonstrate how to perform a task using a remotely controlled robot and the AI models learn by imitation.

“Sonny’s manufacturability at scale makes it an ideal robot not just for most handwork in manufacturing and logistics, but for arbitrary business-critical applications across the physical economy,” Tutor co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Josh Gruenstein wrote in a blog post. “Data collected by our Sonny fleet trains our largest and most capable robot foundation models at the frontier of rate and reliability.”

Tutor sells its robots under a usage-based pricing model. It removes the need for customers to make a large upfront purchase, which lowers the entry barrier. The company disclosed today that the number of facilities where its robots are used has nearly quadrupled over the past year.

Tutor will use its newly raised funding to enhance its AI models and speed up robot production.

#5465. Synova Global partners with Eventus to leverage Validus trade surveillance platform for its markets

NativX compute marketplace will be Synova Global's first exchange to deploy Validus upon its launch

AUSTIN, Texas and BOULDER, Colo., Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Eventus, a leading provider of comprehensive, at-scale trade surveillance and financial risk solutions, and Synova Global, the newly launched exchange-as-a-service company, today announced that Synova will leverage the Eventus Validus platform as part of its exchange infrastructure offering for the markets it introduces. The partnership will kick off with the deployment of Validus for compute marketplace NativX, Synova Global's first market.

Synova Global officials said that trade surveillance is central to its mission of creating stable, reliable markets, with robust surveillance protecting market integrity, deterring manipulation and bad actors, and ensuring market participants will feel secure and confident trading on NativX and other markets the company launches in the future.

Cole Crawford, founder and CEO of Synova Global and founder and chairman of NativX, said: "AI's continued growth depends on turning compute from a fragmented, unpredictable operating cost into transparent, manageable market infrastructure. But a market is only as strong as the trust its participants place in it. As accelerated compute becomes an asset class, institutions and regulators need confidence that every price is fair and every trade is monitored. Eventus has earned the trust of regulators and brings deep experience across exchanges, futures commission merchants (FCMs) and broker-dealers. This partnership gives NativX traders institutional-grade surveillance from day one, built to scale as the world's newest commodity market grows."

Eventus CEO Cameron Routh said: "Eventus has a powerful track record of establishing the benchmark for best-in-class trade surveillance across new and emerging markets, including digital assets and, more recently, prediction markets. We're excited to now bring this expertise into the important new compute capacity space, where NativX is forging new ground with its innovative marketplace. We are particularly excited to partner with Synova Global on its exchange-as-a-service offering as the company grows and introduces new markets."

Synova Global markets will leverage Validus' real-time monitoring and advanced surveillance tools. The company expects that NativX will use the Frank AI solution Eventus introduced last fall into Validus as relevant use cases permit the exchange to further automate and enhance its surveillance operations.

Last month, Frank AI earned Validus recognition as Best AI Solution for Trade Surveillance in the second annual AI in Capital Markets Awards hosted by A-Team Group.

Eventus provides state-of-the-art, at-scale trade surveillance software across all lines of defense. Its powerful, award-winning Validus platform is easy to deploy, customize and operate across equities, options, futures, foreign exchange (FX), fixed income, digital asset and prediction/information markets. Validus is proven in the most complex, high-volume, and real time environments of Eventus' rapidly growing client base, including tier-1 banks, broker-dealers, futures commission merchants (FCMs), proprietary trading groups, market centers, buy-side institutions, energy and commodity trading firms, and regulators. Clients rely on the platform, coupled with the firm's responsive support and product development, to overcome their most pressing trade surveillance regulatory challenges. For more, visit www.eventus.com.

Headquartered in Boulder, Synova Global is the market layer for real-world assets: exchange infrastructure as a service. The company licenses its full trading and settlement stack, including the Titan matching, settlement engine and the Venue front end. With security at the foundation, any operator can launch a compliance-ready, on-chain, white-label market for any asset class today. Learn more at www.synova.global.

NativX develops the benchmarks and market infrastructure for verified compute and connectivity capacity. It publishes NxCI, the NativX Compute Index, and operates nx.exchange and the NX Flow interface on technology licensed from Synova Global. Based in San Juan, Puerto Rico, NativX is building a common market reference for the delivered output of AI infrastructure across hardware generations and providers. Learn more at www.nativx.net.

#5464. Beyond Finance Leader Vanessa Hering Wins 2026 Herizon Award

Award recognition honors Hering for transforming customer service through an empathetic, innovative approach to helping people overcome debt

CHICAGO, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Vanessa Hering, client success officer at Beyond Finance, one of the country's leaders in financial wellness and debt consolidation, has been recognized with a 2026 Herizon Award for leading the company's human-centered model for addressing the financial and emotional dimensions of debt.

Hering was recognized as an Executive Influencer who transformed a team or department and a finalist in the category of transforming a company. As Beyond Finance's client success officer and executive vice president of strategy and operations, she leads teams that combine financial solutions with empathy, education, technology, and financial wellness support. In 2025, Beyond Finance's approach to financial wellness helped consumers resolve $4.7 billion in debt and generated $1.1 billion in client savings from reductions in debt, after fees.

Under Hering's leadership, Beyond Finance has expanded client support beyond debt resolution. Certified financial therapists provide weekly financial wellness sessions, while educational resources and technology help clients understand their finances, monitor progress, and build healthier habits. This approach is supported by a Client Success team of more than 500 people who provide clients with 24/7 assistance. This model is making a measurable impact: The company achieved 93% customer service interaction satisfaction, and in a survey of over 10,000 respondents, program graduates self-reported a 42% improvement in their financial habits.

"This award truly belongs to Beyond Finance's Client Success team who support our clients every day with professional guidance and compassion," said Hering. "It's an honor to work with them year after year and be inspired by their commitment to providing the service that helps hundreds of thousands of our clients build a more secure future. I'm proud to be recognized with the Herizon Award on their behalf."

As an executive leader and advocate for human-centered innovation, Hering continues to challenge conventional approaches within the debt consolidation industry. Her work demonstrates how empathy, operational excellence, and technology can come together at scale to improve consumers' lives while delivering strong organizational performance.

"Vanessa is redefining financial wellness and debt relief for millions of Americans," said Russ Fordyce, Chief Recognition Officer, Business Intelligence Group, the organization behind the Herizon Awards. "Her empathetic approach, built on education, behavioral science, and personalized support, helps people reclaim their financial independence."

Recognized Among a Select Group of WomenThe 2026 Herizon Awards honored 57 winners across five nominee roles and four countries, spotlighting women whose leadership has transformed individuals, teams, companies, and industries. Every nomination is read and scored by experienced business professionals. Judges highlighted the measurable behavior change produced by Beyond Finance's model, as well as Hering's commitment to applying the same empathetic approach within the company to support employees' career development and well-being.

#5463. How Xatoms is using AI to solve the global water crisis

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

Every September, Climate Week and Global Citizen Week in New York bring together policymakers, investors and innovators focused on the world’s most pressing problems.

It’s also when Cisco Systems Inc. and Global Citizen recognize the winner of the Global Citizen Prize: Cisco Youth Leadership Award. Cisco and Global Citizen created the award in 2018 to honor a young leader who uses technology to help end extreme poverty, and this year’s recipient may have the most compelling story yet.

Diana Virgovicova (pictured) is the founder and CEO of Xatoms (pronounced “X-Atoms”), a Toronto-based company that uses artificial intelligence and quantum chemistry to design sunlight-activated materials that break down pollutants in water. The award comes with a $250,000 grant, and Xatoms was chosen from more than 2,000 applications.

Most of the AI conversation at Climate Week focused on what AI takes from the planet: power, land and, increasingly, water. Xatoms offers a positive counterpoint, a case study in AI giving back.

Most founders find a market. Virgovicova found a problem the hard way. She grew up in a village of about 800 people in Slovakia, surrounded by farms that used heavy amounts of pesticides. “I got sick when I was 14 years old,” she told me. “I was diagnosed with ovarian cancer because of the water I drank.”

After her diagnosis, she persuaded her mother to go backpacking across Asia. On trains in India, she heard from women facing the same thing. “I learned that there is a girl in Slovakia who got sick. There is a girl in India who’s getting infections. There is a girl in Africa who has to spend long hours every single day searching for clean water,” she said. “So, we need to find a solution, and it is affecting mainly women across the globe.”

Globally, women and girls spend 250 million hours a day collecting water, more than three times the time men and boys spend. “While boys go to school, the girls are responsible for bringing a bucket of water home, and they start missing school very early on,” Virgovicova explained. “It’s an educational, economic and health problem.”

And it’s growing. “We have 2 billion people that don’t have access to clean drinking water, and this number is actually growing because of flooding, climate change,” she said.

One of the more interesting aspects of Xatoms is where it chose to play. Many water treatment efforts target bacteria such as E. coli because the effects are immediate. Xatoms goes after the harder problem: complex industrial pollutants such as pesticides, pharmaceuticals, forever chemicals and heavy metals.

“I think we are forgetting about these complex contaminants because they don’t make us sick tomorrow. They make us sick in 10 years,” she said. “They give us chronic diseases. They cause infertility.” She made a point I hadn’t considered: Scientific progress is making it worse.

“We are able to create better antibiotics, but these better antibiotics are more complex, thus more difficult to destroy in water,” she said. That’s a second-order problem traditional treatment wasn’t built for, and exactly where advanced computational design has an edge.

At 17, while working with a university professor in Slovakia, Virgovicova used quantum chemistry software to design a new molecule that harnesses sunlight to break down water pollutants. That work earned her a Diploma of Excellence from the Swedish Royal Family and a full scholarship to the University of Toronto.

“What is so exciting about this science is that we can use computers to design new materials, and we don’t have to create them in the lab,” she said. “We can see these materials, how they react, and what their properties are before we even synthesize them.”

Quantum chemistry gets far fewer headlines than quantum computing, so I asked her to explain it. “Quantum helps us understand these molecules at a fundamental level, including how the atoms within the molecule interact,” she said. “When we know these fundamental properties, we can understand what makes each molecule good at something, and that helps us design an even better molecule, a better material.”

The output is a photocatalyst powder. “Initially, it was a molecule in a computer, but we were able to synthesize it in a lab,” Virgovicova said. “We put this photocatalytic powder into water. It splits water into OH radicals, and the OH radicals then destroy contaminants.”

Because it’s a catalyst, it isn’t consumed, so a small amount can treat “hundreds of gallons,” she said. Earlier photocatalysts required ultraviolet light; her design works with visible light, such as sunlight or LEDs, eliminating the need for expensive UV reactors.

AI is the accelerant. “It would take a decade if we did it without AI,” she said. “We can do it in 30 days.” That’s the real story for business leaders. Materials discovery has historically been slow, expensive and lab-bound, and Xatoms has transformed it into a computational pipeline.

Here’s where it matters for technology buyers. Data centers consume enormous volumes of water for cooling, and the AI buildout is making that worse. I asked Virgovicova whether Xatoms can flip the script. “There are a lot of problems with contaminants within the data center,” she said. “The data center water needs to be completely clean for cooling,” she said. “We are able to use this catalyst to help reuse the water in data centers.”

This is an underappreciated opportunity. Hyperscalers and neoclouds face mounting pressure over water use, and the industry’s response has largely focused on cooling design. Reuse through improved treatment is a different and more planet-friendly solution.

Xatoms works with Indigenous communities in Canada under longstanding boil-water advisories, as well as in Kenya and South Africa. Virgovicova told me the footprint now includes Japan and Azerbaijan. Every engagement is customized.

“We collect a water sample. Recently, we shipped the sample from Azerbaijan all the way to Canada,” she said. “We identify the contaminant and then determine which of these 88 options would be the best.”

Customers define the outcome. “Some of them want to take yellow water and decolorize it. Some of them have a specific contaminant in mind that they want to remove or reduce,” she said.

Next up are Turkey, where co-founder Kerem Topal Ismail Oglou grew up, and the broader Middle East, driven by textile manufacturing and oil and gas. She also met South Africa’s water minister during Climate Week ahead of a trip to Cape Town.

Being named a global winner of the World Economic Forum’s Water Resilience Challenge opened doors with large enterprises. “We had the chance to interact with some of the biggest Fortune 500 companies, which helped us create pilots and partnerships,” she said.

The Cisco grant is moving directly into execution. “We have more than six major projects coming up, so we need help with lab work,” she said. “We need to figure out the best way to manufacture more materials.” The goal is to “commercialize this technology as fast as we can.”

When I joked that billionaires are hunting for water on Mars while we haven’t solved it here, she pointed out a funding gap. “About 3% of climate VC funding goes to water only,” she said. Water underpins industry, agriculture and now AI infrastructure, yet it remains capital-starved.

Virgovicova mentors young founders, especially women in science and climate, and her advice is very direct. “There’s always going to be skepticism in every single room you go into at first,” she said. “It’s very important that you know how to present yourself and that you’re confident. You can really prove everyone wrong as long as you know your stuff.” With women still scarce among Fortune 500 CEOs, she added, “If I can do it, you can do it as well.”

Her favorite piece of advice: “If you focus on watering your grass, you don’t care about someone’s grass being greener.” And the AI myth she wants gone? “That it’s going to destroy the world. I think it’s a tool for improving the world.”

Cisco uses this award to make a point it rarely gets credit for: technology’s value is measured by what it does for people. Xatoms applies two of the decade’s most hyped technologies, AI and quantum, to a tangible, urgent problem.

For technology leaders, there are three key takeaways. First, AI’s biggest payoff may come from scientific discovery, where compressing a decade of work into 30 days can reshape an entire industry’s economics. Second, AI’s water problem has solutions beyond cooling design, and data center builders should be evaluating treatment and reuse partners now. Third, water deserves far more capital than it receives.

In 10 years, Virgovicova wants Xatoms to be “a global leader in discovery of these materials,” with solutions for many toxic contaminants worldwide. Given how far she has come from a village of 800 people, I wouldn’t bet against her.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

Executives from TMB (Trusted Media Brands), FAST Studios, FUEL TV, and Swerve TV to discuss streaming monetization strategies at Future of Video, November 17â18 in Marina del Rey, California

PLANO, Texas, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- New research from Parks Associates finds the US streaming market has 275 subscription video-on-demand (SVOD) services, 141 advertising-based video-on-demand (AVOD) services, and 60 FAST platforms, highlighting the growing diversity of business models competing for consumer attention and advertising revenue.

Research from the firm's Streaming Video Tracker also identifies 243 premium SVOD services, 85 transactional video-on-demand (TVOD) services, 110 FAST channels, 55 ad-supported SVOD services, and eight virtual multichannel video programming distributors (vMVPDs). Categories may overlap as streaming providers increasingly combine subscription, advertising, and free content offerings.

The session, moderated by Michael Goodman, Director, Entertainment Research, Parks Associates, features executives representing content owners, streaming platforms, and FAST channel operators:

"The streaming market is evolving beyond traditional subscription models, with companies testing new combinations of advertising, premium content, and free services," Goodman said. "Streaming providers must identify sustainable revenue models that balance advertising, pricing, content investment, and customer retention."

#5461. Automated Drone Technology Further Transforms Polish Mountain Rescue Operations

How Poland's TOPR Team is Revolutionizing Mountain Rescues with Automated DJI Docks

SHENZHEN, China, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- With its steep peaks, deep valleys, and harsh winter conditions, the Tatra Mountains present immense challenges for search and rescue operations. Powered by DJI Enterprise's next-generation automated drone technology, TOPR (TatrzaÅskie Ochotnicze Pogotowie Ratunkowe), Poland's dedicated volunteer mountain rescue service, is actively transforming its emergency response in rugged regions.

Building on their successful integration of DJI Enterprise equipment like the DJI Dock 3, TOPR recently initiated a pilot program with the newly released DJI Dock 4. The concept is groundbreaking for alpine rescues: launching a drone from an automated rooftop dock before the ground rescue team has even left the base.

"Certain locations are completely inaccessible by car, bike, or even snowmobile during winter," explains Marcin JÃ³zefowicz, a TOPR rescuer and Head of Cybertech. Traditionally, a full mountain deployment could take up to two hours just to assemble the team and reach the trailhead on foot. To overcome this critical bottleneck, TOPR is looking to the sky.

This early deployment means a drone can reach a reported accident site in minutes instead of hours. "Crucially, we can assess the situation before we begin a physical operation," says JÃ³zefowicz. This rapid aerial reconnaissance allows duty officers to determine if a rescue is genuinely needed, how many volunteers to dispatch, and exactly what equipment is required.

Once on the scene, the DJI Matrice 5TD helps TOPR make contact with people on the ground. Rescuers can use its loudspeaker to give instructions and ask whether assistance is needed, with hikers responding through gestures. If they indicate that they do not need help, the team can continue searching elsewhere. In total darkness, advanced thermal fusion imaging provides operators with near-daylight clarity, allowing them to pinpoint hikers' headlamps and read topographic details simultaneously.

To conquer the mountainous terrain that frequently blocks standard communication signals, TOPR's trial creatively utilizes a network of DJI O4 video transmission ground stations. By placing relay stations on observation towers and distant peaks, the drone can seamlessly roam between them. "This infrastructure allows us to extend our flight range even into neighboring valleys," JÃ³zefowicz notes.

With automated flight triggers and a dock capable of swapping batteries in just 25 seconds for continuous operations, TOPR is exploring the ultimate future of mountain rescue. Beyond active missions, the automated fleet is testing the waters for daily hazard reconnaissance and trail monitoring. For TOPR's dedicated volunteers, this continuous innovation serves one ultimate goal: reaching the injured faster, safer, and more effectively in the unforgiving Tatras.

#5460. VCs bet $30M on Larridin’s ability to help enterprises demonstrate AI’s value for money

As enterprises jack up their spending on artificial intelligence tools, it’s only right for senior executives to want to know exactly what they’re getting in return for their costly investments. Larridin Inc., a startup focused on AI adoption measurement, has just raised $30 million in early-stage funding to try to provide them with the answers.

Today’s Series A round was led by Pelion Ventures and saw participation from existing backers Andreessen Horowitz and Gradient Ventures, as well as new investors like GFT, W23, Thayer, DG Daiwa Ventures, Cougar Capital and Alumni Ventures. The round brings the company’s total amount raised so far to $47 million.

Larridin’s funding comes at a time when enterprise leaders are facing growing pressure to demonstrate the value they’re getting for their spiralling token consumption costs and application programming interface bills. Shareholders of publicly traded companies, especially, are eager to see those investments are driving real growth, and aren’t easily swayed by vanity metrics showcasing adoption without value.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Russ Fradin says this pressure stems from the flawed way in which most organizations evaluate their AI investments. He argues that traditional adoption metrics such as seat licenses and login counts do not reflect the true operational impact of AI.

Indeed, one of Larridin’s own customers is a case in point. That organization’s own surveys showed that 92% of its engineers were active AI users, which seems like a good rate of adoption. But when it started using Larridin’s tools to dig deeper, it found that a single engineer accounted for 65% of the company’s entire AI budget.

These aren’t the only kinds of blind spots AI has created. In Larridin’s newly released Engineering AI Impact Report, based on a survey of more than 1,000 developers, it found that though AI-assisted pull requests increased from 35% in April to 62% in September, it didn’t provide much value for enterprises because it simply created bottlenecks further downstream. For instance, organization’s median code review wait times increased more than 50% over the same timeframe.

Fradin says this is why companies cannot just monitor AI output volume. What’s needed is a complete picture that also covers the cost and quality of AI outputs, and the friction it creates.

Larridin’s goal is to give companies more visibility into their AI technology with what it says is the industry’s first AI value measurement platform. It links data on AI tool adoption with employee productivity metrics and expenditure data, and also looks at the value generated by, and the cost of autonomous AI agents that do work on behalf of humans.

By tracking complete workflows, Larridin can help companies to identify where and how AI is actually driving value and where spend is being wasted. It can also highlight new processes that are ripe for agentic automation.

Such insights can be extremely compelling. In one case, Larridin identified a 66-fold cost discrepancy per shipped code change between two competing AI coding tools that were being used by different employees for similar tasks. The customer was able to cancel its subscription for the much more expensive tool without any impact on productivity.

“Companies must be able to prove tangible business value from skyrocketing AI spend,” Fradin said. “Our investors share that conviction, and our Series A reflects the belief in our technology and its ability to solve this critical challenge.”

Larridin’s customer base includes enterprises such as SurveyMonkey Inc., Vertiv Holdings Co., Kalviyo Inc. and Gainsight Inc., and it’s planning to build on this traction by expanding its go-to-market and engineering teams.

Pelion Ventures’ Jeff Kearl said he’s backing Larridin because it fills a vital gap in enterprise analytics by tying every dollar spent on AI directly to measurable business outcomes. “As AI adoption scales, Larridin empowers executive teams with the intelligence to maximize their return on investment and build a clear path to long-term value creation,” he said.

#5459. Pump.fun Perps on Hyperliquid: How the 0.10% Builder Fee Works

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On a $10,000 Bitcoin perpetual order placed through Pump.fun, Pump.fun can charge up to $10.

Hyperliquid, the exchange that actually matches and settles the trade, charges a standard taker $4.50. Only one of those fees has a written rule sending it toward a token burn, and it's Hyperliquid's.

Most launch coverage focused on whether to buy HYPE or SOL. The more useful question for PUMP holders is where each dollar of perps fees goes. When you compare Pump.fun's fee schedule, its buyback methodology and Hyperliquid's fee documentation, then, you'll see they don't connect the way many people assume.

Pump.fun didn't build a derivatives exchange. Its perps run on Hyperliquid's order books through builder codes, a feature that lets outside apps send user orders to Hyperliquid and add their own fee on top. Hyperliquid's engine handles matching, margin and liquidations.

The product first appeared in Pump.fun's API around October 9, when Wu Blockchain spotted a /coins/perps endpoint showing prices, funding rates, open interest and maximum leverage, all pulled from Hyperliquid's mainnet. The same endpoint also listed SOL, Nvidia, Tesla, gold and crude oil contracts. Trading launched around October 16 and 17, with up to 40x leverage on BTC and 25x on ETH reported at launch.

Pump.fun updated its terms and conditions on October 17. The perps feature is blocked for users in the United States and Ontario, along with sanctioned parties.

Pump.fun's official fee schedule splits the cost of a perp trade into separate parts.

Here's the math on a $10,000 market order at entry-tier rates, assuming Pump.fun charges its full maximum:

For a maker order, the gap is wider: $1.50 to Hyperliquid and up to $10 to Pump.fun. At full rate, the app routing the trade earns more per order than the exchange that runs it. Note that 0.10% is the published maximum, not a confirmed rate for every trade.

This side of the trade has the clearest documentation. Hyperliquid says its fees are "entirely directed to the community," meaning its HLP vault, the assistance fund and market deployers.

The assistance fund converts trading fees into HYPE automatically as part of the chain's execution.

According to Hyperliquid's documentation,

So every Pump.fun perp trade feeds part of Hyperliquid's own token-burn mechanism through standard protocol rules. That share never touches Pump.fun's treasury.

There's one more possible layer. Some of the markets in Pump.fun's API, such as stocks and commodities, are the kind of contracts that third-party HIP-3 deployers usually run on Hyperliquid. Those deployers can set their own fee share. If Pump.fun lists them, another party joins the split.

Under Hyperliquid's builder code rules, the builder fee goes to the builder's address on Hyperliquid. Builders claim it through the standard referral-reward process. The fee is charged in the collateral asset, so for these markets it builds up in USDC on Hyperliquid, not in SOL on Solana.

That matters once you check Pump.fun's PUMP buyback methodology. The program puts 50% of revenue toward buying and burning PUMP. It defines revenue as income from:

Perps builder fees and bridge fees aren't on that list. The page also says buybacks aren't a commitment to future purchases, except as "deterministically programmed prior to April 29, 2026." Perps launched in October, so they weren't covered by that commitment.

To be fair to Pump.fun, the absence of a rule isn't proof that the money stays out of buybacks. Pump.fun could add perps to its revenue definition at any time. But as of today, no published Pump.fun document links a perps fee to a PUMP burn. Any connection would also need USDC moved off Hyperliquid and converted, because the buyback table records purchases in SOL.

This also changes how to read the buyback numbers I've covered before. The PUMP page shows $490.65 million in cumulative buybacks on its dashboard and $465 million in Newsletter #14. It also says the fee dashboard has misreported revenue and buyback amounts since Custom Pairs launched and that this "will be fixed soon." If perps revenue grows, Pump.fun's total income and the share that actually reaches PUMP burns could move further apart.

Hyperliquid makes the builder side of this traceable. It publishes daily fill files for each builder at:

[https://stats-data.hyperliquid.xyz/Mainnet/builder_fills/](https://stats-data.hyperliquid.xyz/Mainnet/builder_fills/){builder_address}/{YYYYMMDD}.csv.lz4

The builder address must be entirely lowercase. A builder's total collected fees also appear in Hyperliquid's referral info query.

Without Pump.fun's builder address in its fee schedule, terms or announcements, nobody outside the company can add up the actual perps revenue, which is the number that would show whether this product is a side feature or a real revenue line. Once that address is public, the next step is to check whether a matching amount ever shows up in the PUMP buyback table.

Until then, the honest answer is this: Hyperliquid's share has a documented path to a HYPE burn, while Pump.fun's share has a documented path into Pump.fun's own wallet.

NEW ORLEANS, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Rep Data has launched the Verified Intelligence Platform (VIP), an end-to-end research and insights solution that takes teams from business questions to actionable insights, with data quality verified throughout. The platform allows researchers to design studies, source verified respondents, detect fraud and low-quality responses, and analyze results in one connected system, with the flexibility to manage research themselves or work with Rep Data's experts.

The platform builds on RepData's sample sourcing and fraud prevention technology, adding survey design, behavioral data quality assessment and advanced analytics through its recent acquisitions of ReDem, OWL and SightX. It incorporates RepData's curated participant network and quality checks at the source, respondent and response levels. The launch establishes Verified Intelligence as a new category of research with data quality verified at every step and visible to customers.

"Insights teams shouldn't have to make high-stakes decisions on questionable data or choose between quality and speed," said Patrick Stokes, CEO and Founder of RepData. "We've built the only research platform that offers this level of capability, technology and transparency in one place. Quality has been part of our DNA since day one, and VIP sets a new standard for conducting research and making decisions with confidence."

Verification is integrated throughout the platform, with customers able to see how data quality is assessed at each stage:

#5456. Enterprise architecture: Dell and Microsoft integrate hybrid AI

How can software and cloud giant Microsoft Corp. translate its platform vision into fully deployed enterprise architecture in the age of AI?

This central question has defined the next chapter in a decades-long partnership between Microsoft and Dell Technologies Inc. Dell provided some answers at this year’s Dell Technologies World by expanding its private cloud offering to deploy the latest Microsoft software implementations.

Since that event, Microsoft has worked to enable a disaggregated architecture, simplifying operations across Dell PowerEdge compute, Dell PowerStore storage and Azure Local. Flexibility is the key attraction for enterprise customers evaluating Dell and Microsoft’s joint solutions, according to Paul Nashawaty, principal analyst at theCUBE Research.

“Microsoft and Dell are moving beyond infrastructure partnerships to deliver a more integrated go-to-market strategy for enterprise AI, hybrid cloud and application modernization,” he said. “Since Dell Technologies World in May, the focus has been on connecting Microsoft Azure Local, SQL Server and hybrid-cloud capabilities with Dell’s automation platform and enterprise infrastructure to help customers deploy, govern and operate AI workloads wherever their data resides.”

This feature is part of SiliconANGLE Media’s exploration of the architectural shifts powering continuous, production-grade AI. Be sure to check out theCUBE’s “Dell AI Data Platform Event: From Ambition to AI at Scale,” and past coverage of this year’s Dell Technologies World. (* Disclosure below.)

The market opportunity for both Dell and Microsoft centers on the need to operationalize AI applications. Meeting this goal requires integration across the full AI deployment lifecycle.

Dell Automation Platform and Dell Private Cloud provide an operational backbone for deploying Azure Local on-premises and managing the hardware lifecycle, including firmware and updates. Azure Arc provides consistent management across environments. SQL Server can be run in virtual machines or Kubernetes containers without learning separate skill sets for cloud and on-premises environments.

“The key architecture for AI capabilities is integrating with things like embedding models for vector searching or chat completion models for AI agents, but we do it all inside … the SQL Server Engine,” Bob Ward, principal architect at Microsoft, told theCUBE. “We [formed a] partnership with Dell so that we can connect to anything on premises. I can connect to Azure Local, Dell [and] Nvidia Factory. We just got a framework built in. It doesn’t matter where you’re running these AI models; we can easily integrate with it.”

A central element of Dell and Microsoft’s partnership involves integrating database, automation and hybrid cloud capabilities into a stack that can feed AI the data it needs. Data fragmentation is often cited as a top blocker to scaling AI beyond pilots, and integrating the two companies’ services addresses a pressure point that surveys have identified across enterprise information technology.

Data fragmentation remains a barrier to scaling AI beyond pilots. Dell and Microsoft’s partnership brings database, automation and hybrid cloud capabilities into a common stack.

“From an AppDev perspective, that integration matters because the challenge is no longer simply building AI applications, but operationalizing them securely, consistently and at scale,” said Nashawaty. “TheCUBE AppDev Research highlights the execution gap: Approximately 88% of AI pilots fail to reach production, while 64% of enterprise AI teams identify integration complexity as a leading barrier to adoption.”

Dell’s partnership with Microsoft also extends to unstructured data storage. The two companies are bringing familiar storage capabilities into hybrid and multicloud environments.

Dell PowerScale for Microsoft Azure brings Dell’s OneFS file system software into Azure as a managed storage service. Customers can provision file storage directly from the Azure portal while retaining familiar PowerScale management capabilities.

The solution supports a wide range of production workloads across industries. These industries increasingly depend on high-throughput, low-latency file access to drive the next generation of agentic AI and advanced analytics. Media and entertainment firms can use it to handle massive video files, real-time editing and tight production timelines. Semiconductor and electronics design houses can accelerate simulation and modeling using large datasets.

“This isn’t really about running the software just in the cloud,” said Rachna Lalwani, senior consultant, director and product manager at Dell, in an interview with theCUBE. “It’s about creating a truly integrated experience that empowers businesses to do more with their data. What they really gain is the operational consistency across their entire storage landscape.”

A recent IDC analysis found that 95% of enterprises already run at least one AI agent workflow in production, and it predicted 2.5 billion agents by 2030. With the rise of agentic AI, Dell and Microsoft are collaborating on solutions designed to help enterprises deploy autonomous agents while controlling costs.

Managing the cost of tokens, the fundamental units of data processed by large language models, is one of AI’s financial challenges. To help address it, Dell introduced Deskside Agentic AI in May in collaboration with Microsoft and Nvidia Corp., providing a local environment for building and testing AI agents.

“What’s resonating with customers right now is that the cost of tokens is through the roof,” explained Jon Siegal, senior vice president of Dell portfolio marketing at Dell. “We know even though the cost of a token has come down pretty dramatically, the amount of tokens that are being consumed right now is just astronomical. The cloud costs are just pretty high right now. How do customers balance that out and run the right workload in the right place? We’re trying to give customers a place to start. The PC is a great place to start.”

In early October, Dell announced an expansion of its Windows PCs and workstations for agentic AI. In partnership with Microsoft, Dell broadened its AI development portfolio to provide creators, developers and enterprises with more choice in how they build, test and scale agentic AI on Windows.

This marked a key step in the evolution of Windows, where the platform has evolved into a broader resource for agentic AI. Tools such as Windows AI Foundry give developers a structured path to build, package and scale agents inside a governed environment.

“With Windows, we’re going beyond just it being an operating system — we’re thinking about it as really a canvas for AI,” said Mary Ann Anderson, worldwide marketing director of Dell partnerships at Microsoft. “Pretty soon there’s going to be a point where individual employees are managing their own agents, maybe a small army of agents. You have to do that in a way that is governed and is very secure.”

Dell and Microsoft see a significant market opportunity in closing the gap between AI development and production deployment.

“Microsoft and Dell have an opportunity to address that gap by simplifying deployment, automating infrastructure operations and giving partners repeatable solutions they can take to market,” said theCUBE Research’s Nashawaty. “The real measure of success will be whether their combined ecosystem helps enterprises move from AI experimentation to production-ready applications with stronger governance, predictable costs and measurable business outcomes.”

(* Disclosure: TheCUBE is a paid media partner for the Dell AI Data Platform Event. Neither Dell, the sponsor of theCUBE’s event coverage, nor other sponsors have editorial control over content on theCUBE or SiliconANGLE.)
