#5455. Top tips for long flights from frequent travelers

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Make your next long-haul flight more comfortable with expert tips for better sleep, smarter packing, in-flight snacks and an easier arrival

A long-haul flight can test even the most enthusiastic traveler. After hours in a cramped seat, the cabin starts to feel stuffy, your legs need a stretch and the snacks you packed suddenly seem less appealing. While you can't control every part of the experience, a little planning can make a big difference between arriving ready to explore and stumbling off the plane feeling completely wiped out.

Frequent travelers have learned to make those hours more manageable. Some rely on practical comforts, such as packing a personal amenity kit or choosing a seat with sleep in mind. Others have built routines around staying hydrated, getting up to move or adjusting to a new time zone before landing. A few even treat long flights as a chance to catch up on work without the usual interruptions.

Reader’s Digest spoke with frequent travelers to gather their best advice for making long flights more comfortable. Their suggestions cover everything from what to wear and pack to how to spend your time in the air. Whether you're crossing the country or heading overseas, these tips can help you settle in, make the most of your seat and arrive feeling a little more human.

A long flight is no time to assume you'll be hungry at exactly the moment the airline serves food. Reader’s Digest recommends bringing a mix of snacks, including something salty and something sweet, along with a drink purchased at the airport. In-flight service can be delayed, and it's easy to sleep through the beverage cart or simply not feel like asking for something between scheduled services.

Having your own snacks gives you more control over when and what you eat. It also means you're not stuck waiting if you get hungry during a long stretch without service. Spending a little extra at the airport may feel unnecessary, especially when you've already paid for your ticket, but having food within reach can make the flight more comfortable. Think of it as a small investment in your own in-flight peace of mind.

Airplane cabins can get cold, and a stylish outfit won't do much for you if you're uncomfortable halfway through the flight. According to Reader’s Digest, wear breathable, cozy layers if you can. Wearing an oversized hoodie and thick socks, and bringing a neck pillow and eye mask, can help create a warm, dark space for sleeping.

Prioritize comfort over an outfit designed just for the airport. A soft layer is easy to add or remove as the cabin temperature changes, and it can save you from relying on a thin airline blanket.

There's nothing worse than needing a toothbrush, face wipe, or change of clothes, and realizing the item is buried in your overhead suitcase. Keeping a well-stocked amenity kit in your personal item, where you can reach it throughout the flight, can be extremely helpful.

Your kit can include basics such as a toothbrush, toothpaste, makeup-removing wipes, and hair products. Also, according to Reader’s Digest, packing a change of underwear can go a long way in case checked luggage goes missing. or doesn't arrive when you do.

Rather than rummaging through your carry-on or waiting until you reach your hotel, you have the things you need to freshen up close at hand. Put together a small kit before you leave home and keep it in the bag that stays under the seat in front of you. It's one less thing to worry about when you're tired and ready to land.

Long flights come with plenty of familiar cabin smells, from reheated meals to stale air. For example, notes Reader’s Digest, scented balms can make the environment feel more pleasant.

The scents can be subtle, so as not to overwhelm nearby passengers. If you want to try the idea, keep any scent you bring understated. A strong fragrance can quickly become unpleasant for people sitting nearby in a confined cabin. The point is to create a small comfort for yourself, in an otherwise somewhat stale environment.

The hours spent in an airplane cabin can leave some travelers feeling less than refreshed. Keeping up with those small routines can go a long way to feeling good upon arrival. Additionally, according to Reader’s Digest, a few familiar products can make it easier to freshen up during a long journey, especially if you're heading straight into sightseeing, a meeting or another connection.

You don't need to bring your entire bathroom cabinet. Choose a few travel-size products you already use and keep them somewhere accessible in your personal item. That way, you can freshen up without unpacking your luggage or waiting until you reach your destination.

Shoes that feel fine at the airport may become uncomfortable after hours in the air. According to Reader’s Digest, choose slip-on shoes without laces and go up half a size. Tight sneakers became increasingly uncomfortable as your feet will possibly swell during lengthy journeys.

Easy-to-remove shoes also make it simpler to get comfortable in your seat without wrestling with laces. Just remember that you'll want footwear that's practical for walking through the airport, too. The goal is to avoid shoes that feel restrictive after several hours, not to sacrifice comfort as soon as you reach the gate.

If you're planning a long-haul trip, think about how your shoes will feel near the end of the journey, not just when you first put them on. A little extra room can make those hours much easier.

#5454. SlidesAI Expands Beyond Google Slides With Standalone AI Presentation Platform

Users can now create, edit and share presentations directly in their browser, alongside integrations with Google Slides, Microsoft PowerPoint and ChatGPT.

SHARJAH, UAE, Nov. 3, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- SlidesAI, an AI presentation maker that began as a Google Slides add-on, has expanded into a standalone presentation platform with its own browser-based workspace.

First released earlier this year, the SlidesAI web app lets users turn ideas, notes and documents into presentations without installing an add-on or working inside Google Slides or PowerPoint. It brings presentation planning, content creation, design and editing into one workspace.

"We started as a Google Slides add-on, then a PowerPoint add-in, and that's where we found our first users and grew to over twelve million," said Anurag Bhagsain, founder of SlidesAI. "But honestly, the product outgrew that framing."

The standalone platform extends SlidesAI's role across the presentation process. Users begin with a topic, notes or a document, then specify their audience, tone, language and slide count. Before generating the deck, they can review the outline, reorder slides and refine the content. Once the presentation opens in the editor, they can edit text directly or request AI revisions, review the suggested changes and accept them.

The need for help across those steps is reflected in a recent SlidesAI onboarding survey. Among more than 18,000 responding new users, roughly two-thirds selected design and visuals as a presentation challenge, while nearly half selected the time required. Respondents could select multiple challenges.

Those responses illustrate why generating slide text addresses only part of the work. Turning that content into a structured, visually coherent presentation also requires decisions about sequence, layout and design. SlidesAI's web-based AI presentation maker lets users work through those stages within the same environment.

For organizations creating recurring presentations, Brand Kit lets users import an existing PowerPoint template and apply their colors, fonts, logos and layouts to generated decks. Finished presentations can be presented directly, shared through a link or exported to PowerPoint or Google Slides.

SlidesAI also continues to support its existing integrations. Users can create and refine presentations through the PowerPoint add-in, work directly within Google Slides, or use ChatGPT to generate presentations directly in their SlidesAI account.

SlidesAI is an AI presentation creation and editing platform for professionals, educators and students. Available as a standalone web app and through integrations with Google Slides, Microsoft PowerPoint and ChatGPT, SlidesAI helps users turn ideas and source material into editable presentations. Learn more at  https://www.slidesai.io/.

#5453. PagerDuty debuts Paige AI agent with renamed PD Reliability Platform and PD Labs

Operations management software company PagerDuty Inc. today introduced Paige, an artificial intelligence agent for site reliability engineering that is built to work as a member of operations and engineering teams.

Paige runs on the company’s flagship product, which as of today is called the PD Reliability Platform. Alongside both, PagerDuty opened PD Labs to put early features in front of customers while they are still being built.

The launch is aimed at a problem PagerDuty says is getting worse as AI coding tools write more production software, much of it shipped with little human review. Applications built on AI models also break in their own ways. Chief Executive John DiLullo pointed to model drift, token runaway and leaked personal data as examples. The only way to stay resilient, he said, is “to fight fire with fire, using AI itself as part of how we keep systems running.”

Customers set Paige’s permissions team by team. A team that keeps a person in the loop gets faster triage with remediation held for approval, and the agent acts on its own only in well-understood, low-risk scenarios the team has explicitly authorized. In March, PagerDuty said its SRE Agent would start joining escalation policies as a “virtual responder.” Paige, billed as the company’s next-generation SRE agent, can now be put on call that way. A lower-priority incident may never reach a human at all.

Paige’s recommendations arrive with evidence and a confidence level attached. By the time a responder reads one, many possible causes have been ruled out already. PagerDuty argues the bigger payoff comes later, once a resolved incident has been written into a shared memory that Paige consults whenever something similar fails. In a benchmark report released with the launch, the company says Paige did better than leading AI coding agents at diagnosing simulated information technology incidents.

The renamed platform, known until today as PagerDuty Operations Cloud, is where Paige gets its operational context. Incident commanders and team managers also get a new PD Reliability Platform Console, which puts incidents, on-call rotations and AI agents in one view. The console shows which agents are switched on and what each one is doing. Paige’s suggested fixes can be acted on from the same screen.

Responders can run an incident end to end in Slack or Microsoft Teams. A trigger opens a dedicated channel and a conference bridge without anyone having to set them up.

Steve Miller, director of business development at Slack, said having Paige and the platform inside Slack gives responders speed and visibility, which he called critical as “agentic and human teams operate side-by-side in the same channel.” Nobody has to write the post-incident review, which is generated as soon as the incident is resolved, and its follow-up actions come with owners and due dates already assigned.

Canadian telecommunications company Telus Corp. has wired the platform into its own centralized internal incident tool. Kulvir Gahunia, director of the Site Reliability Office at Telus, said PagerDuty’s Scribe Agent now runs through every incident, so responders “don’t have to stop and document what is happening.”

The earlier-stage work runs through PD Labs, which PagerDuty is building in the open with design partners who get early access and a direct line to the engineers writing the code.

Three experiments are in preview to start. Topology keeps a live map of an organization’s services, assembled from its code, infrastructure and runbooks. No configuration management database is needed, and the map scopes the blast radius of a problem automatically as conditions change.

Deep Investigation has Paige test several root-cause hypotheses at once while showing its reasoning on each as new evidence comes in. SRE Workbench gives people and agents one workspace to tackle a problem side by side, and whatever they find is saved to the same memory Paige learns from.

IT teams want measurable results from their spending on AI agents, according to Snow Tempest, research manager for IT service management at International Data Corp. Better uptime counts, as does time handed back to responders who would otherwise be “chasing logs and assembling the right people for an incident.” More organizations also want to prevent incidents, Tempest said.

Paige and the PD Reliability Platform are generally available today, and SRE Workbench is open to try through PD Labs. The platform is sold for a fee tied to operational scale that comes with a starting allotment of ingested events, automation actions and user seats. Customers who outgrow it can buy flexible credits without having to forecast usage ahead of time.

#5452. Many workers break rules to help customers. Their bosses punish them anyway

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Most managers punish everyone the same way for breaking a rule. Employees step out of line for four reasons, and only one is personal gain

A version of this article originally appeared in Quartz’s Leadership newsletter. Sign up here to get the latest leadership news and insights straight to your inbox.

Plenty of managers write up an employee as soon as they find out he or she broke a rule. They handle every case the same way because it seems fair, and they want the rest of the team to see that nobody gets a pass. And many of them assume the worker was only looking out for himself or herself.

Some employees do put themselves first. Others bend a rule to help a customer, cave to pressure from coworkers or a deadline, or follow their profession's ethics over a company policy, according to a review of more than 250 studies by Oxford's Michael Gill. Gill has watched a lot of managers treat all four kinds of employee alike.

"If your first move is to punish someone, you may be solving the immediate issue but missing the real cause," Gill told Harvard Business Review. "And that can hurt the business in the long term." Once the boss files the write-up, he or she never hears what the employee was trying to do. He or she also never learns whether others on the team have been making the same call for the same reason.

Front-line workers will often bend a company rule to help a customer. In an experiment by Su Kyung (Irene) Kim of the University of British Columbia and Yujie Zhan of Wilfrid Laurier University, service staff answered voicemails for a pretend children's dance school. One message came from a mother with two kids in a Monday class. She had missed a deadline by a few days, and her bill had gone up $142. She asked to keep last year's rate, and more than half the staff let her pay it.

Kim and Zhan also had retail clerks, nurses, hotel workers, and others describe the last time a customer wanted something their company didn't allow. Most had said yes anyway. Afterward, they felt more in control of their work and closer to the people they served. A month later, they were less worn out and liked their jobs more. Those clerks and nurses are often exactly the people a business can least afford to lose.

If a boss punishes everyone the same way, the employees most willing to help customers take the same hit as the ones cheating the company. So they stop helping, and the rule stays in place.

When everyone on a team keeps doing something they've been told not to do, Gill doesn't start by blaming them. "If a rule has been broken over and over again and that is an issue," he said, "then that speaks to a more fundamental problem about the rule itself rather than the rule breakers."

Managers write instructions for the job as it is at the time. Then the work changes, and nobody goes back to update them, Gill said. Front-line staff notice first. They're the ones who have to tell customers no, but many quietly start saying yes.

They usually know how the job should be done instead. Workers feel especially capable after going against instructions they already think make no sense, according to Kim and Zhan. They also suggest more ways to improve service afterward. They're the first people a leader should ask.

They won't say much, though, if they suspect they're about to be disciplined. "If your people believe they are in trouble, they'll shut down," Gill told HBR, "but if they think you're trying to understand what happened before coming to your final conclusions, they are more likely to open up." Once staff decide the boss doesn't care about their reasons, some follow the rulebook to the letter and stop making their own calls. Others keep doing the job their own way and make sure nobody finds out. In both cases, the boss never learns what needs to change.

Asking why doesn't mean letting everyone off. Gill said employees tend to explain themselves right away if they have a good reason, and say much less if they're looking out for themselves. He thinks managers should discipline workers who break a rule for their benefit, as long as they know what they're doing and what it could cost them. For everyone else, he said, the boss should start by explaining what's at stake for the company.

Some rules are worth keeping even when breaking them would help a customer. Delinea, a San Francisco cybersecurity company, sells through resellers, and they decide what buyers pay. Its own employees aren't supposed to talk price at all. Some answered customers' questions about cost on the spot anyway, instead of making them wait, CEO Art Gilliland told HBR. But if a Delinea employee names a figure, the company can break regulations and face price-fixing claims. Even though everyone involved was trying to help, they still had to stop answering those questions.

Gilliland responded by asking how often an employee gave a customer a number. If the answer was once, a manager would explain why Delinea leaves pricing to its resellers and coach the person on what to say next time. Usually, nobody needs a second talk. "If someone continues breaking a rule after coaching and support, eventually you must make the call to let them go," Gilliland said.

Gilliland blames the person when one employee keeps quoting prices after being shown the right way. Gill, by contrast, looks at the company's instructions once a whole team stops following them. Before rewriting a rule or letting someone go, a leader has to know whether one person is ignoring it or everyone is.

A CEO only hears about either problem if someone speaks up, and in many companies nobody does. Employees often keep quiet when they see a coworker break a rule, and managers rarely tell their own bosses. Gill would give staff an anonymous way to speak up, or someone neutral to go to. He also wants senior leaders to spend some time doing front-line work themselves. A rule that seems obvious from the executive floor can look very different behind the counter.

#5451. Zebec ZBCN Buyback: 40.5M Tokens Held, Not Burned, as Supply Stays Unchanged

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zebec says it bought back 40.5 million ZBCN in the third quarter and is keeping them "out of circulation."

On-chain, those tokens didn't reach Zebec's buyback treasury wallet during the quarter. They arrived on October 21, three weeks after Q3 ended, the same day Zebec announced the buyback, sent from what Solscan labels a Crypto.com hot wallet.

The amount matches Zebec's claim almost to the token. But the wallet's history also shows something "out of circulation" doesn't usually suggest: it has moved 59 million ZBCN out before. Let's go through the wallet to check what Zebec's buyback claim actually covers.

Zebec Network announced on October 21, in an X post, that it repurchased 40,536,539 ZBCN in Q3 for about $100,000. That implies an average price of roughly $0.00247. The money came from Zebec Cards and payroll fees across Zebec Enterprise and the SuperApp.

Zebec's explainer, Inside the ZBCN Buyback Program, says buybacks are "funded by operating revenue" from payroll, payments, cards and related services, not from treasury reserves. That's a real point in Zebec's favor.

The scale is small. ZBCN has a 100 billion maximum supply, so 40.5 million tokens is about 0.04% of it.

Zebec says the repurchased tokens "will not re-enter circulation." They weren't burned. ZBCN's total supply is exactly the same as it was before the buyback.

That's a deliberate policy. The program began in 2023 under the old ZBC token and originally included burns. In early 2024, the Zebec DAO approved ZIP-4, which paused burns while keeping recurring buybacks. Zebec says the DAO expects to decide by the end of 2026 whether to propose bringing burns back. Governance happens through the Zebec DAO portal.

The practical difference matters. A burn permanently destroys tokens. "Out of circulation" depends on Zebec continuing to hold them and on data providers leaving them out of circulating supply. The blockchain doesn't enforce either one.

Zebec's blog says repurchased tokens are held "in the designated on-chain Buyback Treasury Wallet and with Uphold Institutional," but doesn't give the address. The account linked with the announcement is EkXEg6de172aoLvr7w86YzQ2rf5oEFD3iUt8uQsLQuQW. ZBCN's Solana mint address is ZBCNpuD7YMXzTHB2fhGkGi78MNsHGLRXUhRewNRm9RU.

As of October 22, Solscan shows the wallet holding 108,256,701.48 ZBCN, worth about $246,157 at $0.002273.

The Q3 check passes. On October 21 at about 14:11 UTC, the wallet received two ZBCN transfers from an address Solscan labels "Crypto.com Hot Wallet":

Together, that's 40,535,224.09 ZBCN, just 1,315 ZBCN (about $3) short of Zebec's figure. That's a 99.997% match. The small difference is likely due to fees or rounding.

One detail stands out: the account is off-curve. Solscan shows "isOnCurve: FALSE," which means the address is derived by a program and has no private key of its own. Accounts like this are usually controlled by a program such as a multisig, so moving tokens requires that program's approval. That's a better setup than a single person's wallet, but it isn't a lock.

The timing shows how the program works. The wallet's transfer history suggests a repeating pattern, with each batch arriving after its quarter has ended:

Those three batches add up to the wallet's current balance within 0.01 ZBCN. So the "buyback treasury" holds the last three quarters of deliveries and nothing else.

This means that during each quarter, the purchased tokens weren't in the on-chain treasury. The pattern points to buying on an exchange, with tokens sitting in an exchange account until they're withdrawn to the treasury around announcement time. The chain doesn't show when the Q3 purchases actually happened, so for July 1 to September 30, the "$100,000 Q3 buyback" can't be checked on-chain. Only the October 21 delivery can.

That's common practice and not a sign of wrongdoing. But it means the on-chain record confirms delivery, not the purchases themselves.

If the balance only covers the last three batches, what happened to earlier buybacks? The transfer history answers that, too. The wallet has sent ZBCN out twice, both times to the same address, shown on Solscan as 9Sq2nZ...4TEine:

That's about 58.97 million ZBCN moved out of a wallet described as holding tokens that "will not re-enter circulation."To be fair, Zebec says tokens are "periodically consolidated with Uphold Institutional for custody," and these outflows may be exactly that. There's no confirmation that 9Sq2nZ...4TEine belongs to Uphold. Once tokens leave this wallet, readers can't follow them using Zebec's disclosures. These transfers also show what a burn would prevent: tokens in this wallet can, and do, move.

The Q3 claim holds up better than I expected. The wallet received almost exactly 40.5 million ZBCN, and the balance reconciles to the token. What the chain can't show is when the tokens were bought, or where earlier buybacks are now.

Three disclosures would close those gaps:

For now, Zebec did buy and deliver its Q3 tokens, and the supply is the same as it was before.

#5450. AI optimism meets data center backlash as protesters disrupt Seattle AI Week kickoff

by Todd Bishop on Oct 26, 2026 at 10:44 pmOctober 27, 2026 at 11:21 am

The Washington Technology Industry Association kicked off the third annual Seattle AI Week on Monday with a reminder that AI affects everyone, from engineers and artists to “someone who learned about ChatGPT today,” as WTIA’s Nick Ellingson put it.

“All of us should be a part of that conversation,” he added.

A few people in the audience took that statement literally.

Members of Troublemakers, a Seattle climate activism group, interrupted the week’s opening panel on AI and economic growth several times before they were led out by security. Outside on Elliott Bay, others floated in kayaks with a banner: “Power for People, Not for Tech.”

“These are not your constituents — we are,” one protester told Beau Perschbacher, Gov. Bob Ferguson’s senior policy advisor, as he addressed the large crowd of tech and startup leaders at Seattle’s AI House. Perschbacher was on a panel with Joe Nguyen of the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce and Mattie Zazueta of OpenAI, the event’s presenting sponsor.

The group’s main message, according to members who spoke with GeekWire: the rush to build data centers and roll out AI is putting the state’s communities, jobs and environment at risk, and Washington should be investing in green jobs and clean energy instead.

The protest comes amid a broader backlash against data centers in Washington state and across the country. The Seattle City Council voted unanimously in June to pause new large data centers in the city for a year, and Washington AI Resistance organized at least 19 protests around the state this month calling for a statewide moratorium.

The event also came the same day Microsoft offered voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, roughly a quarter of its workforce, as it spends tens of billions of dollars on data centers and AI infrastructure.

The backlash contrasts with a push from the business and tech community for Washington state and the Seattle region to do more to stay competitive in the AI era.

“Washington helped build the technology economy of the last generation. We have an extraordinary opportunity to lead the AI economy of the next,” said former Gov. Chris Gregoire, now CEO of the business group Challenge Seattle, in her opening remarks at the AI Week event.

Gregoire cited efforts to put AI to work on the region’s own problems, including an AI permitting pilot in Everett that she said could cut the median wait for an accessory dwelling unit permit from 252 days to 90. She highlighted the AI-driven protein design work of Nobel laureate David Baker of the University of Washington, with applications in areas including the environment, agriculture and health care.

She also warned that Washington is close to the bottom for its business climate, even though it ranks second in North America for tech talent, as other states court its companies and jobs.

On the panel, Perschbacher said Ferguson’s administration has been focused on data centers since taking office, setting up a work group early last year to study their impact. The group looked for a Washington community that had been harmed by a data center and couldn’t find one, he said.

He added that the state won’t permit data centers to run diesel generators around the clock, and that their water use turned out to be “not out of line with a typical industrial user.”

Electricity is a different story. Data centers “use a really significant amount of electricity,” he said, and with demand also rising from EVs and heat pumps, getting enough power “is a major challenge.”

Perschbacher addressed the protesters directly, saying Washington has some of the strictest environmental laws in the country and that the state’s data center work group reinforced those rules rather than weakening them. Bills on ratepayer protections and transparency for data centers are likely to come back in the next legislative session, he said.

The issue also came up in the event’s second panel, on AI policy. State Sen. Marko Liias, who sponsored a bill this year on high-risk uses of AI, said data centers that want to locate in Washington need to meet “stringent expectations,” including adding clean energy to the grid, recycling water and dropping nondisclosure agreements that keep communities in the dark. Washington’s goal “has never been to be the cheapest or easiest place,” he said.

“When energy becomes scarce, I do think we need to be clear that our communities deserve access to that energy before the data centers do,” Liias said.

Joe Braidwood, founder of AI governance startup Glacis, which works out of AI House, said on the same panel that it was the first event he’d attended there with a public protest. “I think that’s actually kind of promising that people care enough to want to come together and talk and disagree and figure this out,” he said.

Zazueta, OpenAI’s global head of community programs, said in the opening panel that the industry needs to do a better job showing people the benefits of AI. Many people “read about these scary headlines,” she said, but don’t see how the technology applies to their daily lives.

OpenAI runs AI literacy workshops and trains libraries and community groups to lead their own, she said. The company opened an expanded office in Bellevue in March, its largest engineering center outside San Francisco.

Speaking with GeekWire outside the event on Monday afternoon, one of the protesters who had interrupted the panel singled out that remark. She said it dismissed public concerns about AI as the product of bad headlines, and she objected to the idea of using community groups to win people over to the benefits of artificial intelligence.

“They want to infiltrate our communities,” she said.

The opening panel with Zazueta, Perschbacher and Nguyen was titled “The Abundance State: Washington’s Chance to Lead the AI Future.” The protester objected to that framing, saying the panelists’ idea of abundance came down to easing permits for data centers.

It wasn’t the first time the group has protested the tech industry’s energy use. In 2024, it blocked entrances at Amazon’s Seattle headquarters to protest the company’s plans to power data centers in Oregon with natural gas.

Inside the event on Monday, as the interruptions continued, Nguyen, a former state senator who now leads the Seattle chamber, had responded to the protesters directly. “If you want to have your own event, have your own event,” he told them.

After they were led out, Nguyen said he agreed with the protesters, calling their passion “very warranted.” Those concerns are one reason Washington created some of the most stringent energy policies in the country, he said, adding that everyone would be better off if data centers elsewhere were held to the same standards.

“I think we’re very unique in Washington state to be able to actually do this in a way that really is mindful of our values, of the environment, and also pushing for innovation as well,” he said.

At the same time, Nguyen said demand for AI and data centers is market-driven, and it isn’t fair to criticize data centers while using them every day.

“For anybody who’s upset with data centers, I hope that when you email me, don’t email me,” he said. “Print it off and walk it to my office.”

Update, Oct. 27: Protesters interrupted the opening session of WTIA’s Seattle AI Summit six times Tuesday morning, during an on-stage interview of OpenAI’s Vijaye Raji by GeekWire’s Todd Bishop. They objected to AI-related job losses, the climate impact of data centers, OpenAI’s ties to the Trump administration and the leadership of OpenAI CEO Sam Altman.

#5449. From Trump University to Yeezy, 5 celebrity brands that failed or faltered

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These celebrity businesses that flopped or stumbled, from Trump University to Planet Hollywood and Yeezy, ran into lawsuits, bankruptcies, settlements and broken partnerships

Fame can draw a crowd to a launch. It cannot settle a lawsuit, satisfy a creditor, answer a regulator or keep a corporate partner on board. The celebrity businesses that flopped or stumbled in this list show where that limit sits. Each one carried a famous name. Each one still faced the same pressures that test any other company.

A recognizable founder lowers the cost of getting attention. Fans already know the name on the label before the first product ships. That head start does not change how a business is judged once it is open. Customers still decide whether to come back. Courts still hear complaints. Regulators still review what a company says about its products. Partners still weigh whether an association helps or hurts them.

The five cases here took different turns. Trump University was a real estate seminar program. It drew a lawsuit from the New York attorney general and class actions from students. Donald Trump agreed in November 2016 to pay $25 million to settle those suits. His Trump Steaks and Trump Vodka products were also discontinued.

Planet Hollywood opened in New York in 1991. Its backers included Arnold Schwarzenegger, Bruce Willis, Sylvester Stallone and Demi Moore. The restaurant chain filed for bankruptcy protection in 1999 and again in 2001. Gwyneth Paltrow started Goop as a newsletter in 2008. In 2018, the lifestyle brand paid $145,000 to settle a civil case with California district attorneys over unsupported health claims. Adidas ended its Yeezy partnership with Kanye West in October 2022 after his antisemitic remarks. Kim Kardashian's KKW Beauty line took a new name, SKKN by Kim, in 2022.

Not every one of these ventures disappeared. Goop still operates. Planet Hollywood still runs at a much smaller scale. The lawsuits against Trump University ended in a settlement. Adidas cut its ties with West and sold off the remaining Yeezy inventory. The KKW Beauty name was retired.

This is a selection of celebrity business failures and setbacks, not a ranking or a complete list. Each slide covers one celebrity's venture or group of products and the event that marked its turn: a lawsuit, a bankruptcy filing, a regulatory settlement, a terminated partnership or a rebrand.

Trump University, a real estate seminar program carrying Donald Trump's name, ended in court. In November 2016, Trump agreed to pay $25 million to resolve the lawsuits the program drew.

The legal pressure came from two sides. One case was a government action brought by the New York attorney general. The others were class actions filed by former students of the seminars.

A single $25 million agreement covered both the state's case and the students' claims. The settlement closed the litigation without a trial verdict.

The Trump brand also reached beyond education. Trump Steaks carried the name into food. Trump Vodka carried it into liquor. Both product lines were later discontinued.

Taken together, the three ventures stretched one name across seminars, meat and spirits. All three have since ended.

Planet Hollywood, the celebrity-backed restaurant chain that opened in New York in 1991, filed for bankruptcy protection in 1999 and again in 2001. The brand outlasted both filings and still operates, though at a much smaller scale.

Film actors backed the chain. Its investors included Arnold Schwarzenegger, Bruce Willis, Sylvester Stallone and Demi Moore. Their names tied the restaurants to Hollywood from the start.

The first bankruptcy filing came eight years after the New York opening. The second came two years after the first. That timing put the company back under bankruptcy protection soon after its first case.

Neither filing closed the business. The Planet Hollywood name is still in use. It now sits on an operation far smaller than the chain that first sought protection in 1999.

Gwyneth Paltrow's Goop paid $145,000 in 2018 to settle a civil case with California district attorneys. The case involved health claims the brand made about its products, including the jade egg, that were not supported.

The settlement was a regulatory setback for Goop, not the end of the business. The company kept operating after the case and is still in business.

Paltrow founded Goop in 2008. It began as a newsletter before it grew into a lifestyle brand that sells products.

The jade egg was one of the products at the center of the dispute. The case turned on what Goop told customers those products could do for their health.

Goop's trouble came from law enforcement officials, not from creditors, a bankruptcy court or a partner ending a deal. The district attorneys challenged the brand's marketing claims, and the $145,000 payment resolved the civil case.

That places Goop among celebrity business setbacks rather than shutdowns.

Adidas ended its Yeezy partnership with Kanye West in October 2022 after he made antisemitic remarks. The sportswear company later sold off the Yeezy inventory that remained.

Yeezy was the sneaker line Adidas produced with West. The partnership tied a major manufacturer to a celebrity name.

The deal ended because of West's public statements. It did not end with a bankruptcy filing or a court settlement. That sets it apart from celebrity brands that failed under pressure from creditors or lawsuits.

The split left Adidas holding Yeezy products that had already been made. The company chose to sell off that stock after the partnership ended.

The case turned on one party's decision. Once Adidas ended the agreement, the Yeezy line under that partnership stopped.

Kim Kardashian's KKW Beauty name ended in 2022, when the line was rebranded as SKKN by Kim. The rebrand replaced the original label with a new one.

The change was a name switch. It was not a bankruptcy filing, a court-ordered shutdown or a legal settlement.

KKW Beauty is the one case here where the turning point was a change of identity rather than an outside party forcing an end. The KKW Beauty brand name stopped being used in 2022. SKKN by Kim took its place.

#5448. Startup Athena raises $2.5M in pre-seed funding to revamp the revenue model for legal AI

Athena Circle Corp., an artificial intelligence-native legal technology startup that’s automating the nitty gritty of commercial real estate deals, said today it has raised $2.5 million in pre-seed funding.

The round was led by Andreessen Horowitz’s accelerator program, a16z Speedrun. No other investors were named.

Legal AI technology is nothing new, but its adoption in the industry has been somewhat haphazard, for the technology has exposed an awkward problem: Most law firms are still billing their clients by the hour, and that makes automation less lucrative. If a law firm can use AI agents to get a 10-hour contract review done in just a couple of minutes, then it’s going to let an awful lot of billable revenue slip through its fingers, killing any incentive there might be to adopt them.

Athena’s co-founders Cem Ucan (pictured, left) and Kieran John Keenan (right) and founding engineer José Braz all cut their teeth at the pioneering legal AI tech startup Legora AB, where they quickly realized how AI conflicts with the industry’s standard business model. They came up with an entirely different business model to convince legal firms of the benefits of automation. Instead of selling software tools directly, it provides a legal service through its affiliated law firm, charging a fixed fee per transaction that’s typically 30% to 50% lower than standard rates. In this way, it ensures that revenue is better aligned with efficiency.

“Most legal AI companies sell tools to traditional law firms, but we took a different approach,” Ucan said. “Our AI works hand-in-hand with a law firm designed around it from day one, with experienced attorneys focused on the judgment and negotiation that actually move deals forward.”

The startup is focused on automating the intricacies of commercial real estate acquisitions, sales and financing. Its AI agents are designed to automate the creation and review of purchase agreements and loan documents, and will handle all of the due diligence and administrative closing hurdles needed to get deals done, while ensuring human lawyers remain fully in the loop to make all of the final legal determinations.

In this way, Athena basically takes care of the grunt work, giving commercial real estate firms much more agility. That’s a real advantage, because commercial real estate is an industry where speed is of the essence: The faster a law firm gets things done, the more likely it is to actually secure the deal, which is the end result that everyone wants. With investors often submitting dozens of bids for each property listing, the ability to get the paperwork done in a matter of hours rather than weeks or days means buyers can lock in a deal before their rivals know what’s happened.

Keenan, who serves as the startup’s chief technology officer, explained that each new workflow begins with an incoming agreement that’s ingested by its AI agents. They cross-reference the terms of the deal against their standard deal sheets in order to flag inconsistencies, prepare redlines and draft client communications.

This work is informed by historical transactions, which allow its agents to adapt to each client’s negotiating style, Keenan said. Human attorneys then review this work, make strategic judgment calls when required, and approve all deliverables before they’re sent to clients.

“I measure our progress by how quickly an attorney can review an AI agent’s work and confidently stand behind it,” Keenan explained. “A draft produced in minutes can still leave a lawyer with hours of work. Making that review more efficient is how our platform helps us deliver faster legal services with the quality clients expect.”

Athena’s agents are already proving their worth, with the startup having signed up 22 legal firms as clients so far, just two months after launching its service. By learning continuously from attorney’s edits and client’s preferences, its agents have reduced review times by an average of 70%.

L. Miguel Arce, chief executive of the Texas-based multifamily real estate and property management firm Mox Living, said Athena was able to deliver a complete purchase agreement in less than 48 hours, the fastest turnaround he has ever seen. “A lot of firms in our industry have an AI task force in name only,” he said. “What stood out about Athena is that the system learns from every deal, from what the attorneys change to what we prefer. Speed only matters if it’s quality work, and Athena gets us both.”

Keenan said Athena is primed to strike while the iron is hot. He said the industry is bracing itself for a wave of new commercial deals as properties financed through short-term loans in 2021 and 2022 hit their refinancing deadlines, and he’s hoping that the startup can win a significant amount of that business. In any case, growth is on the horizon, for Athena also plans to expand into new markets and property classes and even new legal domains.

A16z Speedrun’s Troy Kirwin said AI automation is all well and good, but clients still demand to speak to a human who can take responsibility for the work that gets done. “Athena is building around that need with a system that can improve through real legal work and a team that’s obsessed with scaling fast,” he said.

#5447. Who’s getting Anthropic’s compute spending? IPO filing shows where the tech giants really stand

by Todd Bishop on Oct 27, 2026 at 6:53 amOctober 27, 2026 at 10:58 am

Anthropic’s IPO filing reads like a ledger of who’s getting paid in the AI boom. The Seattle region’s tech giants are on the list, but they aren’t at the top.

The prospectus, filed Monday with the Securities and Exchange Commission, details more than $750 billion in computing deals, including firm commitments and estimated future spending, and offers clues about what its founders and biggest investors stand to gain ahead of the company’s planned Nasdaq listing under the ticker ANT.

Amazon and Microsoft have invested billions in Anthropic and won high-profile spending commitments from the Claude maker. But both trail Google, chipmaker Broadcom and Elon Musk’s SpaceX in their shares of Anthropic’s planned spending on computing power, the filing shows.

Following the compute money: Google’s chips are the biggest winner. Anthropic has lined up roughly $400 billion in computing capacity, mostly over the next seven years, based on Google-designed AI chips, known as tensor processing units or TPUs.

That total includes $114.5 billion to Google directly through July 2033, $161.2 billion in equipment leases with chipmaker Broadcom, and an estimated $125 billion to $150 billion in additional TPU capacity from 2028 to 2031.

Broadcom’s leases are the largest single arrangement in the filing. The five-year leases provide TPU-based hardware for data centers operated by other companies on Anthropic’s behalf.

Elon Musk’s SpaceX is next. Anthropic agreed to spend up to $120.5 billion through 2029 for computing capacity from SpaceX’s AI subsidiary, formerly known as xAI, which runs a rival AI lab.

The filing says payments will reach about $3.1 billion a month once all the capacity is delivered, which Anthropic expects in December. The agreements run into 2029, though either side can cancel on 90 days’ notice after early 2027.

Amazon is still a big winner. Anthropic committed in April to spend at least $110 billion with Amazon Web Services over 10 years, through April 2036, and AWS Trainium is one of four chip families that Anthropic uses to train and run its models.

Microsoft’s piece is smaller, which reflects its later start. The company was aligned closely with OpenAI for years before striking its own deal with Anthropic.

Anthropic has committed to spend at least $44.9 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud from November 2026 through May 2033, the filing shows. That’s up from the $30 billion Azure deal announced in November 2025. The deal has been amended twice since, most recently this month.

Claude is built into Microsoft 365, and former Microsoft CFO Chris Liddell joined Anthropic’s board in February.

Two smaller providers have deals in the same range as Microsoft’s. Anthropic agreed to spend up to about $44.6 billion with Nscale, a U.K.-based AI infrastructure company, and about $41.3 billion with GPU cloud provider Lambda, both for capacity powered by Nvidia chips, according to the filing.

Will Anthropic need it all? Most of the commitments can’t be canceled, and the deals with Microsoft, Google and Amazon require Anthropic to pay “regardless of actual usage,” according to the filing.

So far, the demand is there. Anthropic’s revenue hit $11.6 billion in the second quarter, up from $787 million a year earlier, and the company posted its first operating profit, $974 million. It still had a $66.3 billion net loss, mostly from accounting charges tied to its soaring valuation.

The company says it has “consistently operated in a compute-constrained environment where customer demand exceeds available compute.”

Its compute commitments assume that demand keeps growing. Anthropic spent less than $2 billion a month on compute and infrastructure in the second quarter. The SpaceX deal alone is expected to cost about $3.1 billion a month at full capacity.

Paper fortunes: Amazon’s biggest payoff is its stake, which it valued at $190.4 billion as of June 30 in its quarterly SEC filing. That includes convertible notes with $6.2 billion in principal that Amazon valued at $97.9 billion. The notes would convert into stock, subject to a 12% ownership cap that Amazon can waive.

Amazon is scheduled to report third-quarter results Thursday, its first earnings report since Anthropic’s filing. The Seattle-based company has updated the value of its Anthropic holdings in each of its quarterly filings this year, so a new number could come this week.

Google put $10 billion into Anthropic’s latest funding round and can invest up to $20 billion more under a March financing deal. The filing doesn’t give ownership percentages for Amazon, Google or Microsoft. It says only that the three companies have each made “significant equity investments” in Anthropic.

Anthropic’s seven co-founders hold roughly 230 million to 245 million shares each, worth about $14 billion apiece at the latest private funding price. The company also gave its own Public Benefit Fund about 847 million shares, or 5% of its fully diluted stock as of June 30, worth about $50 billion at that price.

Anthropic could begin formally marketing its IPO to investors as soon as the week of Nov. 9, Bloomberg reported, citing people familiar with the matter. It is aiming to go public the following week, according to the Wall Street Journal. The company expects the offering to match or beat the size of SpaceX’s IPO, according to Bloomberg. SpaceX raised $75 billion in June, the largest IPO on record.

#5446. Nuclear power at sea: Seattle startup targets Norway for ships and floating power plants

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 27, 2026 at 7:06 amOctober 27, 2026 at 7:15 am

Emerald Nuclear today announced a $2.1 million award from The Research Council of Norway to support its efforts to bring nuclear energy to the shipping industry and offshore power. The Seattle-based startup is developing high-temperature gas reactors that use an encapsulated fuel designed to resist meltdowns.

“This award will enable Emerald Nuclear to work directly with our marine partners to validate integration of our technology with their state-of-the-art marine power distribution and control systems,” said Wesley Deason, co-founder and CEO.

The funding supports Norway’s Marine Nuclear Propulsion System Pilot project, which is being led by Emerald Nuclear’s Norwegian subsidiary.

Shipping accounts for roughly 3% of global carbon dioxide emissions, making it a significant target for lower-carbon energy solutions. Some ferries serving shorter routes are adopting hybrid-electric propulsion. Shipping companies are exploring methanol, ammonia, biofuels and other alternatives to heavy fuel oil, but their climate benefits depend on how those fuels are produced and used.

Nuclear reactors have powered U.S. Navy submarines for more than 70 years. Now, a new wave of companies is working to expand nuclear power’s role in commercial shipping and other marine applications.

The award supports an early development step for Emerald Nuclear, with substantial work remaining before commercial deployment. The company has yet to build its first reactor, and its plans will require additional financing, regulatory approvals and a reliable fuel supply. The startup has previously received an undisclosed amount of funding from angel investors.

Emerald Nuclear has five employees, most of them in Norway, and is targeting two applications: offshore ships that help construct facilities like oil platforms and wind turbines and lay deep-sea cables, and floating power plants for remote communities. Each reactor is designed to produce 5 megawatts (6,705 horsepower), according to the company.

Bringing nuclear to the marine environment poses several significant challenges. They include safety issues, regulations for vessels traveling internationally, management of nuclear fuel and waste, and the way shipping companies frequently buy and sell vessels.

Deason said the company’s approach helps address those concerns:

Emerald Nuclear is designing its technology “to integrate with the unique power needs of the ship, but also to meet the ways that the maritime industry does business,” Deason said.

Other companies pursuing nuclear ship propulsion include Core Power, newcleo and Blykalla. Core Power, Westinghouse, Saltfoss Energy and Prodigy Clean Energy are also developing floating nuclear power stations. Russia’s state-owned Rosatom already has nuclear-powered icebreakers and a floating nuclear power plant in operation.

Prior to launching Emerald Nuclear, Deason, a nuclear engineer, worked for Ultra Safe Nuclear Corp. (USNC) developing reactors for space-based applications.

During his tenure at the Seattle company, a professor from the Norwegian University of Science and Technology approached USNC about applications for the maritime sector. USNC declared bankruptcy in October 2024 and the deal wasn’t pursued. But the idea interested Deason and Hallgeir Juliebø, a Norwegian entrepreneur who had been a consultant with USNC. The two co-founded Emerald Nuclear in 2024 and Juliebø serves as chief commercial officer.

Emerald Nuclear has signed a lease for an engineering center in Norway, where it’s designing and building its first prototype, a non-nuclear thermal device that will be used for the Marine Nuclear Propulsion System Pilot project.

Other partners for the project are VARD Group, Vard Electro, Island Offshore, Norwegian University of Science and Technology, Imperial College London and Maskindynamikk, bringing together nuclear technology, ship design and integration, vessel operations and academic research.

The startup will build its first nuclear reactor, named the Gem Microreactor, at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology, with 2030 as its goal for completion. Emerald Nuclear will integrate equipment from Peregrine Turbine Technologies in Maine to convert the reactor’s heat into electricity.

The target for the first commercial deployment is 2031, on a Norwegian offshore vessel.

Deason is hoping to open a manufacturing site in the future in Western Washington on Puget Sound with an initial focus on floating nuclear power systems that replace diesel generators. That phase of growth is roughly targeted to the early 2030s.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.

#5445. PancakeSwap's 69% CAKE Emission Cut Would Make CAKE Less Deflationary

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Cutting CAKE emissions by 69% sounds like the most token-friendly move PancakeSwap could make. But run last week's burn figures through "The Flip," and CAKE's net deflation doesn't speed up. It falls by about 30%.

That's the part missing from coverage of the vote, which is currently running about 98% against. Reports have focused on the drop from 22,500 to 7,000 CAKE per day. They haven't covered the burn the proposal removes to fund higher LP payouts. I rebuilt the supply math using PancakeSwap's own weekly burn breakdown. The result is more interesting than a straightforward "cut emissions, good for CAKE" story.

The Flip governance vote is a binary For/Against vote. It opened on October 21 at 08:07 UTC and closes on October 24 at 08:07 UTC. As of Thursday afternoon, the vote page showed:

One address, 0x3D...e1ad, cast 765,559 votes against, about 61% of all voting power used so far.

That share has fallen as more voters joined, and the result would be lopsided even without that wallet. Excluding it, "Against" still has more than 95%. With only 32 votes cast, though, this is mainly a verdict from a small group of large veCAKE holders, not a broad community poll.

The proposal, first posted on PancakeSwap's forum on October 14, has two parts.

Emissions: Daily CAKE emissions would drop from 22,500 to 7,000, with the remaining 7,000 going to a new ecosystem fund called the Pantry. The cut happens in two stages: first to 11,000 per day, then to 7,000 once CAKE reaches its Tokenomics 3.0 goal of about a 20% supply reduction.

PancakeSwap estimates LPs would have earned about $62 million more if this split had applied to 2025 volume.

Here's PancakeSwap's burn report for the week ending October 20, as published in its weekly update:

Current emissions are 22,500 per day, or 157,500 per week. That puts this week's net deflation at about 201,000 CAKE.

Now apply The Flip to the same week. The v3 and Infinity burns are mostly gone, while v2 and "Other" stay, leaving about 190,000 CAKE of weekly burn. At stage one, emissions fall to 77,000 a week, so net deflation drops to about 113,000 CAKE, a 44% decline. At stage two, emissions fall to 49,000 a week, and net deflation recovers only to about 141,000 CAKE. That's still 30% below where it is today.

The emission cut saves 108,500 CAKE a week at full rollout. But the removed v3 and Infinity burn totaled 168,600 CAKE that week. The burn being given up is larger than the emissions being saved.

The previous week tells the same story. Working backward from the week-over-week changes, the burn was about 530,000 CAKE: roughly 272,000 from v2 and 191,000 from v3. Net deflation was about 373,000. Under The Flip, it would have been about 249,000 at stage two, which is 33% lower.

There's one real offset. The non-stablecoin part of the new 12% treasury fee still funds buybacks, and PancakeSwap hasn't said how large that is. So my figures are a floor, not an exact forecast. It's also possible that higher LP payouts attract more liquidity and volume, and the team projects up to 30% more liquidity. That would increase v2 burns over time.

PancakeSwap's own estimate, based on 10 weeks of activity, is that v2 burns alone would keep CAKE net deflationary by about 190,000 CAKE a week after emissions. That's plausible, and CAKE would keep shrinking. But it's still a slower pace of deflation than what CAKE has been running at, sold under the headline of a 69% emission cut.

The final cut to 7,000 a day depends on reaching the 20% supply reduction target. CAKE supply is 329,915,408, down 11.5% from 372,837,045 in April 2025. The roughly 20% target sits near 298.3 million, which leaves about 31.6 million CAKE still to burn.

Coverage has suggested stage two could arrive about 12 months after stage one. Here's how long 31.6 million CAKE actually takes at stage-one net deflation:

Hitting the target in 12 months would require about 608,000 CAKE of net deflation every week. That's more than CAKE's gross burn in either recent week. On these numbers, stage one could stay in place for years. The "69% cut" headline is really a 51% cut for the foreseeable future.

LPs aren't the ones voting this proposal down. Voting power comes from veCAKE, which means locked CAKE, not liquidity positions. LPs are the group that stands to gain the most, with an 88% fee share.

veCAKE holders have different incentives. Today, they direct the 22,500 daily emissions through gauge voting, and an ecosystem has grown around that control. The Flip would reduce that budget to a 7,000-a-day fund managed by PancakeSwap's team. It would also cut the burn support that has been shrinking supply. For someone holding CAKE for its scarcity, The Flip gives up a definite burn today in exchange for a possible liquidity gain later.

That's why the vote is so one-sided. The people being asked to approve The Flip aren't the people it pays. If it fails on Saturday, I'd expect the next version to keep some v3 burn share. Otherwise, the emission cut doesn't do what the headline suggests.

#5444. From Hamilton to Salt Lake City: 10 NHL franchises that changed cities

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These 10 NHL teams that moved left cities such as Hamilton, Quebec City and Hartford, and here is where each franchise started and where it ended up

A hockey franchise is not always tied to the city on its jersey. Several current NHL clubs began life somewhere else, often under a different name and always in a different arena. The New Jersey Devils started in Kansas City, Missouri. The Calgary Flames started in Atlanta. The Dallas Stars started in Minnesota. Tracing those paths shows how much of the league's map has changed since its early decades.

Some cities appear on both sides of the ledger. Winnipeg lost its original Jets to Arizona in 1996. It then gained a different franchise from Atlanta in 2011, and that team took the Jets name. Atlanta has lost two NHL teams, the Flames in 1980 and the Thrashers in 2011. Denver hosted the Colorado Rockies from 1976 to 1982 and later gained the franchise that became the Colorado Avalanche. Minnesota lost the North Stars to Dallas in 1993. It received a new team, the Wild, which began play in 2000.

This guide to NHL teams that moved covers a selection of 10 relocations, not every move the league has had. Each slide names the city a franchise left, the city it went to and when the move happened. It also traces what happened to the team afterward, including any Stanley Cup won in its new home.

A few patterns run through these NHL franchise relocations. Three of the clubs — the Quebec Nordiques, the original Winnipeg Jets and the Hartford Whalers — entered the NHL in 1979 from the World Hockey Association. All three later left their original markets in the 1990s. Several franchises that changed cities won a championship after the move, including the Avalanche in their first season in Colorado. One franchise, the California Golden Seals, moved to Cleveland as the Barons and merged with the Minnesota North Stars in 1978. Another, the Kansas City Scouts, moved twice before settling in New Jersey.

The slides run in chronological order of the moves. The list starts with the Hamilton Tigers, whose players went on strike over pay in 1925. The franchise was then sold and became the New York Americans. It ends with the 2024 move of the Arizona Coyotes' hockey operations to Salt Lake City. The team played the 2024-25 season there as the Utah Hockey Club, and the Utah Mammoth name was announced in 2025. In between are moves from the 1970s, 1980s, 1990s and 2010s.

The NHL franchise based in Hamilton, Ontario, moved to New York in 1925 and became the New York Americans. The move followed a pay strike by the Hamilton Tigers players and their suspension by the league.

The Tigers joined the NHL in 1920. Hamilton sits in southern Ontario, at the western end of Lake Ontario. The club played five seasons in the city before a labor dispute ended its stay.

The dispute was about wages. In 1925 the Tigers players went on strike over their pay. The NHL responded by suspending the players who had walked out.

The franchise was then sold to New York interests. That sale took the club out of Canada and into the U.S.

In its new city, the franchise took the name New York Americans. The team played its home games at Madison Square $SQ Garden in Manhattan.

The Americans stopped operating in 1942, 17 years after the club left Hamilton. The franchise did not relocate again or resume play under another name. No current NHL club traces its history back to the Tigers.

That ending sets this move apart from many other NHL teams that changed cities. The Calgary Flames and the Dallas Stars, for example, still play under the names they took on after relocating.

Hamilton has not had an NHL team since the Tigers left in 1925. The city's time in the league is limited to those five seasons in the early 1920s.

The New Jersey Devils began in Kansas City, Missouri, as the Scouts in 1974, moved to Denver as the Colorado Rockies in 1976 and relocated to New Jersey in 1982. Each move brought a new name. As a result, the club's history runs through three identities.

The Scouts entered the NHL as an expansion team in 1974. They played two seasons in Kansas City before the franchise left Missouri. That made the Missouri chapter the shortest of the franchise's three stops in the NHL.

Denver became the franchise's second home in 1976. The team took the name Colorado Rockies there and played six seasons in the city. That stay was longer than the one in Kansas City, but it also ended in a relocation.

The second relocation came in 1982. The franchise moved east and became the New Jersey Devils. Its new base was the Meadowlands in East Rutherford, New Jersey. The move took the club from the Mountain West into the New York metropolitan area.

The Rockies are not the same franchise as today's Colorado Avalanche. The two clubs share a state but not a history. Each keeps its own records.

The Devils won the Stanley Cup in 1995, in the franchise's 13th season in New Jersey. The club had needed more than a decade in its third city to reach that point. Two more championships followed, in 2000 and 2003. All three came within a span of nine seasons. That stretch remains the only period in which the franchise has won the Cup.

None of those titles came during the Kansas City or Denver years, which covered the franchise's first eight seasons. Every championship in the club's history belongs to the New Jersey era. The two earlier cities produced a name change each, while the Stanley Cup arrived only after the second move.

The NHL franchise that began in Oakland, California, in 1967 moved to Cleveland in 1976 and became the Barons. Two years later, in 1978, the Barons merged with the Minnesota North Stars and stopped playing as a separate club.

The franchise entered the league in 1967 as an expansion team. It was first called the California Seals. It later took the name California Golden Seals, which it carried until it left the Bay Area.

The Minnesota North Stars also joined the NHL as an expansion team in 1967. They played in Bloomington, Minnesota. The two clubs that eventually combined had entered the league in the same year.

The 1976 relocation took the franchise from Northern California to Ohio. It arrived with a new name and played in Cleveland as the Barons. That made it one of two NHL teams that changed cities in 1976. The Kansas City Scouts moved to Denver that same year and became the Colorado Rockies.

The Barons lasted in Cleveland until the 1978 merger. After that, the franchise no longer existed as its own club. Its history continued inside the Minnesota organization rather than under the Barons name. Cleveland has not had an NHL team since then.

That ending sets this franchise apart from most of the NHL teams that changed cities in this selection. The others in the list either still play in their new homes or kept operating for many years after relocating. This one moved once and then folded into another club.

From its 1967 start in Oakland to the 1978 merger, the franchise played 11 seasons as its own club. It spent nine of those seasons in Oakland and two in Cleveland.

Any link between the old Seals and a current NHL team runs through that merger. The North Stars, the club that absorbed the Barons, later left Minnesota for Texas and became the Dallas Stars.

The Atlanta Flames moved from Atlanta to Calgary, Alberta, in 1980, and the franchise kept its name in the new city. The result was the Calgary Flames, who went on to win the Stanley Cup in 1989 against the Montreal Canadiens.

The franchise entered the NHL in 1972. It was one of two expansion teams added to the league that year. The other was the New York Islanders.

In Atlanta, the Flames played home games at the Omni Coliseum. The downtown arena opened in 1972, the same year the team arrived.

The name had roots in Georgia history. It referred to the burning of Atlanta in 1864, during the Civil War, when Union forces under William Tecumseh Sherman burned much of the city.

That historical reference did not travel to Alberta, but the name did. The team's logo changed from a flaming letter A to a flaming letter C.

Calgary had hosted major professional hockey before the Flames arrived. The Calgary Cowboys played in the World Hockey Association from 1975 to 1977. The relocated Flames gave the city its first NHL team.

The club's first Calgary home was the Stampede Corral, an older arena on the city's Stampede grounds. In 1983 the team moved into the Olympic Saddledome. The building was constructed in part for the 1988 Winter Olympics, which Calgary hosted. It was later renamed the Scotiabank Saddledome.

The Flames reached the Stanley Cup Final in 1986 and lost to Montreal. Three years later, the same two teams met again in the Final.

This time Calgary won. The Flames clinched the 1989 championship in Game 6 at the Montreal Forum. They became the only visiting team to win the Stanley Cup on Forum ice against the Canadiens.

Defenseman Al MacInnis received the Conn Smythe Trophy as the most valuable player of the playoffs. Veteran forward Lanny McDonald scored in the deciding game. It was the final game of his NHL career.

The Minnesota North Stars left Bloomington, Minnesota, for Dallas in 1993 and became the Dallas Stars. The franchise dropped "North" from its name and carried the Stars identity to Texas.

The North Stars joined the NHL in 1967 as an expansion team. Bloomington, a suburb of Minneapolis, was their home. The club played 26 seasons in Minnesota before the move.

The franchise also absorbed another club that had changed cities. In 1978 the Cleveland Barons, which began in Oakland, California, merged with the North Stars. Through that merger, the Dallas Stars' lineage connects to two of the relocations in this list.

Dallas won the Stanley Cup in 1999. The Stars beat the Buffalo Sabres in the final. The title came in the franchise's sixth season in Texas. It was the club's first championship under either name.

Minnesota went seven seasons without an NHL team. The gap ended when the Wild, a new franchise, took the ice.

The Wild do not carry the North Stars' records. That history moved to Texas with the team. The 1967 expansion club and today's Dallas Stars are one franchise under two names.

The Quebec Nordiques left Quebec City for Denver after the 1994-95 season and became the Colorado Avalanche. The renamed team won the Stanley Cup in its first season in Colorado.

The Nordiques did not begin in the NHL. The club played in the World Hockey Association before the NHL admitted it in 1979.

Quebec City hosted the franchise for 16 NHL seasons, from 1979-80 through 1994-95. That run puts Quebec City among the former homes of current NHL teams.

The move came through a sale. A new ownership group bought the franchise and took it to Denver. There the team adopted the Avalanche name.

The change of city and owners did not create a new franchise. The club the NHL admitted from the WHA in 1979 is the same club that plays in Denver today. Its NHL history runs from Quebec City to Colorado without a break.

The 1996 Stanley Cup Final matched Colorado against the Florida Panthers. The Avalanche won all four games of the series.

That sweep gave the franchise its first Stanley Cup. The Nordiques' 16 NHL seasons in Quebec City had ended without one. The title arrived as soon as the franchise reached Denver.

The original Winnipeg Jets left Manitoba for Arizona in 1996 and became the Phoenix Coyotes. The move ended 17 NHL seasons in Winnipeg. That run began when the club entered the league from the World Hockey Association in 1979.

The franchise's history started before its NHL years. The Jets were a founding member of the WHA, which began play in 1972 as a rival major league. That year, the Jets signed Bobby Hull away from the Chicago Black Hawks. Hull was one of the NHL's top scorers at the time. The Jets went on to win the WHA championship, the Avco World Trophy, three times, in 1976, 1978 and 1979.

The WHA shut down after the 1978-79 season, and the NHL absorbed four of its clubs. Winnipeg entered the league alongside the Edmonton Oilers, the Quebec Nordiques and the Hartford Whalers. The Whalers had played as the New England Whalers in the rival league.

In the NHL, the Jets played home games at Winnipeg Arena. The team took Dale Hawerchuk with the first overall pick in the 1981 NHL Entry Draft. The center won the Calder Trophy as the league's top rookie in 1982. In the 1992-93 season, Teemu Selänne scored 76 goals for Winnipeg, which remains the NHL record for a rookie.

Phoenix had never had an NHL team before the Coyotes arrived. The relocated club opened in downtown Phoenix at America West Arena, a venue built for the NBA's Phoenix Suns. The Coyotes shared that building with the Suns until 2003.

The team then left downtown for a suburban arena in Glendale, Arizona, which opened in 2003. That building carried several sponsor names over the years, including Jobing.com Arena and Gila River Arena. The franchise also changed its own name in 2014, becoming the Arizona Coyotes.

Winnipeg's current Jets, who began play there in 2011, are a separate franchise with their own history.

The Hartford Whalers left Hartford, Connecticut, for North Carolina in 1997 and became the Carolina Hurricanes. The franchise spent two seasons in Greensboro, settled in Raleigh in 1999 and won the Stanley Cup in 2006.

The club's roots are in the World Hockey Association, not the NHL. It began play in that league in 1972 as the New England Whalers, based first in Boston before moving to Hartford. The Whalers won the WHA's first championship in 1973.

The team entered the NHL in 1979, when the WHA ceased operations and four of its clubs joined the older league. It took the name Hartford Whalers. Its home rink was the Hartford Civic Center in downtown Hartford.

Peter Karmanos, the team's owner, moved the franchise south after the 1996-97 season. Hartford has not had an NHL team since the Whalers left.

The Hurricanes did not open in their permanent home. Their new arena in Raleigh was still under construction when the team arrived. For their first two seasons, they played at the Greensboro Coliseum in Greensboro, North Carolina.

The team moved to Raleigh in 1999, when the new arena opened that fall. The franchise has played its home games in Raleigh ever since.

Carolina reached the Stanley Cup Final in 2002 and lost to the Detroit Red Wings. The team returned to the Final in 2006 and beat the Edmonton Oilers in seven games. The deciding game was played in Raleigh.

That series matched two former WHA clubs. Edmonton had joined the NHL in the same 1979 merger that brought in the Whalers. Cam Ward, a rookie goaltender, won the Conn Smythe Trophy as the most valuable player of the playoffs. Rod Brind'Amour captained the team.

The Hurricanes have also acknowledged the franchise's Hartford years. Starting in the 2018-19 season, the team has worn Whalers throwback jerseys for occasional home games.

The Atlanta Thrashers moved to Winnipeg in 2011 and became the current Winnipeg Jets. True North Sports & Entertainment bought the franchise that year and relocated it to Manitoba. The new owners gave the team the Jets name, which the city's earlier NHL club had used.

The Thrashers began play in 1999 as an expansion team. That gave Atlanta its second NHL franchise, after the Flames. The club took its name from the brown thrasher, the state bird of Georgia. Home games were at Philips Arena in downtown Atlanta. The building opened the same year the team debuted.

The Thrashers had several notable players during their 12 seasons. The club drafted Ilya Kovalchuk first overall in the 2001 NHL draft. Dany Heatley won the Calder Trophy as the league's top rookie in 2002. The team's postseason history was brief. The Thrashers won the Southeast Division in 2006-07 and made their only playoff appearance that spring. The New York Rangers swept them in the first round.

The 2011 sale brought the NHL back to Winnipeg. True North, led by chairman Mark Chipman with backing from David Thomson, moved the team into the downtown arena then known as MTS Centre. The building is now called Canada Life Centre.

The Jets name carried over, but the franchise history did not. The current Jets and the original Jets are separate franchises. The team playing in Winnipeg today traces its records to Atlanta in 1999. It does not claim the history of the club that previously wore the same name in the same city.

The relocated team spent its first two seasons in the Southeast Division, the grouping the Thrashers had played in. The league's 2013-14 realignment moved Winnipeg to the Central Division. That placed the Jets with teams such as the Minnesota Wild and the Chicago Blackhawks.

In 2018, the Jets reached the Western Conference Final, where the Vegas Golden Knights eliminated them. That run was the furthest the franchise had advanced in the playoffs in either city.

The Arizona Coyotes' hockey operations moved from Tempe, Arizona, to Salt Lake City in 2024. The NHL approved the sale of those operations to Smith Entertainment Group that year, and the team's players went with them to Utah.

The club's last Arizona home was a college building. In its final seasons in the state, the team played at Mullett Arena in Tempe, which Arizona State University owns. The arena is also home to the university's Sun Devils men's hockey program.

The transaction covered the team's hockey operations. The players moved with that side of the organization to Salt Lake City.

Smith Entertainment Group is the company led by Ryan Smith, and it also owns the NBA's Utah Jazz. In Salt Lake City, the hockey team began playing at the Delta Center, the downtown arena the Jazz already used. The move gave Utah its first NHL team.

The team played its first season in Utah, 2024-25, as the Utah Hockey Club. That name identified the club by its state and its sport, with no nickname attached.

A nickname followed the next year. The Utah Mammoth name was announced in 2025.
