#5443. Seattle startup Avante raises $30M to bring AI agents to corporate benefits teams

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 27, 2026 at 9:03 amOctober 27, 2026 at 9:29 am

Avante, the maker of an AI platform to help companies manage employee health care and other benefits, has landed a $30 million Series A round.

Frist Cressey Ventures led the round, with participation from Sorenson Capital, Hearst Ventures, Morgan Stanley Next Level Fund and existing investor Fuse. The new funding, announced Tuesday, brings Seattle-based Avante’s total raised to $40 million, following a $10 million seed round led by Fuse in 2024.

Benefits are one of employers’ biggest costs. Avante’s AI agents do work like comparing vendor contracts against actual claims, reviewing plan documents for errors and preparing for renewals. Employees can also use the platform to ask questions about their own coverage.

The startup plans to use the cash to expand internationally and develop more AI agents, building on a beta release of its “Ava Agents” last week.

Avante says it now has more than 70 customers, including Samsung Semiconductor, Real Chemistry, Zscaler and News Corp, and that bookings grew nearly fivefold over the past year. The platform reaches more than 385,000 employees and family members, according to the company.

Avante was founded in 2023 by CEO Rohan D’Souza; Carly Eckert, a physician and epidemiologist who serves as head of innovation and impact; and executive chairman Kabir Shahani, the co-CEO of Amperity.

D’Souza and Eckert previously worked as executives at health care automation company Olive AI, which shut down in 2023. The startup emerged from stealth in early 2024 and launched publicly in April 2025.

“Benefits teams are responsible for one of the largest and most consequential investments their companies make, yet they’re still operating with outdated information, archaic spreadsheets, and technology built for another era,” D’Souza said in a statement.

Avante is pitching its software as employers face rising health care costs. Large employers are projecting a median 9.2% increase for 2027, the company said.

The startup competes with benefits and HR software providers such as Workday, ADP, Deel and Rippling. It has also signed partnerships with benefits advisory firms including Gallagher, OneDigital, Segal Benz, Howden and USI Insurance Services.

Avante ranks No. 156 on the GeekWire 200, our list of top Pacific Northwest tech startups.

#5442. Seattle’s Kivo Health raises $10M to bring lung disease rehab into patients’ homes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 27, 2026 at 10:19 amOctober 27, 2026 at 10:52 am

Seattle-based Kivo Health today announced $10 million in funding to help increase access to its services, which target older adults with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). The Series A round brings the startup’s total funding to more than $16 million.

Kivo ships equipment to patients’ homes and provides a nine-week program of therapist-led, live video sessions focused on exercise, breathing techniques and disease management. The company provides ongoing support following the program and says it uses AI to handle administrative tasks and communicate with patients, supporting its clinicians.

“We’re using the funding to build our AI health coach to blend AI-led care with human-led care,” Dr. Victor Sadauskas, Kivo’s co-founder and CEO, said via email. That pairing, he added, will help patients manage their chronic disease over the long term.

The company has approximately 50 employees, including clinicians.

COPD is an incurable lung disease in which damaged airways and air sacs make breathing difficult and can worsen over time. Common symptoms include shortness of breath, a persistent cough and fatigue. COPD is the third leading cause of death globally and the fifth in the U.S.

However, there are effective treatments to improve the condition, though many patients are not able to easily access care. A study of Medicare beneficiaries with COPD found that only 3.7% received pulmonary rehabilitation in 2012.

Kivo reports that a peer-reviewed study of its program found improvements in participants’ symptoms, physical function and mental health. The company also funded an analysis that estimated its model could reduce annual health care spending by $8,245 per member through fewer hospitalizations, ER visits and time in nursing homes.

Kivo says its program is covered by Medicare, Medicaid and private insurers including UnitedHealthcare, Humana, Blue Cross, Aetna and Priority Health.

“By thoughtfully combining high quality clinical care with AI, we can now scale proactive, accessible care to every senior, improving symptoms and reducing avoidable costs,” Sadauskas said in a statement.

Sadauskas launched Kivo in 2023 with co-founder and Chief Technology Officer Vaughn Koch. Sadauskas previously was an emergency medicine physician for Kaiser Permanente and a senior investment fellow with Life Science Angels. Koch is a serial entrepreneur who sold his startup Movity to Trulia in 2010.

While its current focus is COPD, Kivo aims to expand into other costly chronic conditions affecting older adults.

Allumia Ventures led the round, with participation from Corewell Health Ventures, Y Combinator, Heuristic Capital and MassMutual Ventures.

#5441. The 10 longest bridges in the world

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Seven of the world's 10 longest bridges stand in China, and a Louisiana causeway is the lone entry outside Asia.

Most drivers cross a bridge without a second thought. Road bridges fold into the daily landscape, lifting traffic dozens of meters above rivers and valleys. A handful of engineering projects pierce that indifference with their scale and with the technical demands their builders had to meet. Height offers one way to stop a viewer. France's Millau Viaduct climbs to 341 meters. In China, the Beipanjiang bridge hangs 565 meters above the Beipan River. Each turns the plain act of getting from one bank to the other into a spectacle.

Length can impress as much as altitude, and it tests a structure in a different way. A tall bridge commands one point on the map. A long one claims a whole stretch of it, carrying its deck over kilometer after kilometer. Italy supplies a useful yardstick. The country's longest viaduct, at Coltano on the A12 motorway, runs 9.6 kilometers. The runner-up, an A19 motorway viaduct over the Fichera stream, covers seven kilometers, 2.6 fewer than Coltano. Both distances give readers a baseline for judging the reach of the crossings that follow.

We Build Value, Webuild's digital magazine, ranked the world's 10 longest bridges in an article dated May 17, 2021. The magazine ordered the list on a single measure, how far each bridge extends from end to end, and gave no other criteria. Asia dominates the field. Nine of the 10 stand on that continent, seven of them in China, with one each in Taiwan and Thailand. The 10th sits in the U.S. Europe, home to the Millau Viaduct and Italy's top two, places no entry among the 10. The group serves several modes of travel, from high-speed rail lines to roads to an urban subway. The list captures the picture as of spring 2021, and new construction can reorder such a lineup. Each entry below draws on the magazine's measurements, locations, and completion dates.

The Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge runs 164,800 meters, a distance no other bridge on Earth matches. Its path cuts through Jiangsu province in China, linking Shanghai and Nanjing. High-speed trains on the Beijing-Shanghai line travel along its deck. The record holder doubles as working rail infrastructure. It occupies part of the Yangtze River delta. It stretches more than four times as far as the Wuhan Metro Bridge, the shortest entry among the world's 10 longest.

Canals, rivers, lakes, and rice fields crowd the land beneath the route, and builders needed every one of those meters to clear them. Soft ground near the Yangtze River created a second engineering problem. Designers answered with a viaduct broken into smaller segments, with arches and pillars bearing each one to prevent collapse. The result resembles a chain of modest structures joined end to end, each sized for ground too weak to carry a single massive one.

Nine kilometers of the crossing pass above the waters of Yangcheng lake. The lake section makes up about 5.5% of the total, leaving roughly 94.5% over farmland and smaller waterways. Piers carry the deck across the lake. Some portions rise high enough for naval vessels to slip beneath. Flexible diagonal cables lend extra support, making the bridge cable-stayed as well. Over Yangcheng lake, the bridge had to serve trains above and shipping below.

Construction began in 2006 and wrapped up in 2010, a four-year effort that employed more than 10,000 workers. The project cost $8.5 billion in total. Per meter, the price comes to about $51,600. Divide the length by the workforce and each person accounts for less than 17 meters of bridge. Crews averaged about 41 kilometers of finished bridge a year over that period. At that rate, the crews added the equivalent of Italy's Coltano viaduct roughly every three months.

Taiwan's Changhua-Koahsiung Viaduct stretches 157,317 meters, enough to make it the second-longest bridge in the world and leave it 7,483 meters behind China's Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge. Across two structures that each exceed 150 kilometers, a gap of about seven kilometers counts as a narrow margin. The viaduct covers more than 95% of the Chinese leader's distance. China's Cangde Grand Bridge, in third, sits 41,417 meters behind the Taiwanese structure, more than five times the gap at the top. The two front-runners form a class of their own, well clear of the remaining eight.

Of the other two entries outside China, neither comes within 100 kilometers of the viaduct. Thailand's Bang Na Expressway, the closer of the pair, trails it by 103,317 meters. The Taiwan crossing extends more than 16 times as far as Italy's Coltano viaduct, the longest in that country.

High-speed trains run over the viaduct, a key segment of the Taiwan High-Speed Rail line. Vertical bearings and transverse shear keys support the box girder spans along that railway. Rail service ties the viaduct to its neighbors on the list. Danyang-Kunshan and Cangde, the entries on either side of it, both carry China's Beijing-Shanghai high-speed line. The world's three longest bridges all serve rail traffic.

Builders completed the viaduct in 2007, three years before crews finished the Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge in 2010. Weinan Weihe, done in 2008, arrived later but runs 77,585 meters shorter. The Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge, completed a decade after the viaduct in 2017, measures 101,600 meters less. From 2007 until 2010, the viaduct stood as the longest finished structure among these 10.

The geography of the area between Baguazhang and Zuoying forced the viaduct's builders to meet strict anti-seismic criteria. Taiwan's builders applied the standard across a structure reaching beyond 150 kilometers. The viaduct shows that a bridge held to demanding earthquake standards can approach the world record in length.

The Cangde Grand Bridge lifts 115,900 meters of high-speed track off the ground on 3,092 pillars, a reach that earns it third place among the world's longest bridges. Each support carries an average of about 37 meters of deck. Italy's Coltano viaduct would fit inside the Chinese structure more than 12 times.

The pillar count shows how a crossing of this scale takes shape. Workers set more than 3,000 supports into the soil along the route, each one a separate point where the deck meets the earth. The bridge owes its extent to repetition, with one modest span following another across the full distance.

The viaduct belongs to the Beijing-Shanghai high-speed line, the same corridor that carries the Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge. Crews finished both structures in 2010. Within a single year, one rail route gained two of the world's three biggest bridges. The line holds an outsized share of the planet's elevated rail. Work on the Tianjin Grand Bridge ended in 2010 too. Every bridge in the top four except Taiwan's Changhua-Koahsiung Viaduct, which came earlier, reached completion that year.

Cangde's standing hinges on an uneven pair of gaps. It falls 48,900 meters short of the Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge and 41,417 meters short of the Changhua-Koahsiung Viaduct. Below it, the Tianjin Grand Bridge trails by 2,200 meters. The cushion beneath Cangde amounts to less than one-twentieth of the deficit separating it from first place.

In distance terms, Cangde has more in common with the next Chinese viaduct down the list than with the two giants above it. The top pair form a class of their own, and Cangde heads the tier that follows.

The Tianjin Grand Bridge stretches 113,700 meters between Langfang and Qingxian in China, a distance that secures fourth place among the world's longest bridges. A mere 2,200 meters separate it from the Cangde Grand Bridge, the crossing one spot higher. The Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge, at the head of the list, outstrips it by 51,100 meters. Below the Tianjin span, the gap yawns wider. The bridge closes out a group of four giants that pulls clear of the remaining six.

The Chinese rail bridge runs more than twice the length of Thailand's Bang Na Expressway, which held the global record until 2004. It measures close to three times the length of the first of the two parallel bridges that make up Louisiana's Lake Pontchartrain Causeway. It covers more than double the length of the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge, which opened in 2018. Work on the Tianjin Grand Bridge started two years after the Bang Na Expressway lost its crown. Ten years after the Bang Na Expressway's 2000 completion, China had built a railway crossing reaching beyond 113 kilometers.

The Tianjin Grand Bridge serves China's railway network. SlashGear reports that the bridge carries the Beijing-Shanghai High-Speed Railway on an elevated structure. Box girders weighing several hundred tons apiece went into the build, according to SlashGear. The raised track crosses dry ground in some sections and bodies of water in others.

Construction ran four years, from 2006 to 2010, and the bridge's formal inauguration followed in 2011. The Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge, the top entry of all, kept the identical timeline, breaking ground in 2006 and wrapping up in 2010. Builders finished the Cangde Grand Bridge in the same year. Crews finished the Beijing Grand Bridge, farther down the list, in 2010 and opened it the following year, matching the Tianjin sequence. China completed three of the four bridges at the top of this list in a single year, 2010, the Tianjin Grand Bridge among them.

The Weinan Weihe Grand Bridge runs 79,732 meters, trailing the fourth-place Tianjin Grand Bridge by 33,968 meters. One other step in the list opens a wider gulf, the 41,417-meter drop between the second and third entries. The four structures above Weinan Weihe form a separate tier, each longer than 110 kilometers. The Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge covers more than twice its distance.

Weinan Weihe is the list's sole entry on China's Zhengzhou-Xi'an High-Speed Railway. Danyang-Kunshan, Cangde, and the Beijing Grand Bridge all serve the Beijing-Shanghai high-speed line. Crews finished the bridge in 2008, two years ahead of the three longer mainland viaducts, each of which reached completion in 2010. Taiwan's Changhua-Koahsiung Viaduct, done in 2007, stands as the lone crossing among the four longer ones to beat it to the finish. The Beijing Grand Bridge shares the 2010 date, leaving Weinan Weihe the earliest completed of the five mainland Chinese rail viaducts on the list. The Zhengzhou-Xi'an route had its long crossing in place while work on the Beijing-Shanghai corridor's three viaducts continued.

The viaduct threads water and dry land alike. Trains on the line clear the Wei River and many of the streams that feed it. Roads and farmland lie beneath the deck. A single structure lifts the railway over each of those obstacles.

Weinan Weihe outruns Italy's longest viaduct, at Coltano, more than eight times over. The 10th-place Wuhan Metro Bridge, the list's shortest entry, covers less than half the ground Weinan Weihe spans.

The sixth-place Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge falls 24,015 meters short of Weinan Weihe, a gap 9,953 meters narrower than the one separating Weinan Weihe from Tianjin. In length, the fifth-place viaduct sits nearer the bridge below it than the one above. Weinan Weihe belongs at the head of the list's lower six, the longest of the crossings whose reach runs to double-digit kilometers.

The Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge runs 55,717 meters across the Lingdingyang canal, connecting Hong Kong, Zhuhai, and Macao in the Pearl River delta. Its outline echoes the dragon of Chinese tradition. The crossing edges past Thailand's Bang Na Expressway, the next entry down, by 1,717 meters. Vehicles move along a divided deck with three lanes in each direction, according to ScienceDirect. The bridge's reach extends beyond the three cities in its name. The link forms a vital piece of the main highway system joining the large urban areas around Guangzhou, Shenzhen, Hong Kong, Macao, and Zhuhai.

Close to seven kilometers of the route dips underwater as a tunnel, about one-eighth of the total length, leaving more than 48 kilometers outside it. The tunnel follows an immersed design and passes beneath the Pearl River Estuary's primary shipping channels near Hong Kong International Airport. Artificial islands tie this submerged section to the bridge segments. Cable-stayed spans lift the roadway over other navigation channels so sea-going vessels can pass. Between the tunnel and those raised spans, the layout keeps the estuary's principal shipping routes clear for ocean traffic.

Builders poured 400,000 metric tons of steel into the project, about seven tons for each meter it covers. Work lasted eight years and finished in 2017, a year before the bridge opened in 2018. No other entry among the 10 opened later. An unofficial figure puts the full bill at about $7 billion. Spread across the whole distance, the sum comes to about $126 million per kilometer.

Harsh weather and a conservation zone surround the islands and the tunnel. Those islands and the tunnel face the Ling Ding Channel, where typhoons are frequent and convection and monsoon conditions turn severe. The Chinese white dolphin's core protected area lies nearby. The parts that keep ships moving sit where storm exposure and dolphin habitat meet.

Thailand's Bang Na Expressway stretches 54 kilometers, and apart from a single river crossing, its whole course rides above dry ground. The Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge outruns it by about 1.7 kilometers. So slim a gap separates a sea link from a route that keeps to the land, two opposite engineering problems that produced near-twin lengths.

One river marks the only point where the expressway clears water. Everywhere else, its deck passes over solid earth from end to end. Its reach comes from covering terrain, a trait that distinguishes it from entries earning their places over lakes, canals, or open sea. Builders of those bridges answered to the water in their path. Bang Na shows that dry land alone can call for a bridge on a record-setting scale.

Louis Berger drew up the design in 1994, and crews finished the work in 2000. Six years separated the first plans from the completed structure. Berger is also the only designer the ranking names for any of the 10 bridges. The finish date sets Bang Na among the elders of the group. Only the Lake Pontchartrain Causeway in Louisiana predates it, which makes the Thai expressway the oldest Asian bridge on the list.

Bang Na held the title of world's longest bridge from 2000 until 2004, a four-year reign. Six structures surpass it, and each reached completion between 2007 and 2017, years after that reign ended. Their arrival pushed the former titleholder down to seventh. The expressway lost ground without losing a meter. The Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge, today's record holder, runs about three times as far, a margin that turns the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge's edge into a rounding error. Bang Na outreaches the Beijing Grand Bridge, the next entry, by more than 5.8 kilometers. A structure finished before eight of the other nine has kept its footing in the top seven through a decade of longer construction.

The Beijing Grand Bridge carries the Beijing-Shanghai high-speed line along a 48,153-meter railway viaduct, joining the Danyang-Kunshan, Cangde, and Tianjin grand bridges as the fourth entry from that route among the world's 10 longest.

Its route partners dwarf it. The Cangde Grand Bridge exceeds it by 67,747 meters, and the Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge runs about 3.4 times its length. Yet the junior member of the quartet would swallow Italy's record-holding Coltano viaduct about five times over.

The Beijing viaduct's nearest rivals come from outside the rail corridor. Thailand's Bang Na Expressway adds 5,847 meters to its span, and the Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macao Bridge adds 7,564. Those two crossings sit within a few kilometers of the Beijing viaduct, a tight cluster beside the 65,547-meter gulf that separates it from Tianjin, its closest partner on the line.

The Beijing Grand Bridge holds a clear margin over the two entries below it. It surpasses the Wuhan Metro Bridge by 10,365 meters and the longer of the Lake Pontchartrain Causeway's two parallel spans by 9,738 meters. Its lead over the Louisiana causeway outstrips its deficit to Bang Na, which places the viaduct closer to the crossings above it than to those beneath.

Combined, the Danyang-Kunshan, Cangde, Tianjin, and Beijing viaducts lift 442,553 meters of track off the ground, more than 2.8 times the reach of Taiwan's Changhua-Koahsiung Viaduct. The Beijing span supplies the smallest slice of that total, and it completes the set of four bridges that gives the Beijing-Shanghai high-speed corridor four places on a list of 10.

Crews finished the Beijing Grand Bridge in 2010, and its inauguration followed in 2011. The Danyang-Kunshan, Cangde, and Tianjin grand bridges reached completion in 2010 as well, and Tianjin opened to service in 2011 alongside the Beijing viaduct. One year delivered four of the world's 10 longest bridges, more than any other completion date on the list. The four 2010 finishers match the corridor's four entries exactly, tying the list's most productive year to a single Chinese railway.

The Lake Pontchartrain Causeway carries traffic 38,400 meters over a Louisiana lake on its original span, a reach that holds ninth place and edges the 10th-place entry by 612 meters.

The causeway predates every other structure on the list by decades. Crews finished its first span in 1956, 44 years before Thailand's Bang Na Expressway, the next-oldest entry, reached completion in 2000. Builders completed the remaining eight between 2004 and 2017, most of them for high-speed rail lines. A 1950s road link keeps pace with projects finished nearly half a century or more after it.

Mandeville and Metairie sit at opposite ends of the crossing. Between those two communities, the causeway covers Lake Pontchartrain in its entirety. The Bang Na Expressway rides over dry ground everywhere except a single river. The causeway inverts that pattern, with water beneath the deck from one shore to the other.

Two parallel bridges make up the causeway. A second span joined the first in 1969, 13 years after the original, and measures 15 meters longer at 38,415 meters. The near match shows the newer structure tracing the same path across the lake. The 15-meter bonus still leaves the 1969 bridge 9,738 meters behind the eighth-place Beijing Grand Bridge.

Vehicles split by direction across the pair. Southbound drivers heading for Metairie use the 1969 span, which leaves northbound travel toward Mandeville on the 1956 structure. The arrangement turns two independent bridges into one divided route.

A pivoting section on the northbound bridge turns to let large boats pass. The movable piece lets the causeway serve motorists on its deck and vessels on the lake below. Boats big enough to need that opening show Lake Pontchartrain working as a navigable waterway, and the causeway has to accommodate both.

Combined, the two spans lay 76,815 meters of roadway across Lake Pontchartrain, more than any single bridge from sixth place down covers on its own.

The Wuhan Metro Bridge runs 37,788 meters through Wuhan, China, and carries every meter of Line 1 on the city's subway. One unbroken elevated structure holds the entire route, earning the bridge the title of the world's longest continuous viaduct. Nine entries on the list outdistance it. The title rewards an uninterrupted span, and the Wuhan structure supplies one between the two termini of its line. A trip on Line 1 never leaves the bridge.

Line 1 opened in 2004 and made Wuhan the fifth Chinese city with a subway. The city's first metro route ran its full course on a raised deck. Wuhan's riders entered the subway era above street level. Four Chinese cities had opened subways before Wuhan, and the fifth arrived with its debut route lifted into the air. Among the 10, no other bridge hosts a subway.

Wuhan's 2004 opening makes this bridge the oldest of the seven Chinese structures on the list. The other six reached completion between 2008 and 2017. Five of those six carry railways between cities. Wuhan's structure serves trips that begin and end inside one metropolis. Only Thailand's Bang Na Expressway and Louisiana's Lake Pontchartrain Causeway predate it, and Taiwan's Changhua-Koahsiung Viaduct followed three years later.

The Wuhan crossing falls 627 meters short of the newer Lake Pontchartrain span and 612 meters short of the original one. No neighboring pair among the 10 sits closer together than the Louisiana causeway and the Wuhan bridge. The causeway splits its traffic across two parallel bridges. Wuhan's viaduct keeps its whole line on one continuous structure. It covers less than a quarter of the distance of the Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge. An urban subway line, opened before any of China's high-speed rail viaducts on the list, reaches far enough to stand among the world's 10 longest bridges.

#5439. Microsoft earnings preview: Employee buyouts, AI spending and a new financial scorecard

by Todd Bishop on Oct 27, 2026 at 10:50 amOctober 28, 2026 at 3:02 pm

Update, 10/28: Microsoft’s Azure cloud business brought in $33.2 billion in revenue in the September quarter, up 48% from a year earlier, blowing past the company’s own forecast and beating Wall Street’s expectations. Read the full story.

Microsoft’s earnings report Wednesday will come two days after the company offered buyouts to about 60,000 people, roughly a quarter of its employees. The call gives executives their first chance to say what the offer will cost, and to explain how it fits with the company’s long-term view of its workforce.

Whether or not they go into those details, it’s one of several issues to watch in Wednesday’s report, the first under Microsoft’s new reporting structure. Anthropic’s IPO filing on Monday adds another storyline, showing how much the Claude maker has agreed to spend on Microsoft’s cloud.

Coming into the report, Microsoft’s stock is near its high. Microsoft closed Monday at $532.60, about 2% below its record close of $543.45 on Oct. 13, after gaining roughly $1.4 trillion in market value since late June.

Here are the key numbers and issues heading into Microsoft’s results for the first quarter of its 2027 fiscal year, ended Sept. 30.

Core numbers: Analysts expect revenue of $90.75 billion, up nearly 17% from a year ago, and earnings of $4.72 per share, up 14%, according to Yahoo Finance. Microsoft’s own forecast was $89.85 billion to $90.95 billion, so Wall Street is looking for a result near the top of that range.

In July, Microsoft reported $90 billion in revenue for the June quarter, well above the $87.7 billion analysts expected.

A new scorecard: Microsoft announced in September that it would sort its business into two groups instead of the three it had used since 2015. This is the first quarter under the new setup.

The first, dubbed Agents and Infra, includes Azure, Microsoft 365, Dynamics, LinkedIn’s recruiting and sales tools, and server and productivity licensing. It brought in 81% of Microsoft’s revenue and 88% of its operating income in fiscal 2026, based on figures Microsoft recast under the new structure.

Microsoft expects Agents and Infra revenue of $75.15 billion to $75.75 billion this quarter, which would be growth of about 22% to 23%, by GeekWire’s calculation.

The other group, Devices and Consumer, includes Windows, Xbox and search advertising. Microsoft expects it to bring in $14.7 billion to $15.2 billion, down 5% to 8% from a year earlier.

Azure, in dollars: Microsoft started disclosing Azure’s annual revenue last year, when it passed $75 billion, and topped $100 billion in fiscal 2026. Starting this quarter, it reports the figure every quarter. It also changed what counts as Azure: GitHub’s cloud business and Security Copilot now fall under Microsoft 365, and its healthcare cloud moved to a new industry unit.

Counted that way, Azure brought in $29.4 billion in the June quarter, up 42%. Microsoft expects growth of 44% to 45% this quarter, not counting currency fluctuations, which would put Azure at roughly $32 billion, by GeekWire’s calculation. That compares with the roughly 45% Microsoft projected in July, under the old definition.

Hitting that forecast may not be enough. Investors are looking for about 46%, BNP Paribas analyst Stefan Slowinski wrote in a note Monday. In January, Azure beat Microsoft’s own forecast and the stock still fell 10%, because investors had privately expected more.

“Azure moves the stock, but the read that matters is whether capacity is absorbed as fast as it lands,” wrote Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives in a note last week.

Capital spending: Microsoft expects capital expenditures of more than $50 billion for the quarter, which would be a record. That’s up from $41 billion in the June quarter and $34.9 billion a year earlier.

An accounting change reduces what Microsoft reports as capital spending, without reducing its planned investment. Microsoft now assumes its data center buildings will last 25 years instead of 15. As a result, more of its data center leases will be classified in a way that doesn’t count as capital spending, CFO Amy Hood said on the July earnings call.

That change alone lowered Microsoft’s capital spending estimate for calendar 2026 to about $175 billion, from the roughly $190 billion it projected in April. Hood said the company’s actual spending plans hadn’t changed.

Cloud margins: Microsoft Cloud gross margin came in at 65% last quarter, better than expected but down from a year earlier. Microsoft said it expects the figure to be relatively stable this quarter. It also expects operating margins to be roughly flat with a year ago.

Workforce: The new “voluntary exit” offer, announced Monday by Chief People Officer Amy Coleman, covers participating teams in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. It has no age or tenure requirement and extends to some vice presidents. Employees have until the first week of December to decide, and Microsoft hasn’t said how much the offer will cost or when it will record the charge.

For the spring retirement program, Hood disclosed the cost on the April earnings call: about $900 million, with roughly $350 million in cost of revenue and $550 million in operating expenses. The charge showed up in the following quarter. About 30% of the 8,750 eligible employees accepted.

The new offer is less generous. It matches Microsoft’s standard severance, without the extended healthcare of the spring program, and the company expects a much smaller share of people to take it. But the pool of eligible employees is nearly seven times larger.

Microsoft says the offer doesn’t mean it needs fewer people. Coleman said in July that the company was studying whether to make voluntary exits a regular part of managing its workforce. It has told investors to expect operating margins roughly flat this quarter and down less than a point for the full fiscal year, even with record capital spending.

Nadella has addressed this before. In a July 2025 memo to employees, after Microsoft laid off about 15,000 people, he acknowledged the “uncertainty and seeming incongruence” of thriving financially while cutting jobs. “This is the enigma of success in an industry that has no franchise value,” he wrote.

In his annual shareholder letter last week, he focused on Microsoft’s spending on AI infrastructure. “Based on the demand we see and the efficiencies we are driving, I am confident in the long-term returns on our investments,” Nadella wrote. “We are building against a growing book of business tied to this secular shift.”

Microsoft had about 223,000 employees as of June 30, before it cut 4,800 jobs in July and more in September. The Information reported this month that Azure President Girish Bablani told leaders in his group to find ways to cut costs by at least 20%. Microsoft called the report inaccurate and said Azure leadership had not directed teams to develop cost-cutting plans.

Copilot: Microsoft said in July that businesses were paying for more than 30 million Microsoft 365 Copilot seats, up from 20 million in April. That’s still only about 7% of the more than 450 million commercial Microsoft 365 seats.

The bigger change is in how Microsoft charges for Copilot and its other AI tools. In July it added usage-based billing alongside per-seat pricing. It’s also pushing customers toward E7, a new premium bundle that includes Copilot. Microsoft expects Microsoft 365 commercial cloud revenue to grow about 17% this quarter, not counting currency swings, a number that now includes GitHub.

The BNP Paribas analyst Slowinski, who attended Microsoft’s Frontier Tour event in London last week, wrote that partners are seeing more customers roll out Copilot company-wide. Partners also told him that Microsoft now ties 35% of E7 sales incentives to how much customers use features like Cowork.

Anthropic and OpenAI: Anthropic’s S-1 filing shows the company has committed to spend at least $44.9 billion with Microsoft from November 2026 to May 2033, up from the $30 billion Azure commitment announced last November. That’s well below its minimum commitments to Amazon ($110 billion) and Google ($114.5 billion).

Microsoft agreed last year to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic. Its results for the June quarter included a $3.2 billion gain on that investment.

OpenAI remains the bigger factor. Microsoft’s commercial remaining performance obligation (RPO), the measure of signed contracts it hasn’t yet delivered on, reached $678 billion last quarter, up 84% from a year earlier. Without OpenAI, the backlog grew 25%. OpenAI told investors its annualized revenue approached $50 billion at the end of September, The Information reported, lower than earlier reports of about $70 billion.

Windows: Microsoft expects revenue from Windows licenses sold to PC makers, along with its own devices, to fall a little more than 20%. Higher memory prices are making PCs more expensive, and PC makers are still working through extra inventory.

What’s next: Alphabet also reports Wednesday afternoon, and Amazon reports Thursday, setting up a side-by-side look at Azure, Google Cloud and AWS.

Anthropic is aiming to go public the week of Nov. 16, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Check back Wednesday afternoon for coverage.

#5438. Shopify stock sinks after earnings report as revenue missed expectations

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Shopify reported 32% revenue growth and $119 billion in gross merchandise volume for the quarter ended Sept. 30

Shopify $SHOP stock was headed for a sharp decline after the company reported 32% revenue growth for the quarter ended Sept. 30. Revenue missed expectations, according to MarketWatch.

Adjusted earnings per share came in at 49 cents, compared with 34 cents in the same quarter of the prior year. That topped the 47-cent consensus estimate from FactSet, according to MarketWatch.

Shopify said revenue grew 32% in constant currency and its free cash flow margin was 22%. Gross merchandise volume, or GMV, which measures the total dollar value of orders facilitated through the Shopify platform, reached $119 billion.

"We powered $119 billion in GMV, while continuing to build commerce into every surface, every agent, and increasingly, everywhere," Harley Finkelstein, president of Shopify, said in a statement.

For the fourth quarter, Shopify said it expects revenue to grow at a low-thirties percentage rate year over year. It expects gross profit dollars to grow at a high-twenties percentage rate and operating expenses to equal 29% to 30% of revenue. Stock-based compensation is projected at $155 million, and the free cash flow margin is expected to match the fourth quarter of 2025.

Shopify's management team will hold a conference call on Tuesday at 8:30 a.m. ET to discuss the results. A webcast will be available on the company's investor relations website.

Shopify in September partnered with Meta $META Platforms to let Meta's Muse AI agent browse Shopify-powered stores and complete purchases for users. The integration is to be built on Shop Pay, Shopify's one-tap checkout service.

#5437. Tech Moves: Xbox COO’s sudden departure; SeekOut leadership shakeup; Fred Hutch names VP

Tech Moves covers notable hires, promotions and personnel changes in the Pacific NW tech community. Submissions: [email protected]

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 27, 2026 at 2:08 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 1:05 pm

— Xbox Chief Operating Officer Helen Chiang has suddenly left Microsoft after 21 years with the company, just months after landing the role in July. Her past roles include leading Mojang and the Minecraft franchise.

Verge first reported the news on Friday, citing a memo from Xbox CEO Asha Sharma that did not disclose the reason for her departure.

An Xbox spokesperson was likewise mum on details. “We don’t discuss individual personnel matters. We’re grateful for Helen’s years of service and wish her well,” the company said in an email to GeekWire.

In response to speculation around her departure, Chiang offered a LinkedIn post on Nov. 2 refuting rumors that she left because of leaks to the media, to take a role with a competitor, for poor behavior or because she was passed over for a larger role.

“My story is about staying true to your core values, especially when it is hard. That’s the legacy I hope to leave behind,” Chiang wrote, without providing specifics.

Xbox has undergone a massive reorganization that included Chiang’s appointment, roughly 3,200 job cuts through the fiscal year — about 20% of the Xbox workforce — the spinoff of four game studios and a plan to dramatically flatten management.

— Seattle-based tech leader Philip Su has joined Anthropic as a member of technical staff on beneficial deployments. The management role focuses on AI applications in global health, life sciences, economic mobility and education.

Su started his tech career with 12 years at Microsoft and later worked for Facebook. He has launched multiple ventures, including Audere, a global health software nonprofit, and Superphonic, a podcast player. In 2021, he worked at an Amazon fulfillment center to experience the holiday rush.

Su also created and leads an annual course for University of Washington computer science students on how to maximize their personal and professional growth.

— More leadership changes are underway at SeekOut, a Bellevue-based recruiting startup launched in 2017. The company announced Monday that co-founder John Tippett is now president, moving from his role as chief client officer.

In April, SeekOut CEO and co-founder Anoop Gupta retired and passed the reins to enterprise software veteran Sean Thompson. In August, co-founder and chief technology officer Aravind Bala took over as CEO. Thompson is now listed as an adviser to the board.

Tippett will lead day-to-day operations and work with Bala “on the company’s direction,” according to a press release. SeekOut said it wants to integrate AI tools into customers’ operations to reduce recruiters’ workload.

SeekOut is No. 68 on the GeekWire 200, a ranked index of the Pacific Northwest’s top startups.

— Fred Hutch Cancer Center has appointed Michael (Mick) Merritt as vice president of strategy and partnerships, effective Dec. 7.

Merritt joins from Penn Medicine, where he was chief operating officer of Penn Signature Services. He has more than 25 years of experience in academic medicine, consulting, strategy, business development and operations.

— Industrial wastewater treatment startup Membrion has named Alexander Demihovsky as director of applications engineering. He joins the Seattle-based company from Xylem. His past employers include Evoqua Water Technologies and Bechtel National.

“Alex helps turn customer needs into viable project plans, mitigate execution risks and develop competitive proposals,” the company said.

— Marine geothermal energy startup Endurance Energy has named Marty Calvert as the director of turbomachinery. Calvert joins the Seattle startup from Blue Origin. He was previously a turbomachinery engineer at NASA for more than 13 years.

Endurance completed its fifth deployment to the ocean floor last month, testing Adélie, a 100-kilowatt geothermal generator named for a penguin.

#5436. Oil prices climb after U.S. strikes Iran's Qeshm Island in Strait of Hormuz

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Brent crude is up more than 1.7% after a Monday selloff of more than 7%, as U.S.-Iran talks and strike risks continue

The U.S. struck Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday, according to The Wall Street Journal, and oil prices climbed on Tuesday.

Brent crude futures traded near $106.60 a barrel, up more than 1.7%, regaining some of the ground lost in Monday's drop of over 7%. West Texas Intermediate futures gained.

Three U.S. officials described the action as limited and defensive, meant to protect U.S. assets in the region, according to CNN. One official said the strike came after Iranian fire directed at an American aircraft. Washington has conducted a string of limited strikes over recent weeks, and this one is the newest, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi said Tehran retains its right to self-defense and called the incident part of an "ongoing war," according to CNN.

President Donald Trump wrote on social media Monday that an agreement "could happen," according to CNN. Vice President JD Vance told reporters the two sides had "certainly made some progress," according to CNN. Tehran says the Strait of Hormuz could be open again within two days if Washington satisfies seven demands, while the U.S. rejects Iran's claimed authority over the waterway.

U.S. Gulf allies are bracing for the chance of a wider American offensive on Iran, which might provoke reprisals aimed at commercial and civilian facilities throughout the Middle East, according to The Wall Street Journal. Trump has been inclined to order a more sweeping strike following Tuesday's midterms, though he has yet to reach a firm conclusion.

Two vessels were hit Monday by projectiles of unknown origin near the coasts of Saudi Arabia and Oman, according to U.K. Maritime Trade Operations. Both crews were said to be unharmed.

Saudi Aramco CEO Amin H. Nasser said on the company's third-quarter earnings call Tuesday that oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz had not yet returned to levels seen before the conflict, according to The Wall Street Journal. Nasser said ships had to wait a long time before they could transit safely.

Oil prices had fallen on Monday as negotiations to end the conflict eased worries about Middle East supply. Brent had closed out October at a six-month peak. The U.S. and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding on June 17, but the agreement collapsed.

#5435. Etzioni on AI: Is Anthropic worth $2 trillion? Do the napkin math with this handy calculator

by Oren Etzioni on Oct 27, 2026 at 4:45 pmOctober 27, 2026 at 4:45 pm

Anthropic filed to go public on Monday under the ticker ANT, and you may end up owning the stock soon even if you never buy it directly, because index funds and ETFs will be required to buy it within weeks of its debut.

Anthropic’s bankers are reportedly valuing Anthropic between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion. Below is a simple, interactive tool to help you form your own opinion of what’s an appropriate valuation for Anthropic.

Disclaimer: this is highly simplified, and I’m not an investment advisor.

The whole IPO debate comes down to two numbers nobody knows: how much revenue Anthropic will have in 2028, and how much of it will be profit. Pick yours.

Your number = revenue × margin × profit multiple. The IPO valuation is $2 trillion, the top of the reported range. The arithmetic ignores two things that roughly cancel: a 2028 profit is worth about 17% less today than the same profit earned now, and Anthropic’s $132 billion in cash adds about 7% to any result. Big Tech multiples are market value divided by the latest quarter’s operating profit, annualized; margins are operating margins from the latest quarter. Anthropic’s figures are from its S-1 and the forecast it gave investors. This is arithmetic, not investment advice.

#5434. Pfizer is raising its sales forecast after beating earnings expectations

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The drugmaker's full-year revenue outlook is now $62 billion to $64 billion, up from $60.5 billion to $62.5 billion

Pfizer $PFE raised its full-year 2026 guidance for revenue and adjusted earnings per share on Tuesday after reporting third-quarter results that included higher sales of launched and acquired products.

The company now expects revenue between $62.0 billion and $64.0 billion, compared with the $60.5 billion to $62.5 billion range it had forecast earlier. That is a $1.5 billion increase at the midpoint. Pfizer also raised and narrowed its adjusted EPS guidance to $2.95 to $3.05, from $2.80 to $3.00. The EPS range absorbs a single $650 million charge tied to an in-licensing and collaboration deal with Innovent Biologics, which weighs on the figure by roughly 10 cents a share.

Third-quarter revenue was $16.6 billion, flat from a year earlier on an operational basis. Excluding Comirnaty and Paxlovid, revenue grew 7% operationally. Adjusted EPS was 87 cents, unchanged from the prior-year quarter. Net income was $3.24 billion, or 56 cents a share, down from $3.54 billion, or 62 cents a share.

Analysts expected adjusted earnings of 73 cents a share and revenue of $15.87 billion, according to CNBC. Pfizer's results exceeded both figures.

Revenue from launched and acquired products rose 32% on an operational basis. Eliquis revenue rose 25% operationally and Padcev revenue rose 55%. Paxlovid revenue fell 63%, Comirnaty revenue fell 29% and revenue from the Prevnar family fell 10%.

Chief Financial Officer Cecile Guegan said in a statement that the raised guidance reflects the company's year-to-date performance and confidence in its business. Chairman and CEO Albert Bourla said in a statement that the obesity program continued to advance and that recent milestones in oncology, immunology and vaccines show the potential of the pipeline.

Pfizer raised the midpoint of its full-year revenue guidance in August, when it set the $60.5 billion to $62.5 billion range. Guegan became interim CFO that month after Dave Denton left the role. The company said her appointment as CFO took effect Nov. 1.

Pfizer will host a conference call and webcast at 10 a.m. ET on Tuesday.

#5433. CFTC Sets December 14 Deadline to Rewrite "Actual Delivery": Where Exchanges Are Exposed

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The clock is officially ticking on the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s (CFTC) attempt to overhaul its regulatory grip on retail digital asset trading.

While corporate press releases focused on preliminary announcements, the formal publication of Federal Register Document 2026-20888 under RIN 3038-AF80 establishes a strict deadline: public comments close on December 14, 2026.

That date anchors an urgent operational check for digital asset exchanges, custodians, and margin trading desks. While crypto media outlets like The Defiant and TFTC covered the high-level regulatory announcement, this breakdown maps the ANPRM’s exact per-question mechanics directly against the concrete exchange structures they expose. The Advance Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM) represents the Commission’s first attempt to replace its piecemeal enforcement stances with a binding, notice-and-comment framework for "actual delivery" under Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the Commodity Exchange Act (CEA).

Responding by December 14 is not merely an exercise in policy debate; it requires market participants to confront the exact legal and technical mechanics where their existing architectures remain exposed.

Under Section 2(c)(2)(D) of the CEA, any leveraged, margined, or financed retail commodity transaction falls under full CFTC futures regulation unless "actual delivery" occurs within 28 days. Centralized exchanges historically operate in a regulatory gray area by executing off-chain, book-entry updates in internal databases and claiming those entries fulfilled delivery requirements.

The proposed Regulation CTX directly targets that operational model. Through the questions inside the ANPRM 2026-20888, the Commission reveals four critical vulnerabilities that exchanges must address before the comment window shuts:

In its analysis of the proposal, law firm Fenwick & West highlights that the ANPRM leaves open a crucial question regarding how the 28-day actual delivery exception applies to fully-paid transactions maintained entirely on an exchange’s internal ledger.

If an exchange's user agreement or onboarding terms contain broad margin or financing language, the CFTC signals that every transaction on the platform, even fully-paid spot trades could be swept into the CTX umbrella. Without explicit actual delivery, an exchange keeping user assets on internal book-entry databases risks having its entire spot book reclassified as an illegal, unregistered derivatives venue.

The ANPRM questions whether off-chain ledger entries can ever satisfy actual delivery without an explicit on-chain transaction. If the CFTC mandates on-chain settlement, exchanges relying on centralized databases to match order books at high speeds will face severe throughput bottlenecks and surging gas costs.

The notice probes what constitutes true "possession and control" by the buyer. The CFTC specifically asks whether a customer maintains full control if an exchange retains administrative keys, emergency pause functions, or liquidation authority. If retaining risk-management hooks breaks the delivery exception, platforms cannot claim actual delivery while maintaining centralized control over user balances.

Recognizing that instant on-chain delivery for high-frequency retail leverage is technically impractical, the Commission seeks feedback on Alternative CTX framework models. The notice asks whether leveraging registered Futures Commission Merchant (FCM) structures, strict account segregation, and proof-of-reserves audits can provide a viable compliance pathway for platforms choosing not to settle every trade on-chain.

Because this ANPRM RIN 3038-AF80 precedes a formal Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM), the CFTC is using the December 14, 2026 window to gather empirical data on how exchanges manage custody, leverage, and settlement. Platforms can review the docket materials directly via the CFTC Innovation page.

Exchanges relying on internal ledgers to offer retail products must submit technical feedback demonstrating how their custody models preserve user protection. Once the CFTC translates these questions into binding NPRM language, the legal definition of "actual delivery" will solidify, leaving non-compliant exchanges directly vulnerable to federal enforcement actions.

#5432. China and Russia have hypersonic missiles. This $13 billion startup wants the U.S. to catch up

For the last couple of months, when someone asked what I was working on, I’d mention in passing “a hypersonics startup,” and almost always got stopped: Wait, roll that back.

The startup is Castelion, based in Torrance, Calif. and working to produce and scale low-cost hypersonic missiles. The term “hypersonic” may have a sci-fi ring to it, but the technology is very real, and there are many reasons to pay attention. As I write at the top of the feature published this past weekend:

The first thing to know about hypersonic missiles is that they’re air-rippingly fast.

A hypersonic missile, definitionally, moves at least at Mach 5, or five times the speed of sound; one could cross the U.S. coast to coast in under 45 minutes. Unlike ballistic missiles, hypersonics are maneuverable and unpredictable to watchers, with an uncanny ability to fly low, change course, and skirt radar.

The second thing to know about hypersonics is that China and Russia have them, and the U.S. doesn’t—not really. It’s not for lack of trying: Despite years of research costing billions and some successful tests, the U.S. has yet to fully field a hypersonic missile of its own due to testing complications and production issues. The tech’s been around, but it’s been expensive and difficult to produce at scale.

That’s the chasm that startup Castelion, valued at $13 billion, is betting it can close, even if the defense giants have so far fallen short. “Humans have done it, just not Americans,” says Castelion CEO and cofounder Bryon Hargis. “I firmly believe it’s doable.”

In 2022, Hargis, Andrew Kreitz, and Sean Pitt—all previously SpaceX executives—cofounded Castelion to help close America’s hypersonics gap. And the beginning was comically unpromising, a reality the three founders remain unflinchingly honest about. An example, from the story:

In 2022, as Hargis, Kreitz, and Pitt were just getting started, they presented to the Defense Innovation Unit, the Pentagon’s tech acceleration division. It didn’t go well. “It was the tailish end of COVID,” said Pitt. “So, it was a video presentation, and we explained ‘we’re here to make low-cost missiles.’ They asked: ‘Are you going to compete with Lockheed?’ We said yes, and it was not a little laugh. There were a good number of people laughing.”

Not anymore. Now, Castelion is valued at $13 billion and ranks easily among the most valuable defense upstarts in the world. The company’s also at the end of the beginning: With a notable customer in the U.S. Navy (and the program of record to match), Castelion is barreling towards 2027 with a strong need to ramp up and speed up—for the business and to meet a wildly unpredictable geopolitical landscape.

It’s a story about long odds, deterrence, and urgency. But Castelion is also a prism through which we can understand what makes the defense tech boom necessary, challenging—and definitionally high-stakes.

#5431. A new pal for Pluto? Rubin Observatory finds its first dwarf planet candidate

by Alan Boyle on Oct 27, 2026 at 7:54 pmOctober 27, 2026 at 8:23 pm

Astronomers sorting through data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile have found an icy world that has a good chance of joining Pluto in the solar system’s retinue of dwarf planets.

University of Washington astronomer Mario Jurić joined the astronomer who made the discovery, Matthew Holman of the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, to announce the findings today at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society’s Division for Planetary Sciences in Spokane, Wash.

Jurić, the Rubin team’s solar system lead scientist, said the observatory’s capabilities made it possible to detect and characterize the new dwarf planet candidate, known as 2026 ED138.

“Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth, and precision,” Jurić said in a news release. “And the discovery is just the beginning: Once we identify a new object, we can search back months, and sometimes even decades, finding it in images where nobody knew to look. This ability to both discover and ‘precover’ objects is transforming how quickly and accurately we can determine their orbits and understand the distant solar system.”

2026 ED138 traces a tilted orbital path that takes it well beyond Pluto, the solar system’s best-known dwarf planet. It’s currently at a distance of 46 astronomical units, where 1 AU equals the average distance between Earth and the sun. Pluto, by comparison, is currently about 40 AU from the sun.

Astronomers suspect ED138 formed billions of years ago closer to the sun before being flung into a wider orbit by gravitational interactions with Neptune.

Based on an analysis of its distance, brightness and assumed composition, ED138 is thought to be somewhere between 600 and 1,500 kilometers (373 to 932 miles) in diameter. At that size, an icy object should possess enough gravity to pull itself into a round shape — satisfying the primary physical criterion for a dwarf planet.

ED138 may be Rubin’s first dwarf planet candidate, but it almost certainly won’t be the last. Thanks to the observatory’s Simonyi Survey Telescope — named after the family of Seattle software billionaire Charles Simonyi — the Rubin team detected more than 11,000 new asteroids even before June’s official start of a 10-year survey of the southern sky.

Rubin’s researchers analyze the data from those scans to find objects of interest — ranging from asteroids to gamma-ray bursts — and track them over time. On Oct. 13, Holman was running data through a search code that he developed with Kevin Napier, a colleague at the Center for Astrophysics. ED138 stood out due to its exceptional size and brightness.

“My first reaction was one of excited disbelief,” Holman said. “Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong.”

To confirm the discovery, Holman, Jurić and their colleagues found 30 archived observations of ED138 dating back to March 4. The Asteroid Institute’s ADAM Precovery service found still more images of the object, going back to 2016, in the archives of a different astronomical survey.

The precovery data confirmed that ED138 was a special case.

“Finding an object this big, roughly 1,000 kilometers across, is something that happens maybe once in a generation,” Jurić said. “It’s the largest trans-Neptunian object found in about 20 years, and Rubin turned it up while we were still commissioning the telescope.”

In 2006, the International Astronomical Union defined dwarf planets as planetary objects that are big enough to crush themselves into a roundish shape — technically speaking, into a state of hydrostatic equilibrium — but not big enough to clear their orbital neighborhood.

So far, the IAU has classified five solar system objects as dwarf planets — including Ceres in the main asteroid belt, plus Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake in the region beyond Neptune. 2026 ED138 joins a host of other celestial objects that are thought to be dwarf planets but haven’t yet been added to the IAU’s official list.

“The official list hasn’t moved since 2008,” Jurić told GeekWire in an email. “I’m not sure if there’s an active process that reviews candidates, and what are the timelines.”

Jurić and his colleagues hope additional observations will boost ED138’s chances of attaining true dwarf planethood.

“The next step in building the case would be to prove it’s round (in hydrostatic equilibrium),” he wrote. “The means to do that would be directly through occultations (and there’s a good chance of that, given it’s in a dense stellar field), and then thermal measurements plus modeling and light curves (or the absence of variability).”

#5429. Anthropic’s third quarter results mean IPO math and history are not on its side, analysts say

Anthropic’s IPO is looking like an increasingly expensive and risky bet after the company released third quarter financial results yesterday that showed its rate of revenue growth slowing and its expenses climbing at a faster pace compared to prior quarters.Several analysts Fortune spoke to said math and past experience are not in favor of Anthropic producing stellar returns for investors. That may explain why institutional investors are reportedly pushing the company and its IPO advisors to price Anthropic’s shares at the lower end of a $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion valuation range that the company is seeking in its public stock offering.

Even that may be too pricey, according to analysts. Any IPO valuation above about $1.41 trillion would ask Anthropic’s buyers to pay more than $40 for every dollar the company generated in revenue over the past year—a price level achieved by just 14 of the 4,110 IPOs that took place between 1980 through 2024, according to a study from Jay Ritter, director of the University of Florida’s IPO Initiative. What’s more, those IPOs delivered lower average returns than the broader market, Ritter said.

Against the roughly $35.3 billion in revenue Anthropic booked over the past four quarters, a valuation range of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion, would mean investors paying between $43 and $57 for every dollar of sales the company generated in the past 12 months.

To justify a valuation north of $1.4 trillion, Anthropic needs a path toward annual after-tax profits of at least $100 billion, Ritter told Fortune. Only a handful of companies have ever earned that much in a year, he said, including Alphabet, Nvidia, Apple and Microsoft.

In the third quarter, Anthropic’s revenue rose nearly 47% from the previous quarter, while compute and infrastructure expenses climbed about 77% to $9.9 billion. About half of that compute bill, roughly $5 billion, came from the company purchasing short-term capacity. Anthropic typically orders compute 12 to 18 months ahead, but is forced to buy more expensive short-term capacity when customer demand or research needs exceed what it has secured. The company attributed the decline in its adjusted operating margin to 15% from 19%, primarily to those short-term costs.

Tomasz Tunguz, founder and general partner of Theory Ventures, told Fortune that higher compute costs would put increasing pressure on Anthropic’s margins, although he noted that the company’s implied gross margin was still a healthy 85%. Gross margin counts only the cost of serving customers. It excludes the far larger sums Anthropic spends training models and on research, which are booked as separate operating expenses.

The pressure on adjusted operating margins arrived sooner than Tony Trzcinka, an investment grade portfolio manager at Impax Asset Management, said he expected. “The key question is whether revenue can compound fast enough to absorb the future commitments and outpace compute cost,” he told Fortune. He expects the company’s existing obligations and interconnected relationships to limit its ability to borrow at the kinds of low interest rates available to investment-grade companies. This means if Anthropic does need to take on debt to fund its compute capacity, that money will be expensive, further weighing on margins.

But paying more for compute can also help an AI company generate future revenue, Campbell Hutcheson, a senior researcher at Epoch AI, said. Frontier models, such as those Anthropic builds, can command premium prices and help improve the training and inference efficiency of other models, he told Fortune. Because revenue growth often depends on reaching a capability or product threshold first, as with ChatGPT and Claude Code, he said it can be rational for labs to pay a premium to get there first. Hutcheson said Anthropic continued to show “very strong growth, high gross margins” while investing heavily in AI research.

With about $131.8 billion in cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments at September 30, Anthropic has resources to keep investing while it works to improve those economics. Its operations generated $6.6 billion in cash during the first nine months of the year. Ritter said those reserves, combined with IPO proceeds, would allow considerable investment. Trzcinka also views liquidity as a positive for bondholders, while watching for further spending commitments and any borrowing under the company’s revolving credit facility.

In estimating what Anthropic could be worth to shareholders, Aswath Damodaran, a finance professor at New York University’s Stern School of Business, looked a decade ahead. His Oct. 28 valuation—which was produced prior to Anthropic releasing its third quarter results—assumed annual revenue reaching $1 trillion by 2036, a target operating margin of 27.5% and an estimated $100 billion in IPO proceeds. Those assumptions produced an equity value of about $1.475 trillion, which he described as at the lower end of the $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion range.

Damodaran told Fortune that Anthropic’s third-quarter figures gave him little reason to revise his valuation, calling them “the most telegraphed 3rd quarter number of all time.” His earlier post had already discussed slowing revenue growth and continued margin volatility, he said. “If my intrinsic value changed significantly based on this news story, it would be neither intrinsic nor value, just a pricing chase.”

Ritter likewise saw no big surprises in the third quarter numbers, but his research highlights the risk of paying for exceptional growth in advance. In Ritter’s study, the 14 IPOs that commanded the kind of price-to-sales ratio that Anthropic is asking investors to swallow delivered returns averaging 15.4 percent below the broader stock market, measured from their offer prices over holding periods of up to three years, although some companies outperformed. Each company had at least $100 million in revenue over the 12 months before listing, adjusted for inflation to 2025 dollars.

Anthropic has substantial upside potential, Ritter said, but “a lot of things have to go right” for its revenue and profits to grow enough to support such a high valuation.

Wen Shao is a reporting fellow at Fortune covering AI, with a focus on the companies, economics, and infrastructure shaping the industry.

#5427. Amazon earnings preview: AWS is booked up, and Wall Street wants to know what comes next

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 8:11 amOctober 28, 2026 at 8:11 am

Amazon reports third-quarter earnings Thursday afternoon with more demand for its cloud services than it can serve, driven by AI labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI along with growth in its traditional cloud business.

One big question for Wall Street going into the report is what Amazon might signal about next year’s spending as it tries to keep up with that demand.

CEO Andy Jassy said on an Andreessen Horowitz podcast last week that AWS capacity is largely booked for this year and next, along with “a good chunk of ’28.”

Amazon has said it expects to spend about $220 billion on capital expenditures this year, largely on AI and cloud infrastructure, up from its earlier plan of $200 billion. Even at that level, Jassy said, Amazon is “leaving a meaningful amount of demand on the table.”

Past spending pushed Amazon’s free cash flow to negative $7.6 billion for the 12 months ending in June, as the cost to add data centers, chips and other equipment exceeded the cash its operations brought in. Jassy gave no indication of slowing down, saying the company “could invest a lot more and it wouldn’t be a bad use of capital.”

Core numbers: Analysts expect revenue of about $202 billion, up 12% from a year ago, according to Yahoo Finance. That’s at the top of Amazon’s own forecast of $197 billion to $202 billion.

Analysts expect earnings of $1.96 per share, about the same as a year ago.

Amazon’s sales growth will likely look slower this time, about 12%, down from 20% last quarter. A big reason is timing. Prime Day, the company’s biggest sales event of the year, fell in the second quarter this year, rather than the third quarter as it did last year, so this quarter is up against a tougher comparison.

Amazon estimated in July that the shift would take nearly 4 percentage points off its growth rate this quarter. It hits online store sales hardest: analysts expect them to grow only about 3%, according to Zacks.

AWS: Amazon Web Services, the company’s cloud business, generates the majority of its operating profit. AWS revenue grew 37% to $42.2 billion in the second quarter, its fastest pace since 2021 and the fifth straight quarter of faster growth.

Analysts expect AWS revenue of about $45.4 billion this time, up 37.5%, according to Zacks. Wedbush is more optimistic, projecting growth of about 41%.

AWS had $496 billion in signed contracts it hadn’t yet delivered as of June, more than double the year before. That means its growth depends largely on how quickly Amazon can bring new data centers online.

“Capacity, not demand, is the constraint,” Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives wrote of the industry in a note Sunday.

Jassy said on the a16z podcast that running AI models is still “an order of magnitude too expensive” for businesses to use them widely, and that Amazon’s custom chips, including its Trainium AI processors, are a big piece of bringing that cost down. Amazon said in July that its chip business was on pace for more than $25 billion in annual revenue.

Anthropic stake: Amazon’s reported earnings could look very different. That’s because its profit fluctuates significantly depending on the value of its stake in Anthropic.

Last quarter, $53.4 billion in pre-tax gains, mostly on Anthropic, pushed Amazon’s earnings to $5.75 per share, against expectations of $1.82.

Anthropic filed paperwork Monday for a planned IPO on the Nasdaq. Amazon’s stake in the AI company was valued at about $190 billion as of June 30, according to Amazon’s latest quarterly filing. That includes about $92 billion in gains on convertible notes, a form of loan that turns into stock, which haven’t yet been counted in Amazon’s profit. Those notes would convert to Anthropic stock when it goes public.

Anthropic is also one of Amazon’s biggest cloud customers. Its IPO filing shows commitments to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon’s computing capacity into the 2030s, behind the $114.5 billion it committed to Google, as GeekWire reported Tuesday. Anthropic also said in the filing that it has asked its cloud providers for more computing power than they were willing to supply.

Shopping agents: Amazon blocked Meta’s new Muse AI agent from its store last month, escalating a fight over who controls the customer relationship when software does the buying. Amazon said Muse broke its rule requiring agents to identify themselves.

Agents that shop on a customer’s behalf could bypass Amazon’s advertising business, which depends on people browsing its pages. Ad revenue grew 26% to $19.8 billion last quarter, and analysts expect about $20.8 billion this time, up 18%, according to Zacks.

“Investor questions remain on agentic commerce risk, particularly to advertising, but we see limited risk,” Wedbush analyst Ygal Arounian wrote in an Oct. 16 note, citing Amazon’s logistics advantage and its role connecting shoppers with sellers.

Amazon is trying to give shoppers fewer reasons to look elsewhere. It now lists 250 million products sold on other retailers’ sites, about 2.5 times as many as in March, The Information reported Wednesday. On the seller side, Amazon opened its tools to outside AI agents in September, starting with Anthropic’s Claude.

Cloud rivals: Microsoft and Alphabet report quarterly results Wednesday afternoon, a day before Amazon. Microsoft’s report is its first under a new structure that breaks out Azure cloud revenue every quarter.

#5425. Cheap flights in Europe face a fuel cost reckoning as Ryanair’s CEO says fares could rise up to 20% next year because of the Iran war

Americans planning next year’s summer Euro trip may want to start saving now as the Iran war pushes up fuel prices and the CEO of the world’s biggest budget airline warns that the continent’s notoriously cheap short-haul flights could soon become more expensive.

Ryanair CEO Michael O’Leary said on CNBC following the company’s earnings call Monday that he expects European airfares to rise by 10%, and maybe even 20% next year, potentially dealing another blow to Americans hoping to visit multiple European destinations without breaking the bank.

Americans made nearly 24 million trips to Europe in 2025, a 5% increase from the previous year. Summer is one of the busiest tourist seasons for the region, and this year the European aviation network handled an average of 35,959 flights per day between June and August, a 2.4% increase from last year, according to The European Organisation for the Safety of Air Navigation.

But the Iran war, now in its ninth month, has disrupted global supply chains, including by effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz, through which about 20% of the world’s oil passed before the war. That has driven up oil and jet fuel prices increasing the burden on airlines, for which fuel is the second-biggest expense behind labor.

Ryanair, Europe’s largest airline by passenger traffic, shows what could be in store for travelers next year.

Ryanair has been more insulated from rising fuel prices than many of its rivals because of fuel hedging, the practice of locking in prices ahead of time to protect against market volatility.

O’Leary said Ryanair has locked in a price of $67 per barrel for 80% of its fuel needs through March 2027, helping keep costs in check for now.

Beyond that, though, only 25% of its fuel needs for the following fiscal year are hedged at about $95 per barrel, leaving the remainder exposed to higher market prices. Brent crude stood around $110 per barrel Monday, up 70% from a year ago.

Ryanair said in its fiscal second quarter earnings Monday that its annual fuel bill will increase by about  2 billion euros next year (for the fiscal year ending March 2028). O’Leary said fares would need to rise 20%, or about 10 euros per passenger, to cover all of it, but even he said the increase in fares might not fully cover the additional expense. To close the gap, the company said it is reviewing costs, including temporary pay freezes for labor agreements that mature in April and lower crew ratios.

O’Leary’s comments highlight another potential expense for Americans already dealing with increasing inflation, especially in the travel sector.

U.S. airfares rose 22.4% in September compared with a year earlier, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, about six times the overall inflation rate. The average domestic airfare reached $445 in the second quarter, according to the Bureau of Transportation Statistics. Unlike Ryanair, major U.S. airlines abandoned fuel hedging years ago, leaving them more immediately exposed to surging fuel prices.

Pricier jet fuel could also mean fewer flights to choose from. Ryanair has already reduced its annual passenger target from 216 million to 214 million for the fiscal year ending in March, and said it expects winter traffic to stay flat as it limits exposure to more expensive fuel. O’Leary said competing European airlines are already cutting capacity, which could drive up prices as travelers compete for fewer seats.

Still, the higher prices could actually benefit Ryanair. O’Leary argued that competitors facing even greater financial pressure will have little choice but to raise fares, which means his airline can do the same while also maintaining its low-cost advantage.

“They are under much more pressure to get pricing up,” he said during the company’s earnings call.

O’Leary also said Ryanair could maintain or even widen its margins as competitors increase their fares.

For travelers hoping to squeeze several European cities into one vacation, the consequences could add up. A 50 euro flight that rises 20% would cost 60 euros. While that might seem small on its own, multiple family members and destinations could add to the cost.

For his part, O’Leary warned that travelers thinking about waiting for a bargain next summer should instead look at tickets now.

“I would encourage them all to book early, because the longer you wait, the higher fare you are going to pay,” he said.

#5424. Central banks bought gold at fastest pace since 2024, WGC data shows

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Purchases reached 321 tonnes in the third quarter, lifting year-to-date buying 6% above last year's level

One kilogram gold bars and a five hundred gram gold bar in April 2025 (Angel Garcia/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Central banks bought 321 tonnes of gold in the third quarter, the World Gold Council said on Tuesday.

That was the fastest pace of central bank buying since late 2024, according to The Wall Street Journal. Purchases for the first nine months of the year total 675 tonnes, up 6% from a year earlier, the council said.

The council said third-quarter buying exceeded recent typical quarterly levels. Central banks bought 226.3 tonnes in the same quarter of 2025, according to Mining Zimbabwe.

China and Poland led the way among buyers that disclosed their purchases, according to The Wall Street Journal. "Central banks remained an important pillar of demand," said Louise Street, senior market analyst at the WGC, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Other parts of the market moved differently, the council said. Total gold demand, including over-the-counter trading, slipped 1% from a year earlier to 1,369 tonnes. Gold-backed exchange-traded funds added 211 tonnes after outflows in the second quarter. The council said the inflows appeared to reflect worry that public finances may prove unsustainable and that prices could keep climbing.

Jewelry demand fell 17% to 313 tonnes, the lowest reading for any third quarter in the series the council tracks, as high prices remained a headwind. Bar and coin demand slid 19% to 268 tonnes as buyers held off until the path of prices grew clearer. Technology demand rose 3% from a year earlier, driven by AI-related manufacturing.

Gold has slipped under $4,000 per troy ounce over the past few days. Prices stood at more than $5,000 an ounce ahead of the Iran war's outbreak in late February.

The WGC expects central bank purchases for the full year to equal or exceed last year’s total, after buying in the second and third quarters came in stronger than it had forecast, according to Mining Zimbabwe.
