#5422. We have the most powerful technology in history, and we’re using it to stop hiring young people

We hold the most powerful technology in human history, and so far corporate America is mostly using it to write marketing copy and cut headcount.

Through September, U.S. employers announced 573,195 job cuts. Artificial intelligence was cited in 120,136 of them, more than any other reason this year, according to outplacement firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas. Tech companies alone announced 165,925 cuts, up 54% from the same period last year.

To be fair, total announced cuts are down 39% from the first nine months of 2025, and AI was cited in only about 9% of September’s cuts. The bigger effect is on hiring. Using ADP payroll data, Stanford economists Erik Brynjolfsson, Bharat Chandar and Ruyu Chen found that as of June, employment among 22- to 25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed occupations was about 19% below where it would be if it had kept pace with young workers in less-exposed jobs. A year earlier, the gap was 15%. They write that the adjustment works “primarily through reduced hiring of young workers rather than increased separations.”

Companies aren’t firing junior workers; they are simply not hiring them. They’re using efficiency as the excuse.

On paper, the economy looks powerful. Real GDP grew at a 3.4% annual rate in the third quarter, up from 2.2% in the second, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis. Spending on computer equipment, a soft landing for capital expenditure, was a main driver.

But for the common citizen, this year has been anything but a soft landing. Consumer prices rose 3.7% in the year through September, and gasoline rose about 34%. Since the Iran war closed the Strait of Hormuz in March, oil has gone through what the World Bank calls “the largest oil market shock in history.”

In addition, workers now pay an average of $7,471 a year toward family health coverage, up 9% from 2025, according to KFF. Over roughly the same period, wages increased only 3.7%. Effectively, the people took a pay cut.

The AI buildout is also competing with households for the same electricity. In PJM, the largest U.S. grid operator, the independent market monitor estimated that data centers caused 63% of the price increase in 2025/2026, about $9.3 billion in costs, according to the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis. Pepco residential customers in Washington, D.C., saw bills rise about $21 a month starting in June 2025. Roughly $10 of that came from capacity prices.

This is what makes me angry. None of these issues requires new technology to be solved. The models exist, the compute exists, and the capital is already being spent. What’s missing is a decision about where to point it.

The American Society of Civil Engineers estimates a water main breaks every two minutes in the U.S., and about 6 billion gallons of treated water is lost daily. We could use AI to forecast load and balance the grid so data centers pay for the strain they add. We could use AI to find leaks in water systems. We could model drought before it reaches a farm, inspect bridges, harden supply chains, and cut diagnosis costs instead of raising premiums.

In June, in the U.K., Northumbrian Water reported that a six-month trial using AI-powered acoustic sensors to help crews locate hidden leaks was saving nearly 6.4 million liters of water a day. This is the technology we must invest in and deploy immediately.

San Jose Water installed 13,600 fixed acoustic sensors across its 2,400-mile network, and the system found 483 leaks and saved more than 400 million gallons of treated water. Plus, New Mexico’s LeakTracer satellite-plus-AI program identified 216 leaks across 181 miles of pipe in its first year. Completing the needed repairs could recover 328 million gallons and save about $505,000 a year.

First, we must treat energy resilience as a national security issue. Data centers must be required via litigation to pay for the grid upgrades and capacity they drive. Families shouldn’t have to subsidize the infrastructure required by multibillion-dollar tech companies. AEP Ohio already requires new data-center customers to reimburse 100% of buildout costs if they cancel before energization. The company creating the demand, carrying the risk, must be fundamental.

In my home state, New Jersey’s Data Center Fair Share Act was signed in July 2026, creating a separate rate class for large data centers. This requires them to cover their own infrastructure costs, demands financial guarantees covering at least 85% of requested load for 10 years, and lets them offset capacity obligations by paying for demand reductions elsewhere. This could save ratepayers more than $1 billion a year. Other states are moving in the same direction, with large-load tariffs imposing high minimum-demand charges and contribution-in-aid rules so residential customers aren’t charged if a project underdelivers or exits.

Next, go after health costs at the source. Use AI to reduce the volume of unnecessary tests, procedures, and late-stage interventions rather than simply shifting higher premiums onto households. Start by capping excessive hospital prices in public employee health plans, with safeguards for vulnerable hospitals. Oregon capped in-network hospital payments at twice Medicare’s rates and saved an estimated $107.5 million over 27 months. Then require publicly funded health care AI projects to demonstrate lower costs without compromising care. Efficiency isn’t helping if the patient’s bill remains the same.

Third, deploy AI to retrain people faster than it replaces them. By tying public incentives for AI investment and data-center build-out to measurable entry-level hiring and apprenticeship commitments, AI will create efficiency and jobs. As entry-level roles disappear for the benefit of only AI owners, the coming generations are being steered toward economic ruin. Tie public AI incentives to net-new paid apprenticeships and entry-level jobs, with payments after six and 12 months of verified employment and not simply after a training course.

This isn’t some pipe dream; the blueprint exists. In July, the Labor Department awarded nearly $162 million through an apprenticeship program that links payments to verified retention and progression milestones. Reward employers for being job creators and builders. Going forward, any firm receiving tax credits, accelerated permitting, or public power-purchase support for AI capacity must fund or host a proportional number of paid apprenticeships or entry-level roles, with progress reported publicly.

Finally, give public infrastructure the same AI investment private data centers get. One of the most impactful improvements AI could make is in utilities and water. As governments embed AI into power grids and water systems to stabilize national infrastructure, we should use AI-driven material evaluation of roads and highways and continuous monitoring to predict repair needs before learning from injuries and accidents. Funding can be mandated by dedicating a share of data-center tax revenue to local infrastructure technology. Virginia began taxing data-center electricity consumption at 1.1 cents per kilowatt-hour in July. States should direct a portion of that revenue toward leak detection, grid management, and bridge inspection, plus paying the employees who act on the findings.

A dedicated public AI infrastructure fund can be created and financed by a small, transparent tax on large data-center power or compute capacity, matched by federal and philanthropic capital.

When voters go to the polls Tuesday, they won’t vote on GDP. They’ll vote on whether things at home got easier or harder since their last ballot was dropped in the box. With AI, the question isn’t whether we can point this technology at the problems that decide whether people can afford to live and create a solution. We can do that. The real question is whether anyone in charge is willing to, or if they just want to keep eliminating the future of work for the next generations.

#5421. The Asterisk on Robinhood Chain’s $51M Win Over Ethereum

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Take 12 days out of Robinhood Chain's first quarter, and the "3-month-old L2 beat Ethereum" headline turns around.

For the other 80 days, Robinhood Chain earned about $166,000 a day in network fees. Ethereum averaged about $446,000.

ARK Invest's numbers are accurate. Robinhood Chain did generate about $51 million in Q3 against Ethereum's roughly $41 million. But the coverage repeated the comparison without checking how the $51 million was made or who ends up with it. Going back to the underlying data, and the comparison holds up much less well than the headline suggests.

ARK's DeFi Quarterly for Q3 2026 charts "Network Real Economic Value by Blockchain". In it, Robinhood Chain logged about $51 million in its first quarter, while Ethereum logged about $41 million, down roughly 35% from the previous quarter.

The comparison spread quickly. A chain that launched on July 1 beating the network that secures most of DeFi made an easy headline. ARK's wider data has more context: total network value across the chains it tracks rose about 24% to roughly $349 million, the first quarterly increase in five quarters, though still about 47% below a year earlier. Robinhood Chain processed about $65 billion in DEX volume, fourth in ARK's dataset, and hosted about $13.7 billion in tokenized equities.

ARK's DeFi Quarterly glossary defines Real Economic Value (REV) as "the total value a network generates consisting of both in-protocol transaction fees and out-of-protocol tips," using data from Blockworks Research.

In other words, both figures measure the same thing: gross fees users paid to use the chain. Robinhood Chain's $51 million matches the $51.0 million in user network fees reported in growthepie's Q3 review of the chain. It's not app revenue. growthepie puts the revenue of apps on Robinhood Chain separately, at $591.4 million.

So ARK didn't mix up its metrics. The trouble is that the same metric means very different things on these two chains. The Q3 number doesn't show that.

growthepie's report has the detail the headline leaves out. A 12-day surge, from August 30 to September 10, pushed median transaction costs to 31 times their pre-surge average. That surge produced 74% of the quarter's fees. growthepie names Relay as the largest tracked fee payer.

Outside the surge, Robinhood Chain earned about 37% of Ethereum's daily rate. At that pace, a full quarter would come to about $15 million, well under Ethereum's $41 million. The "out-earned Ethereum" result depends almost entirely on 12 days when fees jumped to 31 times normal.

That doesn't make the surge fake. Users paid those fees. But the surge came from congestion and higher prices, not steady growth. Across the quarter's 793.7 million transactions, users paid about 6.4 cents per transaction on average. Median costs that briefly rose to 31 times normal aren't a pricing model an exchange-backed chain will want to repeat.

Even with the same metric, the two figures go to very different places.

On Ethereum, most of the $41 million is the base fee, which is burned. That reduces ETH supply and benefits every holder. The rest goes as priority fees and tips to thousands of independent validators. Ethereum's REV is close to a public measure of what the network's users pay.

On Robinhood Chain, an Arbitrum Orbit rollup, fees go to the chain's sequencer, which Robinhood operates. In practice, the $51 million is a company's gross receipts. Some of it goes back to Ethereum to pay for posting data and settling transactions there, and the rest is Robinhood's margin. As coverage of the report noted, how much reaches Robinhood's income statement is still unclear. The company's earnings report on October 27 may answer that.

So on one side, you have fees paid to a decentralized base layer, mostly destroyed. On the other, you have gross receipts for one company, before costs. Both count as "network value," but they aren't the same kind of income.

Three more things make the head-to-head weaker:

The accurate version of the headline is less dramatic: in its first quarter, Robinhood Chain charged its users more in total than Ethereum's base layer did. About three-quarters of that came from a 12-day congestion spike, and the money went to Robinhood's sequencer, not to a decentralized validator set.

That's still a strong debut. Robinhood Chain's stablecoin growth, $13.7 billion in tokenized equities and nearly 800 million transactions are all real. But "beat Ethereum" tells you more about one busy fortnight in early September than about which chain has the stronger business. Q4 will be the real test: without a surge, can Robinhood Chain's fees come close to Ethereum's on an ordinary day?

Former T-Mobile CEO Mike Sievert is hanging up his magenta hat, leaving the wireless giant’s board of directors and vice chair role effective Nov. 1.

Once the scrappy outsider, Bellevue, Wash.-based T-Mobile currently ranks second among U.S. telecom companies by market capitalization, behind Verizon and ahead of AT&T.

Sievert previously worked at Microsoft, AT&T Wireless, E-Trade, IBM and Procter & Gamble.

#5419. Apple stock fell as rising memory costs sent its holiday margin forecast below expectations

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Apple projected a December-quarter gross margin of 45% to 46%, below the 46.3% analysts expected, according to CNBC

David Paul Morris / Bloomberg via Getty Images

Apple $AAPL forecast a gross margin between 45% and 46% for its holiday-season December quarter, and it cited rising memory chip costs. Apple stock dropped roughly 3% in after-hours trading on Monday, having already lost nearly 2% over the normal trading day.

The company reported fiscal fourth-quarter revenue of $114.5 billion on Monday, up 12% from a year earlier. Gross margin was 47.9%, including about 1 percentage point from tariff refunds. Diluted earnings per share were $2.10, up 14%.

The margin forecast falls short of the 46.3% that analysts were expecting on average, according to CNBC. Analysts had expected earnings per share of $1.99 and revenue of $113.39 billion.

"This includes primarily the impact of higher memory costs, as well as some costs related to the ramp of Siri AI," Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh said on the earnings call, according to CNBC.

CEO John Ternus said memory now costs the company more than it did in prior months of the year. "What we're seeing with memory pricing right now is unprecedented," Ternus said, according to CNBC. "Looking beyond the December quarter, we see the pricing for memory purchases continuing to increase."

Apple expects to have trouble supplying enough iPhones and Macs during the holiday quarter, mostly because of memory. Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan said the company has less room to maneuver across its supplier network than usual. Khan said Apple's purchase obligations grew by $33 billion between the June and September quarters, but he declined to say whether Apple has signed long-term agreements with memory makers.

A drop in the December-quarter margin would be Apple's third straight decline, according to CNBC. The margin was 50.1% in the June quarter. If results land halfway through that range, it would mark the company's weakest gross margin since the final quarter of fiscal 2023.

Ternus became CEO on Sept. 1, according to CNBC.

#5418. Wall Street is bracing for a fresh wave of tariffs, Iran action (and potentially a government shutdown) after the midterms

Though analysts have been wrong before, many observers expect the Democrats to claw back some political power in this week’s midterm elections. Despite that, Wall Street is expecting President Trump to double down on some of his less popular policies, following the vote.At the time of writing, Harvard University’s polling gives a 96% chance that the Democrats take the House, and a 78% likelihood of the Democrats taking both the House and the Senate.Goldman Sachs, for example, wrote to clients this morning that it expects President Trump to increase tariffs in the event the Democrats secure greater Congressional influence. Economists Alec Phillips and Abhay Duggirala reasoned that “Democrats have indicated they would seek to reverse some of President Trump’s tariffs, but we expect this to have a limited effect since the reversals would likely be focused on a few countries (e.g., Canada) or products.”“We expect President Trump to announce new tariff increases after the election that would more than offset those reductions, likely resulting in a rise in the US effective tariff rate of a little under 2pp.”

Tariffs will also likely become an increasingly important revenue source in the coming months. The conflict in the Middle East, for example, is proving costly, and sits against a backdrop of $40 trillion in national debt with calls from budget hawks to reduce deficits to 3% of GDP from its current 6%.

But any efforts to reduce these deficits will likely get bogged down in a more divided government, according to ING’s James Smith. He wrote to clients that fiscal gridlock will likely push attention back to trade policy and how to squeeze more revenue out of import relationships.

“Remember tariffs?” Smith wrote. “After the Supreme Court struck down Trump’s emergency tariffs, temporary 10% blanket rates ultimately gave way to a more permanent structure under Section 301. The issue has since slipped remarkably far down the agenda.”

The White House’s course of action in the Middle East, post-midterms, remains an unanswered question. As UBS’s Paul Donovan described it, the president may become more aggressive in the Gulf war “once freed from the pursuit of popularity.”

According to a Pew Research study last month, just 14% of voters said they strongly approve of President Trump’s handling of the military conflict with Iran, with a further 20% said they “somewhat” approve. With voters disenchanted, Trump’s only remaining motivations for the conflict lie in national security and his personal legacy.

“Where markets will want to focus is on the Republican reaction to the results,” said Donovan. “Does the Republican Party divide over MAGA-related issues, and does President Trump escalate hostilities in the Gulf War with wider economic consequences at home and abroad?”

More broadly, the cost of paying for the action settles into longer-term divisions about the future of government spending. Recent reports on the costs of the Iran war now come to $47 billion, with the conflict initially outlined as a matter of weeks now stretching into months.

“Republicans will likely attempt to pass a reconciliation bill along party lines in the coming weeks that could add substantially to defense spending and potentially address the debt limit, which will have to be dealt with before the late summer/fall of next year,” Deutsche Bank wrote to clients on Friday. “Recall, also, that federal government funding runs out on December 11 which will require bipartisan support for a continuing resolution to prevent a shutdown.”

Trump signed the Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act on September 2, which funded federal agencies through a 72-day window to December 11.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The offer of C$43 a share is a 32% premium to MTY's Oct. 30 closing price, after two earlier approaches were rebuffed

Foodtastic has offered to acquire Canadian restaurant franchisor MTY Food Group for about C$1 billion ($720 million), or C$43 a share, according to Bloomberg. MTY rebuffed two earlier approaches from Foodtastic.

The proposal tops MTY’s Oct. 30 closing stock price by 32% and puts a total valuation of roughly C$1.5 billion on the company once debt is counted, according to Bloomberg. MTY stock gained roughly 1% on Monday to finish at C$32.75, which gives the company a market capitalization near C$748 million.

MTY announced a leadership change on Tuesday, appointing director Victor E. Mandel as chief executive, effective at once. Mandel replaces Eric Lefebvre, who is leaving the company and its board. MTY franchises and operates restaurants under more than 80 banners, with 6,966 locations.

Foodtastic CEO Peter Mammas said in an emailed statement that the company is disappointed with MTY's response, according to Bloomberg. "We are therefore disappointed that MTY has rejected the proposed transaction without engaging in substantive dialogue," Mammas said. He added that Foodtastic is confident MTY's shareholders will see the proposal as "a superior path forward to MTY's standalone strategy."

Mammas also criticized MTY's performance. "MTY is a great company with excellent opportunities, but it has unfortunately not lived up to its full potential in recent years," he said, according to Bloomberg.

The approach follows the conclusion of a strategic review at MTY, which had weighed whether to sell either the whole business or a portion of it, according to Bloomberg. MTY's board, together with a committee made up of independent directors, determined that sticking with its current business plan would generate greater returns for shareholders. On Oct. 9, MTY said it planned to restart share repurchases, weigh a substantial issuer bid, lift its quarterly payout by 35%, to 50 Canadian cents per share, and pare back the portion of its business tied to company-operated restaurants.

Over the 13 weeks ended Aug. 30, MTY's comparable-store sales slid 1.9%, with the U.S. market accounting for a steeper 2.7% drop. Net income dropped to C$24.8 million, compared with C$27.9 million in the same period last year. The company closed a net 74 restaurants over the course of the quarter.

Foodtastic would pay for the transaction together with its financial backers, according to Bloomberg, which cited unnamed sources. Financing is expected to be lined up once a definitive deal is signed, as long as MTY opens its books for closer examination, according to Bloomberg. Foodtastic wants to hold talks with MTY’s board, though it has left open alternative routes if directors say no, Bloomberg said.

Foodtastic, based in Montreal, runs over 1,200 restaurants under roughly 30 brands, among them Milestones Grill + Bar, Second Cup and Freshii, according to Bloomberg. Funds managed by Oaktree Capital Management have backed the company since 2018.

#5416. PicoBrew’s patents are back on the market, six years after the Seattle homebrew startup’s collapse

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 28, 2026 at 10:36 amOctober 28, 2026 at 3:08 pm

The patents behind PicoBrew, the Seattle startup that once promised to do for home beer what Keurig did for coffee, are up for sale again — six years after the company collapsed into receivership and after two changes of ownership.

Hilco Global, an Illinois-based diversified financial services company, announced this week that its Intellectual Property Services group has been retained by PicoBrew’s current owner to market the startup’s technology to potential buyers.

The sale includes 17 patents and patent applications, two of them pending, along with engineering and design files and product concepts. Buyers can bid on all or part of the portfolio, and non-binding indications of interest are due Nov. 18. Hilco is pitching the assets to companies in coffee, tea, kombucha, spirits, beverage appliances and housewares.

The seller is Pico Craft Group, which Hilco described as led by a former PicoBrew investor. After PicoBrew’s 2020 collapse, its bridge lender took over the assets. That lender, PB Funding Group, was managed by former Microsoft software developer Greg Whitten, The Seattle Times reported at the time. Pico Craft Group bought the assets from the lender in 2024 for an undisclosed amount, according to Hilco, which did not say who runs the group.

“PicoBrew was a true innovator in the consumer and commercial craft beverage space, and its portfolio has applications well beyond beer,” Eric Hurwitz, a senior director at Hilco, said in a news release.

The portfolio covers technology from PicoBrew’s full product line, according to the release, including the Pico Pro and Pico C home brewing appliances, the PicoStill accessory for spirits, the Pico U Multibrew platform for beer, coffee, tea and kombucha, and Z-Series brewing machines and KegSmarts kegerators for commercial use.

Bill Mitchell, a former Microsoft vice president and longtime homebrewer, founded PicoBrew in 2010 with his brother Jim Mitchell, a food scientist, and Avi Geiger, an engineer who also worked at Microsoft. Their countertop machines automated the brewing process using PicoPaks, ingredient packs based on recipes from craft breweries.

The startup became a Kickstarter regular. Its 2017 campaign for the Pico Model C raised $1.93 million from 4,301 backers, a record at the time in the site’s food category, and the $549 machine landed at retailers including Best Buy, Williams-Sonoma and Amazon. A 2018 campaign for the Pico U pushed PicoBrew into coffee, tea and kombucha.

But the company struggled to land more funding. In February 2020, after failing to close a new round, PicoBrew entered receivership. It had raised more than $15 million and cut its staff to fewer than 40, down from a peak of more than 80.

PicoBrew ceased operations in 2020, and no one has supported existing devices since, according to Hilco. Any decision about future support would be up to a buyer. The King County Superior Court approved the 2020 sale, which freed PicoBrew’s bridge lender from the company’s liabilities and from responsibility to past customers, The Seattle Times previously reported.

Some owners kept their machines brewing without the company’s servers by using a workaround developed by a Facebook group of PicoBrew users, The Spoon reported in 2020. The founders were let go after the receivership, according to the site.

When PicoBrew went up for sale in 2020, Mitchell told GeekWire that hardware takes time and multiple funding rounds backed by firm investor commitment.

He shared advice he’d gotten from Dan Leviton of Maveron: “Startups only fail for one of two reasons — they run out of heart, or they run out of money.”

#5414. Current price of oil as of November 3, 2026

As of 6:45 a.m. Eastern Time today, oil is trading at $110.45 per barrel, based on the Brent benchmark we’ll explain in a bit. That’s $2.15 below yesterday morning’s level and about $45 higher than where it stood a year ago.

No one can say for sure where oil prices will go next. Many forces shape the market—but at the core, it’s still about supply and demand. When risks like a potential recession or war ramp up, oil prices can change direction quickly.

When you buy gas at the pump, you’re covering more than the cost of crude oil. You’re also paying for every step in the process, including refineries, wholesalers, taxes, and the markup your local gas station adds.

Even so, crude oil has the biggest influence on what you pay, often making up more than half the cost per gallon. When oil prices jump, gas prices usually climb right along with them. But when oil falls, gas prices often slip much more slowly—a pattern sometimes called “rockets and feathers.”

If an emergency hits, the U.S. keeps a backup supply of crude oil called the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. It’s mainly there to protect energy security during crises, such as sanctions, catastrophic storm damage, even war. It can also help cushion the blow when supply shocks send prices soaring.

It’s not meant to solve long-term problems. Instead, it provides quick relief for consumers and helps keep vital parts of the economy moving, like essential industries, emergency services, and public transit.

Oil and natural gas are two of the world’s primary energy sources. A big change in oil prices can affect natural gas by extension. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, which which increases demand for natural gas.

When looking at how oil performs, two main benchmarks stand out:

Of the two, Brent gives a better picture of global oil performance because it prices a large share of the world’s traded crude. It’s also the go-to for tracking oil’s historical trends. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now relies on Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook.

If you look at the Brent benchmark over several decades, oil has been far from stable. It has experienced sharp rises tied to wars and supply cuts, along with steep drops linked to global recessions and oversupply (called a “glut”). For example:

To sum up, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s heavily influenced by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, shifting energy policies, and much more.

Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage:

The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic.

The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing.

In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply.

When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf.

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Pfizer raised full-year revenue guidance by $1.5 billion at the midpoint, to a range of $62.0 billion to $64.0 billion

Pfizer $PFE raised its full-year 2026 revenue and adjusted earnings guidance on Tuesday as it reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of 87 cents per share, flat from a year earlier.

The company expects full-year revenue of $62.0 billion to $64.0 billion, up from a prior range of $60.5 billion to $62.5 billion. It expects adjusted earnings of $2.95 to $3.05 per share, compared with a prior range of $2.80 to $3.00. The earnings range includes a one-time $650 million charge tied to an in-licensing and collaboration agreement with Innovent Biologics, which reduces earnings by about 10 cents per share.

Third-quarter revenue totaled $16.58 billion, down $71 million from a year earlier. Excluding Comirnaty and Paxlovid, revenue grew 7% on an operational basis, which removes currency effects. Revenue from products it has launched or bought rose 32%, measured the same way.

Analysts surveyed by LSEG expected adjusted earnings of 73 cents per share and revenue of $15.87 billion, according to CNBC. Analysts surveyed by Zacks Investment Research expected 72 cents and $16.13 billion, according to The Associated Press.

Eliquis revenue rose 25% operationally, and Padcev revenue rose 55%. Paxlovid revenue fell 63%, Comirnaty revenue fell 29% and the Prevnar family's revenue fell 10%, the company said. Pfizer attributed the Paxlovid decline mainly to lower COVID-19 infections in the U.S. and international markets.

Net income came to $3.24 billion, or 56 cents a share, versus $3.54 billion, or 62 cents a share, a year earlier.

Pfizer appointed Cecile Guegan as chief financial officer and executive vice president, effective Nov. 1. Guegan had filled the role on an interim basis beginning Aug. 16.

"Today, we are raising our full-year 2026 Revenue and Adjusted diluted EPS guidance, reflecting our strong year-to-date performance and confidence in our business," Guegan said in a statement.

Pfizer will host a conference call and webcast at 10 a.m. ET on Tuesday.

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 10:56 amOctober 28, 2026 at 11:05 am

Shares of F5 fell about 20% on Wednesday, a day after the Seattle-based company beat Wall Street’s estimates and said it would boost spending to capitalize on expected growth in the AI security market.

The application security and delivery company’s stock was trading around $368 late Wednesday morning, down from $459 at Tuesday’s close, wiping out about $5 billion in market value. That put F5 on pace for its biggest one-day drop in more than 13 years, according to Barron’s. Before the drop, F5’s shares had climbed nearly 80% this year.

F5’s revenue for its fiscal fourth quarter rose 13% to $917 million, and product revenue jumped 23%. Adjusted earnings of $4.42 a share beat estimates of about $4.30.

Slower growth ahead: Investors seem to be focused on the outlook. F5 expects revenue to grow 8% to 9% in fiscal 2027, down from 11% this year, and adjusted earnings per share to grow 3% to 5%. It’s also projecting lower margins as memory and storage components get more expensive, and as it doubles its team of AI security sellers.

F5’s hardware business is also cooling off. Systems revenue jumped 29% in the quarter as customers replaced aging equipment, but F5 Chief Financial Officer Cooper Werner said on the earnings call that those replacements will taper off in the second half of fiscal 2027.

The AI bet: F5 is spending more to go after AI security. CEO François Locoh-Donou said on the call that the company will double its team of specialist AI security sellers in fiscal 2027 and more than double its marketing in that area. It’s also adding compensation incentives for all of its field sellers to discuss AI security with customers.

F5’s adjusted operating margin fell to 33.7% in the quarter, from 37% a year earlier.

Locoh-Donou said F5’s AI-related bookings topped $100 million in fiscal 2026, up about 300%. Most of that came from AI data delivery, which moves data to and from AI systems, rather than security. More than 300 customers are using an AI-powered web application firewall that F5 launched in March.

The company estimates the AI market it sells into will grow from about $1 billion this year to $11 billion by 2030.

Wall Street reaction: Piper Sandler downgraded the stock to neutral, according to The Motley Fool. Analysts at William Blair, which rates F5 “market perform,” wrote in a research note that “the AI opportunity has yet to contribute meaningfully to the top line.”

We’ve contacted F5 for comment on the stock decline.

F5 has been building out its AI security business, including its acquisition of SurePath AI. Locoh-Donou talked about the company’s path from the early web to AI security on a GeekWire Podcast episode marking F5’s 30th anniversary. He said companies adopting AI are losing track of what those systems can access, and that juggling separate tools to manage it is a burden, which is why F5 is building a single AI security platform.

This week, F5’s board authorized an additional $1.5 billion in stock buybacks, on top of $322 million remaining in its existing program.

#5411. Following a sudden GOP slide, a top data scientist’s model gives Democrats 90% odds of taking the Senate as Kansas trends blue in major shock

Data scientist Thomas Miller’s site handicapping outcomes for the U.S. Senate races now shows overwhelming odds that the Democrats will take control, numbers much more commanding than even the polls and prediction markets are showing.

As of around 9 a.m. ET on Monday, Miller’s site, Virtualtout.io, gave the Democrats a 90% chance of winning at least 51 seats. In recent days, the GOP’s chances of keeping control of the upper chamber have virtually collapsed, dropping from 23% on Oct. 26 to under 10% now.

A major reason from the quick downdraft, and a sign of the blue wave’s strength: Democrats now hold the lead in longtime red stronghold Kansas, and have turned Iowa into a virtual toss-up.

Miller, a professor at Northwestern University, won kudos for correctly forecasting that Democrats would sweep the two Georgia Senate runoffs in early 2021, when the polls and pundits posited GOP wins in both. He scored again by calling a Trump win in 2024.

His methodology: Miller starts by incorporating the “prices” posted on the two prediction markets boasting the highest volumes, Kalshi and Polymarket, and translates those numbers into probabilities of a Democrat or Republican win. He then deploys multiple time series that examine 10 to 12 underlying factors that drive the prediction markets, and continually crunches the numbers to forecast their impact going forward.

Miller updates the probabilities every 10 minutes, and the numbers stream across the top of Virtualtout.io in a continuous band resembling a stock ticker. The NowCast also displays the change over the last 24 hours. Hence, his figures are far more current than the polls.

“They all relate to voters’ perception of the performance of the Trump administration,” Miller told Fortune. “That’s the thread running through all the races. The factors include affordability, the economy, and the war in Iran, the issues that motivate voters. The states don’t move independently of one another. When voters’ view of those issues turns more negative, the Republican numbers drop on all the races.”

In other words, Trump has effectively nationalized the battle for the U.S. Senate.

Miller added that the impact of Trump’s tireless stumping is harder to assess. “People have come to expect certain things from Trump,” he said. “The way he behaves is not a surprise, it’s a continuous thing.”

Most of what the president says on the Senate campaign trail, according to Miller, simply reinforces the view of Trump and his party that voters already hold. “Still, there’s no evidence he’s helping,” Miller said. “It doesn’t appear that his appearances are a positive.”

One instance where his model found that Trump’s rhetoric backfired: The POTUS’s defense of the ad Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy ran in Ohio featuring the mother of his Democratic opponent Amy Acton severely criticizing her daughter. “Following Trump’s praise of the ad, we saw a huge drop in the Republican percentage,” Miller noted.

He pointed out that in the last 10 days, “a lot of contests are moving a little bit” in the Democratic direction from day to day, but the cumulative gains are substantial. In the five elections where the Democrats have long harbored chances for a flip, the GOP stands below 30% in all of them, from a high of 28.4% in Alaska to a low of 2% in North Carolina.

The Republicans’ best chance comes in Maine, where incumbent Susan Collins sits at 34.7%. In Michigan, the probability of a Republican flip via beating Abdul El-Sayed has faded from over one-third in mid-September to a current count of 24.5%.

The Miller model now points to high possibility of Democratic wins in states that, until a few days ago, the GOP counted on as surely in their column. “Those are the races I’ve been watching closely, and the move toward the Democrats in the last few days is surprising a lot of people,” says Miller. In the Iowa run for an open seat, Republican Ashley Hinson held an almost 62% shot at victory as of Sept. 17. Now, she’s dropped to 51.6% as her opponent Josh Turek pulls almost even.

In Kansas, Sen. Roger Marshall looked on track for easy reelection just two months ago at around 75%. His number’s dipped to 43.9% and suffered a 7.1% drop just in the past 24 hours.

Miller highlighted that Virtualtout.io and its NowCast will keep running all through Election Day, and will be first to call races, mainly based on its analysis of the swings in the betting odds.

Of course, the Republicans could hang on by keeping Kansas and Iowa, winning Maine where their odds are still decent, and defying the probabilities in Texas or one other key state. It’s a narrow path that in recent days now looks far narrower as Midwestern strongholds swing blue.

Shawn Tully is a senior editor-at-large at Fortune, covering the biggest trends in business, aviation, politics, and leadership.

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 28, 2026 at 1:38 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 1:47 pm

Seattle startup Ganaz, which provides payroll and HR tech for agricultural workers and employers, has been acquired by Beacon Holdings.

Ganaz co-founder and CEO Hannah Freeman announced the deal Wednesday on LinkedIn, saying the public benefit corporation “is in great hands” at Beacon, which “is building momentum for our next exciting season.”

Freeman indicated she is stepping away from the company to “catch my breath, spend more time with my daughter, and dream about what’s next,” she wrote. “I’ll miss our team & customers, but will be cheering you on from the sidelines.”

Ganaz launched in 2017 and has raised more than $10 million, with its last disclosed funding round in June 2021. That financing valued the company at $26 million, according to PitchBook. Terms of the acquisition were not disclosed.

Beacon, based in Toronto, buys software businesses serving traditional industries and provides shared technology and operational resources. The company said in September that its portfolio included 45 software businesses.

Ganaz’s platform provides employee onboarding, training, communication and analytics tools. It also offers a Mastercard payroll card that gives unbanked workers access to digital banking. Employers save time and money by skipping paper checks, while workers keep more of their pay by avoiding check-cashing and high remittance fees.

Ganaz received GeekWire’s 2023 Geeks Give Back Award. “We founded Ganaz to make life better for farm workers, and we do that by building technology that agricultural employers love and can’t live without,” Freeman told GeekWire in 2023. “We build our tools to help both workers and employers prosper, and that kicks off a virtuous cycle that helps agricultural communities prosper as well.”

At that time, the startup was serving more than 250,000 agricultural workers in the U.S. and Mexico and 100 employers in the sector.

The company has about 17 employees, according to LinkedIn. Freeman did not say in her post whether Ganaz will continue as a subsidiary or whether its employees will receive job offers from Beacon. GeekWire has reached out to Freeman for comment and will update the story with any reply.

#5409. AI agents are deciding who captures the value. Shoppers, workers and voters should have a say

Ask an AI assistant to buy you a coffee machine on Amazon and you have stepped into one of the first legal fights over agentic commerce. Perplexity’s Comet browser can browse the store and place the order for its user. Amazon sued, arguing that the agent entered its store without authorization while disguised as an ordinary Chrome browser, and a federal judge in San Francisco blocked it. On Aug. 4, the Ninth Circuit vacated that order. Because the agent acts only when its user tells it to, the court wrote, “it is the user who ‘accesses’ Amazon’s computers.” In September the court declined Amazon’s request for a rehearing. The underlying case continues.

The dispute matters to shoppers because it is about what they get to see. Search Amazon yourself and the results page mixes sponsored listings with organic ones, flagged in small type, and you can scroll past them. Send an agent and you get back a short list with a sentence of explanation. You do not see the products it dropped, and you cannot tell whether its ranking reflects quality or what a seller paid for placement. Perplexity framed its defense in those terms, accusing Amazon of being “more interested in serving you ads, sponsored results, and influencing your purchasing decisions.” Amazon’s position is that a store may decide which software comes through its door. Both companies are fighting over the same asset, which is control of the moment a shopper makes up their mind.

The price itself is becoming as hard to read as the ranking. In December 2025, Consumer Reports and Groundwork Collaborative asked 437 volunteers to buy the same groceries through Instacart. At one Safeway in Washington, D.C., a dozen eggs came up at $3.99, $4.28, $4.59 or $4.79 depending on the shopper. Instacart described the tests as limited and randomized, said they used no personal data, and ended them within two weeks of the report. The gap between the lowest and highest price for the same eggs was value moving from shoppers to the seller, and only the seller could see all of it.

Cases like these are usually filed under consumer protection. They point to something larger. Each of us meets agentic AI as a consumer, as a worker and as a citizen, and in each role the same question is being settled: who captures the value that agents create. The public debate on AI and the economy has concentrated on productivity and jobs, on how much value AI will add. Far less attention has gone to how that value is divided, which depends on who controls the terms agents operate under.

For workers, the division can already be measured. Researchers at the University of Oxford, working with the nonprofit Worker Info Exchange, analyzed more than 1.5 million trips by 258 Uber drivers in Britain between 2016 and 2024. After Uber introduced a dynamic pricing algorithm in 2023, passengers paid more per trip while drivers’ inflation-adjusted hourly earnings fell from over £22 to just over £19, before costs. Uber’s share of fares rose from around 25% to 29%, and on some trips exceeded half. Uber said it did not recognize the figures. The mechanism deserves attention whatever the exact numbers. One system sets what the passenger pays and what the driver earns, and it sees both sides of every trip. The passenger and the driver each see a single figure, and neither can tell how the other was priced.

For citizens, the stakes are institutional. Friedrich Hayek’s defense of the market rested on the idea that prices emerge from countless decisions and belong to no one. The French philosopher Jean-Pierre Dupuy observed that this anonymity made market outcomes bearable, because a price set by no one offers no address for a grievance. Agentic pricing gives the price an address. When the Justice Department sued RealPage, it treated the vendor of the software that landlords used to set rents as a party to the coordination, alongside the landlords themselves. The proposed settlement announced in November 2025 bars RealPage from feeding its models competitors’ current nonpublic data and from training them on active leases. The rent on an apartment turned out to have an author.

Inside companies, that author is harder to find, a problem two of us call “functional innocence” in our book IA et revenu (Ellipses, 2026): responsibility disappears across a chain of individually defensible decisions. Everyone involved can say in good faith that they decided nothing, which is why someone has to be named who answers for what the system does.

These questions are being settled in court dockets and in the integration meetings where companies plug into assistants, and neither was designed for public deliberation. Where elected bodies have stepped in, the results have been modest and workable. New York now requires businesses that set prices with personal data to state, next to the price, “This price was set by an algorithm using your personal data.” In October 2025 a federal judge dismissed the National Retail Federation’s First Amendment challenge to the law. In Europe, the Platform Work Directive obliges platforms to tell workers when automated systems monitor them or make decisions about them, and member states must transpose it by Dec. 2, 2026. In July the European Commission ordered Google to open Android features to rival AI assistants.

Disclosure is a start, and a real debate would go further using tools that already exist. The German economist Walter Eucken argued that competition is an order that has to be instituted and maintained, because a market left to itself drifts toward concentration. Applied to agents, that principle gives consumers a right to send the agent of their choice to any store they may lawfully enter, and to leave that agent taking with them what it has learned about them. The Ninth Circuit has addressed the first half of that right under a single statute, on a preliminary record. The principle also implies a duty of loyalty for agents that buy on our behalf. European law settled the equivalent question for financial advice in 2014: an adviser who claims to be independent may not keep commissions from the providers whose products it recommends. An agent that shops for you should meet the same standard, or say plainly who pays it.

Business leaders have good reasons to want this debate. Most companies sit on the seller’s side of an agent’s shortlist, and they gain when channels stay open and no single assistant can set the terms of visibility alone.

Executives are consumers, employees and voters as well. The question of who captures the value of agentic AI is being settled now, one ruling and one integration at a time, and leaving it there means accepting answers that few boards and no voters were asked about.

#5408. Yum! Brands posted higher revenue despite Taco Bell's cyclospora slump

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Taco Bell same-store sales fell 4% in the quarter, while KFC same-store sales rose 1% and Yum completed its Pizza Hut sales

Yum! Brands, the parent of Taco Bell and KFC, reported third-quarter revenue of $2.05 billion, up 4% from a year earlier, as same-store sales at Taco Bell fell 4% after a July cyclospora outbreak.

Adjusted earnings per share were $1.56, down 1% from $1.58 a year earlier. Net income reached $1.62 billion, equal to $5.92 per share, up from $397 million, equal to $1.41 per share, in the year-earlier period. The latest quarter also booked roughly $1.7 billion in pre-tax gains tied to the Pizza Hut sales.

Adjusted earnings per share topped the $1.49 analysts expected, and revenue matched the $2.05 billion estimate, according to CNBC.

Taco Bell division system sales fell 2%, and operating profit declined 5%. Operating margin fell to 33.1% from 36.6%. U.S. system sales dropped 3%, while international same-store sales grew 5%. KFC same-store sales rose 1%, though KFC system sales in the U.S. fell 6%.

Health authorities pointed to lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms as the source of the outbreak, according to The Wall Street Journal. Customers cut back on visits to Taco Bell, according to CNBC. Yum executives have described the July 18 weekend as the low point for sales, with results getting better afterward.

"Since the end of September, Taco Bell U.S. has been outpacing the QSR industry on same-store sales growth," CEO Chris Turner said in a statement. "Taco Bell will continue building on this momentum, with differentiated value and innovation that resonate across all consumer groups."

Yum stock gained over 3% ahead of the market open.

Yum finalized the sale of the Pizza Hut mainland China business to Yum China on Aug. 7, then handed the remainder of the brand to LongRange Capital on Sept. 1. Third-quarter results count Pizza Hut's contribution only through the respective closing dates. Excluding Pizza Hut, core operating profit grew 1% for the quarter.

Yum’s second-quarter results didn’t capture the outbreak. Taco Bell same-store sales rose 7% in the second quarter, a period that ended before the outbreak emerged in mid-July, though the company’s risk disclosures in that report already cited its impact on sales and the pace of recovery.

Yum announced in June that it would sell Pizza Hut for $2.7 billion in two transactions: $1.5 billion from LongRange Capital for the operations outside mainland China, and $1.2 billion from Yum China for the mainland business. With both sales closed, Yum operates Taco Bell, KFC and Habit Burger & Grill.

#5407. Microsoft Azure revenue surges 48% to $33.2B, beating expectations as cloud and AI demand grows

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 1:47 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 4:30 pm

Microsoft’s Azure cloud business brought in $33.2 billion in revenue in the September quarter, up 48% from a year earlier, blowing past the company’s own forecast and beating Wall Street’s expectations.

The growth suggests that Microsoft is selling cloud and AI computing about as fast as it can install it. Azure revenue rose $10.8 billion from a year earlier, driven by demand for services across the platform, Microsoft said in its quarterly filing. That came even as some new data center capacity arrived late.

For investors worried about Microsoft’s record capital spending, it’s a sign that the company’s massive AI and cloud infrastructure buildout is turning into sales. Microsoft’s shares rose nearly 4% in after-hours trading following the earnings report.

Overall, Microsoft reported revenue of $92.3 billion for the first quarter of its 2027 fiscal year, up 19% and above the $90.75 billion analysts expected, according to Yahoo Finance. Earnings were $4.89 per share excluding the impact of its OpenAI investment, compared with expectations of $4.72.

It’s the first time Microsoft has reported Azure’s quarterly revenue figure, not just its growth. The disclosure is part of a new financial structure that took effect this quarter, splitting the company into two segments: Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer.

Capital spending came in below Microsoft’s forecast. The company spent $45.2 billion, including finance leases, short of the more than $50 billion it expected. Some data center capacity that third parties were supposed to deliver in the quarter was delayed, the company said.

Google Cloud, which includes Google’s Workspace productivity apps, brought in $30.7 billion in revenue in the quarter, up 103% from a year earlier, Alphabet reported Wednesday afternoon.

Amazon reports earnings Thursday afternoon, including AWS results.

Update, 3:05 p.m.:Microsoft expects Azure growth to accelerate again this quarter, to 49% to 50% excluding currency changes, CFO Amy Hood said on the earnings call. “Customer demand continues to exceed available supply,” she said.

Hood said Azure’s growth came from Foundry, Microsoft’s service for building AI apps and agents, and from engineering work that let Microsoft sell unused capacity on its existing servers. That helped make up for delays in new data center capacity that outside providers were supposed to deliver.

Those delays pushed some spending later into the fiscal year. Microsoft now expects to spend about $170 billion on capital expenditures in calendar 2026, down from about $175 billion. It expects to spend more than $50 billion this quarter, and Hood said spending will accelerate in the first half of calendar 2027.

Hood also said Microsoft may tap additional sources of financing to help pay for the buildout, “when we believe it is attractive to do so.” The company still expects to bring in more cash than it spends this fiscal year.

Microsoft’s expense forecast for the December quarter includes an estimate for the buyout offer it announced Monday, Hood said, though she didn’t give the amount.

The company expects total revenue of $96 billion to $97.1 billion for the December quarter, above the $95.7 billion analysts expected, according to Yahoo Finance.

#5406. Coinbase's October 26 Perpetual Conversion: The Crypto Index the CFTC Waiver Excludes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Coinbase wants six futures contracts to stop expiring on October 26. The CFTC letter it leans on covers five of them by design, and its own footnote points away from the sixth.

The Division of Market Oversight issued Letter 26-29 on October 3, 2026. The CFTC announced it two days later, on October 5, in Release 9308-26. Coverage then focused on the headline that exchanges can now strip expiry dates from perpetual-style index futures. The Merkle flagged the relief's hard October 20 stop on October 19, and outlets like Finance Magnates and FinanceFeeds ran the same window. That coverage, however, predates what Coinbase filed next. This breakdown sets the October 19 filing beside the letter's text, because the two don't line up cleanly.

Meanwhile, the CFTC is working on retail crypto leverage through a different door. As NullTX's earlier breakdown shows, the actual-delivery ANPRM (2026-20888) takes comments until December 14. Perpetuals on registered exchanges skip that process. Instead, they move through staff letters and self-certification.

Coinbase asked for the relief on October 1, and the Division granted it two days later. The letter says staff won't recommend enforcement if a DCM drops expiry dates from existing perpetual-style contracts, as long as the DCM meets eight conditions. First, it must gather feedback from holders of open positions. Next, it must give at least five calendar days' notice and let them close out under the old terms. It must also disclose the risks and change no other material term. Finally, it must file under the CFTC's rules, notify the Division and certify compliance.

Coinbase's Submission #2026-67 then names six contracts: US500, Tech100, Defense10, AI10, China10 and Coin50. It says everything except the expiry stays the same, and that the exchange knows of no substantive opposition. The contract list reached the CFTC by email on October 16.

Letter 26-29 defines its scope by asset class. A footnote shuts out any perpetual-style contract referencing something other than a broad-based security index. Coin50, by contrast, follows the Coinbase 50 Index, and Rule 1148 in the filing itself calls it a futures contract based on a cryptocurrency. In other words, the letter's scope and Coin50's own rule text point in opposite directions.

Crypto contracts did have their own relief. Letter 26-19, issued June 12 to Bitnomial and Coinbase Derivatives, covered digital commodities only and carried the same eight conditions. Even so, it says its positions expire on June 30, 2026. It rests on the Commission's May 29 order and its perpetuals policy statement.

Letter 26-29 sets October 20, 2026 as the day its no-action positions expire. It doesn't say whether implementation itself must happen by then, or only the notice and filing. Coinbase filed on October 19, one day early, but picked October 26 to go live. That choice matters. Ten business days from October 19 lands on November 2, and Coinbase specifically asked to skip that wait. As a result, going live on October 26 depends on the relief still applying.

Without relief, the Division's own words make the path clear. Letter 26-19 says certifications that remove expiry dates will generally draw a stay under Regulation 40.6(c). A stay then gives the Commission another 90 days to review and opens a 30-day public comment period.

Neither side has explained the gap. Searches of news coverage and official channels turned up no statement from Coinbase or the CFTC on whether Coin50 sits inside Letter 26-29, on what authority covers it after October 20, or on why the filing's October 26 date falls after the letter's expiry. We also found no CFTC stay notice and no extension or amendment of Letter 26-29. Likewise, the Coinbase posts we found cover other perpetual launches, not this conversion.

That silence doesn't mean a problem exists. Coinbase may be relying on authority the documents don't mention, and the CFTC may read the letter's dates differently than we do. Still, the paper trail shows a crypto-based contract sitting under relief written for stock indexes, with a start date that falls after that relief expires.

Three developments would settle it: a CFTC stay notice, a new or amended staff letter, or a clarification from Coinbase Derivatives.

Whichever arrives first tells us whether the first U.S.-listed crypto index perpetual goes live on schedule or lands in a 90-day review.

#5405. Who pays for AI’s $2.6 trillion build-out? Look to corporate budgets

Good morning. By 2030, the AI ecosystem will need about $2.6 trillion in annual end-market spending to support data centers, chips, model development, and investor returns, according to a BCG Institute analysis.

Enterprises would account for $1.8 trillion of that total, followed by consumers at $366 billion, hyperscalers’ internal use at $204 billion, and emerging technologies such as physical AI at $200 billion. The estimates represent global spending, excluding China, and reflect infrastructure costs concentrated mainly in the U.S., where most new capacity is being built.

The $1.8 trillion is a measure of what the AI ecosystem would need from enterprises, rather than a forecast of actual spending.

In one illustrative scenario, BCG estimates that companies could contribute that amount by reallocating $857 billion from existing technology budgets and adding $937 billion in new spending. That would put enterprise tech budgets roughly 13% above International Data Corporation’s IT spending forecast, with AI’s share of those budgets rising from 5% today to 25% in 2030.

The scenario underscores how much the AI industry’s growth depends on corporate spending. For CFOs seeking additional AI investment, that means presenting boards with evidence of productivity gains, cost reductions, new revenue or competitive advantage, said Clark O’Niell, BCG’s global lead for AI, infrastructure and cyber. Some strategic benefits, however, may be difficult to capture in traditional ROI calculations.

“The question isn’t just whether AI delivers an immediate financial return,” he said. “It’s also what the cost of falling behind could be.”

That argument deserves scrutiny, too. Fear of falling behind can be a legitimate strategic consideration, but it shouldn’t become a substitute for a business case.

BCG considers the AI build-out as more resilient than past infrastructure booms, partly because hyperscalers have financed much of their investment through cash flow rather than debt. But the ability to finance infrastructure doesn’t guarantee that it will generate adequate returns.

O’Niell identifies two indicators worth watching. The first is how infrastructure investment is financed, with a sustained shift toward debt signaling greater risk. The second is whether deployed compute generates sufficient revenue. As frontier labs enter public markets, their disclosures could reveal whether revenue is keeping pace with compute costs.

The economics leave limited room for disappointment.

BCG assumes AI chips have an average five-year lifespan and estimates that each gigawatt of capacity coming online in 2026 must generate about $15 billion in revenue to cover its costs. Weaker-than-expected demand could trigger price wars and losses for model providers and data-center operators.

For corporate buyers, those pressures have a practical implication. O’Niell advises most to avoid long-term price-per-token commitments as AI prices continue to fall. Contract flexibility could help CFOs capture future cost reductions.

The $2.6 trillion is achievable, he said, “but it’s not guaranteed.” And even if enterprises provide the spending, the question remains whether they will capture enough of the economic value to justify it.

Previously, he worked at Slingshot Aerospace, where he served as VP of finance. Americans are open to AI, but they want a person to make the final call. In a Pew Research Center survey of 3,488 U.S. adults, most respondents said they were comfortable with AI handling routine health care tasks like translating for patients or scheduling appointments, most often with a human doing a final review.

Support drops off sharply as the stakes rise. Only 5% are open to AI deciding an insurance claim on its own, and 46% don't want AI involved in those decisions at all. Trust is also thin: 58% have little or no confidence that health insurers will use AI in patients' best interests; half say the same of AI companies, and 51% expect AI to make the security of personal health information worse.

Views of AI's effect on health care costs are more closely divided: 26% say AI will make costs worse, 19% say it will make them better, and 32% aren't sure. Still, Americans see benefits in some areas.

More say AI will improve access to health care services than say it will worsen it (31% vs. 20%).

#5404. Bigger than Bing or Xbox: Microsoft’s OpenAI haul reaches $10B in quarterly revenue

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 4:28 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 4:33 pm

OpenAI generated $10 billion in revenue for Microsoft in the quarter ended Sept. 30, about 11% of the Redmond company’s total revenue, according to its quarterly filing Wednesday.

The amount is up sharply. In the fiscal year that ended in June, Microsoft recorded $24.1 billion in revenue from its business with OpenAI, or about $6 billion a quarter on average.

That $10 billion surpasses some of Microsoft’s longest-running businesses. Xbox brought in $5.4 billion in the quarter. Search and advertising, which includes its Bing search engine, generated $6.6 billion. Windows licenses sold through PC makers, along with Surface and other Microsoft devices, brought in $3.6 billion.

The total covers revenue-sharing payments from OpenAI, as well as other business between the companies, such as OpenAI’s use of Azure to train and run its AI models. Microsoft didn’t say how much came from each, or how much of Azure’s growth came from OpenAI.

Azure revenue rose 48% to $33.2 billion in the quarter, beating Wall Street’s expectations and the company’s own forecast of 44% to 45% growth.

Microsoft has begun disclosing its revenue from OpenAI because its stake of about 24% makes OpenAI a “related party” under accounting rules, requiring it to report the business they do with each other.

Microsoft first reported the number in its annual report in July, as a full-year total. This is the first time it has given a quarterly figure.

The original AI alliance: Microsoft first invested in OpenAI in 2019, eventually committing $13 billion, and became its exclusive cloud provider. ChatGPT ran on Azure when it launched in late 2022.

The companies have loosened their ties since then. OpenAI restructured as a public benefit corporation in October 2025, and Microsoft gave up its right of first refusal to supply OpenAI’s computing capacity. OpenAI committed to buy an additional $250 billion in Azure services. An April 2026 agreement gave OpenAI broader freedom to use other cloud providers.

OpenAI has also agreed to keep sharing revenue with Microsoft through 2030.

In addition, Microsoft sells access to OpenAI’s models to business customers through its Azure OpenAI Service, and the models became the foundation for its Copilot products, putting Microsoft at the front of the generative AI boom. That revenue comes from Microsoft’s own customers, so it isn’t part of the $10 billion.

Microsoft, for its part, now builds its own AI models and offers models from Anthropic and others.

Many customers, not a few: Asked by Bernstein Research analyst Mark Moerdler whether AI growth on Azure was coming from big businesses or AI-native companies, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella didn’t mention OpenAI.

He said he doesn’t want Azure’s AI business to depend on a few big customers, and that broad adoption by businesses is just getting started.

Nadella described it as “a decade-long thing,” and contrasted it with relying on “four customers who buy a lot of capacity from you” to show a few quarters of growth. That, he said, is “not a business as far as I’m concerned.”

He added that Microsoft has large customers who want to buy capacity, “and as long as the pricing is right, we may sell them some. If not, we will be patient.”

Later in the call, Goldman Sachs analyst Gabriela Borges brought up the fact that OpenAI made up 11% of revenue. Nadella didn’t address the number but praised OpenAI’s latest models and said customers are increasingly mixing models from different companies, or training their own.

He cited Microsoft’s tools for routing each task to whichever AI model handles it best. If you use AI coding agents, Nadella said, you want Anthropic and OpenAI “to compete for your workload, not like once a quarter, but for every task.”

New risk language: Microsoft also expanded a warning in its quarterly filing about the risks of depending on outside AI providers. The company builds products such as Copilot on AI models from outside companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic. It now says it has “limited visibility into or control over” how those models are designed, trained, secured and tested.

Without naming OpenAI or Anthropic, the same section notes that some of these AI partners are also “significant customers of Azure,” and that the benefits Microsoft expects from those relationships “may not be realized or sustained.” It says those partners could change how much they buy, and that Microsoft itself may change how it allocates scarce data center capacity or prices it.

Microsoft is an investor in both companies. According to its latest filing, it owns about 24% of OpenAI, down from about 25% in June and about 27% after OpenAI’s restructuring a year ago, and has put $12.0 billion of a promised $13.0 billion into the company.

In addition, Microsoft agreed last year to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic, and its results for the June quarter included a $3.2 billion gain on that investment. Microsoft hasn’t disclosed the size of its Anthropic stake, and Anthropic’s IPO filing earlier this week didn’t specify it either.

#5403. Zillow agrees to pay $212.5M to settle investor lawsuit over failed home-flipping business

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 6:40 pmOctober 29, 2026 at 7:46 am

Zillow Group will pay $212.5 million to settle a shareholder class action lawsuit over its handling of Zillow Offers, the home-flipping business it shut down in 2021.

The lawsuit alleged that Zillow executives painted an overly positive picture of Zillow Offers in the months before the shutdown, without disclosing how poorly the company was able to predict home prices. That kept the stock artificially high until Zillow revealed the problems and announced the shutdown in November 2021, according to the complaint.

The Seattle-based company disclosed the settlement Wednesday in an SEC filing. About $48 million of the payment is expected to come from insurance. The deal requires court approval and includes no admission of wrongdoing.

In a statement, a Zillow spokesperson said, “We are pleased that the parties have reached a resolution on the matter.”

The settlement comes about three weeks after the U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear Zillow’s challenge to the case’s class status. The U.S. Chamber of Commerce and other business groups backed Zillow’s petition.

Steve Berman, managing partner of Seattle law firm Hagens Berman, the court-appointed class counsel, told Real Estate News he believes it’s the largest single securities settlement in the history of the Western District of Washington, the federal court district that includes Seattle.

Separate shareholder lawsuits filed on the company’s behalf against its leaders, known as derivative suits, remain pending, according to the filing.

Zillow bet its future on buying and selling homes in 2019, when co-founder Rich Barton returned as CEO and projected the business would reach $20 billion in annual revenue within three to five years. The company used its pricing algorithms to buy houses, fix them up and resell them.

The effort unraveled in the fall of 2021. An analyst report found that two-thirds of 650 homes it sampled from Zillow’s inventory were listed for less than the company paid.

Days later, Zillow shut down the business, cut about 2,000 jobs and took a $304 million inventory writedown, with Barton citing the unpredictability of its home-price forecasts. Zillow’s stock fell 32% over two days, according to Reuters.

The original lawsuit, filed that month in federal court in Seattle, cited upbeat statements executives made in the months before the shutdown.

They included a September 2021 remark by Jeremy Wacksman, then Zillow’s chief operating officer and now its CEO, that “the strength and the appeal for Zillow Offers just continues to grow.” Investor Jeremy Jaeger later became the lead plaintiff.

The class covers investors who bought Zillow Class A or Class C shares between Aug. 5 and Nov. 2, 2021. If the judge grants preliminary approval, Zillow will pay the money into a settlement fund within 20 business days.

#5402. These Millionaires Have the Cash to Buy a Home. Here’s Why They’re Renting Instead.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

For a growing number of wealthy households, renting is a choice to seriously consider.

More millionaires are renting, despite being able to afford homeownership. This group of wealthy renters is choosing a different path on purpose.

According to a recent report from apartment search website RentCafe, millionaire renters are growing at a faster rate than millionaire homeowners. The report qualified individuals from households that have a total annual household income of $1 million or more as millionaires.

From 2020 to 2024, the number of millionaire households renting their homes surged 229%, more than tripling in five years, compared with a 193% increase among homeowners in that same time period, according to RentCafe’s analysis of American Community Survey estimates.

Choosing to rent contradicts a long tradition of treating homeownership as a defining symbol of the American Dream, especially for affluent Americans.

“For a growing number of millionaires, renting is now a deliberate choice,” the report said. “That’s because many prioritize mobility without the commitment of owning a home, as well as the ability to relocate without going through the lengthy process of selling a multi-million-dollar house.”

The report also pointed out that many wealthy renters would rather keep their money accessible and pursue returns in a strong stock market rather than lock their funds into a home.

Most millionaires reach that status with two incomes. According to the report, couples with high earnings account for 75% of these households, while individuals make up the remaining quarter.

RentCafe found that millennials represent the largest share of millionaire renters at 49%. However, Gen Z is the fastest-growing group, with its count rising 46-fold from fewer than a dozen households renting in 2020 to more than 400 in 2024. The report revealed that despite that jump, Gen Z still comprises just 2% of millionaire renter households.

Gen Z “was barely entering the workforce in 2020,” Adina Dragos, RentCafe writer and research analyst, said in an interview with USA Today. She noted that “by 2024, the oldest Gen Zers were approaching 30.”

“Many who struck it big early — through the creator economy, crypto or startup equity — were choosing to rent precisely because their wealth isn’t tied to a traditional career ladder,” she said. “With no employer anchoring them to one place, they have little reason to put down roots.”

According to RentCafe, millionaire renters typically hold lucrative white-collar jobs as chief executives, technology professionals and senior financial managers. These roles offer flexibility about where they live and work.

The group also includes less obvious high earners, such as professors and operations managers. It’s “a sign that the millionaire renter isn’t always who you’d expect,” per the report.

New York, San Francisco and Los Angeles remain major hubs for millionaire renters, but their numbers are climbing rapidly in Texas and Florida.

Houston recorded the fastest growth of any major metro, with millionaire renter households rising from 18 in 2020 to 232 in 2024, a 1,189% increase.

“Granted, 232 households is still a tiny fraction of the Houston metro’s roughly 2.7 million households, but the growth rate far outpaces any other major metro,” RentCafe noted.
